title: fix(schema): ModelAlias accepts segments with internal whitespace — resolved refs can never match a model
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolve` / `resolveRef` rejects model references whose provider, model, or variant segments are padded or empty (#436/#437, PR #440), and rejects whitespace-only alias targets (#412) — but a segment with **internal** whitespace passes every check and resolves to a reference that can never match a real model:

Verified this run with a bun probe against `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` on main `e791e497ca` (probe + log: `hidden_files/probe-2026-10-25-creator/` in the sweep workspace):

```
internal-space provider            => RESOLVED: "open ai/gpt-4"
internal-space model               => RESOLVED: "openai/gpt 4"
internal-space variant             => RESOLVED: "openai/gpt-4#hi there"
tab in model                       => RESOLVED: "openai/gpt\t4"
provider alias target (x->"open ai") => RESOLVED: "open ai/gpt-4"
model alias target (f->"open ai/gpt-4") => RESOLVED: "open ai/gpt-4"
variant alias target (hi->"hi there")  => RESOLVED: "openai/gpt-4#hi there"
```

Root cause: the guards in `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` are `hasPaddedSegment` (segment !== segment.trim()) and `hasEmptySegment` — an internal space or tab makes a segment neither padded nor empty, at every check site (input check ~line 52, alias-target checks ~lines 91/122/161, settled-base check ~line 202, final-variant check ~line 237, `checkedVariantTarget`, and `parseRefString`).

## Why it matters

Provider, model, and variant names contain no whitespace (OpenChamber's mirror validator states this invariant explicitly in its `targetReferenceSpellingProblem` comment). A reference with internal whitespace therefore attaches/looks up under a key no real model has, and the failure surfaces later as a confusing model-not-found instead of the clear `Invalid model reference` error the padded/empty spellings now produce. This is the remaining hole in the same spelling-validation family as #412/#436/#437.

## Cross-repo set (one issue, per the set rule)

The same gap is verified in **developing-today/openchamber**: `targetReferenceSpellingProblem` in `packages/web/server/lib/routing/model-routes.js` (on its main `5f3cf10e2`, ~lines 355-378) rejects padded and empty segments but not internal whitespace. Probe against `validateModelRoutes` on that main:

```
"open ai/gpt-4"        => null (accepted)
"openai/gpt 4"         => null (accepted)
"openai/gpt-4#hi there" => null (accepted)
" openai/gpt-4"        => rejected (padded) — existing behaviour
"openai//gpt-4"        => rejected (empty segment) — existing behaviour
```

No copy of either validator exists in developing-today/code (grep for `hasPaddedSegment` / `targetReferenceSpellingProblem` / `ModelAlias` in pkgs: no hits). Port the fix to OpenChamber from this issue; do not file a second issue there.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] In OpenCode, any provider/model/variant segment containing whitespace (space, tab, etc.) is rejected with the existing `Invalid model reference` error — for direct input, model alias targets, provider alias targets, scoped alias targets, and variant alias targets, on both the alias and no-alias (`parseRefString`) paths.
- [ ] Nested model IDs with slashes (`openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`) and slash-containing variants (per #422/#425) still resolve.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover internal-whitespace in each position and via each alias kind; existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] OpenChamber port: `targetReferenceSpellingProblem` (and the variant checks in `validateTarget`) reject internal-whitespace segments/variants with a message in the existing style, with tests in `model-routes.test.js`; the documented "names contain no spaces" invariant then matches the code.

title: fix(cli): Node build still references Bun in ACP and CPU-profile paths — PR #441 fixed only the two import handlers
body:
## Finding

PR #441 (merged, commit `09d93f7ed8b127d543d749d9436d2e19f2db8413`, merge `e791e497ca561d0a372b980e2ad202fbe499f506`) fixed #435 — `Bun is not defined` on the Node build — by replacing `Bun.file(...).text()` with `readFile(..., "utf8")` in the two import handlers, and rode along the identical session-import site for the same root cause. But the same root cause remains live in three other runtime paths in `packages/cli/src` on current main (`e791e497ca`). There is no `Bun` global shim in the Node bundle: grep of `packages/cli/vite.node.config.ts` and `packages/cli/src/node/` finds no `globalThis.Bun` / Bun polyfill (the scripts that use `Bun.*` under `packages/cli/script/` run under Bun themselves and are not the problem).

## Evidence (current main, verified by local grep and `git show origin/main:<path>`)

1. `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/acp.ts:37` — fatal for the whole command:
   ```ts
   const connection = yield* ACP.connect(client, ndJsonStream(Writable.toWeb(process.stdout), Bun.stdin.stream()))
   ```
   The handler is registered at `packages/cli/src/index.ts:40` (`acp: () => import("./commands/handlers/acp")`), so on the Node build (`packages/cli/dist-node/opencode.mjs`) evaluating `Bun.stdin` throws `ReferenceError: Bun is not defined` before any ACP connection is made — `opencode acp` cannot start at all on Node, the same failure class #435 reported for `auth import`.

2. `packages/cli/src/acp/permission.ts:96,137,156` — `Bun.file(path).text()` in `withCompletedDiffs` / `permissionPreviews` / `patchPreviews`. These failures are swallowed (`Effect.orElseSucceed(() => [])` at `permission.ts:49-51` in `ask`, and per-file in `withCompletedDiffs`), so on the Node build ACP permission requests and completed-tool updates silently lose their diff previews instead of crashing — a silent degradation, not an error.

3. `packages/cli/src/cpu-profile.ts:54` — `Bun.write(target, JSON.stringify(result.profile))` in the SIGPROF profile writer. `CpuProfile.listen` is wired into the main entry at `packages/cli/src/index.ts:104`, so on the Node build a captured CPU profile is never written; the failure surfaces only as a caught/logged "Failed to write CPU profile" error.

## Why it matters

#435 established that the Node build is a supported artifact and `Bun` does not exist there. #441 fixed the two sites its reporter hit, but a user of the Node build still cannot run `opencode acp` at all, gets silently preview-less ACP permission prompts, and cannot collect a CPU profile. The PR's own verification ("No `Bun.` references remain in either handler") was scoped to the two handlers it touched, so the remaining sites were never checked.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] No `Bun.` references remain in runtime code under `packages/cli/src` (build/test scripts under `packages/cli/script/` and `*.test.ts` that themselves run under Bun are out of scope), or each remaining site is covered by a documented, tested Node-runtime shim.
  - `acp.ts`: use a Node stream for stdin, e.g. `Readable.toWeb(process.stdin)` (the stdout side of the same call already uses `Writable.toWeb`).
  - `acp/permission.ts`: read files with `node:fs` / Effect FileSystem, as #441 did for the import handlers.
  - `cpu-profile.ts`: write the profile with `node:fs` `writeFile`.
- [ ] `opencode acp` on the Node bundle starts and serves NDJSON over stdin/stdout.
- [ ] ACP permission diff previews are produced on the Node build (not silently empty).
- [ ] A SIGPROF CPU profile file is written on the Node build.
- [ ] A guard (test or lint, e.g. alongside `packages/cli/test/import-boundaries.test.ts`) fails if a new `Bun.` reference is introduced into `packages/cli/src` runtime code, so the next site is caught at review time rather than by a user.

Found by pr-diff-review of PR #441 in developing-today/opencode. Single-repo: the CLI Node build exists only in this repo.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias accepts refs with empty segments — openai//gpt and openai/gpt/ resolve to model IDs that can never exist
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` and `parseRefString` accept model references with empty segments — a doubled slash (`openai//gpt`) or a model ID ending in a slash (`openai/gpt/`). The resolved `id` then starts or ends with `/` (`"/gpt"`, `"gpt/"`, or even just `"/"`), which is not a model ID any provider carries, yet resolution reports success and hands the malformed ref downstream instead of throwing the invalid-reference error. Model IDs legitimately contain single slashes (nested IDs), so the gap is specifically *empty* segments, not slashes in general.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main df5fc16d47)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- The settled-result check (line 191) rejects only a slash at position 0 or at the very end of the whole base string (`slashIdx <= 0 || slashIdx === settledBase.length - 1`). It never inspects the model portion for empty segments, so `openai//gpt` (first slash mid-string) and `openai/gpt/` (first slash mid-string) both pass, and lines 195-196 slice out `finalModel` values of `"/gpt"` and `"gpt/"`.
- `parseRefString` (line 277, the no-alias path) checks only that `id` is non-empty (line ~285); `"/gpt"` and `"gpt/"` are non-empty, so both pass there too.
- The whole-string edge cases *are* caught — alias targets `"/gpt"` and `"openai/"` throw `Invalid model reference after alias resolution` — which shows the intent to reject empty provider/model parts; the check just doesn't extend to empty segments inside or at the end of the model part.

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main df5fc16d47):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ models: { x: "openai//gpt" } }` | `x` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "/gpt", ref: "openai//gpt" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai//gpt` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "/gpt" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai/gpt/` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: "gpt/" }` |
| `{ models: { x: "a//" } }` | `x` | OK — `{ providerID: "a", id: "/", ref: "a//" }` |

Controls that already throw today: alias targets `"/gpt"` and `"openai/"` (whole-string edges), and input `openai/` on the alias path.

## Why it matters

A doubled slash is an easy typo in a config model string or a hand-built ref, and a trailing slash is a common copy/paste artifact. Today both sail through the one component whose job is to canonicalize and validate refs, producing an `id` that can never match a provider model — the failure then appears as a generic model-not-found far from the typo, in both the alias and no-alias paths.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reference with an empty segment — `//` anywhere in the base, or a model portion ending in `/` — throws the invalid-reference error, on both the alias path and the `parseRefString` (no-alias) path.
- [ ] Legitimate nested model IDs with single slashes (e.g. `openrouter/anthropic/claude-sonnet-4`) still resolve unchanged.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the doubled-slash and trailing-slash shapes via direct input and via a model alias target; all existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] Dedup checked 2026-10-25: `gh search issues` for "double slash", "empty segment", and "segments" returns no matching issue, open or closed; the #398-#422 series covered `#` shapes, padding, prototype keys, and slash-in-variant routing, not empty segments.

Single-repo: `ModelAlias` lives only in this repo's schema/core packages.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias input reference segments are never checked for padding — padded provider/model/variant resolve into refs that can never match
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` rejects alias *targets* whose provider/model/variant segments carry leading or trailing whitespace (`hasPaddedSegment`, added for #411/#412), but it never applies the same check to the *input reference itself*. A user-typed or config-supplied reference with padded segments resolves "successfully" into a `ResolvedRef` whose `providerID`, `id`, or `variant` contains spaces — values that can never match a real provider, model, or variant, so the failure surfaces later and further from the cause instead of as the invalid-reference error every other malformed shape gets.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-25 on main df5fc16d47)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- `resolveRef` (line 47) trims only the outer ends of the whole input string; nothing validates the individual segments after the `/` and `#` splits.
- The settled result is built at lines 191-197 from `settledBase`/`settledVariant` with only a slash-position check — padded segments pass straight into `finalProvider` / `finalModel` / `finalVariant`.
- `parseRefString` (line 277, the no-alias path) likewise checks only emptiness and `#` placement, so padded segments are accepted there too.
- By contrast, alias targets are rejected for exactly this shape at lines 84, 110, and 151 via `hasPaddedSegment` (line 266), and provider alias targets at lines ~140-147.
- Callers pass raw strings straight in with no segment trimming upstream: `packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts:604,816` (config model strings), `packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts:109`, `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:609`, `packages/cli/src/session-target.ts:97` (CLI value).

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main df5fc16d47):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai /gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai ", id: "gpt-4o", ref: "openai /gpt-4o" }` |
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai/ gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai", id: " gpt-4o" }` |
| `{ models: { zzz: "a/b" } }` | `openai/gpt-4o# fast` | OK — `{ variant: " fast", ref: "openai/gpt-4o# fast" }` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai /gpt-4o` | OK — `{ providerID: "openai " }` via `parseRefString` |
| `undefined` (no-alias path) | `openai/gpt-4o# fast` | OK — `{ variant: " fast" }` via `parseRefString` |

Control: the same padding inside an alias *target* — `{ models: { x: "openai/gpt# fast" } }`, input `x` — throws `Invalid model reference: x` today.

## Why it matters

The input is the most common place padding appears (a stray space in a config value or CLI argument). Today it produces a canonical-looking ref with invisible spaces that no provider lookup will ever match, so the user gets a "model not found"-style failure with no hint that whitespace is the cause. The resolver already decided this shape is invalid for targets; the input deserves the same treatment for consistency.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An input reference whose provider, model, or variant segment has leading/trailing whitespace throws the same invalid-reference error as a padded alias target, on both the alias path and the `parseRefString` (no-alias) path.
- [ ] Whole-input leading/trailing whitespace keeps working (it is trimmed today, line 47).
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover padded provider, model, and variant segments in the input, with and without aliases configured; all existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] Dedup checked 2026-10-25: #411/#412 covered padded/whitespace *alias targets* only; no open or recently closed issue tracks padding in the input reference itself.

Single-repo: `ModelAlias` lives only in this repo's schema/core packages.

title: fix(cli): auth import <file> fails on the Node build with Bun is not defined
body:
On the Node build (`packages/cli/dist-node/opencode.mjs`), `opencode auth import <file>` fails with `Bun is not defined`. The handler reads the file with `Bun.file(file).text()` (`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/import.ts`).

**Repro** (fork main `df5fc16d47`): `node dist-node/opencode.mjs auth import creds.json --standalone` prints `Bun is not defined`.

**Workaround:** pipe the file on stdin instead (`auth import --standalone < creds.json`). That path uses `readStdin()` and works on Node.

**Fix:** read the file with `node:fs/promises` `readFile`, or with the same reader the stdin path uses. Found during the provider-instances end-to-end check (#373).

title: fix(core): settings.baseURL is ignored for opencode-go and its instances
body:
`providers.opencode-go.settings.baseURL` has no effect: requests still go to opencode.ai. The same happens for an `instanceOf: "opencode-go"` copy, so a Go account can't be pointed at a proxy or a local recorder.

**Repro** (fork main `df5fc16d47`, Node bundle, temp HOME, `--standalone`):

```jsonc
"providers": { "opencode-go": { "settings": { "baseURL": "http://127.0.0.1:18998/go-2/v1" } } }
```

Import a key credential for `opencode-go`, then run `opencode run -m opencode-go/glm-5.3 "say hi"`.

- **Expected:** the request reaches the local server at `/go-2/v1/...`.
- **Actual:** the local server gets nothing, and the run fails with `Upstream request failed: Invalid credential` from opencode.ai.

The same override on `openai`, `openai.work` and `anthropic.team` routes to the local server as expected. This was found during the provider-instances end-to-end check (#373).

The models.dev entry for `opencode-go` sets `api: https://opencode.ai/zen/go/v1`. Possibly that URL, or the Console provider overlay, is applied after config and wins over `settings.baseURL`. Not confirmed.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias bare scoped alias target is misrouted when its variant contains a / — slash test looks past the #
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias` scoped model-alias targets in the bare form (`newModel#variant`) are misrouted when the variant itself contains a `/`. Both scoped-alias branches decide "is this target a `provider/model` form or a bare model form?" by testing `target.includes("/")` on the **whole target string, including the part after `#`** — so a slash that belongs to the variant flips the branch, the target is taken verbatim as a provider/model ref, and resolution then fails because the part before `#` has no slash.

## Evidence (verified on main `c79bf55a8e`, Bun probe against `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`)

`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts:113` (original-provider scoped branch) and `:153` (resolved-provider scoped branch, Rule 3) both read:

```ts
if (scopedAlias.includes("/")) {
  current = scopedAlias
} else {
  // hash-split bare form: `${provider}/${scopedModel}#${scopedVar}`
}
```

Probe results:

| Case | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}`, input `openai/old` | **throws** `Invalid model reference after alias resolution: new` |
| `providers: {ds: "openai"}, models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}`, input `ds/old` (Rule 3 branch) | **throws** the same |
| Control — same target with a slash-free variant, `"new#fast"` | resolves to `openai/new#fast` |
| Control — the intended final ref given directly, `openai/new#va/r` (no aliases) | resolves fine, variant `va/r` |
| Control — slash-form target with the same variant, `"other/new#va/r"` | resolves to `other/new#va/r` |

So the bare scoped form is the only one that breaks, and only because the discriminator looks past the `#`. Variants containing `/` are otherwise accepted everywhere in this resolver (the no-alias parser and the alias path both pass them through).

## Why it matters

A scoped alias is the documented way to rename one model under one provider while giving it a default variant. A variant name containing `/` (namespaced effort/variant names occur in the wild) silently turns a valid config into a hard `Invalid model reference` error whose message (`...after alias resolution: new`) points at the model name and gives no hint the variant's slash caused it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolve({models: {"openai/old": "new#va/r"}}, "openai/old")` returns `openai/new#va/r` (both the original-provider branch at :113 and the resolved-provider branch at :153).
- [ ] The form discriminator tests the slash only in the part of the target before `#`.
- [ ] Existing behaviour is unchanged for slash-form targets, bare targets with slash-free variants, and all currently rejected targets (empty, padded, second-`#`).
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the slash-in-variant bare scoped target through both scoped branches; the existing model-alias suite still passes.

Suggested fix: in both branches, compute the discriminator from the pre-`#` segment, e.g. `const hash = target.indexOf("#"); const base = hash === -1 ? target : target.slice(0, hash); if (base.includes("/")) { ... }` — the hash-split else-branch already handles the variant correctly once it is reached.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias alias lookups match Object.prototype members — toString/constructor names crash the #410/#413 validation with TypeError
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), alias lookups read inherited `Object.prototype` members as if they were configured aliases. A model, provider, or variant name that happens to equal a prototype member (`toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`) therefore produces a non-string "target", and the validation added in PRs #410 and #413 crashes with a `TypeError` instead of resolving normally or throwing `Invalid model reference`.

This is visible in the #410/#413 diffs themselves: both PRs changed/introduced guards that assume a lookup returns `string | undefined` —

- PR #413 (commit `837c4e0e1dfb`, merge `0fec462129`): the three model-alias lookups at `model-alias.ts:83` (global), `:109` (scoped under original provider) and `:143` (scoped under resolved provider) now check `!== undefined` and assign the value to `current`.
- PR #410 (commit `e1caf59543f5`, merge `d0ba1110fb`): the provider-alias lookup at `model-alias.ts:132` checks `!== undefined` and then calls `providerAlias.includes(...)`; the variant caller at `model-alias.ts:194` calls `finalVariant.includes("#")` on the value returned by `resolveVariant`, whose bare-key lookup at `model-alias.ts:240` uses the `in` operator (`if (variant in variantAliases)`), which also matches inherited members.

Plain-object alias maps (object literals in tests, and the records produced by config decoding in `packages/core/src/config/normalize.ts`) inherit from `Object.prototype`, so `aliases.models["toString"]`, `aliases.providers["toString"]` and `"toString" in aliases.variants` are all truthy/defined even when the user never configured such an alias.

## Evidence (verified on current main `0fec462129`, the #413 merge)

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "toString")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "constructor")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ models: { other: "openai/gpt-4o" } }, "hasOwnProperty")
  THROWS TypeError: current.indexOf is not a function
resolve({ providers: { other: "openai" } }, "toString/model")
  THROWS TypeError: providerAlias.includes is not a function
resolve({ providers: { other: "openai" } }, "constructor/model")
  THROWS TypeError: providerAlias.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#toString")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#constructor")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
resolve({ variants: { hi: "high" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#__proto__")
  THROWS TypeError: finalVariant.includes is not a function
```

Contrast with the no-alias path, which handles the same names cleanly:

```
resolve(undefined, "openai/gpt-4o#toString")  => "openai/gpt-4o#toString"   // real variant passes through
resolve(undefined, "toString")               THROWS Error: Invalid model reference: toString
```

So with any alias map configured, a bare model named `toString`, a provider named `toString`, or a variant named `toString`/`constructor`/`__proto__` crashes the resolver with a `TypeError`, where the no-alias parser either passes the name through or raises the documented `Invalid model reference` error. Callers in `ModelResolver` and the session runner catch all errors, so in those paths the crash is silently swallowed and alias resolution is abandoned for that request; direct callers (e.g. `packages/cli/src/session-target.ts`) get an unexplained `TypeError`.

Distinct from #412 (whitespace-only alias targets): that issue is about configured string targets; this one is about lookups returning inherited non-string values for names that were never configured at all.

## Why it matters

Alias resolution sits on the model-selection path for every configured deployment. Names colliding with `Object.prototype` members are not exotic in generated or user-authored config (a variant literally named e.g. `constructor` is legal input to the no-alias parser today), and the failure mode — a `TypeError` from inside validation code, or silently skipped alias resolution where callers catch-all — is far from the actual cause. The #410/#413 hardening made the resolver stricter for configured targets; the lookups themselves should be own-property lookups so unconfigured names behave exactly as they do with no aliases.

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

## Acceptance criteria

- Alias lookups in `resolveRef`/`resolveVariant` only match own properties of the alias maps (e.g. `Object.hasOwn` guards or `typeof === "string"` checks): `toString`, `constructor`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, and `__proto__` as a model, provider, or bare variant name behave exactly as they do on the no-alias path (pass through where the plain parser passes them through, `Invalid model reference` where it rejects) — never a `TypeError`.
- A genuinely configured alias whose key is one of those names and whose target is a string still resolves (own-property check, not a blocklist).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover at least: bare model `toString` with a models map present, provider `toString/model` with a providers map present, and variant `openai/gpt-4o#toString` with a variants map present.
- Existing model-alias tests (24/24 on main `0fec462129`) all still pass.

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias whitespace-only alias targets yield blank provider/model/variant segments instead of erroring
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), alias targets are validated only against the empty string, `/` and `#`. A **whitespace-only (or whitespace-padded) target segment passes every check** and becomes the provider, model or variant of the resolved ref — producing refs whose segments are blank spaces, which the no-alias parser rejects for the equivalent input.

## Evidence (verified on main `d0ba1110fb`, the #410 merge)

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ providers: { x: " " } }, "x/model")                 => " /model"              // provider is a single space
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": " " } }, "openai/pro")      => "openai/ "             // model is a single space
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": "  " } }, "openai/pro")     => "openai/  "            // model is two spaces
resolve({ models: { bad: "openai/ " } }, "bad")               => "openai/ "             // global target, model is a space
resolve({ models: { bad: " /gpt-4o" } }, "bad")               => " /gpt-4o"             // global target, provider is a space
resolve({ variants: { hi: " " } }, "openai/gpt-4o#hi")        => "openai/gpt-4o# "      // variant is a single space
resolve({ variants: { hi: "\t" } }, "openai/gpt-4o#hi")       => "openai/gpt-4o#\t"     // variant is a tab
resolve({ models: { bad: "openai/gpt-4o " } }, "bad")         => "openai/gpt-4o "       // trailing space kept in model id
```

Why it happens:

- The initial `input` is trimmed (`const trimmed = input.trim()`), but alias targets substituted into `current` mid-loop are never trimmed or re-checked for whitespace.
- Provider-alias validation (Rule 2) rejects only `!providerAlias || includes("/") || includes("#")` — `" "` passes.
- Variant validation after `resolveVariant` rejects only `!finalVariant || includes("#")` — `" "` / `"\t"` pass.
- The settled-ref check rejects only `slashIdx <= 0 || slashIdx === settledBase.length - 1` — a model consisting solely of spaces has non-zero length, so it passes.

Contrast with the no-alias path: `resolve(undefined, "openai/ ")` throws (the input trim turns it into `openai/`), and `resolve(undefined, " /gpt-4o")` throws (trimmed to `/gpt-4o`). The alias path is therefore more permissive than the plain parser for the same final ref — the same class of divergence closed for empty/`#` targets in #398, #406 and #407.

## Why it matters

Alias config is user-authored; stray whitespace from editing or generated config currently produces a resolved ref with blank segments that downstream model lookup cannot match, surfacing as a confusing "model unavailable"-style failure far from the config mistake instead of an `Invalid model reference` error at resolution time.

## Acceptance criteria

- An alias target segment (provider name, model name, or variant name) that is whitespace-only, or that carries leading/trailing whitespace, causes `resolve`/`resolveRef` to throw `Invalid model reference` — for provider aliases, global and scoped model aliases, and variant aliases alike.
- Refs whose segments are already well-formed are unchanged (`packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` existing tests all still pass).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover at least: whitespace-only provider target, whitespace-only scoped model target, whitespace-only variant target.

Related but distinct: #411 (empty scoped model alias target silently ignored — the truthiness-guard counterpart of this validation gap).

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias empty scoped model alias target is silently ignored instead of erroring
body:
## Summary

In `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`), a **scoped model alias whose target is the empty string is silently ignored**: resolution proceeds exactly as if the alias did not exist, so a mistyped/emptied config entry silently does nothing instead of erroring like every other invalid alias target.

## Evidence (verified on main `d0ba1110fb`, the #410 merge)

The two scoped-model lookups guard on truthiness, so an empty-string target never reaches any validation:

- `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` — orig-provider scoped lookup: `const origScopedAlias = aliases.models?.[origScopedKey]; if (origScopedAlias) { … }`
- `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` — resolved-provider scoped lookup: `const scopedAlias = aliases.models?.[scopedKey]; if (scopedAlias) { … }`

Probe (bun, importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` directly):

```
resolve({ models: { "openai/pro": "" } }, "openai/pro")
  => "openai/pro"            // alias silently dropped, input returned unchanged

resolve({ providers: { ds: "deepseek" }, models: { "ds/pro": "" } }, "ds/pro")
  => "deepseek/pro"          // provider alias applied, empty model alias silently dropped
```

Contrast with the sibling alias kinds, which were fixed to validate with an explicit undefined check:

- Provider aliases use `if (providerAlias !== undefined && …)` and throw `Invalid model reference` for an empty target (#407/#410).
- Variant alias targets that are empty throw (#406/#410).
- Even a **global** model alias with an empty target throws (indirectly, when the settled ref has no `/`), though its message names the input rather than the target.

Only the scoped model path swallows the empty target completely.

## Why it matters

Alias config is user-authored. An entry like `"openai/pro": ""` (emptied while editing, a templating mistake, a generated config bug) currently fails silently: the model the user believes is remapped is not, and there is no error anywhere to chase. Every neighbouring alias kind treats the same mistake as an `Invalid model reference` error.

## Acceptance criteria

- `resolve` (and `resolveRef`) throws `Invalid model reference: <input>` when a scoped model alias that matches the input has an empty-string target — for both scoped lookups (original provider name and provider-alias-resolved name).
- Existing behaviour for non-empty scoped targets is unchanged (`packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` tests 4, 5 and 13 still pass).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the empty scoped target under both the original and the resolved provider name.
- Related nicety (optional): the global empty-target error message could name the alias target rather than only the input.

Single-repo: the `ModelAlias` resolver lives only in developing-today/opencode (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`).

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias provider alias target containing / silently reshapes the ref instead of erroring
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` applies a *provider* alias target verbatim without validating it is a plausible provider ID. A provider alias whose target contains `/` (or `#`) does not error — it silently reshapes the reference, splitting the target at its first `/` so part of the supposed provider becomes part of the model ID.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-24 on main c45147f4b3)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- Rule 2 (lines 153-157): `provider = providerAlias` with no validation, then line 176 rebuilds `current = \`${provider}/${model}\``.
- On the next loop iteration the rebuilt string is re-split at the first `/`, so a target of `a/b` turns provider `a`, model `b/<original model>`.

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main c45147f4b3):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ providers: { x: "a/b" } }` | `x/model` | returns `{ providerID: "a", id: "b/model", ref: "a/b/model" }` — no error; the alias target's second segment became part of the model ID |

A provider ID containing `/` can never be a real provider: the reference grammar is `provider/model[#variant]`, split at the first `/` (`parseRefString`, lines 236-252), so `a/b` as a provider is unrepresentable in the very format the resolver outputs. A `#` in a provider alias target fares no better — it is reinterpreted as a variant separator on the next iteration.

## Why it matters

A malformed `providers` alias entry in user config (a stray `a/b` pasted where a provider ID belongs) is silently reinterpreted as a *different provider and a different model* instead of an error at resolution time. The request then goes to a provider/model the user never named, or fails downstream as "model unavailable" with no hint the alias config was the cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A provider alias target containing `/` or `#` (or empty) throws an invalid-reference error at resolution time, naming the offending reference — it never silently reshapes provider/model.
- [ ] Valid provider alias chains still resolve (existing test 13's `p1 -> p2 -> final-provider` chain passes unchanged).

title: fix(schema): ModelAlias variant alias target is never validated — empty or #-containing target yields a malformed ref
body:
## Problem

`ModelAlias.resolveRef` validates variants typed in the input and variants arriving via a *model* alias target (fixed for #398 in PR #403), but it never validates the value returned from the *variant* alias map (`aliases.variants`). A configured variant alias whose target is empty or contains a `#` produces a malformed or internally inconsistent `ResolvedRef` instead of the invalid-reference error every other path throws.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-24 on main c45147f4b3)

File: `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`

- `resolveVariant` (lines 202-233) returns `variantAliases[...]` verbatim, with no check that the target is non-empty and `#`-free.
- The caller (lines 186-196) assigns that value straight to `finalVariant` and builds `canonicalRef` from it, so the bad value lands in both `ResolvedRef.variant` and `ResolvedRef.ref`.
- By contrast `parseRefString` (line 245) throws when a variant is empty or contains `#`, and the alias loop (lines 82-84) throws for the same shapes arriving in the input or via a model alias target.

Reproduction (Bun probe importing `packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts`, main c45147f4b3):

| Aliases | Input | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `{ variants: { hi: "high#extra" } }` | `openai/gpt-4o#hi` | returns `{ variant: "high#extra", ref: "openai/gpt-4o#high#extra" }` — a ref `parseRefString` itself rejects |
| `{ variants: { hi: "" } }` | `openai/gpt-4o#hi` | returns `{ variant: "", ref: "openai/gpt-4o" }` — variant silently dropped, and `variant` is `""` while `ref` carries no variant |
| `{ variants: { hi: "#" } }` | `openai/gpt-4o#hi` | returns `{ variant: "#", ref: "openai/gpt-4o##" }` |

Control: `ModelAlias.resolve(undefined, "openai/gpt-4o#high#extra")` throws `Invalid model reference`.

## Why it matters

A typo or bad value in the `variants` alias map (user config) is silently turned into a canonical ref no other parser in the repo accepts, so it fails later — further from the cause — or is passed to a provider as a variant name that can never match. The empty-target shape is worse: resolution appears to succeed while quietly dropping the variant the user asked for, and `ResolvedRef.variant === ""` contradicts `ResolvedRef.ref`, which has no variant segment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A variant alias target that is empty or contains `#` throws the same invalid-reference error as the no-alias path, naming the offending reference.
- [ ] `ResolvedRef.variant` is never `""`: it is either a non-empty variant or `undefined`, and it always agrees with `ResolvedRef.ref`.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-alias.test.ts` cover the `#`-containing and empty variant-alias-target shapes (bare and scoped/wildcard variant keys); all existing model-alias tests still pass.
- [ ] Dedup checked 2026-10-24: #398/PR #403 covered input variants and model-alias targets only; no open or closed issue tracks variant-alias (`aliases.variants`) targets.

Single-repo: `ModelAlias` lives only in this repo's schema/core packages.

title: fix(core): OAuth durations parse with bare parseInt — DigitalOcean expires_in "1e3" becomes a 1-second credential, OpenAI device interval "0x10" becomes 16s

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

Two OAuth flows in `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/` parse server-supplied **string** durations with bare `Number.parseInt`, which silently truncates or reinterprets non-plain-decimal spellings instead of falling back:

1. **DigitalOcean `expires_in`** — `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/digitalocean.ts:74` (field is `Schema.optional(Schema.String)` at line 32):
   ```ts
   const expires = Number.parseInt(body.expires_in ?? "0", 10)
   // used when: Number.isFinite(expires) && expires > 0 ? expires : 60 * 60 * 24 * 30
   ```
   The parsed value becomes the OAuth credential's lifetime (`expires: now + payload.expiresIn * 1000`).

2. **OpenAI Codex device `interval`** — `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/openai.ts:197` (typed `interval: string` in the device-code response):
   ```ts
   const interval = Math.max(Number.parseInt(device.interval) || 5, 1) * 1000
   ```
   Note there is **no radix argument**, so `parseInt` also auto-detects hex. The value is the device-code polling interval.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0b51b19b33`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator/probe.js`, Node) evaluating the exact expressions above:

| Input | DigitalOcean result | Intended behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `"3600"` | 3600s | 3600s ✓ |
| `"1e3"` | **1s** — credential expires almost immediately | fallback (30 days) or 1000s, never 1s |
| `"0x10"` | 0 → **30-day fallback** for a 16s token | fallback is fine, but by accident of truncation, not grammar |
| `"3600junk"` | **3600s accepted** | malformed → fallback |
| `"3600.9"` | 3600s (truncated) | malformed → fallback |

| Input | OpenAI result | Intended behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `"5"` / `"10"` | 5000 / 10000ms | ✓ |
| `"1e1"` | **1000ms** polling (10× too fast) | 10000ms or 5s fallback |
| `"0x10"` | **16000ms** (hex auto-detect, no radix) | 5s fallback |
| `"5junk"` | **5000ms accepted** | malformed → fallback |
| `"2.9"` | 2000ms (truncated) | malformed → fallback |

This is the same defect class the repo has repeatedly removed elsewhere by adopting a plain-decimal grammar before parsing: ToolInputRepair (#715), retry-after (#682/#686), Modal pricing (#724), file-URL line ranges (#728), McpxDiagnose (#769). These two OAuth sites were missed because `parseInt` truncates instead of reinterpreting whole-string — the failure is quieter but the value that reaches the credential expiry / poll loop is still not the value the server wrote.

## Why it matters

- A DigitalOcean token whose `expires_in` arrives in a non-plain spelling gets a credential lifetime of 1 second (constant re-auth) or 30 days (a short-lived token believed valid for a month — requests fail with auth errors long after the client thinks the credential is fresh).
- A Codex device flow with a malformed `interval` polls 10× too fast (rate-limit risk against the auth server) or 3× too slow (login appears hung).
- Both values come from a remote server response, i.e. exactly the untrusted-spelling surface the plain-decimal fixes were for.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both sites accept only a plain unsigned decimal integer spelling (the grammar used by the #715/#724 fixes, or a stated equivalent); every other spelling takes the existing fallback (DigitalOcean: 30 days; OpenAI: 5s, still clamped to ≥1s).
- [ ] Tests pin: `"1e3"`, `"0x10"`, `"3600junk"`/`"5junk"`, `"3600.9"`/`"2.9"` → fallback at both sites; `"3600"` / `"5"` still parse as before.
- [ ] No behaviour change for numeric (non-string) inputs or for absent values.

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "digitalocean expires_in", "parseInt expires", "device interval parseInt", "oauth parseInt", "expires_in" — no hits. The sibling grammar issues (#715/#724/#728/#769) cover other files only.

title: fix(core): TmpGuard stdlib list misses annotationlib, antigravity and cProfile — diffed against CPython 3.14 sys.stdlib_module_names

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The hardcoded Python stdlib name list in `TmpGuard` (`packages/core/src/tmp-guard.ts`, added for #132 in PR #748) is incomplete against the very version it claims to cover. Its header comment (lines 5–12) says the set is "Python standard-library top-level module names (CPython 3.14; underscore-prefixed private internals omitted)", but three non-underscore top-level names from CPython 3.14 are missing, so a file with any of these names in the shared tmp root shadows the stdlib with no warning:

- `annotationlib.py` — `annotationlib` is a new top-level stdlib module in Python 3.14 (PEP 649/749).
- `antigravity.py` — `antigravity` is a long-standing top-level stdlib module present in `sys.stdlib_module_names`.
- `cProfile.py` — `cProfile` is a top-level stdlib module; the list has `profile` (line 120) but not its mixed-case sibling `cProfile`. Note the existing test in `packages/core/test/tmp-guard.test.ts` pins `Re.py` as a non-collision, so case handling is deliberate — `cProfile` is not a case variant of a listed name, it is simply absent.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `cd21eab1de`)

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-tmpguard/` (Python 3.14.7): the name set was regex-extracted from the shipped `tmp-guard.ts` (byte copy of main) and diffed against the interpreter's own authoritative list:

```
python: 3.14.7
missing-from-guard (non-underscore): ['annotationlib', 'antigravity', 'cProfile']
in-guard-not-stdlib: []
antigravity in stdlib: True | annotationlib in stdlib: True
```

So the guard has no false extras — it is purely missing these three. `findCollisions(["annotationlib.py", "antigravity.py", "cProfile.py"])` therefore returns `[]` today, while e.g. a stray `cProfile.py` in the tmp root is imported by any `python3 -m cProfile`-style or `import cProfile` run started from that directory ahead of the real stdlib module.

## Why it matters

#132's failure mode is a misleading traceback in every Python run from the shared tmp root. The guard's list is a hand-maintained copy of an upstream list that changes every Python release (3.14 alone added `annotationlib` and `compression` — the latter made the list, the former did not), so this class of gap will recur silently unless the missing names are added and the list gains a regression check against a real interpreter's `sys.stdlib_module_names`.

## Acceptance criteria

- `annotationlib`, `antigravity`, and `cProfile` are recognised: `TmpGuard.findCollisions(["annotationlib.py", "antigravity.py", "cProfile.py"])` returns all three, and `isStdlibPythonFile("cProfile.py")` is `true` without breaking the deliberate case-sensitivity pinned for names like `Re.py`.
- A test pins the three names as collisions in `packages/core/test/tmp-guard.test.ts`.
- The header comment's coverage claim stays accurate (it names the CPython version the list was checked against), and the fix notes how the list was verified (diff against `sys.stdlib_module_names` on that version, underscore-prefixed names excluded).
- No other names are added or removed beyond what that diff justifies (the verified diff shows no extras to remove).
- Existing tmp-guard tests keep passing.

title: fix(core): TmpGuard.scan misses package directories and symlinked .py files — json/__init__.py and a colorsys.py symlink shadow the stdlib with no warning

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`TmpGuard` (added for #132, merged in PR #748) warns when a stdlib-named `.py` file sits in the shared tmp root, but `scan()` only sees one of the three forms that actually shadow the Python standard library for a `python3` process started in that directory. Two shadow forms pass completely undetected:

1. **Package directories** — a directory named after a stdlib package containing `__init__.py` (e.g. `json/__init__.py`, `email/__init__.py`).
2. **Symlinked `.py` files** — a symlink such as `colorsys.py -> /somewhere/else.py`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `cd21eab1de`)

Code — `packages/core/src/tmp-guard.ts`:

- `isStdlibPythonFile` (line 207) only matches names ending in `.py`, so a directory named `json` can never match.
- `scan` (lines 219–224) filters readdir entries with `entry.isFile()`. Node `Dirent.isFile()` follows lstat semantics: it is `false` for a directory entry and `false` for a symlink (even a symlink whose target is a regular file), so both forms above are filtered out before the name check.

Reproduction — laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-tmpguard/` (Python 3.14.7, the version the guard's list claims to cover):

- Layout `pkg/json/__init__.py` containing `MARKER = "shadow-json"`: running `python3 -c "import json; print(json.__file__, json.MARKER)"` with cwd `pkg/` prints the probe file's path and `shadow-json` — the stdlib `json` package is shadowed. The same directory listing run through scan's exact fs logic (`readdirSync(..., { withFileTypes: true })` → `isFile()` → `.py` filter) yields `[]`: no warning.
- Layout `pkg2/colorsys.py` as a symlink to a file containing `MARKER = "shadow-colorsys"`: `python3 -c "import colorsys; ..."` with cwd `pkg2/` loads the symlink target (marker present) — stdlib `colorsys` is shadowed. Scan's logic yields `[]` for this directory too (`colorsys.py` reports `isFile=false, isSymbolicLink=true`).

Existing test coverage gap: `packages/core/test/tmp-guard.test.ts` (scan describe block) covers a plain file, a nested file, and a directory literally named `json.py`, but never a stdlib-named package directory or a symlink.

## Why it matters

The guard exists because one stray stdlib-named file in the shared tmp root breaks every Python run from that directory with a misleading traceback (#132). Package directories and symlinks are realistic ways such a file lands there (an unpacked project, a linked scratch file), and today they defeat the warning while the built-in instruction text (packages/core/src/instructions/builtins.ts:45) tells agents the `python3 -I` workaround is the mitigation the warning is supposed to trigger. A shadow the guard cannot see is worse than no guard: it reads as "checked, clean".

## Acceptance criteria

- `TmpGuard.scan` reports a stdlib-named package directory (a directory whose name is a stdlib top-level package — e.g. `json`, `email`, `http` — containing `__init__.py`) as a collision, naming it clearly in the warning text.
- `TmpGuard.scan` reports a symlinked `.py` file whose link name is a stdlib module name (target followed, e.g. via `fs.statSync` semantics rather than Dirent lstat semantics).
- Plain namespace directories with no `__init__.py` do not produce false positives beyond what Python itself would shadow (a bare directory without `__init__.py` must not be reported if it cannot shadow a regular stdlib package — verify against Python's import rules and pin the behaviour in a test).
- Existing behaviour is unchanged for plain files, nested files, and a directory literally named `json.py` (current tmp-guard tests keep passing).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/tmp-guard.test.ts` pin both new forms (package directory, symlink) plus the no-`__init__.py` negative case.
- Files are still never deleted, moved, or modified — warning only, as today.

title: fix(core): MessagingVars membership tests use `in` — prototype names (constructor, toString, __proto__) are falsely rejected as built-in variables

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Messaging variable handling in `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts` tests membership in the built-in variable tables with the `in` operator, which also matches inherited `Object.prototype` members. Variable names that are perfectly legal under the module's own name grammar (`/^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/`) — `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `isPrototypeOf`, `__proto__` — are therefore treated as if they were built-in computed/time/constant variables:

- `MessagingVars.set` rejects them with `{constructor} is computed and cannot be overridden` (or "is built in"), so a custom variable with one of these names can never be stored, even though no built-in variable by that name exists.
- The variable list silently drops a configured variable with one of these names from the configured-vars section.
- The time-variable and session-field gates take the same false-positive branch (they happen to return `undefined` afterwards, so resolution is not corrupted — but the gates are wrong and the next edit that trusts them will be).

The rest of the codebase already uses `Object.hasOwn` for exactly this hazard (e.g. `packages/core/src/rpc.ts`, `packages/core/src/workspace/driver.ts`), and the same collision class was fixed for provider IDs in #673 and alias lookups in #414. These five sites in `vars.ts` were missed.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-28)

- `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:203` — `if (!(key in MessagingTemplate.sessionFields)) return undefined`
- `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:211` — `if (name in MessagingTemplate.timeVars) return timeValue(name, now)`
- `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:373` — `.filter((name) => !(name in MessagingTemplate.constants))` (variable list)
- `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:418` — `if (input.name in MessagingTemplate.contextVars || input.name in MessagingTemplate.timeVars)` → rejects with "is computed and cannot be overridden"
- `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:424` — `if (input.name in MessagingTemplate.constants)` → rejects with "is built in"
- The tables are plain object literals: `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts:29` (`constants`), `:204` (`sessionFields`), `:218` (`contextVars`, built by spreading `Object.fromEntries(...)` into a literal), `:251` (`timeVars`) — none is prototype-free, so `in` sees `Object.prototype`.
- Laptop probe (probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-vars-proto/` on the laptop; imports the real `MessagingTemplate` from the laptop clone at `b0633cc697`, whose `vars.ts`/`template.ts` sha256 are byte-identical to sandbox main): for each of `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `__proto__`, `isPrototypeOf` — `in constants === true`, `in timeVars === true`, `in contextVars === true`, while `Object.hasOwn(constants, name) === false` and `constant(name) === undefined`. Controls behave correctly: `separator` is an own constant (`constant() === "/"`), `system_time`/`unix` are own time vars, `session_id` is an own context var. The `NAME` regex at `vars.ts:110` accepts all six prototype names.
- Existing tests pin the true-positive rejections that must keep working: `packages/core/test/messaging.test.ts:196` (`session_id` rejected as computed) and `:200` (`separator` rejected as built-in).

## Why it matters

`setVar` is exposed to sessions and the user (via `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:433`). A legal variable name is refused with a misleading reason ("computed"/"built in" when it is neither), and there is no workaround — the name is simply unusable as a messaging variable, and a configured variable with that name vanishes from the variable list while still resolving. It is the same silent prototype-collision class the fleet has already fixed twice (#673, #414); leaving a third instance invites the next one to corrupt data instead of merely refusing a name.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All five membership tests in `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts` (lines 203, 211, 373, 418, 424) use own-property checks (`Object.hasOwn` or equivalent), matching the house pattern in `rpc.ts` / `workspace/driver.ts`.
- [ ] `setVar` accepts and stores custom variables named `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `valueOf`, `isPrototypeOf`, and `__proto__`, and such a variable resolves normally in template rendering; storing `__proto__` must not mutate any object's prototype (the value lives in the DB / a `Map`, and the fix must keep it that way).
- [ ] True positives still reject: `session_id` (context) and `system_time` (time) as computed, `separator` (constant) as built-in — the existing tests at `messaging.test.ts:196,200` keep passing.
- [ ] A configured variable named e.g. `toString` appears in the variable list output instead of being filtered out.
- [ ] New tests in the messaging test set pin at least `constructor` and `__proto__` as settable/resolvable custom variables, plus the list-visibility case.
- [ ] No change to resolution order (args → facts → custom → configured constants) or to any real built-in variable's behaviour.

title: fix(core): webfetch HTML→Markdown renumbers hex-spelled ordered lists — bare parseInt reads start="0x10" as item 16 instead of 0

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The HTML→Markdown converter used by webfetch reads an ordered list's `start` and an item's `value` with a bare `Number.parseInt(...)` (no radix). `parseInt` auto-detects a `0x` prefix as hexadecimal, so a hex-spelled attribute is reinterpreted as a hex number — while HTML's own integer parsing (optional sign, then ASCII digits only, stop at the first non-digit) reads the same attribute as `0`. The converted markdown silently renumbers the list.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-28)

- `packages/core/src/tool/html-markdown.ts:403` — `const start = Number.parseInt(attributes.start ?? "1")` (no radix argument).
- `packages/core/src/tool/html-markdown.ts:411` — `const value = Number.parseInt(attributes.value ?? "")` (no radix argument).
- Laptop probe (probe dir `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-htmlmd/` on the laptop; imports the real `convertHTMLToMarkdown` from the laptop clone, whose `html-markdown.ts` sha256 `49333c55…` is byte-identical to sandbox main `b0633cc697`; run with bun from `packages/core`):
  - control `<ol start="3">` → `"3. a\n\n4. b"` ✓
  - `<ol start="0x10">` → `"16. a\n\n17. b"` — HTML parsing reads `0x10` as 0, so a browser renders this list starting at 0
  - `<ol start="-0x10">` → `"-16. a\n\n-15. b"` — HTML parsing reads it as 0 (`-0`)
  - `<ol><li value="0x20">` → `"32. a\n\n33. b"` — HTML parsing reads `0x20` as 0
  - controls that agree either way: `start="1e2"` → 1, `start="08"` → 8
- The converter is the webfetch path: `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/webfetch.ts:9` imports `convertHTMLToMarkdown` from this module, so fetched pages reach the model with the renumbered lists.
- Dedup: searched open/closed issues for `parseInt`, "ordered list", `htmlparser` on 2026-10-28 — #246 covers TUI editor/IDE ports parsed with `parseInt`, a different surface; nothing covers html-markdown list numbering.

## Why it matters

Webfetch output is ground truth the model reasons from. A page whose list is numbered from 0 (or whose items carry explicit values) comes back numbered from 16/32 instead, with no error anywhere — cross-references in the page text ("see step 16") then point at the wrong items, and quoted numbering is silently corrupted.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `start`/`value` attributes are parsed with HTML integer grammar (optional sign + decimal digits; trailing non-digits ignored the way the HTML parser ignores them), never radix auto-detection: `0x10` → 0, `-0x10` → 0, `0x20` → 0.
- [ ] Ordinary values are unchanged: `start="3"` → 3, `start="08"` → 8, `start="1e2"` → 1, negative decimal starts keep working, and a missing/unparseable `start` still defaults to 1 while an unparseable `value` still leaves the counter untouched.
- [ ] New tests in the html-markdown test set pin the hex-spelled `start` and `value` cases plus the decimal controls.
- [ ] No change to unordered lists, nested-list counters, or the markdown byte budget behaviour.

body:
## Problem

The `jules-daily-upstream-sync` workflow records failures on a tracking issue whose own body promises it will be closed once a sync succeeds — but no step in the workflow ever closes it. A single transient failure therefore leaves a permanent open `chore(deps): automated upstream sync failing` issue that keeps telling the Muse repo tasks to take over a sync that has long since recovered.

## Evidence (verified this run, 2026-10-28)

- `developing-today/opencode` `.github/workflows/jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml` (main `b0633cc697`, step added by PR #731):
  - The only issue-managing step is `Record a sync failure for the Muse tasks`, gated `if: failure()` — it creates the tracking issue or comments on repeat failures.
  - The created issue body says verbatim: "This issue is maintained by the jules-daily-upstream-sync workflow: repeat failures comment here; **close it once a sync run succeeds**."
  - The workflow contains no `if: success()` step and no `gh issue close` anywhere (full file read this run) — the promised success path does not exist.
- Cross-repo set — the same flaw in `developing-today/openchamber`: its `.github/workflows/jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml` on live main has the identical failure step and identical promise, and likewise no success/close step (verified via `gh api` file read this run; 0 matches for `if: success`).
- `developing-today/code` does NOT have this workflow (its Jules workflows are `jules-daily-flake-sync.yml` / `jules.yml` / `jules-daily-codebase-ideation.yml`, none with this tracking-issue pattern) — the set is opencode + openchamber only.
- Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "upstream sync" on 2026-10-28 — prior sync issues (#36, #41, #136, #151, #184) cover setup/pin/concurrency faults, none covers the never-closing tracking issue.

## Why it matters

The tracking issue is an escalation signal: while it is open, Muse repo tasks are told to reproduce and land the upstream sync themselves. If it never closes after recovery, the signal becomes permanent noise — duplicate manual sync work can be started against a healthy daily sync, and a later real failure is indistinguishable from the stale one (it only adds a comment to an already-open, already-escalated issue).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] On a successful `jules-daily-upstream-sync` run in opencode, an open tracking issue with the exact title `chore(deps): automated upstream sync failing` is closed with a comment linking the successful run; when no such issue is open, the success step is a no-op and the run stays green.
- [ ] The success step is idempotent and failure-tolerant in the same style as the existing failure step (exact-title match, not a fuzzy search hit).
- [ ] The same change is applied to `developing-today/openchamber`'s identical workflow step (one set, tracked here; downstream PR references this issue by URL).
- [ ] The tracking issue body text and the workflow behaviour agree — either the close-on-success behaviour exists, or the promise is removed from the body.
- [ ] Repeat failures after a recovery re-open the cycle correctly: a new failure creates a fresh tracking issue (the closed one is not mistaken for the live one — the existing lookup already filters `--state open`).

## Suggested shape

Mirror the existing failure step with an `if: success()` step reusing the same exact-title lookup, then `gh issue close <n> --comment "Upstream sync succeeded: <run_url>. Closing per the workflow's tracking-issue contract."` when a number is found.

body:
## Summary

Custom-command templates expand a `$0` placeholder into garbage: the literal string `undefined` when other placeholders are present, or just the last argument when `$0` is the only placeholder. Positional placeholders are `$1`…`$N` (the highest one consumes the remaining arguments) plus `$ARGUMENTS`; there is no `$0` argument, so a template author who writes `$0` — or a template ported from a system where `$0` means all arguments / the command name — gets silently corrupted prompt text instead of the placeholder being left alone or rejected.

## Evidence

`packages/core/src/config/plugin/command.ts:200-210` on main `01e71bb02a`:

```ts
const args = parseArguments(input)
const placeholders = template.match(placeholderRegex) ?? []
const last = Math.max(0, ...placeholders.map((item) => Number(item.slice(1))))
const expanded = template.replaceAll(placeholderRegex, (_, index) => {
  const position = Number(index)
  const argIndex = position - 1
  if (argIndex >= args.length) return ""
  if (position === last) return args.slice(argIndex).join(" ")
  return args[argIndex]
})
```

with `placeholderRegex = /\$(\d+)/g` (`command.ts:250`), which admits `0`.

For `$0`: `argIndex` is `-1`. When another placeholder makes `last >= 1`, the callback returns `args[-1]`, which is `undefined`, and `String.prototype.replaceAll` stringifies the callback result — the word `undefined` lands in the prompt. When `$0` is the only placeholder, `last` is `0`, `position === last`, and the callback returns `args.slice(-1).join(" ")` — only the last argument.

Verified this run on the laptop (node, replicating the exact expansion code above; no sandbox probe):

| Template | Input args | Expansion | Sane result |
|---|---|---|---|
| `run $0 $1` | `hello world` | `run undefined hello world` | no `undefined` |
| `run $0` | `hello world` | `run world` | not just the last arg |
| `run $00 $1` | `hello` | `run undefined hello` | no `undefined` |
| `run $1 $2` (control) | `hello world` | `run hello world` | ✓ unchanged |

The existing tests in `packages/core/test/config/command.test.ts` pin `$1`, `$2`, and `$ARGUMENTS` interpolation (including literal-input safety for `$&`/`$$` inputs) but have no `$0` case.

## Why it matters

- The expanded text is the prompt a session actually receives: a stray `undefined` or a dropped-arguments expansion is silent prompt corruption in a user-authored command, with no error anywhere.
- `$0` is a plausible thing to write: shell scripting trains `$0`, and several other agent tools' command templates use 0-inclusive or all-args spellings. The failure mode should be boring (placeholder left as written, like other unrecognised `$` forms) rather than inventing text.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A template containing `$0` (or `$00`) never expands it to the string `undefined` and never to a slice of the arguments; it is left as written in the output (consistent with unrecognised `$` forms), or another explicitly tested behaviour replaces this.
- [ ] `$1`…`$N` and `$ARGUMENTS` expansion is unchanged, including the rule that the highest placeholder consumes the remaining arguments and the literal-input cases already pinned in `packages/core/test/config/command.test.ts`.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/config/command.test.ts` pin `$0` alongside another placeholder, `$0` alone, and `$00`.
- [ ] No change to argument parsing (`parseArguments`) or shell interpolation (`!`…`` ` ``) behaviour.

title: fix(core): named route windows resolve silently — an unknown or unparseable window name drops the gate/rule with no diagnostic (PR #649)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Finding

PR #649 added named route windows (`experimental.model_route_windows`) referenced by name from schedule `when`s and target `window` gates. Every name-resolution failure is silent:

- An **unknown** window name in a target gate drops the gate — the target becomes *always eligible*, the opposite of the author's intent (they wrote the gate to restrict it).
- An unknown name in a schedule `when` drops the whole weight rule.
- A **defined-but-unparseable** window (e.g. `start: "25:99"` — the schema types `start`/`end` as plain strings, so this passes config decode) is dropped by `configuredWindows` without any diagnostic, which makes every reference to it fail the same silent way.

No diagnostic, log line, or decision-log entry records any of this, so a one-character typo in a window name silently removes a peak-hour eligibility gate and routes traffic onto the target the operator meant to keep off-peak. This is the #238 pattern (a misconfigured pool "disappears with no diagnostic") in the new windows feature.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/649 (merge commit `ae8738e08278eae4edbdbc8554826c5b0090a51a`)
- Current main `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:176-186` — `configuredWindows`: `const parsed = ModelRouteSchedule.parse(window); if (parsed) windows.set(name, parsed)` — unparseable entries vanish with no record.
- Current main `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:190-195` — `resolveWindow`: "An unknown name resolves to undefined, which drops the rule."
- Current main `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:198-206` — `gateFor`: "An unknown name drops the gate, leaving the target always eligible."
- Current main `packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts:42,161` — the drop behaviour is documented in the schema descriptions, but nothing surfaces it at load time or run time.

Verified against current `origin/main` at review time; deduped against open + closed issues (no issue covers window-name resolution diagnostics; #723 covered gate handling inside nested groups, a different defect, and is fixed).

## Why it matters

Eligibility gates are a cost/quota control: a DeepSeek target gated to off-peak that silently becomes always-eligible burns peak pricing/quota with no visible signal. Silent drops were the right call for *applying* a bad rule (don't apply what you can't read), but the drop itself needs a surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- Loading config with a target gate or schedule that names an undefined window produces a discoverable diagnostic (config diagnostics and/or a decision/config log entry) naming the window name and where it was referenced.
- A defined window that fails `ModelRouteSchedule.parse` likewise produces a diagnostic naming the window, instead of vanishing from `configuredWindows`.
- Valid named windows, inline windows, and the drop-don't-apply semantics are unchanged; tests in `packages/core/test/model-routes-expand.test.ts` (or the config suite) pin the diagnostic for the unknown-name and unparseable-definition cases.

body:
## Finding

PR #641 guarded `ModelPlan.readNotes` against `limit <= 0` (where `slice(-0)` returned every note), but a non-finite limit still slips past the guard: `NaN <= 0` is `false`, so `readNotes({ limit: NaN })` falls through to `matching.slice(-NaN)`, and `slice(-NaN)` is `slice(0)` — it returns **every** matching note, the exact contract break #542/PR #641 fixed for zero.

Probe (plain JS semantics, verified this run): `[1,2,3].slice(-NaN)` → `[1, 2, 3]`.

The `plan_info` tool schema validates its own `limit` input (Finite, 1–500), so the tool path is covered; `readNotes` itself is the exported contract other/future callers use, and its documented contract is "keeping the newest `limit`" — a NaN limit keeps everything instead of a bounded newest set (or an error).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/641 (merge commit `dce697ca6c79a1a64b954427e6b2cbacc2d03ff6`)
- Current main `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:348-350`:
  ```ts
  // slice(-0) is slice(0): a limit of 0 (or less) must keep no notes, not every note.
  const limited = filter.limit === undefined ? matching : filter.limit <= 0 ? [] : matching.slice(-filter.limit)
  ```
  The guard enumerates `<= 0` only; `Number.isFinite(filter.limit)` is never checked.
- `NoteFilter.limit` (`packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:294`) is a plain optional `number` — NaN is representable.

Verified against current `origin/main` at review time; deduped against open + closed issues (#542 covers limit 0 only; #621 covers sort order — neither covers a non-finite limit).

## Why it matters

A caller that computes a limit (e.g. from unparsed input or arithmetic that yields NaN) silently gets the unbounded note history back — unbounded context for the `plan_info` consumer and a repeat of the #542 surprise, one input class over.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readNotes` with `limit: NaN` does not return every note: it either returns no notes (consistent with the `<= 0` treatment) or throws a clear caller error — one behaviour, pinned by a test.
- Positive finite limits and the `limit <= 0` behaviour from PR #641 are unchanged.
- A regression test in `packages/core/test/model-plan.test.ts` pins the NaN case (and, if the chosen behaviour covers it, `Infinity`).

title: fix(core): Form validateWhen accepts when values an external target can never answer — eq false / neq true on an acknowledgement-only field (PR #630)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix

body:
## Finding

PR #630 made external form fields valid `when` targets by treating them exactly like boolean fields in `validateWhen`. But an external field's only valid answer is the `true` acknowledgement — `validateAnswer` rejects any other value — so two of the four condition combinations it now accepts can never match:

- `when: { key: <external>, op: "eq", value: false }` — the target can never be answered `false`, so `matches` never hits.
- `when: { key: <external>, op: "neq", value: true }` — the target is always answered `true`, so `matches` always hits and `neq` always returns false.

A field gated either way is silently dead: it is never active, a value for it is rejected as "not active", and a required gated field never raises missing-required (required only bites while active). This is the same never-answerable-`when` class that #705 (numeric), #708 (string) and #712/#706 rejected for the other target types — external targets were left out because PR #630 lumped them in with booleans, for which `false` *is* an answerable value.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/630 (merge commit `e9d6bc57d4fd17319ff3436bfee312110f19a2ba`)
- Current main `packages/core/src/form.ts:353-356` — `validateWhen`: `if (target.type === "boolean" || target.type === "external") { if (typeof when.value !== "boolean") return ...; return }` — any boolean condition value is accepted for an external target.
- Current main `packages/core/src/form.ts:242-244` — `validateAnswer`: `if (field.type === "external") { if (value !== true) return "External form field must be acknowledged: ..." }` — the only answerable value is `true`.
- Current main `packages/core/src/form.ts:266-270` — `matches`: `eq` returns the hit, `neq` returns its negation; with the target pinned to `true`, eq/false and neq/true are constant-false.

Verified against current `origin/main` at review time; deduped against open + closed issues (the #705/#708/#712 set covers numeric/string/required targets — none covers external targets).

## Why it matters

Form authors get no create-time error for a gate that can never open, so the gated field simply never appears — the exact silent-never-matching failure mode `validateFields` exists to prevent, per its own header comment.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateFields` rejects a `when` on an external target whose value/op combination can never match (`eq` with `false`, `neq` with `true`), with an error naming the field pair, in the style of the existing never-answerable checks.
- `eq` with `true` and `neq` with `false` on external targets remain accepted; boolean targets keep accepting both boolean values.
- Regression tests in `packages/core/test/form.test.ts` pin all four external combinations (and that boolean eq/false still validates).
