body:
## Summary

File-attachment line ranges (`?start=…&end=…` on a `file://` URI) are parsed with bare `Number()` at both consumers, so non-decimal spellings are silently reinterpreted as line numbers instead of being ignored: core's `positiveInt` reads `start=0x10` as line 16 and `start=1e3` as line 1000 and slices those lines into the prompt, and the app's `selectionFromFileUrl` additionally treats a missing parameter as line 0 and accepts fractional lines. The producers of these URLs only ever emit plain decimal integers, so anything else is a malformed or hand-edited URL being trusted.

## Evidence

On main `e1b8222f12`:

- Core: `packages/core/src/session/prompt.ts:230-234` —
  ```ts
  function positiveInt(value: string | null) {
    if (value === null) return
    const parsed = Number(value)
    return Number.isInteger(parsed) && parsed > 0 ? parsed : undefined
  }
  ```
  Used at `:162-163` for the `start`/`end` search params of a file attachment URI; the result drives the line slice at `:118-125` (`.slice(resolved.start - 1, resolved.end)` on the file's lines for `text/plain` attachments). `Number()` accepts hex (`0x10` → 16), exponent (`1e3` → 1000), fraction-with-zero (`5.0` → 5), and surrounding whitespace (`" 5 "` → 5) — all pass the integer/>0 guard.
- App: `packages/app/src/composer/prompt.ts:44-62` `selectionFromFileUrl` — `Number(params.get("start"))` with only a finiteness check. A query string without the params gives `Number(null) === 0`, which is finite, so it returns a selection of `{startLine: 0, endLine: 0}` for a file URL that carries no selection at all; `start=2.5` yields a fractional line; `start=0x10` yields 16. Used at `:101` and `:200` when restoring a prompt's inline files into the composer.
- Producers emit only plain decimals: `packages/app/src/composer/request.ts:58` builds `` `?start=${selection.startLine}&end=${selection.endLine}` `` from numeric line fields, and `packages/tui/src/component/prompt/autocomplete.tsx:256` sets the params with `String(lineRange.startLine)`.

Verified this run with a runtime probe on the laptop (node, the exact conversions — probes are never run on the sandbox): `Number("0x10")` → 16, `Number("1e3")` → 1000, `Number("5.0")` → 5, `Number(null)` → 0, `Number("2.5")` → 2.5 (finite, so the app check passes it).

## Why it matters

- The core path is the substantive one: a hand-written or tool-generated `@file://…?start=0x10` mention (or one pasted from another tool that writes hex/exponent forms) silently attaches the *wrong lines* of the file to the prompt — the model reads lines 16+ instead of the intended range, with no error and no visible sign in the attachment.
- The app path corrupts composer state on restore: a file URL with an unrelated query parameter (or no range) restores with a bogus 0,0 selection, and a fractional/hex range restores as a selection no editor produced.
- This is the same bare-`Number()` grammar hole the repo has been closing surface by surface (#715 tool-input-repair, #711 route-limit windows, #724 modal pricing); these two parsers are the remaining file-URL consumers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Core `positiveInt` accepts only a plain unsigned decimal integer spelling (`/^\d+$/`-style grammar) for `start`/`end`; hex, exponent, signed, fractional-with-zero, and whitespace-padded spellings are treated as absent (undefined), like other invalid values already are.
- [ ] App `selectionFromFileUrl` returns undefined when either param is absent, and accepts only positive integer line numbers in the same plain-decimal grammar (no 0, no fractions, no hex/exponent).
- [ ] URLs produced by the existing producers (`request.ts`, TUI autocomplete) parse exactly as before, and the pinned cases in `packages/app/src/composer/prompt.test.ts` / `request.test.ts` keep passing.
- [ ] New tests pin the rejected spellings at both sites, plus the app missing-param case.
- [ ] No change to how a valid range slices content (core `prompt.ts` slice semantics) or to any other attachment handling.

## Summary

The client-side form validators still accept calendar-invalid `date-time` answers that core rejects: the TUI's `formValidateValue` and the CLI auth form's `validateText` check a `date-time` value only for `NaN`, so `2026-02-30T10:00:00Z` (rolls to Mar 2) and `2026-01-01T24:00:00Z` (rolls to Jan 2) pass locally — while core's `Form` validator rejects both, a contract established by #656 (calendar-invalid date part) and #666 (hour 24). Neither of those issues covered the client copies; both client files already round-trip the sibling `date` format, so `date-time` is the inconsistent remainder in each.

## Evidence

On main `e1b8222f12`:

- Core (the fixed reference): `packages/core/src/form.ts:461-487` `isDateTime` — after the NaN check it round-trips the ISO date part through a real calendar date and rejects an ISO time part with hour > 23; used at `form.ts:416`.
- TUI: `packages/tui/src/util/form.ts:92` — `if (field.format === "date-time" && Number.isNaN(new Date(value).getTime())) return "Expected a date and time"` — NaN is the only check. The same file's `validDate` (`:142-146`, used at `:91`) does round-trip `date` values, so the asymmetry is visible in one function. `formValidateValue` is the shared client gate: `packages/tui/src/component/dialog-integration.tsx`, `packages/tui/src/mini/footer.form.tsx`, `packages/tui/src/routes/session/form.tsx`, and the CLI auth flow imports it as its final validation (`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/form.ts:5,44`).
- CLI: `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/form.ts:194` — `if (field.format === "date-time" && Number.isNaN(Date.parse(value))) return "Expected a date and time"` in `validateText`, the inline prompt validator. Its own `date` branch directly above (`:189-193`) round-trips via `toISOString().slice(0, 10) !== value`.

Verified this run with a runtime probe on the laptop (node, evaluating the exact parse calls these validators make — probes are never run on the sandbox):

- `new Date("2026-02-30T10:00:00Z")` → `2026-03-02T10:00:00.000Z` (not NaN → both client validators accept; core rejects)
- `new Date("2026-01-01T24:00:00Z")` → `2026-01-02T00:00:00.000Z` (not NaN → both client validators accept; core rejects)
- Controls: `new Date("2026-02-28T10:00:00Z")` parses as itself; a garbage string is NaN in all three validators.

## Why it matters

- The three validators are supposed to be one contract at three layers (prompt-time, client-submit, core). A value the TUI/CLI wave through is rejected later by core's `validateAnswer`, so the user completes a form — including provider auth forms in the CLI — and only learns at submission that an answer the UI explicitly validated is invalid, with no inline guidance to fix it.
- Worse, the rolled instant is a *different real date*: any client-side logic that displays or compares the accepted value before core sees it is working with Mar 2 when the user typed Feb 30.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] TUI `formValidateValue` rejects a `date-time` value whose ISO date part is calendar-invalid (Feb 30, month 13, non-leap Feb 29) and one whose ISO time part carries hour 24, matching core `isDateTime` semantics; non-ISO parseable forms keep their current lenient behaviour (no format restriction added).
- [ ] CLI `validateText` applies the same calendar/hour check for `date-time` (sharing the logic with the TUI validator where the package dependency direction allows; a local equivalent otherwise).
- [ ] Valid date-times (including leap-day `2024-02-29T10:00:00Z` and offset forms) are unchanged in both validators, and the existing `date`-format behaviour is untouched.
- [ ] New tests pin the calendar-invalid and hour-24 cases alongside valid controls in the TUI form util tests and the CLI auth form tests (`packages/cli/test/auth-form.test.ts`).
- [ ] No change to core `packages/core/src/form.ts` — it is the reference behaviour.

body:
## Summary

`ModalModels`' price conversion still reinterprets non-decimal number spellings as prices: the #678 fix made blank and negative pricing fall back to the template cost, but the conversion is a bare `Number(value)`, so a remote price string in a radix spelling — `"0x10"`, `"0b101"`, `"0o17"` — is read as 16, 5, and 15 (times a million) instead of falling back. A malformed or adversarial Modal proxy payload can turn a $5-per-million model into a $16,000,000-per-million one in the derived catalog.

## Evidence

`packages/core/src/modal/models.ts:85-90` on main `ae8738e082`:

```ts
function price(value: string | number | undefined, fallback: Money.USDPerMillionTokens) {
  if (value === undefined) return fallback
  if (typeof value === "string" && value.trim() === "") return fallback
  const parsed = Number(value) * 1_000_000
  return Number.isFinite(parsed) && parsed >= 0 ? Money.USDPerMillionTokens.make(parsed) : fallback
}
```

The schema admits any string for `pricing.prompt` / `completion` / `input_cache_read` (`models.ts:25-31`), and the only guards are blank, finiteness, and non-negativity — all of which radix spellings pass. Sibling surfaces in this codebase that read authored decimal strings from remote data use a plain-decimal grammar instead (e.g. `SpeechStream.headerUsage`, `packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts`: `/^\d+(?:\.\d+)?$/`, #687; the retry-after grammars, #682/#686).

Verified this run with a laptop probe (bun 1.4.2, temporary test in `packages/core/test/modal/`, removed after, tree clean) calling the exported `ModalModels.derive` against a template costing input 5, output 10, cache.read 1, cache.write 2 (USD per million tokens):

| Remote pricing | Resulting cost | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `prompt: "0x10"` | input **16,000,000** | template 5 |
| `completion: "0b101"` | output **5,000,000** | template 10 |
| `input_cache_read: "0o17"` | cache.read **15,000,000** | template 1 |
| `prompt: "0.000001"` (existing pinned control) | input 1 | 1 ✓ |
| `prompt: ""` / `"-0.000003"` (#678 controls) | template kept | ✓ |

## Why it matters

- The derived `Model.Info` cost drives cost accounting and the session header. #678 already established that a present-but-invalid price must fall back rather than replace a known template cost; a radix spelling is the same class of invalid-as-a-decimal-price value, just one that produces an astronomically *large* cost instead of zero/negative — recorded spend for a session on such a model would be fiction in the other direction.
- The payload is remote data decoded tolerantly (`load()` flatMaps per-item decodes, `models.ts:52-71`): one weird proxy build or a hand-written mock server emitting hex is enough.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Pricing strings that are not plain decimal spellings (hex `0x…`, binary `0b…`, octal `0o…`) fall back to the template/default cost, like blank, negative, and non-numeric values already do.
- [ ] Valid plain-decimal string/number pricing is unchanged, including an authored `0` / `"0"` (free model) and `"0.000001"` → 1 (existing tests in `packages/core/test/modal/models.test.ts` keep passing).
- [ ] New tests in the modal models test home pin the radix spellings for `prompt`, `completion`, and `input_cache_read` alongside the #678 blank/negative cases.
- [ ] No change to the remote schema's shape or to `limit()`'s behaviour.

title: fix(core): a gate-closed leaf inside a nested route group strands ready siblings — hasReady/factor ignore inner gates and walk never falls back

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

Window gates (#639, PR #649) are honoured for a route's direct children, but not inside a nested group: `ModelRoute.nextTarget`'s readiness and weight helpers ignore gates below the chosen child, and `walk` does not fall back when the group it chose turns out to have no gate-open leaf. A nested pool whose only target is currently gate-closed is therefore selected as if it were available, the recursion finds no candidates, and resolution returns `undefined` — even when a ready, gate-open sibling target sits next to the group. The production caller treats that `undefined` as "no target at all" and stops resolving.

## Evidence

`packages/core/src/model-route.ts` on main `ae8738e082`:

- `hasReady` (:878-886) — a nested node counts as ready when any leaf under it is `ready` and untried; gates on the children inside that node are never consulted:

```ts
const hasReady = (nodeIndex: number): boolean => {
  const node = definition.nodes[nodeIndex]
  if (!node) return false
  return node.children.some((child) =>
    child.leaf !== undefined
      ? ready.has(child.leaf) && !tried.has(child.leaf)
      : child.node !== undefined && hasReady(child.node),
  )
}
```

- `factor` (:903-912) — the group's effective weight is averaged over `leaves(nodeIndex).filter(ready && !tried)` (:908), again ignoring gates, so a gate-dead group keeps its full weight and wins ranking.
- `walk` (:928-937) checks `gateOpen(child.gate, now)` only for the gate on the child position itself; for a node child it trusts `hasReady`. At :1051 it recurses into the chosen node and returns that result directly:

```ts
return selected.node === undefined ? undefined : walk(selected.node, rules, nodePath)
```

  When the recursion finds `positions.length === 0` it logs `no-candidates` and returns `undefined` — the parent never tries its remaining positions.
- Production impact: `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:481-490` loops on `nextTarget(...)` and does `if (index === undefined) break` — one gate-dead nested group ends the whole resolution attempt instead of failing over to the ready sibling.

## Reproduction (verified this run)

Laptop probe (bun 1.4.2, temporary test in `packages/core/test/`, removed after; laptop main `e3fa1c0bf4`, whose gate code is the merged #649 code also at sandbox main `ae8738e082`): a route with root children `[{ node: 1 }, { leaf: 1 }]`, where node 1's only child is `{ leaf: 0, gate: { name: "peak", window: <tomorrow-only, UTC> } }` (gate closed now), both leaves in `ready`:

- `ModelRoute.nextTarget(route, ready, new Set(), undefined, false)` → `undefined` (expected: `1`)
- `ModelRoute.orderTargets(route, ready, undefined, false)` → `[]` (expected: `[1]`)
- Control, identical shape with the gate removed → `orderTargets` → `[0, 1]` ✓

The existing gate tests (`packages/core/test/model-route.test.ts:686-754`) cover gates on node positions at the level being walked and gates on direct leaves, but never a gate on a leaf *inside* an ungated nested node — which is exactly the shape `expand()` produces when a target inside a nested route carries a `window` (`packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, gate attached at the leaf's own node).

## Why it matters

- Named windows + gates are the #639 mechanism for time-based eligibility ("model X only off-peak"). A pool structured as nested routes — the normal shape once routes compose — silently loses *all* resolution whenever one nested group's targets are all gated off, instead of serving from the remaining pools. The failure is total (no target) rather than degraded, and it appears/disappears with the wall clock.
- The decision log makes it worse: the parent logs the dead group as `chosen`, then the child logs `no-candidates`, so the record reads as if nothing was available.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `nextTarget`/`orderTargets` skip a nested group whose leaves are all gate-closed (at the current instant) and resolve a ready gate-open sibling instead of returning `undefined`.
- [ ] Gate state is taken into account at every depth: `hasReady` (or its replacement) and the group weight (`factor`) treat a gate-closed leaf as unavailable, including gates on positions inside nested groups and inverted gates.
- [ ] If `walk`'s chosen group nonetheless yields no target, it falls back to the node's remaining available positions before returning `undefined`.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/core/test/model-route.test.ts` pin: gate-closed only leaf inside an ungated nested node with a ready sibling (resolves the sibling); the same with the group gate-open (resolves the inner leaf); a fully gate-closed route still returns `undefined`.
- [ ] Existing gate behaviour is unchanged: gates on direct leaves and on node positions at the walked level (#639 tests) keep passing, and the decision log's `window-gate-closed` exclusion reason still reports gated leaves.

title: fix(core): ModelPlan date handling rolls calendar-invalid dates over — bare Date.parse in readNotes' since filter, daysSince and addNote turns '2026-02-30' into Mar 2

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`ModelPlan`'s date handling still uses bare `Date.parse`, which silently rolls calendar-invalid dates into the next month instead of failing — so a date that does not exist is treated as a real, different day on every plan-notes surface:

- `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:297-299` — `readNotes`' `since` filter: the guard throws only when `Date.parse` returns `NaN`. `"2026-02-30"` parses fine (as Mar 2), so the documented caller error — "A `since` that does not parse is a caller error and throws" (doc comment :289-292) — never fires, and notes are silently filtered from Mar 2.
- `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:347-349` — `daysSince`: a recorded `verifiedAt` of `"2026-02-30"` counts whole days from Mar 2, understating the plan data's age by two days; a month-13 or day-32 date rolls a full month/year.
- `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:324,333-334` — note timestamps (`note.at`) are compared and sorted through the same bare `Date.parse`, so a note recorded with a calendar-invalid `at` is placed at its rolled instant in `since` filtering and ordering.
- `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:267` — `addNote` derives the note id from `Date.parse(now)`, silently embedding the rolled instant for a calendar-invalid `now` while storing the original string as `at`.

The repo already built the check for exactly this: `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime` (`packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:48-70`) — "Date.parse silently rolls overflow days such as Feb 30 into the next month instead of returning NaN, so an ISO date's components must round-trip through a real calendar date" — and the quota consumers use it (`QuotaSnapshot.resetAtOf`). `ModelPlan` is the remaining bare-`Date.parse` consumer on the plans surface.

## Evidence (verified this run on main d5d4969001)

- Line-level reading of all five sites above on current main: each takes `Date.parse(...)` with at most a `Number.isNaN` guard (`readNotes` since :298, note.at skip :325, sort :335-336, `daysSince` :348). `addNote` (:267) has no guard at all.
- Runtime probe run this run on the laptop (bun 1.4.2, the repo's runtime; probes are never compiled on the sandbox): `Date.parse("2026-02-30T00:00:00Z") === 1772409600000`, i.e. `2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z`, and `Number.isNaN(...)` is `false` — so the `readNotes` throw at :298-299 cannot fire for this input and the filter instant is Mar 2. `Date.parse("2026-02-30")` (date-only form) rolls identically.
- Neighbouring ModelPlan date bugs were different holes and are closed: #557 (unparseable `since` → NaN comparison emptied results; fixed by the throw that calendar-invalid input now bypasses), #558 (`daysSince` returning -1 for future timestamps), #621 (notes sorted as strings). None covers calendar validity.
- Dedup: searched open and closed issues for 'ModelPlan parseAbsoluteTime', 'readNotes calendar-invalid since', 'daysSince', and 'addNote Date.parse' on 2026-10-28 — hits are #557, #558, #621 only (plus #609, which built `parseAbsoluteTime` for the quota-reset surface). No issue covers ModelPlan's sites.

## Why it matters

Plan notes and `verifiedAt` dates are the fleet's record of when provider plan data was checked and what changed. A typo'd or model-written date like Feb 30 does not exist; rolling it to Mar 2 makes stale plan data look two days fresher in `daysSince`, silently re-windows the `since` filter instead of surfacing the caller error the API promises to throw, and misplaces notes in chronological order. Every other date consumer in this codebase (`parseAbsoluteTime` and its callers, QuotaSnapshot, MessagingTemplate, Form) was given the calendar check for exactly this failure mode; ModelPlan's were missed because its NaN guards look like validation while letting the rolled dates through.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readNotes` with a calendar-invalid `since` (e.g. `"2026-02-30"`, `"2026-13-01"`, hour-24 ISO time) throws the same caller-error message as an unparseable `since`, instead of filtering from the rolled instant.
- `daysSince` returns `null` for a calendar-invalid date, matching its existing unparseable-date behaviour.
- Note `at` values that are calendar-invalid are treated like unparseable ones in `readNotes` (skipped and counted under a `since` filter; sorted with the unparseable group), and `addNote` does not silently embed a rolled instant in the note id for a calendar-invalid `now` (reject or fall back consistently — implementer's choice, pinned by a test).
- The fix reuses `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime` where the input is ISO-shaped, or an equivalent component round-trip check; non-ISO `Date.parse` forms that are calendar-valid (e.g. `"Jan 5 2026"`) keep their current behaviour — this is a calendar-validity check, not a format restriction.
- New tests in the model-plan test home pin the calendar-invalid cases for `since`, `daysSince`, and note ordering, alongside the existing valid-date controls (#557/#558/#621 cases unchanged).
- No change to the note file format, the `Note` schema, or the throw message for genuinely unparseable `since` values.

title: fix(core): ToolInputRepair coerces non-decimal number spellings — "0x10" becomes 16, "0b101" becomes 5, "1e3" becomes 1000

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low

labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The tool input repair plugin coerces a model's string argument to a number/integer schema target with bare `Number(value)` (`packages/core/src/plugin/tool-input-repair.ts:76-82`), so every spelling `Number()` accepts is silently reinterpreted as a decimal number the model never wrote:

- `"0x10"` → `16` (hex)
- `"0b101"` → `5` (binary)
- `"0o17"` → `15` (octal)
- `"1e3"` → `1000` (exponent)
- `"+42"` → `42`, `"5."` → `5`

The plugin's own documented contract (file header, `tool-input-repair.ts:8-16`) promises only decimal repairs — `'{"limit":"20"}' -> { limit: 20 }`, `{ count: "2" } -> { count: 2 }`. A non-decimal spelling is not a stringified decimal; left unrepaired it would fail schema validation visibly, and the model could correct it. Repaired, the tool executes with a different value than the argument the model produced, with no trace.

## Evidence (verified this run on main d5d4969001)

- The plugin hooks `execute.before` for every tool call (`tool-input-repair.ts:21-36`): it looks up the tool's input schema and runs `repair(event.input, schema, schema, 0)`.
- The number/integer branch (`tool-input-repair.ts:76-82`):

  ```ts
  if (schema.type === "number" || schema.type === "integer") {
    if (typeof value !== "string" || value.trim() === "") return value
    const parsed = Number(value)
    return Number.isFinite(parsed) && (schema.type !== "integer" || Number.isSafeInteger(parsed)) ? parsed : value
  }
  ```

  The only guards are finiteness and (for integers) safe-integer range. `16`, `5`, `15`, `1000` all pass both.
- Runtime probe run this run on the laptop (bun 1.4.2, the repo's runtime; probes are never compiled on the sandbox): `Number("0x10") === 16`, `Number("0b101") === 5`, `Number("0o17") === 15`, `Number("1e3") === 1000`, `Number("+42") === 42`, `Number("5.") === 5` — each `Number.isSafeInteger(...) === true` where integral. Behaviour follows deterministically from the quoted branch: any of these strings in a numeric tool argument is replaced by the reinterpreted number before the tool executes.
- This is the one numeric-string consumer on the tool-call surface that was missed by the fleet's grammar hardening elsewhere: the ai executor's retry-after parsers reject hex/exponent/sign spellings with anchored grammars (`packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:24-27`, #682), `SpeechStream.headerUsage` rejects them for usage headers (`packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts:111-122`, #687), and `ModelRouteLimits.windows` was filed as #711 for the same `Number()` width. No test in `packages/core/test/plugin/tool-input-repair.test.ts` pins a non-decimal spelling.
- Dedup: searched open and closed issues for 'repair coerces hex tool argument', 'tool-input-repair Number', 'tool input repair hex' on 2026-10-28 — no hit covers this branch (the only 'repair' hits are #407 in developing-today/code, a cross-repo env-var item, and #578, terminal capability detection).

## Why it matters

This repair layer sits in front of **every** tool execution. Its job is to rescue mechanical stringification (`"20"` for `20`); reinterpreting radix-prefixed or exponent spellings crosses from rescue into invention: a count, offset, limit, port, or timeout the model expressed in a notation the schema never invited becomes a different number at execution time, silently — the tool runs, the result is wrong, and neither the model nor the user sees that the argument changed. The fleet has closed this exact hole on the header, quota, and retry surfaces; the tool-argument surface is the highest-traffic one of all.

## Acceptance criteria

- The number/integer repair branch accepts only a plain decimal grammar (optional leading `-`, digits, optional fraction for `number`; `-?\d+` for `integer`): `"20"`, `"-3"`, `"2.5"` (number only) repair exactly as today.
- Non-decimal spellings are left unrepaired (returned as the original string, so normal schema validation reports them): `"0x10"`, `"0b101"`, `"0o17"`, `"1e3"`, `"+42"`, `"5."`, `" 42 "`-with-internal-junk, `"Infinity"`, `"NaN"`.
- Blank/whitespace-only strings keep today's behaviour (left unrepaired), and already-numeric (non-string) values are untouched.
- New tests in `packages/core/test/plugin/tool-input-repair.test.ts` pin the rejected spellings for both `number` and `integer` targets and the accepted decimal controls, alongside the existing repair cases.
- No change to the boolean, object, array, union, tuple, or dictionary repair branches, and no change to the plugin's hook registration or depth limits.

title: fix(core,ai): both retry-after date branches roll calendar-invalid dates over — bare Date.parse in WebSearch.cooldownMillis and the ai executor turns '2026-02-30' into a wait until Mar 2

body:
## Summary

Both retry-after HTTP-date branches still parse the header with bare `Date.parse`, which silently rolls calendar-invalid dates into the next month instead of failing — so a malformed date becomes an invented wait computed from a day the provider never said:

- `packages/core/src/websearch.ts:228-229` — `WebSearch.cooldownMillis`: `Date.parse(value)` with only a finiteness check; anything else takes the result as the cooldown.
- `packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:48-49` — `retryAfterMs`: `Date.parse(value)` with only a NaN check; anything else becomes `retryAfterMs` on the rate-limit details.

The delay-seconds grammar of both parsers was hardened in #682/#686 (hex/exponent/sign spellings now fall through / take the fallback), and this repo's shared calendar check `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime` exists precisely because "Date.parse silently rolls overflow days such as Feb 30 into the next month instead of returning NaN" (`packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:48-53`). Neither retry-after date branch uses a calendar check — they are the remaining bare-`Date.parse` consumers on the retry/cooldown surface.

## Evidence (verified this run on main d5d4969001, line-level)

- WebSearch: `cooldownMillis` at `packages/core/src/websearch.ts:220-230`. Blank → 60s fallback (:221); plain digits → delay-seconds (:223-226); other `Number()`-finite spellings → 60s (:227, the #686 fix); everything else reaches `const date = Date.parse(value)` (:228) and `Math.max(0, date - now)` is returned as the cooldown (:229). The cooldown is set on a 429 in random mode at :204-ish (`cooldowns.set(provider.id, …)`) and `randomProvider` excludes the provider until it expires.
- AI executor: `retryAfterMs` at `packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:31-51`. `retry-after-ms` and delay-seconds `retry-after` are grammar-guarded (:35, :43, the #682 fix); the fallthrough is `const date = Date.parse(value)` (:48), returned as `Math.max(0, date - Date.now())` (:49) and carried on `HttpRateLimitDetails.retryAfterMs` into provider-error classification and the route observer.
- Deterministic consequences, from the calendar behaviour this repo has already probed and documented repeatedly (#609, #655, #666, and the `parseAbsoluteTime` doc comment itself):
  - `retry-after: 2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` — `Date.parse` rolls Feb 30 to Mar 2, so both branches compute a wait to Mar 2. WebSearch sidelines the provider until then instead of taking its 60s fallback for an unusable value; the executor reports the rolled instant as the provider's stated wait. (An ISO-shaped value reaches the date branch in both parsers: neither restricts the branch to IMF-fixdate, and the existing WebSearch test table already exercises the branch with a non-delay-seconds string.)
  - `retry-after: 2026-01-01T24:00:00Z` — hour 24 rolls to Jan 2 (#666 probed exactly this roll in V8), inventing roughly a day of wait from a time that does not exist.
  - Controls behave correctly today and are pinned: `"120"` → 120s, `"Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:02:00 GMT"` → 120s, `"invalid"`/`""`/`"-1"` → fallback (`packages/core/test/websearch.test.ts` Retry-After table).
- No runtime probe this run: the laptop probe host was unreachable over SSH for the whole run and probes are never compiled on the sandbox; the rollover behaviour is established by the repo's own documented probes for the identical `Date.parse` call, and the behaviour of both branches follows deterministically from the quoted code. The packet's regression tests double as runtime confirmation.
- Dedup: searched open and closed issues for 'retry-after calendar', 'cooldownMillis Date.parse', 'retryAfterMs Date.parse invalid date', and 'Feb 30 retry-after' on 2026-10-28 — hits are #686 (this function's number grammar, a different hole since fixed) and #656 (Form's date-time validator). No issue covers calendar validity in either retry-after date branch.

## Why it matters

A retry-after date is an instruction to stop calling a provider until a stated instant. Trusting a rolled date means the fleet waits until a day nobody stated — potentially days of unnecessary cooldown in WebSearch's random rotation, and a fabricated `retryAfterMs` in the executor's rate-limit record that downstream classification and logging treat as the provider's own words. Every other date consumer on these surfaces (`parseAbsoluteTime`, QuotaSnapshot, MessagingTemplate, Form) was given the calendar check for exactly this reason; the two retry-after branches are the ones that were missed, in the same passes (#682/#686) that hardened their number grammars.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both date branches reject a calendar-invalid ISO date part (overflow day such as Feb 30, month 13) and an ISO time part with hour 24, instead of computing a wait from the rolled instant: WebSearch takes its 60s fallback; the executor returns `undefined` from that branch.
- Valid dates keep working unchanged in both branches, including the IMF-fixdate form (`"Thu, 01 Jan 1970 00:02:00 GMT"`) and valid ISO timestamps; a valid date in the past still yields a 0 wait, not a rejection.
- Non-ISO `Date.parse` forms that are calendar-valid keep their current behaviour (the fix is a calendar-validity check on the parsed result / ISO components, in the spirit of `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime`, not a shape restriction to one date format). The `ai` package may need its own local check, following the local-guard pattern its sibling parsers already use.
- New tests pin the calendar-invalid cases in both homes: `packages/core/test/websearch.test.ts` (cooldown falls back for `2026-02-30…` instead of cooling down until Mar 2) and the ai executor/response-hook tests (`retry-after: 2026-02-30T00:00:00Z` yields no `retryAfterMs`), alongside the existing valid-date controls.
- No change to either parser's delay-seconds grammar (#682/#686 behaviour), the blank handling, or the 60s WebSearch fallback value.

body:
## Summary

`Form.validateFields` still accepts required field definitions that no answer can ever satisfy, because `required` imposes an effective minimum of one answer — one non-empty string, one selection — that the create-time checks never compare against a zero cap or an empty closed option list:

- a required **string** field with `maxLength: 0`
- a required **string** field with closed `options: []` (options present, `custom` not set)
- a required **multiselect** field with `maxItems: 0`
- a required **multiselect** field with closed `options: []`

#681 added the pairwise checks (`minLength > maxLength`, `minItems > maxItems`) and #696 added two effective-bound checks (closed multiselect `minItems > options.length`, integer range containing no integer). The required-field effective minimum of 1 is the same kind of bound, and it is not checked anywhere: in each case above the effective minimum (1) exceeds the effective maximum (0).

## Evidence (verified this run on main d5d4969001, line-level)

- Schema allows every shape: `maxLength` and `minItems`/`maxItems` are `NonNegativeInt` (`packages/schema/src/schema.ts`, `isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0)`), so 0 is a legal value; `options` is a plain `Schema.Array(Option)` in both `StringField` and `MultiselectField` (`packages/schema/src/form.ts`), so `[]` is legal; `required` is an optional boolean on the shared field base.
- Create time (`packages/core/src/form.ts:291-323`, `validateFields`): the string branch checks only `minLength > maxLength` when **both** are set (:292) and that the pattern compiles; the multiselect branch checks only `minItems > maxItems` when both are set (:317) and `minItems > options.length` when `minItems` is set (:321). Nothing reads `field.required` in `validateFields` at all, and nothing rejects an empty closed options list.
- Answer time (`validateField`, same file) makes each shape unsatisfiable for an always-active (no `when`) field:
  - String, `maxLength: 0`: `""` → `Missing required form field` (:355, required + length 0); any non-empty string → `Form field is too long` (:357, length > 0).
  - String, closed `options: []`: `""` → missing required (:355); any other string → `Invalid option for form field` (:370-372, no option can match an empty list).
  - Multiselect, `maxItems: 0`: `[]` → `Missing required form field` (:388); any non-empty array → `Too many selections` (:396-397).
  - Multiselect, closed `options: []`: `[]` → missing required (:388); any entry → `Invalid option for form field` (:398-400).
- Controls that must keep creating: the same fields **without** `required` are satisfiable by omission (`validateAnswer` at :246-251 only demands a value from a required active field); a required string with `maxLength: 1`, a required multiselect with `maxItems: 1` and one option, and a `custom: true` field with `options: []` (answers are not limited to declared options) are all answerable.
- No runtime probe this run: the laptop probe host was unreachable over SSH for the whole run and probes are never compiled on the sandbox; the behaviour is deterministic from the quoted paths, the same verification basis as #707/#708/#711.
- Dedup: searched open and closed issues for 'maxLength 0 required', 'required maxItems', 'empty options required form', and 'validateFields required' on 2026-10-28 — the only hit is #707 (duplicate selections, a different check). #681/#696 cover the pairwise and two effective-bound cases, not the required effective minimum.

## Why it matters

`validateFields` is the create-time contract (its header at :272-276 of the current numbering in `form.ts` promises to reject conditions/definitions that can never be satisfied so authoring mistakes surface to the caller instead of silently never matching). A form created with one of these fields can never be answered: every submission fails validation, and the user is told their answer is missing, too long, too many, or an invalid option — never that the definition itself is impossible. The form's creator (an MCP elicitation or integration caller, via `integration.ts:611/764/789`, which run `validateFields` before `validateAnswer`) gets no signal at the point the mistake was made.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateFields` rejects a required string field with `maxLength: 0`, and a required multiselect field with `maxItems: 0`, with a clear per-field error naming the field key.
- `validateFields` rejects a required field whose closed options list is empty (string with `options: []` and `custom` not set; multiselect with `options: []` and `custom` not set).
- Satisfiable controls still create: the same shapes without `required`; required with `maxLength`/`maxItems` of 1 (and at least one option where options apply); `custom: true` with empty options; a required field gated by a `when` is treated the same as any required field (the definition is still unsatisfiable whenever it is active — triage may note this explicitly, but it is not a reason to leave the check out).
- New tests in `packages/core/test/form.test.ts` pin all four rejected shapes alongside the satisfiable controls, in the style of the #681/#696 tests.
- No change to `validateAnswer`/`validateField` answer-time behaviour or to the schema (0 remains a legal cap for optional fields).

body:
## Summary

`ModelRouteLimits.windows` parses the `remaining` and `limit` rate-limit header values with bare `Number()`. #672 fixed the blank spelling (`""` read as 0), but the other spellings `Number()` accepts are still trusted as counts: `"0x0"` reads as a spent window (0 remaining), `"0x10"` as 16, `"1e3"` as 1000, and `"+5"` as 5. A rate-limit count is a plain unsigned decimal — the house grammar the sibling parsers already enforce — so a value in any other spelling should drop the window (the `"lots"` behaviour), not be reinterpreted as a number the provider never said.

## Evidence (verified this run on main d5d4969001, line-level)

- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:158-172` (`windows`): the only guards are the #672 blank check (`raw.trim() === ""` at :160) and `Number.isFinite` at :162/:167. Between them, `const remaining = Number(raw)` (:161) and `const limit = Number(value.limit?.[name])` (:163) accept every spelling `Number()` accepts: hex (`0x…`), binary (`0b…`), octal (`0o…`), exponent (`1e3`), and signed (`+5`, `-5`).
- The values arrive verbatim from provider response headers: `packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts` `rateLimitDetails` copies `x-ratelimit-remaining-*` / `anthropic-ratelimit-*-remaining` (and the matching limit headers) into the record as raw strings, and `ModelRouteLimits.holdUntil` (`model-route-limits.ts:208-221`) consumes `windows()` — a window with `remaining <= 0` is held until its reset (or `UNKNOWN_RESET_MS` 60s with no reset), and `remaining / limit <= NEAR_FRACTION` (0.05) counts as nearly empty. The hold is applied by `ModelRoute.observeRateLimit` (`packages/core/src/model-route.ts:568`).
- Deterministic consequences by JS semantics (no runtime probe this run — laptop SSH unreachable fleet-wide; the behaviour follows directly from the quoted code, the same verification basis as #707/#708):
  - `remaining: "0x0"` → `Number` gives 0 → the window reads as spent and the target is held back, the exact failure #672 fixed for `""`, through a spelling its guard does not catch. `"+0"` and `"0b0"` do the same.
  - `remaining: "1e3"` → 1000 and `limit: "0x64"` → 100 → the near-empty fraction is computed from numbers the provider never stated, so a hold that should fire can be skipped (or vice versa).
  - Control spellings behave correctly today and are pinned by tests: `"lots"` drops the window (`model-route-limits.test.ts:85-87`), `""`/`"  "` drop it (:89-96), plain decimals parse.
- The house grammar is already established in the sibling parsers this surface feeds and is fed by: `executor.ts` retry-after parsing rejects hex/exponent/signs with the comment that both forms "reject the other spellings Number() accepts" (`packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:21-27`, #682); `SpeechStream.headerUsage` restricts usage headers to `/^\d+(?:\.\d+)?$/` with the same rationale (`packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts:117-128`, #687); the WebSearch cooldown was restricted to delay-seconds grammar in #686. `windows()` is the remaining bare-`Number()` parser on this header surface.

## Why it matters

`holdUntil` decides when a route target is benched after a provider response. An invented 0 benches a healthy target for up to the stated reset; an inflated remaining/limit pair keeps sending traffic at a window the provider reported in a form we could not actually read. Both failure directions come from trusting a spelling instead of dropping an unreadable value, which is the contract every sibling parser on this surface now follows.

## Acceptance criteria

- `windows()` treats a `remaining` or `limit` value that is not a plain unsigned decimal (digits with an optional fraction, as in `headerUsage`) as unparseable: hex, binary, octal, exponent, and signed spellings drop the window / yield an undefined limit instead of being reinterpreted.
- Plain decimal values (`"0"`, `"42"`, `"3.5"`), the blank behaviour from #672, and the `"lots"` drop behaviour are unchanged.
- New tests in `packages/core/test/model-route-limits.test.ts` pin the rejected spellings for both `remaining` and `limit` (including the `"0x0"` → no-hold case through `holdUntil`) alongside the existing decimal controls.
- No change to `resetMs`, `holdUntil` thresholds, or the header capture in `executor.ts`.

body:
# fix(core): Form validateFields accepts when values a string target can never answer — a value failing the target's format, pattern, or length bounds

## Evidence (verified this run on main `213b97ed36`, by line-level code reading)

`validateWhen` (`packages/core/src/form.ts:334-350`) validates a `when` condition against its target field. For string targets it checks only that the value is a string, plus membership when the target's options are closed:

```ts
if (typeof when.value !== "string") return "Form field condition value must be a string"
const closed = target.type === "multiselect" ? !target.custom : target.options !== undefined && !target.custom
if (closed && !target.options?.some((option) => option.value === when.value)) {
  return "Form field condition value must be one of the field's options"
}
```

But a string target's own answers are subject to further constraints in `validateField` (`form.ts:356-369`) that `validateWhen` never consults:

- `minLength` / `maxLength` (`form.ts:356-357`)
- `pattern` (`form.ts:358-364`)
- `format`: `email` (`:365-366`), `uri` (`:367`), `date` (`:368`, via `isDate`), `date-time` (`:369`, via `isDateTime`)

So `validateFields` accepts definitions whose condition value no valid answer to the target can ever equal, for example:

- a `date`-format field gated field with `when { op: "eq", value: "not-a-date" }` — the eq gate can never match (any answer equal to it would be rejected as `Expected date`), so the gated field is permanently inactive; with `op: "neq"` the gate is permanently active for every valid answer.
- a string field with `minLength: 5` and a `when` value `"abc"` (length 3), or `maxLength: 3` with value `"abcdef"`.
- a string field with `pattern: "^\\d+$"` and a `when` value `"abc"`.

This contradicts the module's stated create-time contract (`form.ts:272-276`: reject conditions that would silently never match). It is the string-target counterpart of #705, which fixed the brief for numeric targets only — #705's filing explicitly scoped string targets out ("String-format when values (date/uri targets) — noted in the issue body as adjacent, left to triage"), and its queue packet lists string-format when values under `scope.exclude`. This issue is that deferred remainder, widened to the target's full answerability constraints (format, pattern, length), not a duplicate of #705.

Verification note: a runtime probe could not be run this run — the laptop (the fleet's designated probe host) was unreachable over SSH for the whole run (repeated connection drops), and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. The behaviour follows deterministically from the two short functions quoted above, both read in full this run; the regression tests in the acceptance criteria double as the runtime confirmation. Dedup search this run (open + closed, "when format date string target", "validateWhen string") hits only #705 (numeric, string scoped out) and #601 (external references).

Scope note: for a string target with closed options, the existing membership check already decides answerability and stays as-is. The gap is for targets whose binding constraints are format/pattern/length — no options, or `custom: true` (where answers are not limited to the options but must still pass format/pattern/length).

## Why it matters

Same failure shape as #705, on the most common field type: a form author gates a field on a value the gate field can never hold, and nothing complains at creation or answer time — the gated field is silently always hidden (eq) or always shown (neq). Date/uri/email-gated flows (e.g. "show the expiry field when the start date equals …") are exactly where a mistyped or stale condition value is plausible.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `validateFields` rejects a `when` condition whose string value cannot be a valid answer to the target string field because it violates the target's `format` (email/uri/date/date-time), `pattern`, or `minLength`/`maxLength`, for both `eq` and `neq`, with an error in the existing "Form field condition value must be …" style.
- [ ] Matchable conditions are unchanged: values satisfying the target's constraints, all closed-options targets (existing membership check), custom string targets with unconstrained values, and boolean/external/multiselect/number/integer targets behave as before (#705's numeric checks untouched).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/form.test.ts` cover at least: a date-format target with an invalid-date when value, a patterned target with a non-matching when value, a minLength target with a too-short when value, and the matchable controls for each.
- [ ] The fix reuses the target's own answer validation (or the same predicates — `isDate`, `isDateTime`, the email/uri checks) rather than duplicating a divergent copy of the format rules.

body:
# fix(core): Form validateAnswer counts duplicate multiselect entries as separate selections — minItems is met by repeating one option, maxItems rejects one distinct selection repeated

## Evidence (verified this run on main `213b97ed36`, by line-level code reading of the whole answer path)

`validateField`'s multiselect branch (`packages/core/src/form.ts:386-396`) counts raw array length and checks each entry's option membership individually — nothing anywhere in the answer path deduplicates:

- `form.ts:389-392` — `minItems` / `maxItems` compare against `value.length`, duplicates included.
- `form.ts:393-395` — the closed-options check tests each item on its own, so `["a", "a"]` passes membership twice.
- The answer schema imposes no uniqueness either: `Form.Value` is a plain `Schema.Array(Schema.String)` and `Form.Answer` a plain record (`packages/schema/src/form.ts:142-150`).
- The live callers pass the supplied answer straight through with no dedup: `packages/core/src/integration.ts:611,764,789` call `Form.validateFields(...) ?? Form.validateAnswer(...)` on the answer as given.

Consequences, by construction from the code above:

1. **minItems bypass:** a closed multiselect with options `[a, b]` and `minItems: 2` accepts the answer `["a", "a"]` — one distinct selection presented as two. A custom multiselect with `minItems: 3` accepts `["x", "x", "x"]`.
2. **maxItems over-strictness (the same bug in the other direction):** with `maxItems: 1`, the answer `["a", "a"]` is rejected as "Too many selections" although it names one distinct selection.
3. **Contract contradiction with #704:** the create-time check added for #704 rejects a closed multiselect whose `minItems` exceeds its option count on the stated premise that "a closed multiselect's answers may only contain declared options, so asking for more selections than there are options can never be satisfied" (`form.ts:320-323`). That premise holds only if selections are distinct — answer-time validation does not enforce the distinctness the create-time check assumes.

Verification note: a runtime probe could not be run this run — the laptop (the fleet's designated probe host) was unreachable over SSH for the whole run (repeated connection drops), and probes are never compiled on the sandbox. The behaviour follows deterministically from the three short code paths quoted above, each read in full this run; the regression tests in the acceptance criteria double as the runtime confirmation.

This was flagged as an adjacent observation in #696's body ("validateAnswer counts duplicate selections toward minItems") but was never filed as its own issue; #696/#704 fixed the create-time satisfiability side only. Dedup search this run (open + closed, "duplicate selections multiselect", "multiselect duplicates") hits only #696.

## Why it matters

Forms are the structured-input surface for integration auth/setup flows (`integration.ts`). `minItems` is an authoring contract — "the user must pick at least N things" — and today it can be satisfied by picking one thing N times, silently weakening any flow that relies on the count (e.g. selecting multiple scopes, regions, or fallback contacts). The maxItems direction misleads in the opposite way, rejecting an answer whose distinct selections are within bounds.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A multiselect answer whose entries contain duplicates is handled under one stated rule — either duplicates are rejected with a clear error (e.g. `Duplicate selection for form field: <key>`), or counts are computed over distinct entries — and the chosen rule is applied consistently to `minItems`, `maxItems`, the required/empty check, and closed-option membership.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/form.test.ts` cover: `["a", "a"]` against `minItems: 2` (options `[a, b]`), `["x", "x", "x"]` against a custom multiselect with `minItems: 3`, and `["a", "a"]` against `maxItems: 1`.
- [ ] Answers without duplicates behave exactly as before, including the `when` inclusion semantics (`eq` = selection includes value) pinned by existing tests.
- [ ] The rule chosen is consistent with #704's create-time premise (closed answers are selections from the declared options); if distinct-count semantics are chosen instead of rejection, the `form.ts:320-323` comment is updated to match.

body:
## Problem

`Form.validateFields` (packages/core/src/form.ts:277) is the create-time check whose stated job (comment at form.ts:272-276) is that each `when` condition must "carry a value matching that field's type, and use a declared option when the field's options are closed", so authoring mistakes are rejected at creation "instead of silently never matching". For string and multiselect targets that contract is enforced (options membership, form.ts:331-334). For number and integer targets, `validateWhen` (form.ts:319-330) checks only `typeof when.value === "number"` — it never checks whether the value is a value the target field could ever be answered with:

- **Fractional value on an integer target:** integer field `count` (minimum 1, maximum 10) gating a field with `when {key: "count", op: "eq", value: 1.5}` is accepted. Answers to an integer field must be integers (validateField, form.ts:362), so `matches` (form.ts:266-270) can never see 1.5: the gated field is permanently inactive and can never be answered.
- **Out-of-bounds value on a numeric target:** number field `score` (minimum 10, maximum 20) gating with `when {key: "score", op: "eq", value: 5}` is accepted. Every valid answer is within [10, 20], so the condition can never hold.
- The `neq` forms are the mirror image: the same unmatchable values make the condition true for *every* valid answer, so the gated field is permanently active — also not what the author wrote.

## Evidence (verified this run on main b1d8160d69)

Bun probe on the laptop running the verbatim validation section of form.ts (lines 235-415 spliced unchanged; form.ts md5 37f044e29b8f600cb9bb6bf12deade48, byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-0535/probe.ts, removed after):

- `validateFields([integer count 1..10, string gated by eq 1.5])` -> `undefined` (accepted); scanning every valid answer 1..10, none ever activates the gated field (answering it yields "Form field is not active").
- `validateFields([number score 10..20, string gated by eq 5])` -> `undefined` (accepted); no score in [10, 20] ever activates the gated field.
- `validateFields([integer count 1..10, string gated by neq 1.5])` -> `undefined` (accepted), and the gate is active for a valid answer (count=3 + gated answer validates) — permanently on.
- Controls: integer target with `eq 3` and number target 0..20 with `eq 5` are accepted by validateFields AND activatable via validateAnswer — matchable values work exactly as intended.

## Why it matters

This is the remaining hole in the contract #601 and #681/#696 have been closing piece by piece: validateFields rejects unmatchable option values for closed string/multiselect targets and unsatisfiable field bounds, but a numeric `when` value that no valid answer can equal slips through. The failure mode is silent: the form is created successfully, and a field the author intended to appear conditionally simply never appears (or, for `neq`, always appears), with no error at creation or answer time pointing at the cause. The module's own doc comment names "silently never matching" as exactly what this validation exists to prevent.

Adjacent observation, left to triage: the same gap exists in principle for string targets carrying a `format` (e.g. a `date`-format target gated by `eq "not-a-date"` can never match a valid answer); the numeric cases above are mechanical to check, the format case is noted only for completeness.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateFields` rejects a `when` condition whose value is fractional when the referenced earlier field is an integer field.
- `validateFields` rejects a `when` condition whose value lies outside the referenced number/integer field's declared [minimum, maximum] bounds (whichever bounds are declared).
- The rejection applies to both `eq` and `neq` conditions (an unanswerable value makes `eq` never match and `neq` always match), with an error message in the existing style naming the condition (e.g. alongside the existing `Form field condition value must be ...` messages, suffixed with `: <field> -> <target>` as today).
- Matchable conditions are unchanged: in-bounds integers on integer targets, in-bounds numbers on number targets, and all existing string/multiselect/boolean/external `when` validation behave exactly as before.
- Regression tests in packages/core form tests cover: fractional value on an integer target, out-of-bounds value on a number target, the `neq` forms, and the matchable controls.

body:
## Problem

`SpeechStream.sampleRate` (packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts:76-79) parses the `rate=` parameter of a provider-declared media type with a `\d+` regex, which guards the grammar — but not the value: `rate=0` parses to the sample rate `0`, which is not a valid sample rate.

Both callers combine the result with nullish fallbacks, and `0` is not nullish, so the bogus zero defeats every fallback:

- **Google Speech** (packages/ai/src/protocols/google-speech.ts:113): `SpeechStream.sampleRate(state.mimeType) ?? DEFAULT_SAMPLE_RATE` (24000) yields `0`, and the result is reported as the PCM media info via `SpeechStream.pcm("pcm_s16le", sampleRate, ...)` at :117 (or `container("wav", sampleRate)` at :116).
- **Deepgram Speech** (packages/ai/src/protocols/deepgram-speech.ts:113): `SpeechStream.sampleRate(mediaType) ?? context.request.providerOptions?.sampleRate ?? headerless.sampleRate` yields `0`, overriding even an explicitly configured provider-options sample rate and the encoding's known headerless rate (24000/8000, :96-98).

## Evidence (verified this run on main f6edddd729)

Bun probe on the laptop running the verbatim `sampleRate` function (spliced unchanged from speech-stream.ts; the function text is byte-identical on both checkouts — the file md5 differs only because the laptop checkout predates PR #688's headerUsage change elsewhere in the file; probe at laptop ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-0455/probe.ts, removed after):

- `sampleRate("audio/L16;codec=pcm;rate=0")` -> `0`
- Google finish expression with `rate=0` -> `0` (not the 24000 default)
- Deepgram expression with `rate=0` and providerOptions 44100 -> `0` (not 44100, not the headerless rate)
- `sampleRate("audio/L16;rate=0000")` -> `0`
- Controls: `rate=44100` -> `44100`; no `rate=` -> `undefined`; `rate=abc` -> `undefined` (regex-guarded grammar works as intended)

## Why it matters

This is the remaining half of the #690 problem in the sibling parser. #690 / PR #691 fixed ElevenLabs `describeOutput` to reject non-plain and **non-positive** rates; #690's packet explicitly scoped `SpeechStream.sampleRate` out as "regex-guarded", which is true of its grammar but not of zero. A provider media type declaring `rate=0` (or `rate=0000`) currently manufactures media info claiming a 0 Hz sample rate and suppresses the sane fallbacks both callers already have, so downstream consumers that interpret the returned audio by its declared rate get a value that can never be correct.

## Acceptance criteria

- `SpeechStream.sampleRate` returns `undefined` for a `rate=` value of `0` (including zero-padded forms such as `0000`); a non-positive rate is treated as "rate unknown", exactly like an absent or non-numeric rate.
- Positive rates are unchanged: `rate=44100` -> `44100`, `rate=8000` -> `8000`; absent/non-numeric rates still return `undefined`.
- With `rate=0`, the Google finish path falls back to `DEFAULT_SAMPLE_RATE` (24000) and the Deepgram path falls back to providerOptions / the headerless encoding rate.
- Regression tests in packages/ai/test/ speech protocol tests cover `rate=0`, `rate=0000`, and the positive/absent controls.

body:
## Problem

`Form.validateFields` (packages/core/src/form.ts:277) rejects unsatisfiable field bounds after #681 / PR #683 — but only the pairwise `min > max` cases (form.ts:295-308). Two unsatisfiable definition shapes still pass create-time validation, so the form is created and can then never be answered with a legitimate answer:

1. **Closed multiselect whose `minItems` exceeds its option count.** For a multiselect with `custom` unset/false, answers may only contain declared option values (validateField, form.ts:377-379), so at most `options.length` distinct selections exist. A field with 2 options and `minItems: 3` passes `validateFields` (only `minItems > maxItems` is checked, form.ts:305-308), yet every legitimate answer fails with "Too few selections".
   - Schema surface: `minItems` is a `NonNegativeInt` and `options` is a plain array (packages/schema/src/form.ts:96-97, MultiselectField) — nothing upstream bounds `minItems` by the option count.
2. **Integer field whose `[minimum, maximum]` interval contains no integer.** `minimum`/`maximum` on IntegerField are plain `Schema.Number` (packages/schema/src/form.ts:79-80), so `minimum: 1.2, maximum: 1.8` passes the #683 check (`1.2 <= 1.8`), but no integer satisfies it: `1` is "too small" (form.ts:363) and `2` is "too large" (form.ts:364), and non-integers are rejected at form.ts:362.

## Evidence (verified this run on main f6edddd729)

Bun probe on the laptop running the verbatim validation section of form.ts (lines 235-415 spliced unchanged; form.ts md5 37f044e29b8f600cb9bb6bf12deade48, byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop ~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-0435/probe.ts, removed after):

- `validateFields([{key:"tags", type:"multiselect", options:[a,b], minItems:3}])` -> `undefined` (accepted)
- `validateAnswer(same, {tags:["a","b"]})` -> `"Too few selections for form field: tags"` — the maximum legitimate selection still fails
- `validateFields([{key:"n", type:"integer", minimum:1.2, maximum:1.8}])` -> `undefined` (accepted)
- `validateAnswer(same, {n:1})` -> `"Form field is too small: n"`; `validateAnswer(same, {n:2})` -> `"Form field is too large: n"`
- Controls behave correctly: multiselect `minItems:2` with 2 options accepts `["a","b"]`; integer `minimum:1, maximum:2` accepts `2`.

Adjacent observation, left to triage: the multiselect case is currently bypassable only by repeating a selection — `validateAnswer(same multiselect, {tags:["a","a","a"]})` returns `undefined`, because validateField counts duplicate entries toward `minItems` and never rejects duplicates. Whether duplicate selections should be rejected (or deduplicated) in `validateAnswer` is a separate contract question; the create-time fix below does not depend on it.

## Why it matters

#681's rationale applies unchanged: rejecting authoring mistakes at creation surfaces them to the caller immediately, instead of creating a form that stalls forever because no respondent can submit a valid answer. These are the two remaining unsatisfiable shapes in the same function that #683's pairwise checks do not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- `validateFields` rejects a closed (`custom` not true) multiselect whose `minItems` is greater than its number of options, with a clear per-field error naming the field key; a `custom: true` multiselect (respondents may add values) is NOT rejected on this basis, and `minItems <= options.length` still creates.
- `validateFields` rejects an integer field whose `[minimum, maximum]` interval contains no integer (e.g. minimum 1.2 / maximum 1.8, or minimum 0.5 / maximum 0.9), with a clear per-field error naming the field key; intervals containing at least one integer (including equal integer bounds, and one-sided bounds) still create. Number (non-integer) fields are unaffected.
- Regression tests in packages/core/test/form.test.ts cover both rejections plus the satisfiable controls (custom multiselect, integer interval containing an integer, equal integer bounds).
- The duplicate-selection observation is either addressed or explicitly left as a follow-up in the fix PR — not silently ignored.

body:
# Finding (pr-diff-review lane B, PR #623)

PR #623 (MERGED, commit `aa47d642`, for #592) made `MessagingTemplate.parseTime` magnitude-aware for bare epochs: exactly 10 digits are epoch seconds, exactly 13 are epoch milliseconds, and **any other bare-digit string now returns `undefined` immediately**. Before the PR, a bare-digit string that was not a 10+-digit epoch fell through to `Date.parse` — which accepts the ISO year-only form. So `parseTime("2026")`, previously parsed as 2026-01-01, now raises the callers' Invalid time error instead.

## Evidence

- PR #623 diff, `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts`: the old fallthrough was `if (/^\d{10,}$/.test(...)) return Number(...)` followed by `Date.parse(input)`; the PR replaced it with exact 10/13-digit checks plus `if (/^\d+$/.test(bare)) return undefined`, so no pure-digit string can reach `Date.parse` any more.
- Current main, `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts:513-516`: the same three checks remain (line 516 is the catch-all rejection), followed by the calendar-checked `Date.parse` path at line 521 that a bare year can no longer reach.
- `Date.parse("2026")` is `1767225600000` (2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z) — the year-only form is a valid ISO 8601 date and parsed fine before #623 (verified this run).
- The PR's regression tests pin 9/11/14-digit rejections as *epoch misreadings*; a 4-digit string was never an epoch candidate in the old code either (the old epoch branch required 10+ digits) — it was a date, and its behaviour changed as a side effect, not as part of the #592 fix.
- The schema contract for these filters (`packages/schema/src/messaging.ts`, updated by the same PR) describes `since` as "ISO time, relative age such as 2h or 3d, or a bare epoch" — a bare year is ISO time, so the documented contract and the implementation now disagree for this form.

## Why it matters

`parseTime` backs the messaging since/until filters. A user or script passing a year (`since: "2026"`) to mean "from 2026" got a working filter before #623 and gets an Invalid time error after it — a silent regression in an unrelated input class, introduced by a fix aimed at epoch misreading.

## Acceptance criteria

- `MessagingTemplate.parseTime("2026", now)` returns `Date.parse("2026")` (2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z), as it did before PR #623.
- The #592 behaviour is unchanged: 10 digits are epoch seconds, 13 are epoch milliseconds, and the epoch-length rejections the PR pinned (9/11/12/14 digits) still return `undefined`.
- A regression test in `packages/core/test/messaging-template.test.ts` pins the bare-year case alongside the existing bare-epoch cases.
- If triage instead decides the year form is deliberately unsupported, the schema `since`/`until` descriptions are narrowed to say so — the disagreement between contract and code is closed either way.

Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/623 · Parent issue: #592

# Finding (pr-diff-review lane B, PR #624)

PR #624 (MERGED, commit `7e716228`, for #600) made `ErrorSummary.from` keep a thrown primitive as a `{type: "unknown", message: String(value)}` entry instead of returning `[]`. The primitive gate lists `string`, `number`, `boolean` and `bigint` — but not `symbol`, the one remaining primitive type JavaScript allows to be thrown. A thrown symbol is still dropped entirely, and a cause chain bottoming out in a symbol loses its final entry.

## Evidence

- PR #624 diff, `packages/core/src/util/error-summary.ts`: on decode failure the entry is pushed only when `typeof error` is `"string"`, `"number"`, `"boolean"` or `"bigint"`.
- Current main, `packages/core/src/util/error-summary.ts:27-34`: the gate is unchanged — `symbol` is not in the list, so a symbol falls through to `break` with nothing recorded.
- A symbol does not decode against the struct schema (it is not a record), so it reaches exactly this gate — the same path #600/#624 fixed for the other primitives.
- `String(Symbol("boom"))` is `"Symbol(boom)"` — explicit `String()` conversion is the one safe way to stringify a symbol, and it is what the existing code already does, so including the type needs no new conversion logic.
- The PR's own framing in #600: `ErrorSummary.from` is the only diagnostic for credential and MCP OAuth failure logs (`Cause.squash` passes whatever was thrown). Whatever can be thrown can land there; `throw Symbol(...)` is legal JavaScript and libraries do throw non-Error values of every type.

## Why it matters

Small, but it is the same silent-diagnostic-loss bug #600 was filed for, left behind for one primitive type by the PR that fixed it. When it happens, the failure log records nothing at all — no type, no message — for a throw that carried information.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ErrorSummary.from(Symbol("boom"))` returns one entry whose message identifies the symbol (e.g. `"Symbol(boom)"`).
- An `Error` whose `cause` is a symbol keeps the symbol as the final entry of the chain, mirroring the existing string-cause test.
- `null`/`undefined` still return `[]`, and all existing `error-summary.test.ts` cases still pass.
- Regression tests land in `packages/core/test/util/error-summary.test.ts` beside the #624 tests.

body:
# Finding (pr-diff-review lane B, PR #622)

PR #622 (MERGED, commit `a228498d`, for #562) clamped `retry()` attempts with `Math.max(options.attempts ?? 3, 1)` so non-positive values still invoke the operation once. The clamp does not handle non-finite values, and `NaN` reproduces the exact #562 symptom the PR set out to fix — the operation is never called and the promise rejects with `undefined`. `Infinity` is worse: the loop-exit guard can never fire, so a transient failure is retried forever.

## Evidence

- PR #622 diff, `packages/util/src/retry.ts`: the only change is `const attempts = Math.max(options.attempts ?? 3, 1)`; regression tests cover `attempts: 0` and `attempts: -1` only.
- Current main, `packages/util/src/retry.ts:35`: the clamp is unchanged. `Math.max(NaN, 1)` is `NaN`; `Math.max(Infinity, 1)` is `Infinity`.
- Current main, `packages/util/src/retry.ts:42-51`: the loop runs `for (let attempt = 0; attempt < attempts; attempt++)` and falls through to `throw lastError`. With `attempts = NaN` the condition is false immediately, `lastError` is still `undefined`, and the function throws `undefined` without ever calling the operation. With `attempts = Infinity`, the in-loop exit `attempt === attempts - 1` is never true (`Infinity - 1` is `Infinity`), so a retryable error loops indefinitely at the capped delay.
- Standalone probe of the verbatim loop logic (this run): `retry(op, { attempts: NaN })` → `calls = 0`, threw `undefined` — identical to the #562 report ("never calls the operation and throws undefined").
- `attempts` is a caller-supplied option (`RetryOptions.attempts`, `packages/util/src/retry.ts:2`); any caller deriving it from parsed config or arithmetic (division, `parseInt` of a bad string) can produce `NaN` without a type error, since `NaN` is a valid `number`.

## Why it matters

#562 was filed because a zero attempt count silently turned `retry()` into a throw-`undefined`. The merged fix closes the integer cases but leaves the same silent, undebuggable failure — and an unbounded-retry hang — one input class away, in a utility used across the client, CLI and app packages.

## Acceptance criteria

- `retry()` with `attempts: NaN` invokes the operation exactly once and propagates its result/error, like the clamped positive cases.
- `retry()` with `attempts: Infinity` terminates: it behaves as a finite attempt count (the triage decision — clamp to the default or a documented maximum — is pinned in the test).
- Regression tests in `packages/util/src/retry.test.ts` cover both non-finite inputs alongside the existing 0 / -1 cases.
- Fractional attempts behaviour, if changed by the normalisation, is pinned by a test rather than left incidental.

Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/622 · Parent issue: #562

body:
# Finding (pr-diff-review lane B, PR #620)

PR #620 (MERGED, commit `78f7e1de`, for #556) made the config substitution comment guard string-aware via a shared `commented()` helper in `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts`, so `{env:...}` and `{file:...}` references in a trailing `//` comment no longer expand. The helper only recognises `//` comments. The config text it guards is JSONC — it is parsed with `jsonc-parser` in the same module — and JSONC also allows `/* ... */` block comments. References inside a block comment still expand in both substitution passes.

## Evidence

- PR #620 diff, `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts`: new `commented()` scans the token's line prefix for a `//` outside a double-quoted string and nothing else; both the env pass and `substituteFiles` now rely on it exclusively.
- Current main, `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts:37-51`: `commented()` is unchanged — no `/*` handling, and for a multi-line block comment it only ever sees the token's own line prefix, which contains no marker at all.
- Same module parses the text with `jsonc-parser` (`parse(raw, errors, { allowTrailingComma: true })`); jsonc-parser accepts `/* ... */` comments unless `disallowComments` is set, so block comments are valid in this config format.
- Standalone probe of the verbatim `commented()` logic (this run): `'{ "v": "x" } // example: {file:secret.txt}'` → guarded (`true`); `'/* example: {file:secret.txt} */ { "v": "x" }'` → **not guarded** (`false`); a token on a middle line of a multi-line `/* ... */` comment → **not guarded** (`false`).
- This is the same harm #556/#547 fixed for `//`: a `{file:...}` example inside a block comment is read from disk and inlined, and an `{env:...}` value containing a newline can break out of the comment into live config text (the env pass's own comment names exactly that breakout as the reason the guard exists).

## Why it matters

A commented-out example in a block comment — a normal way to document a config file — can still read a local file into the config text or let an env value escape the comment and become live configuration. PR #620's stated goal was one shared guard that actually covers comment text; block comments are the remaining hole in it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ConfigVariable.substitute` leaves `{env:...}` and `{file:...}` references inside `/* ... */` block comments (same-line and multi-line) literal, in both substitution passes.
- References after a closing `*/` on the same line, and live references elsewhere, still expand — including the #620 case of a `//` inside a quoted URL string not suppressing a live reference.
- Regression tests in `packages/core/test/config/config.test.ts` next to the #556 test pin: same-line block comment, multi-line block comment, and a live reference after `*/`.
- The fix keeps one shared guard for both passes (no divergent per-pass comment logic).

body:
## Summary

`describeOutput` in the ElevenLabs speech protocol (`packages/ai/src/protocols/elevenlabs-speech.ts:165-170`) derives the reported audio `sampleRate` from the output-format string with a bare `Number(rate)`: any finite result is accepted, so a malformed format manufactures invalid metadata — `pcm_abc` yields a `NaN` sample rate, `pcm_-44100` a negative one, `pcm_0` a zero rate, and hex/exponent spellings are reinterpreted (`wav_0x10` → 16, `pcm_1e5` → 100000). The format is not a closed enum at runtime: `ElevenLabsOutputFormat` is `OpenString<...>` (`elevenlabs-speech.ts:18`) and the value arrives via `providerOptions.outputFormat` (`:50`, resolved at `:98-99`), so any string a caller passes reaches this parser unchecked.

## Evidence

`packages/ai/src/protocols/elevenlabs-speech.ts:165-170`:

```ts
const describeOutput = (format: string) => {
  const [codec = format, rate] = format.split("_")
  const sampleRate = rate === undefined ? undefined : Number(rate)
  const encoding = PCM_CODECS[codec]
  return encoding === undefined ? SpeechStream.container(codec, sampleRate) : SpeechStream.pcm(encoding, sampleRate)
}
```

The result feeds the finish event's audio media info (`...describeOutput(yield* outputFormat(context.request))` at `:178`, into `SpeechStream.finish`). A `NaN` sample rate also serializes as `null` in JSON, so downstream consumers see a present-but-null rate rather than an absent one.

The sibling parser in the same surface already does this safely: `SpeechStream.sampleRate` (`packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts:76-79`) extracts the rate with a `/rate=(\d+)/` regex, so only plain digits ever reach `Number(...)`.

Verified on main `cf43cf4a4b` via a bun probe on the LAPTOP running the verbatim `describeOutput` + `PCM_CODECS` body (`elevenlabs-speech.ts` md5 `b2e674c85670a0b69f0948005d567351`, byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-0335/probe.ts`, removed after):

| Input | Resulting `info.sampleRate` | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| `pcm_44100` (control) | 44100 | 44100 ✓ |
| `ulaw_8000` (control) | 8000 | 8000 ✓ |
| `mp3_44100_128` (control) | 44100 | 44100 ✓ |
| `opus_48000_32` (control) | 48000 | 48000 ✓ |
| `pcm_abc` | `NaN` | `undefined` — rate unknown |
| `pcm_44.1k` | `NaN` | `undefined` |
| `pcm_-44100` | -44100 | `undefined` |
| `pcm_0` | 0 | `undefined` |
| `wav_0x10` | 16 | `undefined` — not a plain rate spelling |
| `pcm_1e5` | 100000 | `undefined` |

## Why it matters

- The `sampleRate` in the finish event's media info is what players, resamplers, and transcription/alignment consumers use to interpret the returned PCM/container audio. A `NaN`, negative, or zero rate is not a degraded reading — it is a fabricated one that can break playback math (division by the rate) or silently mislabel the audio.
- A typo'd or gateway-mangled `outputFormat` (the type explicitly allows open strings) currently fails silently into wrong metadata instead of the honest `undefined` ("rate unknown"), which the code already uses when the format carries no rate segment at all (bare `pcm` → `undefined`).
- Same defect family as #687 (`headerUsage` in the same speech surface), but a separate parser: that one reads a provider *response header*; this one reads the *request-side* format string. #687's scope explicitly excluded sample-rate parsing on the assumption it was regex-guarded — that is true of `SpeechStream.sampleRate`, but not of this parser.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A rate segment that is not a plain positive integer (at minimum `abc`, `44.1k`, `-44100`, `0`, `0x10`, `1e5`) yields `sampleRate: undefined` in both the `pcm` and `container` results.
- [ ] Plain formats are unchanged: `pcm_44100` → 44100, `ulaw_8000` → 8000, `mp3_44100_128` → 44100, `opus_48000_32` → 48000, bare `pcm` → `undefined`.
- [ ] No `NaN`, negative, or zero `sampleRate` can reach the speech finish event's media info from `describeOutput`.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the malformed and control formats above, in the speech protocol tests under `packages/ai/test/` (e.g. `speech.test.ts`).
