body:
## Problem

`ModelRouteReview.Member.weightLayers` is documented as the per-layer weight attribution "from the most recent selection it was a candidate in" (`packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts:71-73`, shipped in #589 / PR #618), and `route_stats` presents it to the user as the member's current weight explanation. In production it actually returns the **oldest** selection in the window that carries layers.

## Evidence (verified on main e73d850df8)

- The only production caller passes decisions in newest-first order: `ModelRouteLog.decisionRows` is documented "Selections in the window, newest first" and orders `desc(RouteDecisionTable.time)` (`packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts:630-643`); `route-stats.ts:75` feeds those rows straight into `ModelRouteReview.summarize` (`route-stats.ts:112`).
- `memberOf` (`packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts:231-235`) overwrites on every decision that carries layers for the target:

  ```ts
  let weightLayers: WeightLayers | null = null
  ...
  weightLayers = layersOf(decision.detail)[target] ?? weightLayers
  ```

  Iterating a newest-first list and overwriting means the **last** writer wins — the oldest decision with layers in the window.
- `Decision` carries no timestamp (`model-route-review.ts:33-41`), so `summarize` cannot reorder; the ordering contract is entirely implicit, and nothing pins it.
- Laptop probe (real module imported from the laptop checkout; `model-route-review.ts` md5 `4d66ac6f2d8f7726b3412f34f5dfa73b`, byte-identical to sandbox main; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-1335/probe.ts`, per the no-sandbox-probes rule): decisions in production order (newest first, layer `base` values 99, 50, 1) → `weightLayers.base = 1` (the oldest). The same decisions oldest-first → `99`. The result depends purely on caller order, and the production order gives the opposite of the documented answer.
- The existing test (`packages/core/test/model-route-review.test.ts:179-195`, "surfaces the per-layer weight attribution of the most recent decision") uses a **single** decision, so the overwrite ordering is untested.

## Why it matters

`route_stats` (route-stats.ts, `describeMember`) prints "weight layers: base …, scheduled …, prefer …, adjustment …, final …" as the explanation of a member's *current* weighting. Whenever a member's weights changed during the window (a schedule kicked in, a learned adjustment landed, a demotion started), the tool explains the stale, oldest weights — the exact situation the attribution was built to diagnose (#589). The misdirection is silent: the numbers are real, just from the wrong end of the window.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With decisions supplied in the production (newest-first, `decisionRows`) order, `weightLayers` is the attribution from the **first** (most recent) decision that carries layers for the target; a later-in-list decision never overwrites it.
- [ ] A decision without layers for the target does not clear or replace an attribution already found (pre-#589 rows keep the current fall-through behaviour).
- [ ] The ordering contract `summarize` relies on is stated where it is consumed (doc comment on `summarize`/`memberOf` or on `Decision`), so a future caller feeding a different order is visibly out of contract.
- [ ] New regression test: at least two decisions carrying different layers for the same target, supplied newest-first, asserting the newest one's layers are reported; the existing single-decision test passes unchanged.
- [ ] All existing `model-route-review` and `model-route-log` tests pass.

title: fix(core): ModelPlan.readNotes sorts notes as strings, not chronologically — mixed-format timestamps misorder and limit keeps the wrong notes

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Bug

`ModelPlan.readNotes` (`packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:305-315`) orders notes with a string comparison but filters them chronologically:

```ts
.filter((note) => since === undefined || Date.parse(note.at) >= since)
.sort((left, right) => left.at.localeCompare(right.at))
return { notes: filter.limit === undefined ? matching : matching.slice(-filter.limit), skipped }
```

The `since` filter parses each `at` with `Date.parse` (true chronology), but the sort compares the raw strings. String order only equals chronological order when every timestamp is the exact `Date.toISOString()` shape. The notes file is a shared cross-app format — the module header says "the tools here and OpenChamber read and write the same file" — and the `Note` schema accepts any string for `at`, so a writer that omits milliseconds (`2026-10-27T09:00:00Z`) or uses a UTC offset (`2026-10-27T10:30:00+02:00`) produces notes that sort wrong:

- `2026-10-27T09:00:00.500Z` sorts **before** `2026-10-27T09:00:00Z` (`.` < `Z`), though it is half a second later.
- `2026-10-27T10:30:00+02:00` (= 08:30 UTC) sorts **after** both, though it is the earliest.

Because the result keeps the newest `limit` via `slice(-limit)`, the misorder is not cosmetic: `plan_info` reads with `{ limit: 5 }` (packages/core/src/tool/plugin/plan-info.ts:82) and lists with `limit ?? 50` (:181), so the tool can silently surface the **oldest** notes as the newest and drop the actual newest ones.

## Evidence (verified this run)

Probe run on the laptop against the real module on main `6b51ceda5d` (file md5-identical between the sandbox clone and the laptop clone; probe in `~/git/fleet/probe-readnotes-sort/` on the laptop). Scratch data dir with three schema-valid notes, written oldest-file-order shuffled:

| id | `at` | true instant |
|---|---|---|
| n_offset | `2026-10-27T10:30:00+02:00` | 08:30Z (oldest) |
| n_nomillis | `2026-10-27T09:00:00Z` | 09:00:00.000Z |
| n_half | `2026-10-27T09:00:00.500Z` | 09:00:00.500Z (newest) |

Observed:
- `readNotes({})` order: `n_half,n_nomillis,n_offset` — expected chronological `n_offset,n_nomillis,n_half`.
- `readNotes({ limit: 1 })` returned `n_offset` — the **oldest** note — instead of `n_half`.

## Why it matters

Plan notes are the user's recorded experience/expectations about quota and plans; the `plan_info` tool feeds the newest few to the model when advising on routing and plan questions. Returning stale notes as "newest" — and dropping the genuinely newest — silently corrupts that advice, and the trigger is another app (or an older/newer writer) using a different but valid ISO-8601 spelling, exactly what a shared file format invites.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readNotes` orders notes by parsed instant (`Date.parse`), consistent with its own `since` filter; equal instants keep a stable, deterministic order.
- A note whose `at` does not parse still behaves sanely (define and pin the behavior: e.g. it sorts deterministically and is not silently treated as newest).
- Regression tests in `packages/core/test/model-plan.test.ts` cover: mixed fractional-second precision, a UTC-offset timestamp, and `limit` keeping the chronologically newest notes.
- Existing model-plan tests pass (`bun test test/model-plan.test.ts` from `packages/core`).

Related but distinct: #557 (unparseable `since` empties the result), #542 (limit 0), #543 (slug trailing dash) — none cover the sort comparator.

title: opencode-auto-continue (v1 plugin): can it run on opencode v2, or should it be archived?

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: kind/question
labels.description: A decision or question to resolve

body:
## What this is

`opencode-auto-continue` is a standalone OpenCode plugin (its own repo:
https://github.com/developing-today/opencode-auto-continue) that automatically
sends "continue" to a session when a transient/retryable error occurs (API
errors, provider issues, context overflow, connection resets, tool failures),
with configurable error patterns, a retry throttle, a delay, and a max
consecutive-retry cap. It registers `/auto-continue` (alias `/ac`) commands for
runtime management. It was built against the **v1** plugin API and has not been
touched since 2026-04-06 (last origin commit `aceb217`, a CI dist rebuild).

Drew's question (2026-10-27): can it run on opencode **v2**, or should it be
archived?

## Where it lives

- Laptop checkout: `/home/user/opencode-auto-continue` (user `user` on the
  Framework laptop) — single branch `main`, working tree clean as of the
  2026-10-27 cleanup. Note the local `main` is 21 commits behind `origin/main`
  (CI `ci-build` dist rebuilds); one untracked session ledger found during
  cleanup was preserved on branch `preserve/2026-10-27/continuity-ledger` in
  that repo.
- Its own GitHub repo (above); installed by users via a release-tarball URL in
  the `plugin` array of `opencode.jsonc` (see its README).
- Entire implementation is one file: `src/index.ts` (965 lines).

## The v1 API surface it depends on (evidence from the plugin source)

- `src/index.ts:3` — `import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"`;
  `package.json` peerDeps pin `@opencode-ai/plugin >=1.0.0` and
  `@opencode-ai/sdk >=1.0.0` (devDep `@opencode-ai/sdk 1.2.27`). The plugin
  default-exports a v1 hooks object.
- `src/index.ts:873-884` — `config` hook: mutates `opencodeConfig.command` to
  register the `auto-continue` / `ac` commands.
- `src/index.ts:886-890` — `"command.execute.before"` hook intercepts those
  commands and handles them by throwing a sentinel error after replying.
- `src/index.ts:892-965` — `event` hook switching on `event.type`:
  `session.error` (:894, reads `event.properties.sessionID` / `.error`),
  `message.updated` (:914, reads `event.properties.info`, incl.
  `info.metadata.done` to reset the retry counter), and `session.idle` (:947,
  triggers the pending continue after `delayMs`).
- `src/index.ts:422-428` — sends the continue through the v1 SDK client:
  `client.session.promptAsync({ path: { id: sessionID }, body: { parts:
  [{ type: "text", text: "continue" }] } })`.

## What v2 changes (from this repo, developing-today/opencode @ 2.0.30)

- The plugin model changed shape: `packages/plugin/src/promise/plugin.ts`
  defines `Plugin` as `{ id, setup(context) => Cleanup }` with a `Context` of
  domain APIs (`session`, `event`, `command`, `messaging`, …) — not the v1
  hooks-object (`config` / `event` / `command.execute.before`) the plugin
  returns today. `@opencode/plugin` here is version 2.0.30 with `./promise`
  and `./effect` surfaces.
- The v1 event names mostly do not exist in the v2 schema
  (`packages/schema/src/session-event.ts`): there is no `session.error` and
  no `message.updated`; the nearest equivalents are
  `session.execution.failed` (:259), `session.step.failed` (:385), and
  `session.retry.scheduled` (:582). `session.idle` survives but moved
  (`packages/schema/src/session-status-event.ts:47`).
- The v1 SDK client (`@opencode-ai/sdk`, `client.session.promptAsync`
  path/body shape) is replaced by `@opencode/client`'s `SessionDomain.prompt`
  (`packages/plugin/src/promise/session.ts`, `PromptInput` from
  `@opencode/schema/prompt-input`).
- Command registration in v2 goes through the plugin `command` domain rather
  than mutating config in a `config` hook.

So a straight drop-in is unlikely: at minimum the plugin entry shape, the
event subscriptions, and the prompt call all need rework. Whether v2's own
`session.retry.scheduled` behaviour already covers part of the use case is
part of the assessment.

## Acceptance criteria

- (a) **Assess compatibility**: load (or attempt to load) the current plugin
  build under opencode v2 and record exactly what breaks; map each v1
  dependency above to its v2 equivalent or note its absence; state whether
  v2's built-in retry behaviour makes the plugin redundant in whole or part.
- (b) **Decide and execute one outcome**:
  - *Port*: a scoped step list (entry shape, events, prompt call, command
    registration, packaging/install URL) with an effort estimate, filed as
    follow-up issue(s) in this repo or the plugin repo; or
  - *Archive*: tag the plugin repo's final state, add an archive note to its
    README (and archive the GitHub repo if that is the decision), and note
    where the last-known-good v1 build remains available.
- (c) **Record the decision** as a comment on this issue (decision, rationale,
  links to any follow-ups) and close the issue with that comment as the
  resolution.

Filed by the repo-health fleet at Drew's request (2026-10-27 git cleanup).

title: fix(core): quota-reset parsers accept calendar-invalid dates — Date.parse rolls Feb 30 to Mar 2 and shadows later valid resets

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The quota-reset date parsers accept calendar-invalid dates because `Date.parse` silently rolls overflow days into the next month instead of returning `NaN`. A provider (or a user note) stating a reset of `2026-02-30` is read as 2026-03-02, and `2026-04-31` is read as 2026-05-01 — a reset instant nobody stated. Worse, the rolled date is returned immediately, so it shadows a later, valid reset stated in the same message, defeating the scan-past-invalid behaviour #582/#533 deliberately built.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `8afba8bcc5`)

Probe on the laptop importing the real module (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-quota-date/probe.ts`; `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts` md5 `0653b83f91369ad42f6029e29e7216ec`, byte-identical on both checkouts):

- `resetAtFromMessage("quota reset at 2026-02-30", 2026-01-01)` → `2026-03-02T00:00:00Z` (should state no reset)
- `resetAtFromMessage("quota reset at 2026-02-30, back at 2026-03-05T00:00:00Z", …)` → `2026-03-02` — the rolled date shadows the valid 2026-03-05
- `resetAtFromMessage("quota reset at 2026-02-28", …)` → `2026-02-28` (valid control, correct)
- `resetAtFromMessage("quota reset at 2026-13-01", …)` → `undefined` (month overflow yields `NaN` and is skipped — the asymmetry is the bug: day overflow rolls, month overflow doesn't)
- `resetMs("2026-02-30", at)` → 5,184,000,000 ms (60 days, to Mar 2) instead of `undefined`
- `retryHintFromMessage("try again at 2026-04-31", …)` → a wait to May 1

Sites, all in the quota/reset surface:

- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:102-105` — `resetAtFromMessage` returns the first candidate whose `Date.parse` is not `NaN`
- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:59-60` — `resetMs` falls through to `Date.parse(text)` for header reset timestamps
- `packages/core/src/model-route-tuning.ts:168-172` — `ModelRouteTuning.parseQuotaReset` repeats the identical loop over the shared `ABSOLUTE_TIME` pattern, so it has the identical flaw

In-repo precedent: `Model.parseReleaseDate` (`packages/core/src/model.ts:320-335`) already round-trips the components through a real calendar date for exactly this reason, with a comment documenting that `Date.parse` "silently rolls overflow days such as Feb 30 into the next month". The quota parsers never got the same treatment.

## Why it matters

These instants drive `holdUntil` / quota-state `until` values: a target is held back (or released) until the parsed reset. A rolled date holds a target ~2 days past a February reset the provider never stated, or — for a typo'd day in a user tuning note — silently substitutes a different day than the one written, with no diagnostic. The #533 contract ("an invalid date alone still states no reset", pinned in `model-route-limits.test.ts`) is currently only honoured for the invalid forms that happen to produce `NaN`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A calendar-invalid absolute date (day overflow such as Feb 30 / Apr 31, in date-only or timestamp form) is treated as unparseable by `resetAtFromMessage`, `parseQuotaReset`, and `resetMs`: it states no reset by itself (`undefined`)
- [ ] Scanning continues past a calendar-invalid candidate to a later valid reset in the same message, in both message parsers (extending the #533 tests)
- [ ] Valid dates — including Feb 29 on a leap year, dates with zone designators, and date-only forms — parse exactly as today; all existing `model-route-limits` / tuning quota-reset tests pass unchanged
- [ ] New regression tests pin: Feb 30 alone → no reset; Feb 30 followed by a valid date → the valid date; Apr 31 in `resetMs` → `undefined`
- [ ] The validation is shared (one helper or the shared pattern), so the two message parsers cannot drift apart on this either

title: fix(core): Form validateFields rejects a when referencing an earlier external field — and reports it as 'must reference an earlier field'

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`Form.validateFields` (packages/core/src/form.ts:276-294) rejects a `when` condition that references an earlier **external** field, with an error message that states the opposite of the facts: `Form field condition must reference an earlier field: code -> auth` — even though `auth` *is* defined earlier in the same field list.

The cause is at form.ts:283: the create-time loop does `if (field.type === "external") continue` *before* `earlier.set(field.key, field)`, so external fields are invisible to the reference check. That contradicts three surrounding contracts:

1. **The schema doc** (packages/schema/src/form.ts:30-34): "`key` must reference a field defined earlier in the form's field list" — no exception for external fields, and external fields are members of the same `Field` union.
2. **The duplicate-key check in the same loop** (form.ts:279-281): external fields *do* count as defined fields — a test pins that an external field and a string field sharing a key is a duplicate (packages/core/test/form.test.ts:261-267). So the loop simultaneously treats an external field as defined (for duplicates) and undefined (for `when` references).
3. **The runtime** (form.ts:257-267): `matches` compares an answer value against `when.value` generically, and external answers are booleans (`value === true` is the acknowledgement), so a condition `{ key: "auth", op: "eq", value: true }` would evaluate coherently if such a form could be created. Note `validateWhen` (form.ts:296-310) has no external branch either: if the reference were allowed through, an external target would fall into the string-value branch and demand a string condition value, which can never match the boolean acknowledgement.

## Evidence

Verified on main f1e0c586fe via a bun probe on the laptop running the verbatim validation section of form.ts (lines 235-370, file md5 89b117a66d09a77dd59a8876ef2102c9; the module's workspace imports do not resolve on the laptop checkout, so the probe splices the real functions unchanged — probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-form/probe2.ts`):

- `validateFields([external "auth", string "code" with when {key:"auth", op:"eq", value:true}])` → `"Form field condition must reference an earlier field: code -> auth"`
- Control, boolean field in place of external (same shape) → `undefined` (accepted)
- `validateAnswer` on the external-first form: `{auth: true, code: "x"}` → `undefined` (valid); `{code: "x"}` → `"External form field must be acknowledged: auth"` — the runtime side handles the shape coherently.

Whether gating a field on an external acknowledgement is *useful* is a real design question (every valid reply must acknowledge an external field anyway, per form.ts:242-245 and the pinned test at form.test.ts:288+), so this issue asks for a decision, not a predetermined fix: either external fields become first-class `when` targets (boolean condition semantics, like boolean fields), or the rejection becomes explicit and accurate.

## Why it matters

Form authors (MCP elicitation and question flows build these field lists) currently get a false diagnosis — they are told their field ordering is wrong when it is not — and the schema documentation promises a reference the validator refuses. Silent inconsistency between the wire contract, the create-time validator, and the runtime evaluator is how form definitions that work in one client break in another.

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision is recorded on this issue: external fields either are or are not valid `when` targets.
- If they are valid targets: `validateFields` accepts a `when` referencing an earlier external field with a boolean condition value (and rejects non-boolean values with the boolean message), `validateWhen` handles the external target type explicitly, and tests pin create + reply behavior for a field gated on an external acknowledgement.
- If they are not valid targets: the rejection names the real reason (e.g. "Form field condition cannot reference an external field: code -> auth"), the schema `When` documentation in packages/schema/src/form.ts states the exception, and a test pins the accurate error.
- Either way, the duplicate-key treatment and the reference treatment of external fields agree, and all existing form tests pass.

title: fix(core): ErrorSummary.from returns [] for non-Error thrown values — credential/OAuth failure logs lose the error entirely

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`ErrorSummary.from` (packages/core/src/util/error-summary.ts:17-33) returns an empty array for any thrown value that is not an object matching its struct schema — a thrown string, number, or boolean produces `[]`, so the failure leaves no trace at all in the log line that was supposed to diagnose it.

The function's doc comment promises: "each entry keeps the classification and message of one error in the cause chain." A non-`Error` throw has a perfectly good message (its own string form); it is dropped because `Schema.decodeUnknownOption` on a primitive yields `None` and the loop breaks before recording anything (error-summary.ts:22-24).

## Evidence

Verified on main f1e0c586fe via a bun probe on the laptop importing the real module (probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-form/probe3.ts`):

- `ErrorSummary.from("boom string")` → `[]`
- `ErrorSummary.from(42)` → `[]`
- `ErrorSummary.from(new Error("real"))` → `[{"type":"Error","message":"real"}]` (control)
- `ErrorSummary.from({ message: "plain object" })` → `[{"type":"unknown","message":"plain object"}]` (control: plain objects survive)

Callers pass `Cause.squash(cause)`, which returns whatever was thrown — including non-`Error` defects from SDKs and libraries that throw strings:

- packages/core/src/credential.ts:152, 198, 219, 240, 304 — `errors: ErrorSummary.from(Cause.squash(cause))` on credential create/refresh failure log lines
- packages/core/src/mcp/oauth.ts:88, 510, 529 — same pattern for MCP OAuth failures

With a string defect, those log lines read `errors: []` — the one diagnostic field on the failure is empty, and the actual error text exists nowhere else (the surrounding code logs no message of its own; the cause is squashed into this summary).

Existing tests (packages/core/test/util/error-summary.test.ts) cover only `Error` instances and their cause chains; no test pins the non-object case.

## Why it matters

Credential and OAuth failures are exactly the failures a user hits while setting up a provider, and exactly the ones where the thrown value most often comes from a third-party SDK with loose throwing habits. When that happens today, the log says a failure occurred and nothing about why — the summary mechanism silently defeats its own purpose for the cases least likely to be well-formed `Error`s.

## Acceptance criteria

- `ErrorSummary.from` on a thrown string returns one entry whose message is that string (type may be `"unknown"` or a similarly honest classification); numbers/booleans likewise produce an entry with their string form as the message, rather than `[]`.
- A cause chain that bottoms out in a non-object value keeps the entries above it and appends the primitive's entry instead of ending the chain silently.
- `Error` instances, tagged errors, and plain objects with `message`/`code`/`errno` keep their current summaries (existing tests pass unchanged).
- New regression tests in packages/core/test/util/error-summary.test.ts cover: thrown string, thrown number, and an `Error` whose `cause` is a string.

title: fix(core): McpxDiagnose.attemptParameterRepair floors non-integer strings for integer parameters — "3.9" becomes 3 and "-1.1" becomes -2 in the suggested repair

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`McpxDiagnose.attemptParameterRepair` — the self-healing helper that suggests corrected arguments after a tool call fails — "repairs" a string value for an `integer` parameter by flooring whatever number it parses, and accepts non-finite numbers for a `number` parameter. The suggested repair silently changes the value the caller asked for instead of only fixing its type:

- `"3.9"` for an integer parameter is repaired to `3` (the fractional part is silently discarded).
- `"-1.9"` is repaired to `-2`, and even `"-1.1"` is repaired to `-2` — `Math.floor` moves negative values a full unit away from zero, so the "repair" is not even a truncation of what was written.
- `"Infinity"` for a `number` parameter is repaired to `Infinity`, which is not representable in JSON: when the repair is rendered for the model (`formatAutomaticRepair` uses `JSON.stringify`), it shows up as `null`.

A repair facility exists to correct *trivial* errors (the function's own doc: string-to-number coercion, boolean coercion, JSON parsing, array wrapping). Changing the numeric value is not a trivial correction — it invents data. The safe cases work today and must keep working: `"42"` → `42` and `"3.0"` → `3` are genuine type fixes because the string already denotes an integer.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `e82aa33071`)

- `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/mcpx-diagnose.ts:280-289` — the string-to-number coercion: the only guard is `trimmed !== "" && !Number.isNaN(Number(trimmed))` (line 283), and line 285 applies `expectedType === "integer" ? Math.floor(num) : num` unconditionally.
- Probe on the laptop running the function's verbatim source extracted from the byte-identical file (laptop `~/git/opencode` at `e82aa33071`, md5 `f562013fc7cd88ca8779dbe1153acfca`, matching the sandbox clone; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-27-intrepair/probe.ts` — the module's workspace imports do not resolve on the laptop checkout, so the probe splices lines 127-330 of the real file, which contain `extractSchemaProperties`/`determinePropertyType`/`analyzeArgumentMismatch`/`attemptParameterRepair` unchanged):

```
integer "42"       -> repaired=true value=42
integer "3.0"      -> repaired=true value=3
integer "3.9"      -> repaired=true value=3     (fraction silently dropped)
integer "-1.9"     -> repaired=true value=-2
integer "-1.1"     -> repaired=true value=-2    (a full unit from the stated value)
number  "1.5"      -> repaired=true value=1.5
number  "Infinity" -> repaired=true value=Infinity, JSON-rendered as {"ratio":null}
number  "0x10"     -> repaired=true value=16    (hex string silently reinterpreted)
```

- The repair reaches the model as advice: `diagnoseToolCall` (same file, line 391) attaches `repairedParams`, `formatAutomaticRepair` (line 335, JSON rendering at line 344) prints them under "Automatic Parameter Repair Available", and `enrichToolFailure` puts them in the failure's diagnostic metadata — so a floored or `null`-rendered value is what the next turn is told to send.
- Existing coverage (`packages/core/test/tool-mcpx-features.test.ts`, "detects shape mismatches and auto-repairs parameter types") exercises only the clean cases (`"5000"` → `5000`, `"true"` → `true`); no test pins what happens for non-integer or non-finite strings.

## Why it matters

This helper fires exactly when a tool call has already failed and the model is being told how to fix it. A suggested repair that quietly turns a limit of `-1.1` into `-2`, a count of `3.9` into `3`, or a ratio into `null` teaches the next attempt to send a *different* argument than the one that was intended — a silent data corruption presented as a correction, in the one place whose entire job is trustworthy diagnostics. Declining to repair (leaving the mismatch hint from `analyzeArgumentMismatch`, which correctly flags the string) is strictly better than repairing to a different value.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For an `integer` parameter, a string is only coerced when the parsed number is already an integer (`"42"` → `42`, `"3.0"` → `3` keep working); `"3.9"`, `"-1.9"` and `"-1.1"` produce no numeric repair for that property (the type-mismatch hint still stands).
- [ ] For a `number` parameter, non-finite results (`"Infinity"`, `"-Infinity"`) are not repaired; the repaired params never contain a value that JSON-serializes to something different (`Infinity` → `null`).
- [ ] The coercion's accepted grammar is pinned by tests — including what happens for hex/exponent forms (`"0x10"`, `"1e3"`) — whether they stay accepted or are rejected, the choice is deliberate and tested rather than inherited from `Number()` by accident.
- [ ] New regression tests in `packages/core/test/tool-mcpx-features.test.ts` (or a sibling mcpx-diagnose test file) cover the cases above; existing mcpx tests still pass (`bun test` for the touched test files from `packages/core`).

## Suggested fix

Tighten the guard at `mcpx-diagnose.ts:283-285`: require `Number.isFinite(num)` for both types, and for `integer` additionally require `Number.isInteger(num)` (drop the `Math.floor`). No other repair path changes.

title: fix(core): MessagingTemplate.parseTime reads epoch-seconds timestamps as milliseconds — a 10-digit since/until silently becomes January 1970

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Bug

`MessagingTemplate.parseTime` treats every bare digit string of 10+ digits as epoch **milliseconds**, so an epoch-**seconds** timestamp — the form most other tools emit — silently becomes a moment in January 1970. The messaging query filters that call it then return the wrong window with no error: `since=<seconds>` matches everything since 1970, and `until=<seconds>` matches nothing.

## Evidence

`packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts` (parseTime, end of file):

```ts
if (/^\d{10,}$/.test(input.trim())) return Number(input.trim())
```

Verified this run against the real module (bun probe on the laptop clone, file byte-identical to main `e82aa33071`, md5 `f2bb99e6f75d73e0a2831a096b844472`):

| input | result | as date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `1767225600` (2026-01-01T00:00:00Z in epoch **seconds**) | `1767225600` | **1970-01-21T10:53:45.600Z** |
| `1767225600000` (same instant in epoch milliseconds) | `1767225600000` | 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z |
| `17672256000` (11 digits) | `17672256000` | 1970-07-24T12:57:36.000Z |
| `999999999` (9-digit epoch seconds, 2001-09-09) | `undefined` → callers raise `Invalid time` | — |
| `2026-01-01T00:00:00Z` (ISO) | `1767225600000` | 2026-01-01T00:00:00.000Z |
| `2h` (relative) | `now - 7_200_000` | correct |

So the bare-number contract is internally inconsistent: 9-digit seconds are rejected as invalid, 10-digit seconds are accepted but read as a 1970 millisecond instant, and only 13-digit values behave as the milliseconds the code assumes.

Callers (all in `packages/core/src/messaging.ts`): the `since`/`until` and `hiddenSince`/`hiddenUntil` filters at lines 769–774, 823–824, 1752–1753 and 1826–1827 parse through `parseTime` and only error when it returns `undefined` — a mis-scaled value passes silently into `time_created >= / <=` conditions. The schema annotation for these fields (`packages/schema/src/messaging.ts:167`) documents only "ISO time or relative age such as 2h or 3d"; the bare-epoch form is undocumented, so users who supply the epoch form most tools produce get a silently wrong window.

## Why it matters

These filters back message/log search across sessions. A `since` in epoch seconds — a natural thing to paste from a log line, a `date +%s`, or another tool's output — quietly disables the time bound instead of failing, so searches return unbounded history (or, for `until`, an empty result) and the user has no signal that the time was misread.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A bare epoch value is interpreted by a documented, magnitude-aware rule (e.g. 10-digit values are seconds and are scaled to milliseconds), **or** non-millisecond lengths are rejected so the callers' existing `Invalid time` error fires — either way, no input is silently read as a 1970 instant.
- [ ] `parseTime("1767225600", now)` and `parseTime("1767225600000", now)` agree on the same instant under the chosen rule (or the seconds form errors explicitly).
- [ ] The bare-epoch contract is documented where the fields are described (schema annotation / parseTime doc comment).
- [ ] Regression tests cover 9-, 10- and 13-digit inputs alongside the existing ISO and relative forms; existing messaging tests still pass.

title: refactor(core): PR #569 duplicated the governance catalog construction in session.ts and session/session.ts — extract one shared helper

labels.name: kind/refactor

body:
## Finding

PR #569 (merged) added the governance provider-catalog construction **twice, as two near-identical ~35-line copies** — `governanceConfig` in `packages/core/src/session.ts` and `governanceConfig` in `packages/core/src/session/session.ts`. The duplicated block does the same work in both places: look up the already-initialized location context, read config entries, take the provider snapshot, and build the `ModelGovernance.Catalog` map (per provider: model id → `{ enabled, variants }`), with the same `orElseSucceed` fallback to `{ entries: [], catalog: undefined }`.

## Evidence

- Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/569 (MERGED, head `2c7b02c6`, fixes #530) — its diff adds the catalog-building body to both files, growing the previously small duplicated `governanceEntries` helper in each file into the full duplicated `governanceConfig`.
- Verified on current main (`c3c13e0015`, 2026-10-27): `packages/core/src/session.ts:293` defines `governanceConfig` (used by `assertModelAllowed` at :326) and `packages/core/src/session/session.ts:117` defines its twin (used by `switchAgent` at :158 and the model-selection path at :186). The snapshot→Catalog `new Map(Array.from(snapshot.records, ...))` construction appears verbatim in both.
- No existing issue covers this duplication (searched open + closed issues 2026-10-27; #530, now closed, was about the expansion logic, which #569 *did* share correctly via the new `model-route-expansion.ts`).

## Why it matters

#530/#569 exist because governance and the runtime disagreed about route targets; the fix's own principle was "exactly one expansion implementation, so the two can never disagree." The catalog that feeds governance now violates the same principle one level up: if the catalog slice changes in one copy (e.g. a new per-model field governance needs, or a change to how `enabled`/`variants` are read from the snapshot) and not the other, the **same route will be judged against different catalogs depending on which entry point checks it** (`session.ts` session-creation path vs `session/session.ts` switchAgent / setModel paths) — a drift bug that would present as inconsistent denials and be very hard to trace.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The context→entries+catalog construction exists exactly once (e.g. a shared helper alongside `ModelGovernance` in `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts`, or a new small module), and both `session.ts` and `session/session.ts` call it.
- [ ] Behaviour is unchanged: an uninitialized location still yields `{ entries: [], catalog: undefined }`, a location with no provider service still yields its entries with `catalog: undefined`, and any failure still falls back via the existing `orElseSucceed` semantics.
- [ ] Existing tests pass unmodified: `packages/core` model-governance tests and the session test suites that exercise `assertAllowed` through both entry paths.
- [ ] `grep` for the snapshot→Catalog construction in `packages/core/src` returns exactly one site.

title: pr-shepherd(core): PRs #552 and #583 both rewrite ConfigVariable.substitute's env pass — land them as one integrated change so neither protection is lost

labels.description: Queue packet kind: shepherd an open PR or PR set to merge

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core

body:
## Finding

Two open PRs rewrite the **same function** — the `env()` pass inside `ConfigVariable.substitute` in `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts` — from the **same base blob**, with incompatible signatures. They are complementary security fixes, but they cannot both land as-is: whichever merges second will conflict, and a resolution that keeps only one `env()` implementation silently drops the other PR's protection.

## Evidence

- PR #552 — https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/552 (OPEN, head `dab74133`, fixes #546): rewrites `env()` to return a `Substituted` object (`{ text, authored }` ranges) and changes `substituteFiles(input, text: string)` to `substituteFiles(input, substituted: Substituted)`, so `{file:...}` references that arrived inside an env value or `:-` fallback are never expanded (env values could otherwise read arbitrary local files into config values).
- PR #583 — https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/583 (OPEN, head `24128526`, closes #547): rewrites `env()` to build the output string manually (still returning `string`) and adds a `//` comment-line guard inside the env loop, so `{env:...}` inside a comment is not substituted (value leak into the comment; a newline in the value could break out of the comment and change what the config says).
- Both diffs start from the identical base: `packages/core/src/config/variable.ts` blob `a98bdcd7dbac`. Both also insert their new regression tests at the same anchor in `packages/core/test/config/config.test.ts` (immediately after the test ending at old line 1508).
- Verified on current main (`c3c13e0015`, 2026-10-27): `variable.ts` still contains the pre-fix `env()` (plain `input.text.replace(...)` returning a string, `substituteFiles(input, text: string)` at line 45) — neither PR has landed, and no existing issue covers their overlap (searched 2026-10-27; #546 and #547 track the individual bugs only).

## Why it matters

These are both security-relevant fixes to the same ~15-line pass. A hurried conflict resolution that takes one side wholesale reintroduces either the arbitrary-file-read via env-carried `{file:...}` (#546) or the comment leak / newline breakout via `{env:...}` in `//` comments (#547) — with the other PR's tests then failing or, worse, being dropped as part of the resolution. The interaction also has one subtle case neither PR tests alone: an env token on a comment line stays literal under #583, and that literal text is config-authored text under #552's range tracking, so the integrated version must keep the file pass's own `//` guard as the thing that protects a `{file:...}` on that same comment line (see also #556 for trailing-comment file reads).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One integrated change (one PR rebased onto the other, or a combined branch) contains **both** protections: authored-range tracking for the file pass **and** the `//` comment guard for the env pass.
- [ ] Both PRs' new regression tests pass in the same tree: #552's "does not expand file references introduced by env values or fallbacks" + escaped-repair-pass test, and #583's "does not substitute env references inside // comments" + newline-breakout test.
- [ ] A combined case is covered: a config whose comment line contains an env token **and** a `{file:...}` reference neither substitutes the env value nor reads the file.
- [ ] The superseded PR is closed with a comment linking the integrated PR/this issue; #546 and #547 both close when the integrated change merges.

body:
Sub-issue of the design issue #587 (one quota signal, three consumers). Phase 2 of that design — self-contained observability work with no behaviour change and no open design question inside it.

## Task

Make route selection auditable per weight layer. Today `packages/core/src/model-route.ts` → `weightOf()` composes scheduled `WeightRule`s → user `prefer` overrides → tuner adjustments → quota demotion, and `nextTarget` records only the final effective weight per candidate in the `ModelRouteLog` decision detail. Add a traced computation so the decision record shows, per candidate:

- the weight after each layer: `base`, `scheduled`, `prefer`, `adjustment`, `demotion` (final);
- a slot for gate verdicts (e.g. `gate: root-start 85% — snapshot 97% → excluded`) — the slot ships now, empty until #566's gates exist, so the log schema doesn't change twice.

Surface the attribution through the existing route-review tooling (`packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts`, which already documents "the effective weight each candidate carried in a selection") rather than a new surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decision-log detail for a selection includes the per-layer weights above for every candidate, in the existing `detail` shape style (additive fields only; existing consumers keep working).
- [ ] A test proves traced weights equal `weightOf` weights for representative targets (scheduled rule in force, prefer override present, adjustment active, demoted target) — tracing must never drift from the real computation; ideally the traced path *is* the real computation.
- [ ] No behaviour change: selection order, sticky/continuity behaviour, and demotion semantics are byte-for-byte what they were; existing `packages/core` route tests pass unmodified.
- [ ] Route-review output shows the attribution for a recorded decision (covered by its existing test pattern).
- [ ] `bun run check` from the repo root passes (or failures are pre-existing on `devtoday/main` and named in the closing note).

body:
Sub-issue of the design issue #587 (one quota signal, three consumers). Phase 1 of that design — the phase with no open design question inside it. The design issue carries `user/review` for the overall layering decision; this phase is a pure, behaviour-free derivation that is useful under either decision outcome (it only formalises what `windowReport()` already computes for reporting).

## Task

Add a `QuotaSnapshot` derivation in `packages/core`: a pure function that, given the configured plans (`packages/core/src/model-plan.ts`) and recorded usage (the inputs `packages/core/src/model-usage.ts` → `windowReport()` already uses), produces one snapshot per plan window:

```ts
interface QuotaSnapshot {
  planID: string
  window: string
  providerID: string
  percent: number | null        // null = unknown, never treated as headroom
  remaining: number | null
  resetAt: number | null        // epoch ms when derivable from the window's reset rule; null otherwise
  observedAt: number
  stale: boolean                // observedAt older than the configured max age
}
```

Contract rules (from #587):

- One configured max-age defines `stale`, shared by all future consumers (per-plan override allowed, one definition).
- A window with no limit, or no derivable usage (e.g. no `windowHours` — see #550), yields `percent: null` — never a guessed number.
- Pure and deterministic: same plan + usage inputs + clock ⇒ same snapshots. No I/O, no selection-path changes, nothing in `model-route.ts` reads snapshots yet.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Snapshot derivation exists in `packages/core` alongside `model-usage.ts`, reusing `windowReport()`'s percent/remaining computation rather than duplicating it.
- [ ] Unit tests (run from `packages/core`, per repo `AGENTS.md`) cover: normal window (percent + remaining correct against a hand-computed fixture), missing limit → `percent: null`, missing `windowHours` → `percent: null`, observation older than max-age → `stale: true`, fresh observation → `stale: false`, reset rule that yields a `resetAt` and one that does not (`resetAt: null`).
- [ ] No behaviour change anywhere: no routing, gating, or UI code consumes snapshots in this issue.
- [ ] `bun run check` from the repo root passes (or failures are pre-existing on `devtoday/main` and named in the closing note).

## Context

- Design: #587 and `files/designs/opencode-quota-signal-routing.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.
- Consumers waiting on this contract: #566 (placement gates), #568 (burn-rate controller).
- Evidence: `model-usage.ts` `windowReport()` already derives `percent`/`remaining`/`resetRule` for reporting; `model-plan.ts` owns `QuotaWindow` (limit, unit, `windowHours`, reset rule).

body:
## Problem

`ModelRouteSchedule.active` attributes the tail of a wrapping (past-midnight) window to the wrong local day on the DST fall-back night. For one hour a year per timezone, a window that began the previous evening is reported inactive — and the *next* day's window is reported active in its place.

## Evidence (verified on main `405c9b5bd9`)

`packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts`, in `active`:

```ts
if (wraps && current.minutes < minutesOf(window.end)!)
  // Before the end of a wrapping window means it began on the previous local day.
  return dayMatches(window, partsAt(format, now - (current.minutes + 1) * 60_000))
```

The previous local day is computed by subtracting `current.minutes + 1` **absolute** minutes from `now`. Wall-clock minutes and absolute minutes differ by the DST offset change: on the fall-back night the 01:00 hour repeats, so subtracting 91 absolute minutes from the second 01:30 lands at 00:59 the *same* local day instead of 23:59 the previous one.

Probe importing the real module (bun, `packages/core`), window `{ daysOfWeek: [6] /* Sat */, start: "22:00", end: "02:00", timezone: "America/Chicago" }` on the 2026 fall-back night (DST ends Sun 2026-11-01):

| instant | local | `active` | expected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2026-11-01T04:00Z | Sat 23:00 CDT | true | true |
| 2026-11-01T05:30Z | Sun 00:30 CDT | true | true |
| 2026-11-01T06:30Z | Sun 01:30 CDT (1st) | true | true |
| 2026-11-01T07:30Z | Sun 01:30 CST (2nd) | **false** | true |
| 2026-11-01T07:59Z | Sun 01:59 CST (2nd) | **false** | true |
| 2026-11-01T08:30Z | Sun 02:30 CST | false | false (control) |
| 2026-11-08T07:30Z | Sun 01:30 CST (normal week) | true | true |

Mirror image: the Sunday-only window (`daysOfWeek: [0]`) at 2026-11-01T07:30Z returns **true**, though that instant is in Saturday's window tail, not Sunday's.

## Why it matters

Scheduled weight rules and route overrides are how operators express "use this pool on Saturday night" — exactly the overnight windows that wrap past midnight. On the fall-back night those rules silently apply to the wrong day for the repeated hour: Saturday-night rules switch off an hour early, and Sunday-night rules switch on a day early. It is rare (one hour per year per zone) but silent and self-inconsistent — the same instant is judged against the wrong day's `daysOfWeek` *and* `daysOfMonth` (so a `-1`/last-day or 1st-of-month restriction is also misjudged that hour).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The previous-day attribution for a wrapping window's tail is computed from the local calendar date (e.g. the day before the current local date), not by subtracting wall-clock minutes from the absolute instant.
- [ ] Tests pin the fall-back cases: a Saturday 22:00–02:00 America/Chicago window is active at both 01:30 CDT and the repeated 01:30 CST on 2026-11-01, and a Sunday window is not active at either; a normal-week control still passes.
- [ ] `daysOfMonth` attribution in the tail is likewise the previous local day (e.g. a window restricted to the last day of the month behaves correctly in a tail that falls on the 1st).
- [ ] Existing model-route-schedule tests pass; non-wrapping and non-DST behavior is unchanged.

title: fix(core): a route target's until is ignored when the target references another route — expired nested-route targets stay live in expansion and governance

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

A route target in object form whose `model` references another route (`providerID: "opencode-route"`) and which carries `until` is never dropped when `until` passes — neither by the runtime expansion nor by session model governance. The schema promises the opposite: `packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts` defines `TargetObject.until` (line 29) as "Epoch milliseconds after which this target leaves the route. Used for time-limited pool membership", and the same object's `model` field is documented "A route may reference another route", so an expiring nested-route target is a schema-valid, documented configuration.

## Evidence

Found reviewing PR #569 ("fix(core): judge route governance targets via shared catalog expansion (#530)", merged, commit `2c7b02c6`), which added `until` dropping to governance claiming the target set mirrors the runtime. Verified verbatim on current main `405c9b5bd9403046db1d763800c8e97be4893e08` via both `git show origin/main` and the GitHub contents API:

- Runtime — `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`: inside `expand`'s target loop, the nested-route branch runs first (lines 258–262: `if (ref.providerID === ModelRoute.PROVIDER_ID) { const child = visit(...); ...; continue }`) and the expiry check only follows it (line 263: `if (spec.until !== undefined && Date.now() >= spec.until) continue`). For a nested-route target the `continue` skips the `until` check entirely, so the inner route's leaves stay in the route forever.
- Governance — `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts`: `routeTargets` has the same ordering (lines 210–212): `if (selection.providerID === "opencode-route") return routeTargets(entries, selection.model, seen, selectionVariant ?? requested, catalog)` returns before `if (object?.until !== undefined && Date.now() >= object.until) return []` is reached. PR #569 copied the runtime's ordering, so governance now faithfully mirrors the runtime bug instead of the schema contract.
- Test gap: PR #569's new `until` test in `packages/core/test/session/model-governance.test.ts` (line ~464) covers only a concrete target (`{ model: "test/b", until: 1 }`); no test in either the governance suite or the plugin expansion covers `until` on a target whose model is another route.

Note the deliberate, documented exception does not cover this: governance's comment says an intermediate target object's `defaultVariant`/`variants` never reach the inner route's leaves (matching the plugin) — `until` is not part of that exception; it is a membership bound on the target itself.

## Why it matters

`until` is the mechanism for time-limited pool membership (e.g. a borrowed pool or a provider being retired at a set time). Wrapping the expiring membership as a nested route — the natural way to give it its own selection mode/weights — silently defeats the expiry: traffic keeps flowing to the inner route's targets after the deadline, and governance judges those targets as live members, so no layer ever notices.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A target object with a past `until` whose `model` references another route contributes no leaves in the model-routes plugin `expand` (expiry checked before/regardless of the nested-route branch).
- [ ] `ModelGovernance.routeTargets` likewise contributes no targets for an expired nested-route target, keeping governance and runtime in agreement.
- [ ] Regression tests: plugin/governance coverage for an expired nested-route target (dropped) and an unexpired one (`until` in the future, still expanded/judged).
- [ ] Existing model-routes and model-governance suites pass; concrete-target `until` behaviour from #569 is unchanged.

title: fix(core): MessagingTemplate.render calls an acyclic deep variable chain a self-reference — the depth limit and the cycle check share one false error

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`MessagingTemplate.render` reports **"Variable {name} refers to itself"** for a template-variable chain that contains no cycle at all — the chain simply exceeds the expansion depth limit. The cycle check and the depth check share one error message, so a user (or model) debugging a perfectly legal configuration is told to look for a self-reference that does not exist.

## Evidence (verified on main `9a4174a9c2`)

`packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts` (in `render`'s `expand`):

```ts
if (stack.includes(name) || stack.length >= MAX_DEPTH)
  return yield* new TemplateError({ message: `Variable {${name}} refers to itself` })
```

with `MAX_DEPTH = 8` (same file). Two different failure conditions — an actual reference cycle (`stack.includes(name)`) and an acyclic chain that is merely deep (`stack.length >= MAX_DEPTH`) — produce the identical, and for the second case false, message.

Probe importing the real module (bun, `packages/core`), resolver returning template-valued variables forming an acyclic chain `a → b → c → … → k → "end"` (11 distinct variables, no repeats):

- Rendering `{a}` fails with: `Variable {i} refers to itself`
- Control, a genuine self-reference `x → {x}`, fails with the same wording: `Variable {x} refers to itself`

Chained template values are a normal, built-in idiom in this system — e.g. the `private_link` constant is itself `"{separator}{bidirectional}{separator}"` — and constants, config variables and custom variables all render through this path, so a user-defined chain of nine or more variables is reachable in ordinary configuration.

## Why it matters

The error is the only diagnostic a user gets when a topic/template fails to render. A false "refers to itself" sends them hunting for a cycle in an acyclic configuration, while the actual remedy — shorten the chain, or inline some values — is never suggested. Misleading errors in a configuration surface erode trust in every other diagnostic from the same surface.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A reference cycle and a depth-limit excess produce distinct, accurate error messages: the cycle message names the repeated variable (ideally the chain), and the depth message states that the expansion depth limit (8) was exceeded and names the variable at which it stopped.
- [ ] The depth limit itself is unchanged (or, if raising it is chosen, the new limit is documented where `MAX_DEPTH` is defined and the depth message reflects it).
- [ ] Tests pin both cases: a true self-reference (direct and indirect, e.g. `a → b → a`) reports a cycle, and an acyclic chain deeper than the limit reports the depth limit — plus a chain at exactly the limit still renders.
- [ ] Existing messaging-template tests pass.

title: fix(core): route_stats member speed median counts failed and timed-out attempts — Member.tokensPerSecond documents completed attempts only

labels.name: app/core

body:
## Problem

`route_stats` reports each pool member's `tokensPerSecond` as the "Median output speed of the attempts that completed" (`packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts:55`), but the median is computed over **every** attempt that carries a speed value — including failures, timeouts and interrupted attempts that produced partial output. A target whose only completed attempt was slow can be reported as fast because its failed attempts streamed briefly at a high rate.

## Evidence (verified on main `9a4174a9c2`)

- The field's contract: `packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts:54-55` — `/** Median output speed of the attempts that completed. */ readonly tokensPerSecond: number | null`.
- The computation: `packages/core/src/model-route-review.ts:212,222` — `speeds` is `present(attempts.map((row) => row.tokensPerSecond))` over all attempts passed to `memberOf`, with no outcome filter. (The neighbouring `firstTokenMs` field makes no completed-only claim, and `inputTokens` says "of its requests" — only the speed field promises completed attempts.)
- Failed attempts really do carry a speed: both attempt writers set `tokens_per_second` whenever tokens exist and output started, regardless of outcome — `packages/core/src/session/runner/step.ts:408-411` (outcome on the same record is `failure` / `timeout` / `interrupted` / `success`, set a few lines above) and the route-log observer at `packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts:127-130`.
- Probe importing the real module (bun, `packages/core`), one route, one target, three attempts:
  - `success` at 10 tok/s, `failure` at 1000 tok/s, `timeout` at 2000 tok/s
  - `ModelRouteReview.summarize(...)` reported member `tokensPerSecond: 1000` — the median of all three — where the completed-only median is **10**.

## Why it matters

`route_stats` is the surface the model and the user use to judge pool members (rendered as `N tok/s` at `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/route-stats.ts:160`) and it feeds routing judgement calls. Crediting a flaky target with the speed of its aborted attempts makes failing members look fast, exactly when their failure rate (reported alongside) should be read together with a trustworthy speed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Member.tokensPerSecond` is the median over completed (successful) attempts only, matching its documentation — or, if including partial-output attempts is the intended semantics, the field documentation and the `route_stats` rendering are changed to say so explicitly and a test pins that choice. (Decide and pin one; the current doc/code disagreement is the bug.)
- [ ] A regression test with a slow successful attempt and fast failed/timed-out attempts carrying `tokensPerSecond` pins the chosen semantics.
- [ ] Attempts with no recorded speed remain excluded either way; members with no qualifying attempts still report `null`.
- [ ] Existing model-route-review tests pass.

title: fix(core): MessagingLog.clip exceeds its maximum-characters budget at small limits — the omission marker is not counted when the tail is dropped

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`MessagingLog.clip` is supposed to shorten a log entry to at most `chars` characters — the `log` operation's `chars` field is documented as "Maximum characters per entry" (`packages/schema/src/messaging.ts:392`, `PositiveInt`; same wording at `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/messaging.ts:185`) — but at small limits the clipped output is **longer than the maximum**, in one case more than twice it.

## Evidence (verified on main `9a4174a9c2`)

`packages/core/src/messaging/log.ts:165-170`:

```ts
export function clip(text: string, chars: number) {
  if (text.length <= chars) return text
  const head = Math.ceil(chars * 0.7)
  const tail = Math.max(0, chars - head - 20)
  return `${text.slice(0, head)} …[${text.length - head - tail} chars]… ${tail > 0 ? text.slice(-tail) : ""}`
}
```

The formula reserves 20 characters for the omission marker only by shrinking the tail. When `chars - head` is smaller than the marker itself (≈14–17 chars for typical counts), the tail clamps to 0 but the marker is still emitted in full, so the total exceeds `chars`. Probe importing the real module (bun, `packages/core`), with a 1000-character input:

| `chars` (documented maximum) | clipped length |
|---|---|
| 10 | **22** |
| 20 | **29** |
| 30 | **36** |
| 40 | **43** |
| 50 | 50 |
| 100 | 95 |

The live caller is `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:1847`, which clips every returned log entry with the caller-supplied `chars` (defaults 500 / 4000, but any positive integer is accepted, so a caller asking for a tight per-entry budget to fit a context window silently gets entries up to ~2.2× that budget). At the small end the output also keeps no tail at all while spending ~15 characters on the marker — the least useful possible split of the budget.

The existing test (`packages/core/test/messaging-log.test.ts:175-181`) only pins the loose bound `length < 140` for `chars = 100`, so the small-limit behaviour is unpinned.

## Why it matters

`chars` is the contract a caller uses to bound how much log text enters a model's context. A "maximum" that is exceeded by up to 2.2× at exactly the tight budgets where the bound matters most makes context budgeting unreliable, and the failure is silent — the output looks like a normal clipped entry.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For every positive `chars`, `clip(text, chars).length <= chars` whenever `text.length > chars` (or, if a minimum feasible limit is chosen instead, that minimum is enforced/documented at the schema boundary and `clip` respects every value above it).
- [ ] The omission marker's length is accounted for in the head/tail split at all sizes; at very small limits the marker degrades gracefully (shorter marker or plain truncation) rather than overflowing.
- [ ] The stated omitted-character count stays accurate for the head/tail actually kept.
- [ ] New tests pin the boundary matrix (e.g. `chars` = 1, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100) including length and marker accuracy; the existing `chars = 100` test (head 70 / tail 10 shape) still passes or is updated with the reason recorded.
- [ ] Existing messaging-log tests pass.

title: fix(core): route_usage session targets and plan-window shares ignore the requested window — sessionTargetUsage has no since bound

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`route_usage` session reports mix two different time windows in one report: a session's headline totals are filtered to the requested window (`hours`), but its per-target breakdown — and the plan-window shares computed from it — are summed over **all time**. For any session that started before the window (the common case: default `hours` is 168, plan windows are often 5h), the target rows sum to more than the session's own totals, and a session's "share of the plan window" counts usage from long before that window began.

## Evidence (verified on main `9a4174a9c2`)

- `packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts:681-701` — `sessionTargetUsage(db, sessionIDs)` is the only usage rollup with **no time predicate**: it groups every `route_attempt` row for the named sessions. Every sibling query takes `since`: `sessionUsage` (:659), `targetUsage` (:703), `dailyUsage` (:721), `offerUsage` (:737).
- `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/route-usage.ts:76-84` — `collect` calls `sessionUsage(db, since, …)` and then `sessionTargetUsage(db, sessionIDs)` with no `since`, and feeds both into the same report.
- `packages/core/src/model-usage.ts:190-208` — `sessionReports` builds `targets[]` from those all-time rows, and computes each plan window's `used`/`percent` as `usedOf(window.unit, sum(own.filter(provider)))` over the same all-time rows, despite `SessionWindowUse` being documented (:167) as "what the session used of the window".

Reproduction (temporary bun test against the real Database/ModelRouteLog layer, probe kept by the filer): one session `ses_probe` with two attempts — 900 input tokens at t=1000, 100 input tokens at t=5000.

- `sessionUsage(db, since=3000)` → `{ requests: 1, input: 100 }`
- `sessionTargetUsage(db, ["ses_probe"])` → `{ requests: 2, input: 1000 }`

So `route_usage` with a window starting at 3000 reports a session with 1 request / 100 tokens whose only target row claims 2 requests / 1000 tokens, and any plan-window share for that session is computed from the 1000.

## Why it matters

`route_usage` is the tool the agent and user read to answer "how much of my plan window is gone" and "which sessions used the most". Long-lived sessions are exactly the ones that dominate usage, and they are exactly the ones this corrupts: window shares can be inflated (potentially past 100% of a 5-hour window by days-old usage), and the per-target numbers contradict the session totals in the same output, undermining trust in both.

## Acceptance criteria

- `sessionTargetUsage` (or its call in `route-usage.ts`) is bounded by the same `since` as the rest of the report, so a session's target rows sum to its headline totals for the requested window.
- A session's plan-window share in `sessionReports` is computed from usage inside that plan window (bounded by the window's `windowHours` lookback), not the session's all-time usage — or, if all-time session attribution is deliberately kept for the target list, the window share is computed from a separately window-bounded read and the distinction is documented.
- Regression test: a session with attempts on both sides of the window boundary reports target rows and window shares that only count the in-window attempts (the probe scenario above).
- Existing `model-route-log`, `model-usage` and `route-usage` tests still pass.

Filed by the new-issue-creator (opencode lane) after verification this run; not a duplicate of #550 (that is about windows with no `windowHours` being omitted entirely).

title: fix(tui): Locale.truncate/truncateLeft/truncateMiddle return the whole string at width 0-2 — slice(-0) keeps everything

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/tui
labels.description: Package: tui (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/util
labels.description: Package: util (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The TUI's string truncators return (nearly) the **whole string** when the allowed width is very small — the exact case truncation exists for. The root cause is `slice(-0) === slice(0)`: when the computed keep-count is 0, a negative-index slice keeps everything instead of nothing.

`packages/tui/src/util/locale.ts`:

- `truncateMiddle` (lines 89-97): for `maxLength` 1, `keepStart = 0` and `keepEnd = 0`, so the result is `"" + "…" + str.slice(-0)` = ellipsis + the entire string. For `maxLength` 2, `keepEnd = 0` again, giving first char + ellipsis + the entire string. For `maxLength` 0 it returns ellipsis + all but the first character.
- `truncateLeft` (lines 84-87): for `len` 1, `"…" + str.slice(-(len - 1))` is `"…" + str.slice(-0)` = ellipsis + the entire string; for `len` 0 it drops only the first character.
- `truncate` (lines 51-54): for `len` 0, `str.slice(0, len - 1)` is `slice(0, -1)` = all but the last character, plus an ellipsis.

The same `truncateMiddle` flaw exists verbatim in the second copy at `packages/util/src/path.ts:31-38`.

The neighboring `truncateWidth` in the same file (locale.ts:76-82) handles these cases correctly — `width <= 0` returns `""` and `width === 1` returns `"…"` — which shows the intended contract for the family.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c007c53436`)

Bun probe importing the **real** modules (probe + output kept in the goal's hidden files, `probe-2026-10-27-0335/truncate-locale.ts` / `truncate-real.ts`):

```
Locale.truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 0) → "…bcdefghijklmnop"   (16 chars, max 0)
Locale.truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 1) → "…abcdefghijklmnop"  (17 chars, max 1)
Locale.truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 2) → "a…abcdefghijklmnop" (18 chars, max 2)
Locale.truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 3) → "a…p"                (correct)
Locale.truncateLeft("abcdefghijklmnop", 0)   → "…bcdefghijklmnop"   (16 chars, max 0)
Locale.truncateLeft("abcdefghijklmnop", 1)   → "…abcdefghijklmnop"  (17 chars, max 1)
Locale.truncateLeft("abcdefghijklmnop", 2)   → "…p"                 (correct)
Locale.truncate("abcdefghijklmnop", 0)       → "abcdefghijklmno…"   (16 chars, max 0)
util truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 1)   → "…abcdefghijklmnop"
util truncateMiddle("abcdefghijklmnop", 2)   → "a…abcdefghijklmnop"
```

Widths ≥ 3 (middle) / ≥ 2 (left) behave correctly, which is why ordinary layouts never show this.

## Why it matters

These helpers are called with layout-derived widths that can legitimately reach 1-2 on a narrow terminal or a small dialog:

- `packages/tui/src/ui/dialog-select.tsx:916` — `Locale.truncateMiddle(detail, Math.max(1, width()))`: the caller explicitly clamps to a minimum of 1, i.e. it expects a 1-wide result to work; instead the full detail string is rendered, overflowing the dialog.
- `packages/tui/src/component/prompt/autocomplete.tsx:348,377,514,922` — `Locale.truncateMiddle(..., width)` with widths from the autocomplete layout.
- `packages/tui/src/component/dialog-workspaces.tsx:171` and `dialog-select.tsx:876` — `Locale.truncateLeft(..., titleWidth)` with layout-derived widths.

At exactly the terminal sizes where truncation matters most, the "truncated" text is longer than the original (ellipsis added, nothing removed), breaking the layout the width was computed to protect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] For every `maxLength`/`len` ≥ 0, `Locale.truncate`, `Locale.truncateLeft`, and `Locale.truncateMiddle` return a string no longer than the requested length (with `0 → ""` and `1 → "…"` when the input is longer, matching `truncateWidth`'s contract in the same file).
- [ ] The `truncateMiddle` copy in `packages/util/src/path.ts` gets the same fix (or the two copies are unified); results for widths ≥ 3 are unchanged in both.
- [ ] Regression tests cover widths 0, 1, and 2 for each fixed function (existing tests: `packages/util/src/path.test.ts` for the util copy; TUI locale tests per the repo's tui-tests skill if a suitable test home exists, otherwise unit coverage for the util copy plus the shared contract stated in both places).
- [ ] `bun test` for the touched test files passes from their package directories.

title: fix(core): ModelRouteOverrides.parse drops a malformed schedule and keeps the override — a time-boxed instruction becomes always-on

labels.name: kind/bug
