body:
## Problem

Relative quota-reset times stated in provider error messages are misread when the amount is decimal or compound:

- "in 1.5 hours" is ignored entirely (returns `undefined`) — no retry hint, no quota skip.
- "in 1 hour 30 minutes" is read as 1 hour only — the trailing 30 minutes are silently dropped, so the target is retried / un-skipped half an hour early.

Both message parsers in `packages/core` share the flaw, because both use the same single-integer, single-unit relative-time pattern:

- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:67` — `RELATIVE_TIME = /in\s+(\d+)\s*(second|minute|hour|day|sec|s)s?(?![a-z])/` used by `resetAtFromMessage` (:78) and `retryHintFromMessage` (:93). `retryHintFromMessage` is consumed by the session runner (`packages/core/src/session/runner/step.ts`), and `resetAtFromMessage` by tuning predictions and user notes (`model-route-tuning.ts:137`, `:211`).
- `packages/core/src/model-route-tuning.ts:170` — `parseQuotaReset` repeats the identical `/in\s+(\d+)\s*(...)/` pattern.

## Evidence (verified this run on main c792e04fe0)

Probe run as a temporary `bun test` in `packages/core` (at = `Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1, 14)`), then removed:

- `ModelRouteLimits.resetAtFromMessage("try again in 1.5 hours", at)` → `undefined`
- `ModelRouteLimits.retryHintFromMessage("retry in 1.5 hours", at)` → `undefined`
- `ModelRouteTuning.parseQuotaReset("quota exhausted, back in 1.5 hours", at)` → `undefined`
- `ModelRouteLimits.resetAtFromMessage("try again in 1 hour 30 minutes", at)` → `at + 3_600_000` (1 hour; expected `at + 5_400_000`)
- `ModelRouteTuning.parseQuotaReset("quota exhausted, back in 1 hour 30 minutes", at)` → `at + 3_600_000`
- Control: `ModelRouteLimits.resetMs("1.5h", at)` → `5_400_000` — decimal amounts are already accepted for duration strings in the same module family (`resetMs`, model-route-limits.ts), and compound durations ("6m0s", "1h2m3.5s") are handled there too. Only the message parsers are limited to one integer + one unit.

## Why it matters

A provider that phrases its reset as "1.5 hours" gets no hold at all: the runner retries into a still-exhausted quota and the tuning review never skips the target. A compound phrasing gets a systematically short hold, so the first retry after the computed reset lands while the quota is still gone. These are exactly the messages `parseQuotaReset`'s own header says it reads ("in 3 hours", "in 30 minutes", "in 45s") — decimal and compound amounts are the natural neighbouring forms, and #523 already fixed the same class of gap for the "45s" short form.

## Acceptance criteria

- Both `ModelRouteLimits.resetAtFromMessage` / `retryHintFromMessage` and `ModelRouteTuning.parseQuotaReset` return `now + 5_400_000` for "in 1.5 hours" and for "in 1 hour 30 minutes" (including "and"-joined and abbreviated compound forms if straightforward, e.g. "1h 30m" in message text is out of scope unless trivial).
- All existing single-unit behaviour is unchanged: "in 45s", "in 45 sec", "in 45 seconds", "in 30 minutes", "in 3 hours", "in 2 days" return the same values as today; non-time messages still return `undefined` (existing tests in `model-route-limits.test.ts` and `model-route-tuning.test.ts` keep passing, including `parseQuotaReset("try in 5 minutes")` → `undefined` because the quota-keyword gate is unchanged).
- New targeted tests cover the decimal and compound forms for both parsers in `packages/core/test/model-route-limits.test.ts` and `packages/core/test/model-route-tuning.test.ts`.
- Tests run from `packages/core` (`bun test` on the two files above).

title: fix(core): route governance judges targets at defaultVariant/remap variants the runtime drops when the model doesn't offer them (PR #512)

body:
# fix(core): route governance judges targets at defaultVariant/remap variants the runtime drops when the model doesn't offer them (PR #512)

## Finding

PR #512 made `ModelGovernance.assertAllowed` judge route targets at their effective variant, but `routeTargets` in `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts` (lines 182–189 on main `dfe3251890`) computes that variant from the **raw config values**:

- `object.defaultVariant` is used unconditionally when no variant is requested;
- `object.variants[requested]` is used unconditionally when a variant is requested.

The runtime never uses those raw values. The model-routes plugin expansion filters both against the target model's **natively offered variants** before they reach the resolver:

- `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:274–276` — `defaultVariant` is kept only if `model.variants.some((item) => item.id === spec.defaultVariant)`;
- `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:278–282` — a `variants` remap entry is kept only if the target model natively offers the remap's *target* variant;
- the filtered values become `targetVariants` (`model-routes.ts:86–89`), and `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:496–502` resolves `target.variant ?? mapped`, where `mapped` falls back to the requested variant only when the target offers it natively, else `undefined` (the target runs bare / at its default).

## Why it matters

When a target's configured `defaultVariant` (or a remap's target variant) is not natively offered by the target model, governance and runtime judge different runs:

- **Governance bypass:** target `{ model: "p/m", defaultVariant: "high" }` where `p/m` offers no `high` variant, with policy `excludedModels: ["p/m#default"]`. Governance judges the target at `#high` and passes it; the runtime drops the default and runs bare `p/m`, whose effective variant is `default` — the excluded variant runs.
- **Allowed-list bypass:** with `models: ["p/m#high"]` as the only allowed entry, governance passes the route; the runtime runs `p/m` at its default variant, which the allowed list does not permit.
- **Over-deny (reverse):** with `excludedModels: ["p/m#high"]`, governance denies a bare route selection even though the runtime would run the target bare, because the unusable `defaultVariant: "high"` never takes effect.
- The same divergence applies to a remap such as `variants: { low: "high" }` when the target model does not offer `high`: the plugin drops the remap (the runtime then runs `#low` if native, else bare), while governance judges `#high`.

PR #512's own tests use a `defaultVariant`/remap that the (mocked) target is assumed to offer, so the unfiltered path is never exercised.

## Evidence

- PR #512 (merged): `routeTargets` in `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts`, diff hunk adding `object?.defaultVariant` / `object?.variants?.[requested] ?? requested`.
- Runtime filtering: `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:274–282`; resolver consumption: `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:496–502`.
- Verified on current main `dfe32518902d896f09dabc9bc84d7f20a7f0e971` by reading both code paths after a fresh `git fetch`.
- Deduped: no open or closed issue covers this (searches for "routeTargets governance variant", "defaultVariant governance", "wildcard route target governance" return only #506, the issue PR #512 fixed).

## Acceptance criteria

- Governance judges a route target at the same effective variant the resolver will run, for the case where the configured `defaultVariant` or a remap target variant is not among the target model's offered variants (governance will need access to the target model's offered variants, or to the plugin's already-expanded/filtered target data, rather than re-deriving from raw config).
- Regression tests in `packages/core/test/session/model-governance.test.ts` cover at least: (a) unusable `defaultVariant` + excluded `#default` denies the bare route; (b) unusable `defaultVariant` + excluded `#<that variant>` does not deny the bare route; (c) a remap whose target variant is not offered is judged at the variant the runtime actually runs.
- Existing #512 tests (usable `defaultVariant`, usable remap, plain target at requested variant) still pass.

title: fix(core): a model-less child is governance-checked against the parent's model but actually runs the global default (PR #468)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Finding

PR #468's governance check computes the model a child will run as: explicit choice → override/default chain → **the parent's model** (spec §4.2: "the parent's model is what gets checked, because that is what the child inherits"). Nothing implements that inheritance:

- `Session.create` stores only `input.model`; a model-less child has `session.model === undefined`.
- At run time, `SessionRunnerModel.resolve` (`packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts` ~:84-88) sees `!session.model` and falls back to `resolver.resolve()` — the **globally configured default model**, not the parent's model.

So a child created with no model is governance-checked against the parent's model (or not checked at all when the parent is also model-less — the check returns early) and then actually runs the global default, which may be outside the subtree's allowed set or on its excluded list.

## Reachability

- `POST /api/session` with `parentID` and an agent that has no configured default model, and no `model` in the request.
- The plugin host's `sessions.create({ parentID })` (`packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts`).
- The same root affects a model-less child's `switchAgent`, whose check also falls back to a model the session will not run.
- The Task tool and command-subagent paths always pass an explicit model and are not affected.

## Evidence

Verified on current main ffbc8562f2: the checked-model chain and early return in `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts` (~:252-257), creation storing only `input.model` in `packages/core/src/session.ts`, and the runner's global-default fallback in `packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts`.

## Acceptance criteria

- A model-less child's effective model is governance-checked as the model it will actually run: either creation resolves and stores the inherited/default model and checks that, or the runner's fallback for governed children is the checked (parent) model — with the behavior consistent between `Session.create` and child `switchAgent`.
- A regression test creates a model-less child under a policy that excludes the global default model and shows the excluded model cannot run (creation denied, or the child runs the checked parent model).

Filed by the pr-diff-review job, 2026-10-26 run (addendum 3: governance reviewer final report reconciled and re-verified by the parent).

title: fix(core): forking a child session launders it out of ancestor governance — fork is projected top-level (parent_id null), switches and descendants escape policies above the source (PR #468)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/high

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

body:
## Finding

PR #468's spec (§6.2, `specs/2026-10-25-subsession-model-governance.md:272`) states: *"`Session.fork` creates a child whose parent is the source session."* The implementation does the opposite, and the difference silently removes governance from a whole subtree:

- `packages/core/src/session/projector.ts` (~:160-172): the forked session is inserted with **`parent_id: null`** (`fork_session_id` records the source instead), copying only the source's own `subagent_policy`.
- The one-time fork check in `packages/core/src/session.ts` validates only the copied model at the fork instant, against the source as parent.

Consequences, all reachable by forking a **child** session (`POST /api/session/:id/fork`):

1. The fork is top-level, so `switchAgent`/`switchModel` skip governance entirely — both guard on `session.parentID` (`packages/core/src/session/session.ts`, child-only checks added by PRs #468/#486). The fork can be switched to any excluded model unchecked.
2. The fork's own children are governed only by the copied policy: the governance (and depth) walks follow `parentID` only and never traverse `fork_session_id`, so every ancestor policy **above** the source — e.g. the primary session's `models`/`excludedModels` — silently drops out of the subtree.

Forking a governed child therefore launders it out of its ancestor policies: same agent, same model, same history — minus the restrictions.

## Evidence

Verified on current main ffbc8562f2: projector insert (`parent_id: null`, `fork_session_id: event.data.parentID`, `subagent_policy: parent.subagent_policy`), spec §6.2 text, the fork-time check in `packages/core/src/session.ts`, and the `parentID` guards in `packages/core/src/session/session.ts`. Existing fork governance tests (`packages/core/test/session-governance.test.ts:167/186`) cover forking a session whose own policy excludes its model, and policy copying — not forking a child out from under a grandparent's policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- Forking a child session does not escape ancestor governance: either the fork stays linked into the governance chain (its switches and its descendants' creation are checked against the source's ancestors' policies as well as the copied policy), or the escape is an explicitly documented, spec-amended decision with the fork-time check applying the full ancestor chain.
- A regression test forks a grandchild under a primary policy that excludes its model and shows the fork cannot be switched to — or launched with children on — the excluded model (or documents the accepted behavior if the design decision goes the other way).

Filed by the pr-diff-review job, 2026-10-26 run (addendum 3: governance reviewer final report reconciled and re-verified by the parent; this corrects the run's first-pass fork disposition, which had verified only the fork-time check).

body:
## Problem

In `packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts` many fields call `.pipe(optional).annotate({ description })`. The `optional` helper wraps the schema in `optionalKey` and `decodeTo`, and a description on that outer schema never reaches the generated JSON schema, so `packages/protocol/openapi.json` and editors show no description for them. The keys added in #233 annotate first and then call `.pipe(optional)`, and #233 moved `autonomy`, `selection` and `weights` over because it rewrote their text.

Still annotated outside `optional`: `defaultVariant` and `until` on a target object, `softLimit` in a budget, every `Health` field, every `Window` field, the `Schedule` and `GlobalSchedule` fields, and `budgets`, `hedgeAfterMs`, `attempts` and `schedules` on a route, plus the `Tuning` and `Log` fields.

#234 edits the `maxResponseTimeMs` and `minOutputTokensPerSecond` descriptions in `Health`, so moving those lines is best done after #234 merges.

Fix: annotate before `.pipe(optional)` for each, then run `bun run generate` in `packages/protocol` and `services/www` and check that `packages/client` `check:generated` stays clean.

Raised by CodeRabbit in review of #233.



## Acceptance criteria

- Every field listed in this issue annotates before `.pipe(optional)`: target `defaultVariant`/`until`, budget `softLimit`, all `Health` and `Window` fields, `Schedule`/`GlobalSchedule` fields, route `budgets`/`hedgeAfterMs`/`attempts`/`schedules`, and the `Tuning` and `Log` fields.
- `bun run generate` in `packages/protocol` and `services/www` is re-run and the descriptions appear in the generated OpenAPI document (`packages/protocol/openapi.json`).
- `packages/client` `check:generated` stays clean.

title: Should a pinned nested pool run its members through their level remaps?

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

labels.name: kind/question
labels.description: A decision or question to resolve

body:
## Question

When a nested pool is pinned as `opencode-route/<id>#<level>`, each member runs at its own native variant of that name. A member's remap for that level is ignored: a target `{ "model": "p/m", "variants": { "max": "high" } }` or a `variantRules` entry mapping `max` to `high` makes no difference, and a member without a native `max` is left out. Selected directly at `max`, the same pool runs that member at `high`.

This is how pins behaved before #233, and #233 keeps it: the test "a nested pool pinned to a variant brings only the matched models that have it, at that variant" in `packages/core/test/model-routes-matching.test.ts` and the pin text in `config.mdx` describe it. #233 does make a pinned pool leave out members that sit the level out with `false`, because `false` promises the member is never used at that level.

Running a pinned pool's members through their remaps would match what selecting the pool at that level does. It would also change existing configurations: a member with a native `max` and a remap `max -> high` would run at `high` under the pin, where it runs at `max` today. That is a behaviour decision, so it is not in #233.

Raised in review of #233 by Copilot.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is recorded on this issue: pinned nested pools either run members through their level remaps, or the current native-variant-only behaviour is confirmed as intended.
- [ ] `packages/core/test/model-routes-matching.test.ts` (or its successor) pins the decided behaviour, including the member-with-`false` exclusion and a member whose remap differs from its native variant.
- [ ] The pin behaviour text in the route-pool docs (`config.mdx`) matches the decision.

body:
## Question

Should we enable `OPENCODE_EXPERIMENTAL_NATIVE_LLM` (OpenCode's own request layer instead of the AI SDK provider packages)? Examine it in detail and adopt it if there is a real advantage.

## Context

- Currently held OFF deliberately (decided 2026-10-20) while the rest of the experimental flag set was enabled.
- Concrete pain the AI SDK layer has already caused here: a custom provider wired with `@ai-sdk/openai-compatible` failed at runtime (`t.responses is not a function`) where `@ai-sdk/openai` worked — provider-package quirks are a real cost.
- The fork's heavy use cases: Codex OAuth models with effort levels, OpenCode Go models, Cloudflare gateway models, custom OpenAI-compatible providers.

## To examine

- Feature parity per provider: streaming, tool calls, reasoning/effort controls, structured output, image input, cache tokens, error surfacing.
- Where native is ahead/behind the SDK packages today (changelog + source), and how fast the gap is moving.
- Failure modes: does native surface errors better than the SDK (which has hidden a 402 as a silent multi-minute stream hang in our testing)?

## Benchmark plan (required before a decision)

- Same prompt set (small/medium/agentic coding tasks) through 3+ providers, native on vs off: time-to-first-token, tokens/sec, total time, error rate, cost accounting accuracy.
- Note any behavioral differences in tool-call formatting or reasoning-effort mapping.

## Decision criteria

Adopt if: parity on the providers above + measurably better latency, error surfacing, or one less class of SDK translation bugs. Otherwise record why not and re-check in a release cycle or two.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Feature-parity matrix for the fork's providers (Codex OAuth, OpenCode Go, Cloudflare gateway, custom OpenAI-compatible) documented in this issue — streaming, tool calls, reasoning/effort controls, structured output, image input, cache tokens, error surfacing — native on vs off.
- [ ] Benchmark results posted for the same prompt set through at least 3 providers, native on vs off: time-to-first-token, tokens/sec, total time, error rate, cost-accounting accuracy.
- [ ] An adopt / do-not-adopt decision recorded in this issue with the evidence; if adopted, the flag is enabled in config with a one-line rollback note.

title: re.py in the OpenCode tmp folder shadows Python's standard re module

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: area/infra
labels.description: Infrastructure, deployment, and operations

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Summary

A file named re.py sits in the shared OpenCode temp folder ~/.local/share/opencode/tmp/opencode/. Python puts the working directory (for python -c and -m) and the script's own directory on sys.path, so any Python process started from that folder imports this file as the standard re module and fails at startup.

## Reproduction

Observed on macOS with nix Python 3.14.7 (/nix/store/...-python3-3.14.7):

~~~
cd ~/.local/share/opencode/tmp/opencode
python3 -c "import json"
~~~

Result (abridged):

~~~
File ".../opencode/re.py", line 25, in <module>
    import logging
...
AttributeError: module 're' has no attribute 'escape' (consider renaming '.../opencode/re.py' since it has the same name as the standard library module named 're' and prevents importing that standard library module)
~~~

uv run with a script inside that folder fails the same way, because the script's directory is put first on sys.path.

## The file

- Path: ~/.local/share/opencode/tmp/opencode/re.py, 8,357 bytes, modified 2026-10-18 02:04.
- Contents: an Alembic helper module from the operations-portal repository (its docstring describes helpers for Alembic revisions). It is not an OpenCode file. How it got into the shared temp folder is unknown.

## Impact

One command in an affected session failed before it ran. The error looked like a broken Python install until the traceback named the file.

## Workaround

python3 -I (isolated mode) keeps the working directory and the script directory off sys.path. Running from another directory also works. The file was left in place because it is not ours to delete.

## Requests

1. Find what writes module-named files (re.py, or any other standard library module name) into the shared tmp root, and stop it.
2. Keep the shared tmp root free of Python modules. A per-session or per-tool subdirectory is enough.
3. Document python3 -I for tools that run Python from the tmp folder.

## Environment

- macOS (darwin), uv, nix Python 3.14.7
- OpenCode tmp folder: ~/.local/share/opencode/tmp/opencode (pre-created, approved for external access)

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The writer of stdlib-named files (`re.py`) into the shared tmp root is identified and stopped, or proven external and a guard/cleanup is in place.
- [ ] The shared tmp root contains no Python modules named after standard-library modules.
- [ ] Verification: `python3 -c "import json"` run from inside the tmp root succeeds.

body:
## Problem

The `unit (linux)` job on current main crashed mid-suite: **turbo itself segfaulted**, so the run's failure reads as ordinary test failures while most of the affected suite never executed — including `@opencode/core:test`, the package the validated merge changed.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-19)

Run [39182188357](https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/actions/runs/39182188357) — `test` workflow, push to main at `b3e93cd0` (merge of PR #88, the #87 subagent-cycle fix), job `unit (linux)` (117837096275), 00:45:17Z–00:48:18Z:

Test summaries actually printed before the crash:

- `@opencode/server:test` — 104 pass / 0 fail (32 files)
- `@opencode/simulation:test` — 47 pass / 0 fail (9 files)
- `@opencode/sdk` test — 37 pass / 2 fail (39 tests; both failures are the already-tracked #62 transport assertions)

Then, at 00:48:12Z, `@opencode/cli:test` started (`cache miss, executing cfbd54e631d40ea2`), and ~1.6s later:

```
error: Failed to run "turbo" due to signal SIGSEGV
... line 6:  2309 Segmentation fault      (core dumped) GITHUB_ACTIONS=false bun turbo test --affected --concurrency=3
##[error]Process completed with exit code 139.
```

No `@opencode/core:test` group ever opens in the log. `packages/core` is where PR #88 landed (`packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts`), so **current main has no unit (linux) verdict for core at all** — the only visible failures are the two pre-existing #62 sdk tests, which makes the run look like a routine known-failure run.

The sibling `unit (windows)` job in the same run completed its suite (failures: the same 2 #62 tests + the known Windows `#!/bin/sh` mcpx ensureDaemon spawn test) — the crash is linux-job-only in this instance.

## Scope check

- Searched the failed logs of 8 other recent `test` workflow runs (39181436767, 39172821410, 39165632602, 39164913828, 39164101664, 39163561017, 39162690752, 39155385642): no other SIGSEGV. This is a **single verified sighting** so far — filed because the crash silently truncates coverage on the current main, not because it is known to be frequent.
- Turbo is used only in this repo among the four fork repos (no turbo in code/openchamber/nix workflows or package.json), so this is a single-repo issue, not a cross-repo set.
- Not #62 (the sdk assertion failures are real but separate, and they did report), not #61 (timeout caps), not #72 (ripgrep cluster did not appear in this run).

## Why it matters

A test-orchestrator crash that leaves the job summary indistinguishable from ordinary test failures silently erases CI signal: reviewers and sweeps triage the visible failures (#62) and move on, while the package that actually changed ships with no unit verdict. It already happened once on the merge that most needed the verdict.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A re-run (or a new push) produces a complete `unit (linux)` run for `b3e93cd0` or a later main head in which `@opencode/core:test` reports a summary, so main has a real core verdict.
- [ ] On any recurrence, the turbo and bun versions in play and the runner's core dump / dmesg tail are captured on this issue (the unit step runs `bun turbo test --affected --concurrency=3`; the sibling `affected` job pins `turbo@2.10.2` — record which binary actually segfaulted).
- [ ] The unit job distinguishes an orchestrator crash from test failures in its outcome — e.g. per-package test steps/jobs, or a wrapper that retries once on exit 139 and annotates the run — so a truncated suite cannot masquerade as a complete red run.
- [ ] If a re-run plus several subsequent main runs show no recurrence, close with that evidence and keep the distinguishing measure (or record why it is not needed).

body:
## What I found

The fork does not bundle mcpx. Its flake builds `opencode` with an optional `mcpx` argument and links the binary only when one is passed:

- `flake.nix`, overlay and packages: `mcpx = final.mcpx or null` and `mcpx = pkgs.mcpx or null`
- `nix/opencode.nix`: `mcpx ? null`, then `lib.optional (mcpx != null) mcpx` on the PATH and `ln -s ${mcpx}/bin/mcpx $out/bin/mcpx`

So `nix build github:developing-today/opencode` gives an `opencode` with no `mcpx` next to it, because nothing in this flake provides `pkgs.mcpx`. The only consumer I know is `dezren39/nix`, which builds mcpx from its own vendored copy and passes it in with `.override { inherit mcpx; }`. That repo is about to drop the copy and take mcpx from `developing-today/code` instead.

The core code depends on the CLI. `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/mcpx.ts` and its tests (`mcpx-daemon-autostart.test.ts`, `tool-mcpx*.test.ts`) start and call the daemon, with `OPENCODE_MCPX_BIN` and related variables to point at it. I did not check what a user sees when the binary is missing.

## Questions

1. What happens in `opencode` when `mcpx` is not on the PATH and `OPENCODE_MCPX_BIN` is unset? Is the failure clear?
2. Should this flake keep mcpx optional, default to the build in `developing-today/code`, or fail the build when it is absent?
3. If a default is added, which rev of code does it pin, and who updates that pin?

The maintainer decides this. Whatever is chosen should be written next to the `mcpx ? null` argument and in the README.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Behavior without mcpx is checked and recorded here.
- [ ] The flake either provides mcpx, or says in a comment and in the README that the consumer must.
- [ ] A check builds `packages.<system>.opencode` and asserts whether `bin/mcpx` exists, matching the decision.

Related: developing-today/code#308 (how downstream flakes consume mcpx).

body:
## Problem

`TODO.md` ("Still open" under the supervisor and handoff section) lists two gaps in the `opencode serve` handover that nothing tracks as an issue.

1. **Systemd is untested.** `Type=notify` needs `NotifyAccess=all`, because when the wrapper starts the server the notifying process is the server child, not the unit's main pid. The handover tests stand in for systemd with a socket the test process owns and a fake notify socket. Nobody has run it under a real systemd user session.
2. **A teardown race remains.** A connection the predecessor accepted in the last instant before it closes can get a `503` (`service_stopping`) or a reset when its request arrives after teardown begins. In `packages/cli/test/serve-handover.test.ts`, about a thousand requests across handovers showed none, and the control run (no supervisor socket) showed one per run. So the race is rare, but it is not shown to be gone.

## What to do

1. Write a unit file with `Type=notify` and `NotifyAccess=all`, run two generations through a real handover on a systemd host, and record the result here.
2. Decide whether the teardown race needs a fix. If it does, the predecessor should keep answering what it has accepted until its drain ends, and the test should run enough requests to show a difference.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A real systemd handover is run and its output is attached.
- [ ] The teardown race is either fixed with a test that fails before the fix, or the measured rate is written in `TODO.md` with the reason it is accepted.

title: fix(core): mcpx daemon client has no timeout and no response-body cap — a hung daemon hangs the tool call forever, oversized bodies buffer whole

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The mcpx daemon HTTP client in `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/mcpx.ts` has **no timeout and no response-body size cap** on any call:

- `send()` (mcpx.ts:207-217) does `await res.text()` for error bodies and `await res.json()` for success bodies — both buffer the whole body unbounded.
- `callDaemon()` (mcpx.ts:219-243) builds the fetch init with method/headers/body only — **no `AbortSignal`** on either the `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` HTTP path (:236) or the unix-socket path (:240). No caller adds one either (call sites at mcpx.ts:361, 396, 449-494 and `mcpx-projection.ts`/`mcpx-secrets.ts` pass `callDaemon` through unwrapped).

The same file already bounds the sibling path: the CLI fallback `runCli` runs with `maxBuffer: 16 * 1024 * 1024` (mcpx.ts:190). The daemon path — the primary path — has no equivalent bound. The package also already owns the bounded reader `readBoundedResponseText` (`packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts`) used by the fixes for #960/#1017.

## Evidence (main ccd0cb2398; verified this run)

Laptop probe with the **real** `callDaemon` imported from the repo, against a local stub daemon (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-mcpx-daemon/probe.ts`, `MCPX_DAEMON_ENDPOINT` pointed at it):

- **Oversized success body:** a 48 MiB JSON body was accepted whole — returned `pad` length 50,331,648; process RSS **+90 MiB**.
- **Oversized error body:** a 48 MiB 500 body became the `DaemonHTTPError` message verbatim — message length **50,331,679 chars**, i.e. the whole body is carried into the error that surfaces as a tool failure.
- **Hung daemon:** an endpoint that accepts the connection and never responds left `callDaemon("/hang")` **still pending after 5,000 ms** — there is no timeout at any layer. This also defeats `ensureDaemon`'s own 1.5 s health-poll deadline (mcpx.ts:305-318): the loop's first `callDaemon("/v1/health")` can block forever, so daemon startup detection itself can hang.

## Why it matters

Every mcpx tool call (`/v1/call`, `/v1/exec`, `/v1/tools`, `/v1/log`, …) flows through this one client. A wedged or misbehaving daemon — a crashed-but-listening process, a daemon stuck mid-reload, a socket answered by the wrong process — hangs the tool call (and the session turn waiting on it) indefinitely instead of failing as `DaemonUnreachableError` and falling back to the CLI, which is the designed degradation (`send`'s own comment, mcpx.ts:205-206). An oversized response (e.g. `/v1/log` or a tool result gone wrong) buffers without bound, and on the error path the entire body is embedded in the exception message shown to the model/user.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `callDaemon` fetches carry a named, explicit timeout (per-call `AbortSignal.timeout` or equivalent); a daemon that accepts but never responds fails within that bound as unreachable/error, letting the existing CLI fallback engage — it must not hang.
- [ ] Success and error bodies are read through a bounded path with a named, documented cap sized for legitimate daemon payloads (the CLI fallback's 16 MiB `maxBuffer` in the same file is the precedent); over-cap bodies fail with an error naming the endpoint and cap, and the error path truncates instead of embedding the whole body in `DaemonHTTPError`.
- [ ] `ensureDaemon`'s health-poll loop can actually observe its 1.5 s deadline when the daemon socket accepts but never answers.
- [ ] Tests pin: small daemon responses unchanged (health/tools/call), over-cap success body rejected, over-cap error body truncated/rejected, and a never-responding daemon failing within the timeout (run via CI or laptop — no sandbox builds).

title: fix(core): MCP OAuth configured discovery fetches the metadata document with no timeout and no body size cap

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

MCP OAuth authorization-server discovery, when the user configures `oauth.auth_server_metadata_url`, fetches that document with **no timeout and no body size cap**:

- `packages/core/src/mcp/oauth.ts:107-121` — `configuredDiscovery()` calls `input.fetchFn(url, { headers: { accept: "application/json" } })` (line 113: no `signal`, so no `AbortSignal.timeout`), then `const body = await response.json()` (line 115: buffers the whole body, no cap).
- The `fetchFn` implementations add neither: the shared `send` (`oauth.ts:43-53`) is a bare `fetch` wrapper whose only extra behaviour is refresh de-duplication, and the `loggedFetch` wrapper (`oauth.ts:55-105`) only logs.

The URL is entirely config-controlled: it names whatever authorization server a configured remote MCP server (or a pasted config snippet) points at. An RFC 8414 metadata document is a few kilobytes. A slow endpoint hangs MCP connect/authorize indefinitely (no timeout to fire), and a fast hostile endpoint can deliver an arbitrarily large body that `response.json()` buffers whole before the zod schemas ever run.

The bounded helper already exists in this package: `readBoundedResponseText` in `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts:39`, and sibling provider paths cap their bodies (#960's 64 KiB utility-title cap; the generated client's 16 MiB cap in #1007).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d2af8df514`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-mcp-oauth-cap/probe.ts`, bun, real `configuredDiscovery` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD, `fetchFn: fetch`) served a 50,331,843-byte metadata document (valid `issuer`/`authorization_endpoint`/`token_endpoint` fields plus a 48 MiB `pad` field) from a local HTTP server:

- `discovery OK issuer: https://issuer.example.com` — the whole 50 MB body was buffered and parsed, no rejection.
- Process RSS grew by **90 MiB** for that one discovery fetch.

Code reading confirms the missing timeout: the only init passed is `{ headers: … }` (`oauth.ts:113`), and neither `send` nor `loggedFetch` injects a signal.

Dedup: `gh` search for "oauth discovery" returns #199 (closed — MCP OAuth SDK adaptation, discovery *probes*/prompt parameter, not body bounds) and #193 (unrelated headless hang). No open or closed issue covers a cap or timeout for `configuredDiscovery`.

## Why it matters

MCP connect is an automatic path: adding or starting a configured remote MCP server triggers this fetch. A malicious or compromised MCP config — a documented supply-chain surface, since configs are commonly pasted from READMEs — gets an unbounded-memory, unbounded-time fetch in the agent process before any schema validation can reject the document.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `configuredDiscovery` fetches with an explicit timeout (named duration, in line with sibling provider fetches' 3–10 s) so a silent endpoint fails discovery instead of hanging connect/authorize.
- [ ] The metadata body is read through a bounded path with a named, documented cap sized generously for an RFC 8414 document (kilobytes in practice), rejecting over-cap declared `Content-Length` before consuming and over-cap streamed bodies in flight with the body cancelled.
- [ ] Failure modes stay legible: timeout and over-cap produce errors that name the discovery URL's origin and the cause, consistent with the existing `HTTP <status>` error style in this function.
- [ ] Tests pin: a normal small metadata document discovers as before; an over-cap body fails; a never-responding endpoint fails at the timeout rather than hanging. Tests run in CI or on the laptop — no sandbox builds.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed metadata under the cap, on either call path (`provider()` discovery state and `authorize()`).

title: fix(client): service probe buffers the whole /api/info body unbounded — response.json() with no size cap in service-probe

body:
## Problem

The client service probe buffers the entire `/api/info` response body with `response.json()` — no size cap, no `Content-Length` pre-check, no streamed byte count:

- `packages/client/src/service-probe.ts:52-60` — `probeResult()` fetches `new URL("/api/info", info.url)` with an `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` (bounds *time*, not *bytes*), then `body: response.status === 404 ? undefined : ((await response.json()) as unknown)` (line 58).

The URL comes from the local service registration (`service.json`, see `fallback()` in the same file): whoever or whatever is registered there decides what this fetch talks to. A healthy response is a tiny struct — `decodeInfo()` in the same file only ever reads `version` (string) and `pid` (non-negative integer) — so every byte past a few kilobytes is pure trust in the registered endpoint.

This is the same failure class the rest of the client already fixed: the generated client's `json()` caps at 16 MiB (#1007) and its binary path now has a cap (#1015). The hand-written probe path was missed.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d2af8df514`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-service-probe-cap/probe.ts`, bun, real `probeResult` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD) served a 50,331,687-byte JSON body `{"version":"1.2.3","pid":4242,"pad":"<48 MiB of x>"}` from a local HTTP server:

- `probe result state: ready compatible: true` — the 50 MB body was buffered and parsed in full, then classified as a healthy service.
- Process RSS grew by **89 MiB** for that one probe.

`probeResult` runs during service discovery/`ensure()` — i.e. automatically, whenever a client starts against a registered service — so the blow-up needs no explicit user action beyond a bad registration or a misbehaving endpoint.

Dedup: `gh` search for "service-probe" returns only unrelated numeric-boundary issues (#1010/#999/#1000/#1004/#957) — no issue covers this body read. The capped generated-client paths (#1007/#1015) are a different file/mechanism.

## Why it matters

An unbounded automatic probe turns a stale, wrong, or hostile registered endpoint into a memory blow-up of the client process at startup, with no error naming the body size as the cause — exactly the pattern #960/#1007/#1015 eliminated elsewhere in this codebase.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `probeResult` reads the `/api/info` body through a bounded path with a named, documented cap sized for the tiny info struct (kilobytes of headroom, not megabytes), rejecting over-cap declared `Content-Length` before consuming and over-cap streamed bodies in flight with the body cancelled.
- [ ] An over-cap or unreadable body keeps the current classification semantics (treated like an unparseable probe answer — `service: undefined`), rather than crashing discovery.
- [ ] The module stays free of the Effect runtime (the file header requires this: it is shared by the Effect and Promise clients).
- [ ] Tests pin: a normal small info body classifies as before; an over-cap body (declared and streamed) does not classify as a ready service and does not buffer the whole body. Tests run in CI or on the laptop — no sandbox builds.

body:
## Problem

The Copilot and Modal model-list loaders buffer the entire `/models` response body with `response.json()` — no size cap, no `Content-Length` pre-check, no streamed byte count:

- `packages/core/src/github-copilot/models.ts:83-95` — `load()` fetches `${baseURL}/models` with only `AbortSignal.timeout(5_000)`, then `decodeResponse(await response.json())` (line 89).
- `packages/core/src/modal/models.ts:60-71` — `load()` fetches `${baseURL}/models` with only `AbortSignal.timeout(3_000)`, then `decodeResponse(await response.json())` (line 67).

A timeout bounds *time*, not *bytes*: a fast local or misbehaving endpoint can deliver hundreds of megabytes inside 3–5 s. Both `baseURL`s are ultimately endpoint-controlled (Copilot: the account/enterprise endpoint discovery; Modal: the configured provider base URL), and a real model list is kilobytes — so the buffered body is almost entirely trust.

The bounded helper already exists in the same package and is the house pattern: `readBoundedResponseText` in `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts:39`, used by the Copilot utility-title path with a named 64 KiB cap (#960). The generated client caps JSON at 16 MiB (#1007). These two loaders were simply never given the same treatment.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `d2af8df514`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-models-cap/probe.ts`, run with bun against the real `CopilotModels.load` / `ModalModels.load` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD) served a 49,200,010-byte `{"data":[…]}` body of decode-dropping junk entries from a local HTTP server:

- `copilot load OK, models: 0` — the whole 49 MB body was buffered and parsed, no rejection.
- `modal load OK, models: 0` — same.
- Process RSS grew by **295 MiB** while handling the two responses.

Dedup: `gh` search for "models list cap", "copilot models", and the `http-body` cluster returns #923 (four core/ai *download* paths — media/skill/ripgrep/CodeMode, not these loaders), #929 (MessagingEmbedding download, closed), #960/#1007 (the caps these loaders should mirror). No open or closed issue covers the Copilot/Modal `/models` loaders.

## Why it matters

Model loading runs automatically at provider load / session start, not on an explicit user download. An oversized or hostile endpoint response turns a routine startup into a memory blow-up (OOM kill of the whole agent process) with no diagnostic naming the cause — the same failure class #960, #1007, #1015 and #923 were filed to eliminate, in two loaders they missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both loaders read the `/models` body through a bounded path (e.g. `readBoundedResponseText` from `tool/http-body.ts`) with a named, documented cap sized generously for a real model list (cf. 64 KiB utility-title cap, 16 MiB generated-client cap — pick and justify one).
- [ ] An over-cap declared `Content-Length` is rejected before the body is consumed; a streamed/chunked over-cap body is rejected in flight and the body is cancelled, matching the helper's existing behaviour.
- [ ] The failure error names the loader/endpoint and the cap, so an OOM becomes a diagnosable error.
- [ ] Tests pin: a normal small model list loads unchanged for both providers; an over-cap body (declared and streamed) fails with the named error. Tests run in CI or on the laptop — no sandbox builds.
- [ ] No behaviour change for well-formed responses under the cap.

title: fix(client,httpapi-codegen): generated client's binary path buffers the whole response with response.arrayBuffer() — no cap, unlike its capped json() and SSE paths

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Problem

The generated client's binary response path buffers the whole body with no size cap — the one response path in that client the #1007 fix (merged as PR #1008/#1012) did not bound:

- `packages/client/src/promise/generated/client.ts:391`: `if (descriptor.binary) return new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer()) as A` — no `Content-Length` pre-check, no streaming byte count, no cap.
- The template that generates it: `packages/httpapi-codegen/src/index.ts:1218` splices exactly that line in when any endpoint has a binary success schema.
- The same generated file's `json()` helper (client.ts:2627-2655, from the #1007 fix) bounds its body at the named `maxJsonBodyBytes = 16 * 1024 * 1024` cap (client.ts:336): it rejects an over-cap declared `Content-Length` up front and counts streamed bytes, throwing `ClientError("ResponseTooLarge")`. The SSE path has its own 16 MiB event bound. The binary path has neither.
- The only endpoint currently marked `binary: true` is `file.read` (`GET /api/fs/read/...`, client.ts:1675) — reading a file through the server. A large (or hostile / misconfigured) server response is therefore buffered whole into memory by any consumer of the promise client, with no way for the caller to bound it.

This is not a re-file of #1007: that issue's scope was `json()`/`response.text()`, it is closed, and its fix's own infrastructure (`maxJsonBodyBytes`, `ResponseTooLarge`, fire-and-forget body cancel on over-cap exits) is exactly what the binary path bypasses.

## Verified behaviour (laptop probe, main `53f0e12541`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-client-binary-cap/probe.ts` — the real `OpenCode.make` promise client from the laptop clone at the same HEAD, with a stub `fetch`:

- control, binary 2-byte body → resolved, `byteLength = 2` (existing behaviour intact).
- binary, 64 MiB streamed body, no `Content-Length` → **resolved, `byteLength = 67108864`** — the whole body buffered, no error.
- binary, 64 MiB body with `Content-Length: 67108864` declared → **resolved, `byteLength = 67108864`** — even the cheap declared-length pre-check `json()` performs is absent.
- control, JSON endpoint (`file.list`) with the same 64 MiB streamed body → **threw `ClientError: ResponseTooLarge`** — the #1007 cap working as designed on the sibling path.

## Why it matters

`file.read` is the client's file-content door: file sizes are user/server-controlled, not protocol-bounded, so an unbounded `arrayBuffer()` turns a big file (or a compromised / wrong server — the client takes an arbitrary `baseUrl`) into an unbounded memory allocation in every embedding process (app, desktop, SDK consumers). The fix pattern, cap constant, and error type already exist in the same generated file — the binary path is the inconsistent outlier, the same shape as #1007 was for `json()`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The generated client's binary path enforces a named size cap (reusing `maxJsonBodyBytes` / `ResponseTooLarge`, or a documented binary-specific cap with a stated rationale): an over-cap declared `Content-Length` is rejected without consuming the body, and a streamed body is counted as it arrives and rejected once over cap (with the body cancelled, matching the `json()` over-cap exit behaviour).
- [ ] The change is made in the `packages/httpapi-codegen` template and the generated client is regenerated (`bun run generate` from `packages/client` per the repo AGENTS.md) — generated files are not hand-edited as the source of truth.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/client/test/promise.test.ts` pin: a small binary body still resolves byte-for-byte (existing `file.read` test passes unchanged), an over-cap streamed binary body rejects with `ResponseTooLarge`, and an over-cap declared `Content-Length` rejects.
- [ ] `json()` and SSE behaviour are unchanged.

body:
## Problem

`ReadToolFileSystem.read` (`packages/core/src/tool/read-filesystem.ts`) never normalises its `PageInput` at the service boundary. The schema (`PageInput`, read-filesystem.ts:69-72) declares `offset`/`limit` as `NonNegativeInt`, but the exported `read(files, input, resource, page)` function (read-filesystem.ts:120) and the `Service` interface (read-filesystem.ts:108) accept the values as plain numbers — any direct service caller (in-process plugins, future callers, JS callers) bypasses the tool-plugin decode in `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/read.ts`. The three paging sites only apply falsy fallbacks:

- read-filesystem.ts:176-177 (multi-chunk text path), 259-260 (`list`), 292-293 (`textPage`): `const offset = page.offset || 1` and `const limit = Math.min(page.limit || MAX_READ_LINES, MAX_READ_LINES)` — no integer truncation, no floor, no rejection.

## Verified behaviour (laptop probe, real module, main `1c7f4d41ad`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-read-page/probe.ts` — drives the real `ReadToolFileSystem.read` over the in-repo memory environment driver, file `l1..l5`, directory with 4 entries. Control `offset:2, limit:2` → `l2\nl3`, offset 2, next 4 (correct).

- `offset: -1` or `-100` (text) and `offset: -1` (directory list) → the read **dies with a defect** `Error: Schema validation failed` (the sliced page is fed into `TextPage`/`ListPage`, whose `offset`/`next` are `PositiveInt`) — an untyped crash instead of the typed `OffsetOutOfRangeError` this module defines for out-of-range offsets.
- `offset: 1.5` → same schema-validation defect.
- `limit: -1` (text) → empty page with `next: 1, truncated: true` — a **non-advancing page**: a caller following `next` re-reads the same page forever.
- `limit: -1` (directory list) → `visible.slice(0, -1)` silently returns all-but-the-last entry (3 of 4) and reports `next: 4, truncated: true` — an entry is dropped with no signal that the limit caused it.
- `limit: 1.5` → text path returns **2** lines (`entries.length >= limit` reached only after the second push) while the list path returns **1** entry (`slice` truncates the end index) — the two paging paths disagree on the same input.
- `limit: 0` → silently treated as absent (`|| MAX_READ_LINES`) and returns the whole file, not an empty page.

## Why it matters

The read tool is the model's primary file/directory paging surface. A malformed page from any non-schema caller either crashes the read with an opaque defect, loops forever on a non-advancing `next`, or silently drops a directory entry — all from values the service could normalise in one place, exactly like the sibling fixes for `SessionStore.messages` (#981), `Shell.output` (#964) and `Messaging` offset (#953). This site is not in design #992 phase 1's migration list (#993 covers session-list, branch-list and `KV.scan` only).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ReadToolFileSystem.read` normalises `offset`/`limit` once at the boundary (shared by the text, multi-chunk and list paths): non-finite → default (offset 1, limit `MAX_READ_LINES`); fractional → truncated; offset floored at 1; limit floored at 1 and capped at `MAX_READ_LINES` — or invalid values fail with the typed `OffsetOutOfRangeError`/a named typed error, per the house pattern chosen; in no case a schema-validation defect, a non-advancing `next`, or a silently dropped entry.
- [ ] Text and list paths behave identically for the same fractional/negative page inputs.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/tool-read-filesystem.test.ts` call `ReadToolFileSystem.read` directly with offset/limit in {-100, -1, 0, 0.5, 1.5, NaN, Infinity} for both a text file and a directory, pinning the normalised behaviour; all existing read tests (including the `toModelContent` cases) pass unchanged for valid pages.
- [ ] Valid-page behaviour is bit-identical: control `offset:2, limit:2` still returns lines 2-3 with `next: 4`.

body:
# fix(client,httpapi-codegen): generated client's json() buffers the whole response with response.text() — no cap, unlike the same client's 16 MiB SSE bound

## Evidence (verified on main `1c7f4d41ad`, 2026-10-30, by line-level reading)

The generated promise client (`packages/client/src/promise/generated/client.ts`, produced by `packages/httpapi-codegen`):

- `client.ts:2618-2635` — `async function json(response)`: after the content-type check it does `text = await response.text()` and `JSON.parse(text)`. **No size cap, no `content-length` pre-check, no streaming bound.** Every non-streaming request (`request()` at `client.ts:386-395`) and every declared-error body (`responseError`, which calls `json()` for declared statuses) flows through it.
- The same generated file *does* know how to bound a body: the SSE path caps its buffer at `maxSseEventBytes = 16 * 1024 * 1024` (`client.ts:334`) and throws `ClientError("SseEventTooLarge")` (`client.ts:423`), a behaviour pinned by a test (`packages/client/test/promise.test.ts:947`). The JSON path simply never got the equivalent bound.
- The template is the source, not the generated file: `packages/httpapi-codegen/src/index.ts:961` emits the client (including the uncapped `json()`), and `index.ts:1218` emits the binary path `new Uint8Array(await response.arrayBuffer())` (`client.ts:389`) — also uncapped, though legitimately larger responses make JSON the clear first fix.
- The client talks to whatever server the user pointed it at — local serve, SSH/WSL remote hosts, or an arbitrary `--server` — so the body is server-controlled, the same trust argument accepted for #987 (`opencode api` against an arbitrary `--server`). A buggy or compromised server returning an endless/huge JSON body OOMs the app/desktop process that hosts the client.

Dedup: `gh` search (open + closed) for "generated client response.text unbounded", "client json response.text", "httpapi-codegen json unbounded", and "ResponseTooLarge" returned nothing. #987 covers the CLI `api` command's own read (`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/api.ts`), not the generated client; #923 covers four download paths in ai/core, not this client.

## Why it matters

This is the client every GUI surface uses for every ordinary API call. One bad response — a runaway session list, a proxy injecting an endless body, a compromised remote — takes down the whole client process instead of failing one request with a clear error, and the codebase's own SSE bound shows the intended pattern was simply not applied to the JSON path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The fix lands in the `packages/httpapi-codegen` template and the client is regenerated (`packages/client` `check:generated` passes); no hand-edits to generated files as the only change.
- [ ] `json()` enforces a stated cap (named constant, in the spirit of `maxSseEventBytes`): a declared `content-length` above the cap fails before the body is read where available, and a streamed/chunked body is bounded in flight; over-cap fails with a distinct `ClientError` reason (e.g. `ResponseTooLarge`) rather than buffering whole.
- [ ] Declared-error bodies go through the same bound (an error response must not be an unbounded back door).
- [ ] Normal responses behave exactly as today, including empty-body `MalformedResponse` and non-JSON `UnsupportedContentType` handling.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/client/test/promise.test.ts` style pin the over-cap behaviour alongside the existing `SseEventTooLarge` test (declared-length and streamed cases).
- [ ] Out of scope: the SSE path (already capped), and the binary `arrayBuffer` path (`client.ts:389`) unless the fix naturally shares the helper — if left uncapped, say so explicitly in the PR.

body:
## Problem

`opencode uninstall` rewrites the user's shell configuration files **in place, non-atomically**:

```ts
// packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/uninstall.ts:91-96 (main 56321bbd1a)
yield* Effect.forEach(shell, (file) =>
  fs.readFileString(file).pipe(
    Effect.flatMap((content) => fs.writeFileString(file, cleanShellConfig(content))),
    ...
```

The files are the user's own rc files — the candidates at `uninstall.ts:138-157` are `~/.bashrc`, `~/.bash_profile`, `~/.profile`, `~/.zshrc`, `~/.zshenv`, and the fish config. Effect's `writeFileString` truncates the file and writes the new content into the same inode: there is no temporary file, no rename, and no backup.

## Why it matters

- An interrupted rewrite — Ctrl-C at the wrong moment, a kill, power loss, a full disk — leaves the user's shell rc file **truncated or partially rewritten**. Unlike the opencode config, a shell rc is hand-maintained, often years old, and not regenerable; uninstall is exactly the moment a user is least able to use opencode to help recover it.
- Every other config writer in the CLI already does this correctly: temp file in the same directory + rename — `packages/cli/src/config/config.ts:43-47`, `config/migrate.ts:27`, `services/service-registration.ts:39`, `services/service-config.ts:173`, and the CLI handler writers in `commands/handlers/plugin/add.ts:70-72` / `plugin/remove.ts:62` (the #977 fix applied the same shape to `mcp add`). The uninstall rc rewrite is the remaining in-place writer.
- There is also **no test anywhere for this path**: `cleanShellConfig` (`uninstall.ts:154-162`) is unexported and no uninstall test file exists, so the line-removal semantics (PATH entry + its `# opencode` marker line) have no regression net either.

## The fix is not a blind copy of the sibling shape

Shell rc files are very commonly **symlinks** into a dotfiles repository, and their permissions are the user's own. A temp+rename that replaces the symlink itself with a regular file would silently break the user's dotfiles setup. The rewrite must resolve/preserve the symlink and preserve the existing file's mode — which is why this is filed as triage rather than a small fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The shell-config rewrite is crash-safe: the on-disk rc file is never a partially written version (temp file + rename over the resolved target, or an equivalently atomic mechanism).
- [ ] A symlinked rc file still resolves to the same target after uninstall, and the file's existing permissions/ownership are preserved; a regular file keeps its mode.
- [ ] `cleanShellConfig`'s transformation is unchanged: only lines matching the `.opencode/bin` PATH entry (and a directly preceding `# opencode` marker line) are removed; dry-run behaviour is unchanged (no writes).
- [ ] Regression coverage exists for `cleanShellConfig` (entry line, marker-line pairing, unrelated PATH lines untouched) and for the write path's symlink/mode preservation; existing CLI tests stay green.

title: router: antigravity-agy / antigravity-ls leaves are never selected by routes (silent zero-expansion)
body:
## Defect

Routes never attempt **antigravity-agy** or **antigravity-ls** leaves. Direct sessions to both providers work (ledger history: antigravity-agy 21 successes, antigravity-ls 42 successes — all with route_id empty, i.e. direct pins/probes). Across all routed traffic there is not one attempt on either provider.

## Evidence (2026-10-30, laptop)

- workhorse-primary (route config in developing-today/code, .opencode/opencode.jsonc) has carried the leg `antigravity-agy/gemini-4-argon#high` at weight 2 of 4 since 2026-10-29. Zero attempts ever.
- 2026-10-30: `opencode-route/sonnet-plan#high` (live door antigravity-ls/claude-sonnet-5-5) added to the same route (code PR #2731), server restarted on the new config (config file mtime 07:17, restart 07:20). Six probe turns through workhorse: **zero** antigravity attempts — every turn went deepseek-flash doors → cline-pass → commandcode → muse/openai.
- Both proxies are healthy: GET /v1/models on :18743 (agy) and :18745 (ls) return 200 with the expected catalogs (gemini-4-argon and claude-sonnet-5-5 present, spelled as configured).
- Other direct-provider leaves in routes work fine (muse, openai, opencode-go.* are attempted constantly), so route expansion itself works — something about the antigravity providers makes their leaves silently expand to zero candidates (the config comments in code describe this exact symptom for a different route: "the route expanded to zero").

## Impact

Two nearly-full pools (Antigravity Gemini ~99% remaining, Claude/GPT ~100% remaining) are unreachable for all routed work, including the temporary primary burn legs Drew ordered on 2026-10-29/30 (Argon, then Sonnet). Sessions can only reach these pools by pinning the provider directly.

## Acceptance

- A workhorse turn can land on antigravity-agy/gemini-4-argon and on antigravity-ls/claude-sonnet-5-5 via route selection, visible as route_attempt rows with route_id set and provider_id antigravity-*.
- If a leaf cannot expand, the router logs/records why (no silent zero-expansion).
- Related: the quota pre-gating issue (companion, filed the same day) — once gates exist, an idle-but-full pool and a walled pool must be distinguishable in candidacy.

title: router: auto-disable providers at 100% quota until a fresh read shows headroom (cline-pass, commandcode, go)

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Drew's directive (2026-10-30)

OpenCode should disable a provider **on its own** when the provider's quota reads 100% (exhausted), and keep it disabled until a regular quota read shows less than 100% again. Fix at the source (the router), not by editing pools in config. Named cases: **cline-pass** and **commandcode**; the mechanism must be general (opencode-go workspaces hit the same wall).

## Live evidence (laptop route_attempt ledger, 2026-10-30)

Six probe turns through the default workhorse route after the 07:17 CDT server restart. Every single turn walked the same gauntlet before succeeding:

1. opencode-go.personal / .lab / (base) — `QuotaExceeded` "Go usage limit exceeded" (retry-after ≈ 313,773s)
2. cline-pass — `RateLimit` 429 "You have reached your monthly Clinepass limit" (monthly 100%, resets ~Nov 5)
3. commandcode ×2 — `UnknownProvider` wrapping "insufficient credits" (its $10 credit is spent; resets Nov 2)
4. muse / openai — success

Last 6h totals: cline-pass 138 attempts, 138 failures. Last 30 min: 253 attempts for 164 successes — roughly a third of all attempts are known-dead doors being tried first. Each doomed attempt costs a network round trip before the first token, so this is also the fleet's biggest avoidable TTFT tax.

## Required behavior

- The router already ingests quota signal (route_attempt.quota; the laptop quota-gatherer records per-pool reads). When a provider's current quota read is ≥100% / exhausted — or an attempt returns a quota-exhaustion error (429 limit, QuotaExceeded, insufficient-credits) — mark the provider gated and exclude it from route candidacy **before** attempting.
- The gate lifts automatically when a subsequent regular quota read shows <100% (or the recorded reset time passes and a probe/read confirms headroom). No config edit, no restart, no manual step.
- Gating is per provider (per workspace for opencode-go.*), never per model.
- Ledger: gated providers should still be visible in diagnostics as gated-with-reason, not silently absent.

## Acceptance

- With cline-pass at monthly 100%, a workhorse turn records **zero** cline-pass attempts.
- Same for commandcode while its credits read exhausted, and for any opencode-go workspace whose limit is hit.
- When a pool's read drops below 100% (e.g. OpenRouter/Command Code resets), its leaves rejoin routes without a config change or restart.
- Existing behavior otherwise unchanged: failover across live leaves still works; quota demotion semantics already in the router are the starting point — this makes the gate pre-attempt instead of post-failure.

title: fix(core): SessionStore.messages limit is never validated at the service boundary — a negative or NaN limit returns every message, a fractional or infinite one defects the read

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

`SessionStore.messages` passes its `limit` to the query untouched. Unlike the sibling `list` input — a schema class with `PositiveInt` — `MessagesInput` is a plain TypeScript type with no runtime validation anywhere at the service layer, so a direct in-process caller can pass values the HTTP door would never admit: a negative or NaN limit silently returns **every** message in the session (the drizzle dialect drops the LIMIT clause entirely), and a fractional or infinite limit binds into SQLite `LIMIT ?` and dies with a `datatype mismatch` defect that kills the whole read.

## Evidence (main `654a398bbf`)

- `packages/core/src/session/store.ts:44-53` — `MessagesInput` is a plain type: `limit?: number`, no schema. Contrast `store.ts:20` where the sibling list input declares `limit: PositiveInt`.
- `packages/core/src/session/store.ts:171` — `input.limit === undefined ? query.all() : query.limit(input.limit).all()`, verbatim.
- `packages/core/src/session.ts:544` — `Session.messages` forwards the input to the store unchanged.
- The only validation is at the HTTP door: `packages/protocol/src/groups/message.ts:8-13` restricts `limit` to an integer in [1, 200], and `packages/server/src/handlers/message.ts:9,45` defaults it to 50. In-process callers of `Session.Service` / `SessionStore` bypass both — the service-boundary pattern of #948/#953/#964.
- Drizzle's SQLite dialect drops an unusable limit instead of failing: `drizzle-orm/sqlite-core/dialect.js` `buildLimit` emits the clause only when `typeof limit === "number" && limit >= 0` — so negative **and** NaN limits produce *no LIMIT clause at all* (all rows), while a fractional or infinite limit is bound as a parameter.

## Reproduction (laptop probe, bun:sqlite — the store's engine)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-diff-context-parsetime` (`probe2.ts`, 10-row table, `SELECT … LIMIT $l`):

| LIMIT | result |
|---|---|
| `-5` / `-1` | all 10 rows (no limit) |
| `0` | 0 rows |
| `1.5` / `2.9` | `SQLiteError: datatype mismatch` |
| `NaN` | `datatype mismatch` when bound; through drizzle the clause is dropped → all rows |
| `Infinity` | `datatype mismatch` |

Combined with the dialect rule above: through `SessionStore.messages`, negative/NaN ⇒ unbounded read, fractional/Infinity ⇒ the `.all()` defects (`Effect.orDie` at `store.ts:171-173`) and the whole messages call dies.

## Why it matters

Session message reads are on the hot path for context loading, transfer and subagent recovery. A malformed limit from any in-process caller either silently pages in an entire (potentially huge) session history — defeating the protocol's 200-message cap and the handler's 50-message default — or defects the read outright. Today's in-repo callers are sane (handler validated, `session/transfer.ts` deliberately passes no limit, `session/subagent-job.ts` passes 20), which is exactly why the boundary, not the callers, should own the invariant — as #948/#953/#964 established for the messaging and shell services.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SessionStore.messages` (or `Session.messages`) normalises a present `limit` at the service boundary: it is floored to an integer and clamped to a documented positive range (the protocol's [1, 200] is the natural ceiling); non-finite values take the handler's default (50) or another documented default — never "no limit" and never a bound SQLite rejects.
- [ ] An omitted `limit` keeps today's unbounded behaviour — `session/transfer.ts` depends on reading the full settled history.
- [ ] Valid limits behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test` pin negative, NaN, fractional, infinite and zero limits through the service directly, plus omitted-limit and valid-limit controls.
- [ ] No change to the HTTP/protocol schema (already [1, 200]).
- [ ] Check the sibling `SessionStore.list` limit for the same dialect behaviour if a direct caller can reach it without its schema, and note the outcome on this issue.

title: fix(core): Session.diff context is never normalised — a negative, fractional or non-finite context reaches git --unified= raw and fails the whole turn diff

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`Session.diff`'s `context` is never normalised at the service boundary. A negative, fractional, NaN or infinite context reaches `git diff --unified=<value>` verbatim and git rejects it with a usage error (exit 129), so the whole session-turn diff fails as a `Snapshot.Error`. The sibling VCS diff path already normalises exactly this parameter (`diffContext`, fixed for the plugin door in #947); the session diff path — `SessionDiff.turn` → `Snapshot.diff` → `Git.tree.diff` — was missed.

## Evidence (main `654a398bbf`)

- `packages/core/src/session/diff.ts:135` — `context: input.context ?? PATCH_CONTEXT_LINES` passes the caller's number through untouched.
- `packages/core/src/snapshot.ts:213` — `Snapshot.diff` forwards `context: input.context` to the git tree diff.
- `packages/core/src/git.ts:865` — the value is interpolated raw: `` `--unified=${input.context ?? 3}` ``.
- `packages/core/src/session.ts` (`Session.diff`) passes `input.context` straight to `SessionDiff.turn`; the only validation anywhere is the HTTP layer, `packages/protocol/src/groups/session.ts:593` (`NonNegativeInt`), which in-process service callers bypass — the same service-boundary pattern as #948/#953/#964/#965.
- The precedent, `packages/core/src/vcs.ts:34-45`: "`git diff --unified=` / `hg diff --unified` accept only a non-negative integer, so a plugin-supplied context is normalised before it reaches an adapter: a missing or non-finite value keeps the service default (full-file context), and negative or fractional values are clamped to a non-negative integer instead of failing the whole diff with a CLI usage error." `Vcs.diff` applies `diffContext` at `vcs.ts:271`; #947 applied the same fix for the plugin `vcs.diff` door. Neither covers `SessionDiff`/`Snapshot`.

## Reproduction (laptop probe, git 2.55.0)

Probe dir: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-diff-context-parsetime` (throwaway two-commit repo):

| `--unified=` value | exit |
|---|---|
| `-1` | 129 (usage error) |
| `1.5` | 129 |
| `NaN` | 129 |
| `Infinity` | 129 |
| `2147483647` (= `PATCH_CONTEXT_LINES`, the omitted-context default) | 0 |
| `3` | 0 |

So any direct `Session.diff` / `Snapshot.diff` caller passing `-1`, `1.5`, `NaN` or `Infinity` gets a failed diff instead of a clamped one.

## Why it matters

Session turn diffs back the "what changed in this turn" views. One malformed number from any in-process caller (CLI, tool, future plugin surface) takes down the entire diff with an opaque snapshot failure, where the VCS sibling degrades gracefully to a sane context. It is also a consistency hole: two diff doors in the same codebase treat the same git parameter differently.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SessionDiff.turn` (or `Snapshot.diff`) normalises `context` before it reaches git — reusing `diffContext` from `packages/core/src/vcs.ts` or an equivalent: missing/non-finite → `PATCH_CONTEXT_LINES` (full-file, today's omitted behaviour), negative → 0, fractional → truncated.
- [ ] Valid contexts (including the `PATCH_CONTEXT_LINES` default) produce byte-identical diffs to today.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test` pin negative, fractional, NaN and infinite context through the service directly, plus a valid-context control.
- [ ] No change to the HTTP/protocol schema (already `NonNegativeInt`) or to `Vcs.diff` behaviour.

title: fix(cli): mcp add writes the config file in place with default permissions — non-atomic, and a fresh secret-bearing config is created world-readable

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: kind/security

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: source/creator
