labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/cli
labels.description: Package: cli (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`opencode mcp add` is the only CLI handler that edits the user's opencode config file by writing it **in place, with default file permissions**:

```ts
// packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/mcp/add.ts:60-67 (main adaee6e542)
const text = await readFile(configPath, "utf8").catch(/* ENOENT -> "{}" */)
const edits = modify(text, ["mcp", "servers", name], server, { ... })
await writeFile(configPath, applyEdits(text, edits))
```

Two defects follow:

1. **Non-atomic write.** `writeFile` truncates the live config (`opencode.json` / `opencode.jsonc`, in the project or the global config dir) and rewrites it. A crash, kill, or full disk mid-write leaves a truncated/corrupt config that every subsequent opencode launch fails to parse. There is also no protection against a concurrently running opencode process reading the file mid-truncate.
2. **Secret-bearing file created world-readable.** When no config file exists yet, `readFile` ENOENT falls back to `"{}"` and `writeFile` creates the file with the default mode (0666 & umask, typically 0644). The content written can include remote-MCP credentials verbatim: the handler stores `--header` values into the config (`add.ts:14,30-32` — `server = { type: "remote", url, headers }`), and MCP headers are where `Authorization: Bearer …` tokens live.

## The in-repo precedent (every sibling writer does both things right)

- `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/plugin/add.ts:70-72` and `plugin/remove.ts:62` — same kind of config edit, done as write to `configPath + ".tmp"` with `{ mode: 0o600 }`, then `rename()` over the destination.
- `packages/cli/src/config/config.ts:43-47` — global config write: temp file, `{ mode: 0o600 }`, rename.
- `packages/cli/src/config/migrate.ts:27`, `packages/cli/src/services/service-registration.ts:39`, `service-config.ts:173` — same temp + 0600 + rename shape.
- `packages/core/src/database/database.ts:90-94` — the credential database is explicitly forced to 0600, the house norm for secret-bearing files.

Distinct from closed #924 (route-overrides.json atomic write in core) and #99/#85 (Windows rename-EPERM retries for already-atomic writers): this site is not atomic at all and has no explicit mode.

## Why it matters

`mcp add` is the documented way to register MCP servers, and remote servers commonly need an Authorization header. The first `mcp add` on a fresh machine can create the user's global config — now containing a bearer token — readable by every other local user/process, and every `mcp add` risks destroying the whole config (all providers, permissions, MCP servers) if interrupted mid-write.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `mcp add` writes via a temporary file in the same directory + rename, matching plugin add/remove, so the config on disk is never a partial write.
- [ ] A newly created config file is mode 0600 (or the write otherwise matches the sibling writers' permissions); an existing file's contents are updated without widening its permissions.
- [ ] Behaviour otherwise unchanged: same JSONC edit (`modify`/`applyEdits` on `mcp.servers.<name>`), same candidate-path resolution, same stdout message.
- [ ] Regression coverage: a test (or equivalent verification) shows the write goes through temp+rename and a fresh config is created with owner-only permissions; existing CLI tests stay green.

title: fix(ai,core): provider HTTP timeouts have no upper bound — a value over ~24.8 days (or Infinity) makes setTimeout fire in ~1ms and breaks every request on the AISDK route

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai
labels.description: Package: ai (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Provider HTTP timeout settings (`timeout`, `headerTimeout`, `chunkTimeout`) accept any
positive number with no upper bound — including values above 2^31−1 ms (~24.8 days)
and `Infinity`. On the AISDK route those values are fed to raw `setTimeout` /
`AbortSignal.timeout`, where oversized values invert their meaning:

- `setTimeout` clamps any delay above 2^31−1 to **1 ms** (Bun/Node emit
  `TimeoutOverflowWarning: … does not fit into a 32-bit signed integer. Timeout
  duration was set to 1`). So a generous `headerTimeout` such as `3000000000`
  makes the header timer in `packages/core/src/aisdk.ts` abort **every** request
  to that provider after ~1 ms with "Response headers timed out", and an oversized
  `chunkTimeout` makes `wrapSSE`'s per-read timer kill every SSE stream the same
  way.
- `AbortSignal.timeout(Infinity)` **throws** `TypeError: Value Infinity is
  outside the range [0, 9007199254740991]`, so `timeout: Infinity` makes the
  AISDK fetch wrapper throw synchronously on every request instead of disabling
  the whole-request limit (the sanctioned way to disable a limit here is `false`;
  a user reaching for a huge number or Infinity means "effectively never").

Reachable from ordinary config JSON: provider settings are plain numbers in
`opencode.json` (a ms/seconds confusion or a "make it huge" value is all it
takes), and plugin code can also supply `Infinity` programmatically.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `afbe903e5b`)

- `packages/ai/src/schema/options.ts:52` —
  `HttpTimeout = Schema.Union([Schema.Number.check(Schema.isGreaterThan(0)), Schema.Literal(false)])`:
  no finiteness or magnitude bound.
- `packages/core/src/provider.ts:198,210-222` — `Provider.timeouts()` decodes via
  `HttpTimeout` and passes values through unchanged (defaults only when unset/invalid).
- `packages/core/src/aisdk.ts:141-151` — header timer is a raw
  `setTimeout(…, timeouts.headerTimeout)`; whole-request limit is
  `AbortSignal.timeout(timeouts.timeout)`; `:81` `wrapSSE` uses a raw
  `setTimeout` with the chunk timeout.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-timeout-overflow` (real modules, Bun):
  - `HttpTimeout` decode: `3000000000 → 3000000000`, `86400000000 → 86400000000`,
    `Infinity → Infinity`; `NaN / 0 / -5 → undefined` (correctly dropped).
  - `Provider.timeout(3000000000) → 3000000000`, `Provider.timeout(Infinity) → Infinity`;
    `Provider.timeouts({headerTimeout: 3e9, …})` returns `headerTimeout: 3000000000` verbatim.
  - Bun `setTimeout(2147483648)` fired after **7 ms**, `setTimeout(3000000000)` after
    **1 ms**, each with `TimeoutOverflowWarning … Timeout duration was set to 1`;
    `setTimeout(2147483647)` did not fire within 300 ms (control).
  - `AbortSignal.timeout(3000000000)` is accepted; `AbortSignal.timeout(Infinity)` throws TypeError.
- The native route (`packages/ai/src/route/transport/http.ts:144-145`) converts the
  same settings to Effect `Duration`s, so the overflow is specific to the raw-timer
  AISDK consumers — any bound must keep both routes behaving the same.
- No existing issue covers this (searched open + closed for
  headerTimeout/chunkTimeout/timeout overflow/setTimeout/provider timeout settings);
  no tests reference `HttpTimeout` or `Provider.timeouts`.

## Why it matters

A single plausible config value silently turns a provider completely unusable —
every request failing instantly with a misleading "timed out" error — on exactly
the providers a user was trying to give *more* time. The failure mode points at
the provider/network, not at the config, so it is very hard to diagnose.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `HttpTimeout` (or its consumers) reject or clamp values that cannot be
      honoured: non-finite values and values above the largest delay the raw
      timers can represent (2^31−1 ms). `false` remains the way to disable a limit.
- [ ] With `headerTimeout` / `chunkTimeout` / `timeout` set to `3000000000` or
      `Infinity`, requests on the AISDK route no longer abort after ~1 ms and do
      not throw from `AbortSignal.timeout`; behaviour matches the native route.
- [ ] Valid values (including the 300 s / 900 s defaults and values up to the
      bound) pass through unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests cover the boundary: 2^31−1 accepted, 2^31 and `Infinity`
      handled, at the schema/`Provider.timeouts` level (and the AISDK timer path
      if practical).

title: fix(ci): seven workflows can never run since #963 — cancel-in-progress: true combined with queue: max fails every run at startup

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: area/ci
labels.description: CI, workflows, and build infrastructure

labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

PR #963 (commit `ce6c4f00e2`, merged 2026-10-30T08:24:07Z as `198b34765d`, "cancel-in-progress everywhere") flipped `cancel-in-progress: false → true` in seven workflows that also set `queue: max` in the same concurrency block:

- `.github/workflows/docs-update.yml`
- `.github/workflows/jules-daily-upstream-sync.yml`
- `.github/workflows/main-broken.yml`
- `.github/workflows/models-snapshot.yml`
- `.github/workflows/opencode.yml`
- `.github/workflows/review.yml`
- `.github/workflows/stats.yml`

GitHub Actions rejects that combination: `queue: max` is only valid when `cancel-in-progress` is false (the run cannot both cancel the in-progress run and queue behind it). Every run of these seven workflows since the merge **fails at startup with zero jobs** — no step ever executes.

This is the exact failure already fixed in dezren39/nix: nix #1174 / PR #1175 flipped `opencode.yml` back to `cancel-in-progress: false` while retaining `queue: max`, per that repo's `ci-policy.md`. `main-broken.yml`'s own header comment still documents the invariant this change broke: "cancel-in-progress stays false, and this workflow never triggers on issues/pull_request_target, so queue: max is valid here" — the code now says `true`.

## Verified this run (main `afbe903e5b`)

- Diff of `ce6c4f00e2` for `stats.yml`, `review.yml`, `opencode.yml`, `main-broken.yml`: the only change in each is `cancel-in-progress: false → true` beside an unchanged `queue: max`. The commit message states the intent ("every workflow touched here now sets cancel-in-progress: true, groups unchanged").
- Run history: `review.yml` push runs 41026193869 (08:24:12Z, the #963 merge push itself), 41028173095, 41028386720, 41028652184, 41029254767, 41029263067, 41031608536, 41032111192 — all `completed/failure`. `stats.yml` push runs show the same unbroken failure streak from 41026195101 (08:24:12Z) onward; the last pre-#963 stats run (schedule, 2026-10-29T18:11:05Z, 40928384485) completed normally (skipped by its repo guard).
- `gh run view 41031614929` (main-broken.yml @ `afbe903e`): `conclusion: failure`, `jobs: []` — a startup rejection, not a job failure. Seven workflows failed this way within 5 seconds of the `afbe903e` push (09:11:27–09:11:32Z): review, stats, docs-update, jules-daily-upstream-sync, main-broken, models-snapshot, opencode.
- Grep on current main: 13 workflow files carry `queue: max`; exactly the 7 above also carry `cancel-in-progress: true`. The other 6 keep `false` and are unaffected.
- Impact beyond noise: `main-broken.yml` is the watcher that files main-broken issues for the main-tier workflows — it cannot run, so the remediation chain is blind while it is broken. `review.yml` / `opencode.yml` (issue_comment automation) and `models-snapshot.yml` / `docs-update.yml` (push automation) are likewise dead on every trigger.

## Fix shape (per the nix #1175 precedent)

Flip `cancel-in-progress` back to `false` in exactly those 7 workflows, retaining `queue: max` and the existing groups. Do NOT remove `queue: max` — that reintroduces the silent-drop problem closed by #179 ("a third arrival silently drops the pending run"). No other workflow changes; the main-only trigger policy from #963 stays as Drew ordered it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The 7 listed workflows set `cancel-in-progress: false` with `queue: max` retained and concurrency groups unchanged; no other workflows are touched.
- [ ] After merge, a push to main produces runs of these workflows that start (jobs appear) instead of 0-job startup failures — verify at least `stats`/`review`/`main-broken` on the merge push.
- [ ] The stale comment in `main-broken.yml` once again matches the code (it already states the correct invariant; no comment change needed if the flip lands).

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "concurrency queue" and "cancel-in-progress" — #179/#156/#151/#74/#133 cover earlier queue:max additions and group sharing, none covers the #963 flip; no open issue tracks these startup failures.

title: fix(core): detached stop policy is not enforced on a direct interrupt — Session.interrupt stops the target regardless of policy, contradicting the docs (PR #768)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #768's `detached` stop policy is documented as "only force-stop terminates it", but that is only true for interrupts aimed at an *ancestor*. `Session.interrupt` stops its target session unconditionally — the target's own stop policy and the `force` flag are never consulted for the target itself — so a plain (non-force) interrupt sent directly to a detached child's session terminates it. Code and docs disagree, and no test pins the direct-interrupt case either way.

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/768 (merged, commits cdc03c9f / 2c636bdd / f5d00ed7)
- Current main `afbe903e5b4081312a063d393e113701de1eb96d`:
  - `packages/core/src/session.ts:620–622` — `Session.interrupt` computes `selfInterrupted` by interrupting the target session directly; `options.force` only selects which *descendant* walk runs (:623–625). The target's job recovery record / stop policy is never read.
  - `packages/core/src/session/subagent-job.ts` (`start`) — a background subagent's job run is `sessions.resume(childSessionID)`, so interrupting the child's execution settles the job: a plain direct interrupt really does terminate a detached job, not just pause a turn.
  - `services/www/src/docs/content/agents.mdx:128` — the stop-policy table says for `detached`: "Survives plain interrupt and cascade alike. Only force-stop terminates it." and "How to stop: Force-stop the parent or stop the child directly with force."
  - `packages/core/test/subagent-stop-policy.test.ts` — every `sessions.interrupt(...)` call (lines 97, 120, 145, 169, 172, 197) targets `parent.id`; the detached cases pin parent interrupts only. No test interrupts a detached child directly.

## Why it matters

- Users and agents reading the docs will believe a detached job cannot be stopped by a plain interrupt of its own session — and, conversely, anyone relying on the documented guarantee (e.g. a UI stop button that plain-interrupts the child session) gets the opposite behaviour: the "detached" job dies.
- Whichever semantics is intended, the unpinned gap means a future change to either side lands silently.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One semantics is chosen and recorded: either `Session.interrupt` refuses/defers a plain interrupt of a session whose running background job is `detached` (force required, matching the docs), or the docs are corrected to say a direct interrupt always stops the target and `detached` only governs ancestor interrupts.
- [ ] A test in `packages/core/test/subagent-stop-policy.test.ts` pins the chosen behaviour for a direct plain interrupt (and, if enforcement is chosen, a direct force interrupt) of a detached child.
- [ ] `services/www/src/docs/content/agents.mdx` stop-policy table and `tools.mdx` match the implemented behaviour.

body:
## Finding

PR #781 added a node `fs.watch` fallback for recursive directory watches when the Parcel native binding is unavailable (`subscribeDirectoryWithNode`). That fallback is the *only* directory watch on exactly the machines #773 was about, but no test exercises its success path: event delivery, the create/delete typing, and the ignore filtering are all unpinned. The only fallback test on current main covers the failure path (a directory neither backend can watch surfaces `degraded`).

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/781 (merged, commit eb80928c) — the diff touched only `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts` (+53/−3), no test file.
- Current main `afbe903e5b4081312a063d393e113701de1eb96d`:
  - `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts:349` — `subscribeDirectoryWithNode(directory, ignore, publish)`; ignore entries are reduced to path-segment names (:355–368) and `rename` events are typed create/delete by `existsSync` at delivery time (:372–378).
  - `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts:318` — `fallBackToNode` (extended by #797 work) routes every Parcel failure — missing binding, subscribe timeout, inotify exhaustion — into this same untested function.
  - `packages/core/test/filesystem/watcher.test.ts:273` — "reports degraded when neither Parcel nor the node fallback can watch a directory" is the only fallback test; it asserts the ENOTDIR failure path (`subscription` undefined, one degraded cause), never a delivered event.
  - The config reload tests that motivated #773 run against whichever backend the machine has (Parcel on CI), so they do not cover the fallback either.

## Why it matters

- On a binding-less machine (the NixOS laptop environment in #773), a regression in the fallback — e.g. the segment-ignore reduction dropping a real ignore shape, or the `existsSync` race mistyping a delete — silently restores the #773 symptom (edits in `.opencode` never reload) with no failing test anywhere.
- The fallback's semantics deliberately differ from Parcel's (existence-at-delivery typing, segment-name ignores); unpinned, a future refactor can change them invisibly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A test forces the node fallback (e.g. via `Watcher.nativeLayer` with the Parcel binding unavailable, or by calling the fallback path directly) on a real temp directory and pins that creating, modifying, and deleting a file each publish an update with the right path and type (create/update/delete).
- [ ] The same test pins that events under an ignored segment (`node_modules`, `.git` — the `packages/core/src/config/watch.ts:32` ignore set) are not published.
- [ ] The test runs in CI (not gated on the native binding being absent on the dev machine).

title: fix(core): Vcs.branches passes its limit to the provider untouched — invalid values silently return an empty branch list, limit 0 returns every branch

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

`Vcs.branches` passes a caller-supplied `limit` to the VCS provider completely untouched (`packages/core/src/vcs.ts:217-225` on main `198b34765d`):

```ts
provider.branches({ ...scope, ...options }).pipe(Effect.flatMap(decodeBranches))
```

The normalisation built for #945/#946 lives only in the two call-site wrappers — the plugin host's `PluginVcsBranchList.listBranches` (`packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/branch-list.ts:20-27`) and the HTTP handler (`packages/server/src/handlers/vcs.ts:88`), both of which call `branchListLimit()` before invoking the service. The service itself — and any present or future in-process caller that reaches it directly (the exposure pattern behind #948/#949) — gets none of it, while its sibling parameter in the same file, `vcs.diff` context, *was* normalised at the service boundary in #950 (`diffContext`, `vcs.ts`) for exactly this reason.

What a direct service caller can do today, via the git adapter (`packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/git.ts:270`, `...(options?.limit ? [\`--count=${options.limit}\`] : [])`):

- **`limit: -5`, `1.5` or `NaN`** → `git for-each-ref --count=<value>` exits 129 (usage error); `Vcs.branches`' `protect()` wrapper (`vcs.ts:111-120`) swallows the provider failure and returns the `[]` fallback — **the caller is silently told the repository has no branches at all.**
- **`limit: 0`** → falsy, so `--count` is omitted entirely: **every branch is returned**, with none of the documented default page (50) or ceiling (100) applied.

## Verified this run (main `198b34765d`)

- Code read: `vcs.ts:217-225` forwards `options` verbatim; `branchListLimit` is referenced only from `plugin/vcs/branch-list.ts:27` and `server/handlers/vcs.ts:88` (grep over `packages/*/src`); `git.ts:270` interpolates the raw value.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-shell-output/`, real `git for-each-ref` in a scratch repo with branches `main`, `alpha`, `beta`): `--count=-5` → exit 129 "invalid --count argument"; `--count=1.5` → exit 129; `--count=NaN` → exit 129; `--count=0` → all 3 branches; `--count=2` → 2 branches (control OK). Same git behaviour recorded for #945's probe; what changed since is only *where* the guard sits.
- #945 is closed via PR #946, whose fix deliberately placed the guard in the plugin wrapper (+ HTTP handler). This issue is the remaining service-boundary half, mirroring #950's placement for diff context — not a reopen of #945.

## Why it matters

- An empty branch list is a plausible-looking answer: a caller acting on it (branch pickers, worktree flows, review-base logic) proceeds as if the repo had no branches instead of surfacing an error — the worst failure shape for a paging parameter.
- The two VCS paging parameters in the same service now follow opposite conventions (diff context normalised at the service, branch limit only at call sites), which is how the next direct caller reintroduces the #945 bug class.
- The fix is small and mechanical: apply the existing `branchListLimit()` (or an equivalent in `vcs.ts`, next to `diffContext`) inside `Vcs.branches` before dispatch; the wrappers' existing calls become harmless no-ops.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Vcs.branches` normalises `options.limit` at the service boundary (default 50, ceiling 100, non-finite → default, zero/negative/fractional → clamped positive integer — the existing `branchListLimit` semantics), so no caller can reach the git adapter with a raw value.
- [ ] A direct service call with `limit: -5`, `1.5`, `NaN` or `0` returns a correctly paged branch list (never a silent empty list for a repo with branches, never every branch for `0`).
- [ ] The plugin and HTTP paths behave exactly as today (their pre-normalised values pass through unchanged).
- [ ] A test in `packages/core/test/vcs.test.ts` pins the service-level behaviour for the invalid cases above, alongside the existing `diffContext` pins from #950.

Dedup: #945 (closed, plugin/HTTP surfaces) and #947/#950 (diff context, closed) cover the call-site and sibling-parameter fixes; searched open and closed issues for "branches service limit" — nothing tracks the service-boundary gap in `Vcs.branches` itself.

title: fix(core): Shell.output paging is never validated at the service boundary — a negative or NaN limit defects the read, limit 0 returns a non-advancing empty page

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`Shell.output` — the service method that pages through a background shell command's captured output file by byte cursor — never validates its `cursor` or `limit` at the service boundary (`packages/core/src/shell.ts:198-207` on main `198b34765d`):

```ts
const cursor = input?.cursor ?? 0
const limit = input?.limit ?? 65536
if (cursor >= command.size) return { output: "", cursor: command.size, size: command.size, truncated: false }
const start = Math.max(0, cursor)
const length = Math.min(limit, command.size - start)
const buffer = Buffer.alloc(length)
```

The HTTP surface restricts both fields to `NonNegativeInt` (`packages/schema/src/shell.ts:71-74`, used by `packages/protocol/src/groups/shell.ts:58`), but the service itself — called directly in-process, the same exposure pattern as #948/#953 (Messaging) — trusts whatever it is given:

- **Negative or NaN `limit`, or a NaN `cursor`**: `length` becomes negative or NaN and `Buffer.alloc(length)` throws a `RangeError` synchronously inside the generator — the read dies as a defect instead of returning a page or a typed error.
- **`limit: 0`**: `length` is 0, the returned page is empty with `cursor` unchanged and `truncated: false` while `cursor < size` — a paging consumer that follows the returned cursor re-requests the same page forever (or concludes there is no more output while bytes remain).
- **Fractional `cursor`/`limit`**: `start` stays fractional (e.g. 1.5), is passed to `createReadStream`, and the fractional value propagates toward the returned `cursor`, which the `Output` schema declares `NonNegativeInt` (`packages/schema/src/shell.ts:76-84`) — the service can hand back a value its own output contract forbids.

## Verified this run (main `198b34765d`)

- Code read: `shell.ts:198-226` — no floor, no finiteness check, no clamp; the only guard is `Math.max(0, cursor)` on `start`, which does nothing for NaN (`Math.max(0, NaN)` is NaN) or for `limit`.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-shell-output/probe.js`, verbatim arithmetic splice of `shell.ts:198-207`, size=100): control (cursor 0, limit 10) OK; `limit=-5` → **RangeError**; `limit=NaN` → **RangeError**; `cursor=NaN` → **RangeError**; `limit=0` → length 0, stream end −1 (empty non-advancing page); `cursor=1.5` → fractional start/end (1.5 / 10.5) reach the stream and cursor arithmetic.
- In-repo callers are currently sane (HTTP handler via the protocol schema; `session/shell.ts:24` fixed limit; `result()` at `shell.ts:238-239` with `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`/config bytes) — this is a service-boundary hardening gap of exactly the class fixed for Messaging limits in #949 and the `vcs.diff` context in #950, where normalisation was moved to the service because callers reach it directly.

## Why it matters

- Shell output paging is on the hot path for every background command result; a defect here kills the read that delivers a finished command's output to the session.
- The failure modes are silent-or-wrong, not just loud: a 0-limit page reports `truncated: false` with unreturned bytes remaining, and a fractional cursor can produce a response the generated client cannot decode.
- The fix is the house pattern already used twice this week: normalise once at the service boundary (non-finite/negative → defaults, floor to an integer, clamp the limit to a stated ceiling), leaving validated callers byte-for-byte unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `Shell.output` normalises `cursor` and `limit` at the service boundary: NaN/non-finite or negative values take the defaults (cursor 0, limit 65536 or a named ceiling), fractional values are floored to integers, and the returned `cursor` always satisfies the `Output` schema's `NonNegativeInt`.

body:
## Problem

The Copilot utility-title call buffers its whole response body with no size cap. `utilityTitle` in `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/github-copilot.ts:511-556` does:

- `:523-545` — `const response = await send(\`${input.baseURL}/chat/completions\`, …)` then `return response.text()` — no `content-length` pre-check, no streaming bound, no post-read length check.
- `:549-550` — the only bound is `Effect.timeout("20 seconds")`, after which the buffered text is fed to `decodeUtilityCompletion` (a JSON-string decode of a small `choices[0].message.content` struct, `:498-501`).

A chat-completion for a session title is a few hundred bytes in practice. Twenty seconds is an eternity at local/network speeds: the body that arrives in that window is buffered in full, whatever its size.

## Verified this run (main `4064f72a4c`)

- Code read: no size guard anywhere on this path — `send` is `input.fetch ?? fetch` (`:519`), the response goes straight to `response.text()`.
- Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-copilot-title-body/probe.mjs`) reproducing the verbatim read pattern against a local server returning a chunked (no `content-length`) 200 body: **64 MiB was buffered whole by `response.text()` in 278 ms** — i.e. the 20 s timeout, not any size limit, is the only ceiling, and multi-GB bodies fit in it on a fast endpoint.
- The caller is the `session.title` hook (`github-copilot.ts:345-362`), which runs automatically for Copilot sessions when the account has `gpt-4o-mini`; `baseURL` is the loaded provider base URL, which is configuration-controlled (custom/enterprise endpoints), not a hardcoded constant.

## Why it matters

- This is the one response-body read in the provider layer that escaped the fleet's unbounded-download sweep: #923 enumerated four paths (media assets, skill files, the ripgrep archive, CodeMode fetch) and this call is not among them; its out-of-scope list covers own outbound payloads and local files, not a provider response read into memory.
- A misconfigured, compromised, or simply buggy endpoint at the configured base URL can OOM the whole opencode process — every session, not just the one being titled — during an automatic background call the user never explicitly made.
- The house pattern already exists: `collectBoundedResponseBody` (`packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts`) with a named cap, used by webfetch; a title response needs a far smaller cap than webfetch's 5 MB.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `utilityTitle` enforces a stated size cap on the response body (a named constant with a comment, sized for a title completion — orders of magnitude below webfetch's cap): a declared `content-length` above the cap fails before the body is read, and a streamed/chunked body without a declared length is also bounded in flight, not just checked after buffering.
- [ ] An over-cap response fails the utility call cleanly (the title hook already falls back to the normal title path on any failure, `github-copilot.ts:354-361`) — it must not defect the session or be retried in a loop.
- [ ] A normal-sized completion behaves exactly as today (title extracted and used; empty/missing content still fails over to the standard title path).
- [ ] A test in `packages/core/test` (copilot provider tests) pins the over-cap behaviour for both a declared oversized length and an undeclared streamed body, using the injectable `fetch` parameter (`utilityTitle` already accepts `input.fetch`).

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "copilot title", "utility title", "unbounded response" — the only hit is #923, whose four enumerated paths and acceptance criteria do not include this call. This is a companion to #923, not a duplicate.

title: fix(core): SessionStats range is never bounded — an ancient from or far-future to makes one stats request run millions of sequential window scans

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`SessionStats.get` has no bound on the span between `from` and `to`. Its only range guard is `from >= to` (`packages/core/src/session/stats.ts:87-88`). The range is split into fixed 31-day windows (`stats.ts:78`, `windows()` at `stats.ts:354-360`), and **three** sequential passes then run one database scan per window (messages at `stats.ts:122`, tools at `stats.ts:193`, events at `stats.ts:288`). The window count — and therefore the number of SQL scans and the size of the in-memory window array — grows linearly with a span the caller fully controls.

The HTTP surface accepts the values unchecked: `packages/protocol/src/groups/session.ts` declares the `session.stats` query as `from`/`to: Schema.NumberFromString` (optional, no bounds), and `packages/server/src/handlers/session.ts:113-119` passes `ctx.query.from`/`ctx.query.to` straight into `SessionStats.get`.

## Verified this run (main `4064f72a4c`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-stats-windows/probe.mjs`) running the verbatim `windows()` function with `to = 2026-10-30`:

| Supplied range | Windows created | Sequential DB scans (×3 passes) |
|---|---|---|
| `from = 0` (epoch) | 670 | 2,010 |
| `from = -62135596800000` (year 1) | 23,869 | 71,607 |
| `from = -8640000000000000` (minimum Date value) | 3,226,476 | 9,679,428 |
| `to = Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, `from = now` | 3,362,234 (formula) | ~10M |
| `to = year 9999`, `from = now` (default `from`) | 93,929 | 281,787 |

Almost all of those windows are empty — no session data can exist before the database does, or after now — yet each one still costs a full table scan per pass, executed sequentially. Allocating the year-1 window array alone is trivial; the scan loop is the cost, and it runs inside a single `session.stats` request.

## Why it matters

- One request to the experimental stats endpoint with an ancient `from`, a far-future `to`, or an extreme value in either field effectively hangs that request — millions of sequential scans — and keeps a database connection / server worker busy doing provably empty work. The stats app and any API client can supply these values; `NumberFromString` accepts them.
- The existing tests pin only `from >= to` and `from = MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` with the default `to` (which trips the `from >= to` guard) — see `packages/core/test/session-stats.test.ts`. An extreme `to`, or a finite-but-absurd span in either direction, is untested and unguarded.
- This is the same shape the fleet has bounded elsewhere (a caller-supplied number sizing unbounded work), except here the multiplier is three database passes, not a slice or a page size.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `SessionStats.get` bounds the accepted span: a range whose window count would exceed a documented maximum (chosen by the implementer — e.g. reject spans beyond a fixed number of years, or clamp `from`/`to` to a sane envelope around the data / now) fails with `SessionStats.InvalidRangeError` (which the server handler already maps to `InvalidRequestError`) or is clamped with the clamped range reported in the result's `range` — the behaviour is documented in the code.
- [ ] Extreme inputs no longer create unbounded work: `from` at year 1 / minimum Date value, `to` at year 9999 / `MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, and a span covering both, each settle promptly as an error or a bounded clamped range — never tens of thousands (or millions) of window scans.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test/session-stats.test.ts` pin the extreme-span behaviour in both directions (ancient `from`, far-future `to`).
- [ ] Valid ranges behave exactly as today: the default all-time range (derived from the earliest message), ordinary multi-month ranges, and the existing `from >= to` rejection are unchanged.

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "SessionStats", "session stats range", "stats window" — no hit covers a span bound; the only range behaviour tracked anywhere is the `from >= to` guard in the current tests.

title: fix(core): Messaging offset is never validated — a negative offset makes log return the wrong end of the transcript and tail report more on an empty page

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The Messaging service never validates `offset`, and the two unvalidated entry paths disagree with the contract schema, which promises `NonNegativeInt` (`packages/schema/src/messaging.ts`: TopicsInput, SessionsInput, LogInput). Sibling issue #948 covers the same service's `limit`; `offset` is a different parameter with different failure modes and is not covered there.

Two entry paths reach the service without the contract decode:

- The plugin host passes inputs straight through: `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:448-457` (`messaging.query/topics/sessions/log` call the service directly).
- The built-in messaging tool's own schemas accept any integer: `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/messaging.ts:111` (TopicsInput `offset: Schema.Int`), `:158` (SessionsInput `offset: Schema.Int`), and it forwards `offset` verbatim via `pick(...)` at `:580` and `:603`.

What a negative `offset` does, per read (main `01cf577ecf`):

| Read | Code | Negative-offset behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `log` head/pull | `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:1854` `all.slice(offset, offset + limit)` | JS slice wraps from the end: offset `-3`, limit `2` on 10 entries returns entries `[7, 8]` — the tail of the log served as the "head" page, with `more: true` |
| `log` tail | `messaging.ts:1858-1860` | `end = all.length - offset` overshoots the array: offset `-3` returns an **empty page with `more: true`** — a caller paging on `more` makes no progress |
| `log` grep | `messaging.ts:1876` `hits.slice(offset, offset + limit)` | Same end-wrap over the hit list |
| `log` search | `messaging.ts:~1910` `ranked.rows.slice(offset)` | Returns the last-ranked rows instead of the requested page |
| `topics` / `sessions` | `messaging.ts:1573`, `:1765` `.offset(input.offset ?? 0)` | SQLite silently treats a negative OFFSET as 0 (first page returned for a page that was never asked for); a fractional or NaN offset arriving via the plugin host hits the same unvalidated bind path that defects on fractional limits in #948 |

Slice semantics verified this run with a plain language-level check: `[0..9].slice(-3, -3+2) = [7, 8]`; `[0..9].slice(-3) = [7, 8, 9]`; tail arithmetic with offset `-3` yields page `[]` and `more: true`.

## Why it matters

- `log` is how sessions read each other's transcripts; a wrapped page silently returns the *wrong end* of the log labelled as the requested page — worse than an error, because the caller trusts it.
- The tail empty-page-with-`more: true` shape is a paging livelock: the caller is told more data exists and is given none of it.
- The tool schema (`Schema.Int`) actively invites the bad value: a model computing an offset backwards (e.g. `page - 1` underflow) produces exactly this input, and the tool layer — unlike the HTTP layer — does not stop it.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The Messaging service normalises `offset` at its boundary for all reads that accept one (`topics`, `sessions`, `log`): negative, fractional, or NaN offsets never reach SQL `.offset()` or a JS `slice()`; the chosen behaviour (clamp to 0 or reject with `Messaging.InvalidError`) is consistent across all three reads and documented in the code.
- [ ] The built-in messaging tool's `offset` fields (`tool/plugin/messaging.ts` TopicsInput and SessionsInput) match the contract (`NonNegativeInt`-equivalent) instead of bare `Schema.Int`.
- [ ] `log` with a negative offset no longer returns end-wrapped entries for head/pull/grep/search, and tail no longer returns an empty page with `more: true` for a negative offset.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test` (messaging tests) pin negative / fractional offset behaviour for `log` and at least one of `topics`/`sessions`.
- [ ] Valid offsets (including 0 and offsets past the end) behave exactly as today.

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "messaging offset", "negative offset log", "sessions tool offset" — the only hit is #948, which covers `limit` normalisation only; its acceptance criteria do not include `offset` or the tool-schema `Schema.Int` mismatch.

title: fix(core): plugin session.list limit from PR #766 is never normalised — negative returns every session, fractional/NaN defects the store query

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #766 exposed `session.list` to v2 plugins, but the plugin host passes a plugin-supplied `limit` to the session store with no normalisation at all — and neither the session service nor the store validates it at runtime. The sibling plugin surface from the same PR family, `vcs.branch.list`, got exactly this normalisation in PR #946 (`branchListLimit`: missing/non-finite → default, otherwise floored and clamped to a positive integer). `session.list` never did. Issue #935 / PR #940 cover only the missing-limit default (`limit ?? 50`); #935's acceptance criteria explicitly leave explicit-limit behaviour unchanged, so the values below are untracked.

Verified on current main `01cf577ecf4e9d3af6cbddc28f5792c068a56b6e`:

| Plugin `limit` | Result on the plugin path | HTTP `session.list` |
|---|---|---|
| `-5` | SQLite `LIMIT -5` is unlimited → **every matching session returned** | rejected: query schema requires a positive integer |
| `2.5` | store query fails with SQLite `datatype mismatch`, wrapped in `Effect.orDie` → the plugin's list call defects | rejected: positive integer only |
| `NaN` / `Infinity` | same `datatype mismatch` defect path | rejected: positive integer only |
| `0` | empty page (safe, but diverges from the HTTP contract, which rejects 0) | rejected: positive integer only |

## Evidence

- PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/766 (merged, commits `2f5f7b6bd0` / `075d054d33`)
- `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:611` — `sessions.list(sessionListInput(filter, query.limit, decoded?.anchor))` passes the caller's limit through.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:746` — inside `sessionListInput`, `const bounded = limit` is a no-op rename; nothing floors, clamps, or rejects the value (PR #940, open, changes only the `undefined` case to `?? DefaultSessionsLimit`).
- `packages/core/src/session.ts:526-528` — `Session.list` forwards the input to the store with no schema decode, even though the store's `ListInput` declares `limit: PositiveInt` (`packages/core/src/session/store.ts:20`) — that schema is a type, never enforced on this path, and the host builds the input with an `as Session.ListInput` cast (`host.ts:749-752`).
- `packages/core/src/session/store.ts:135` — `input.limit === undefined ? query.all() : query.limit(input.limit).all()` piped through `Effect.orDie`: a non-integer limit becomes a defect, a negative one becomes an unbounded read.
- SQLite semantics probe (in-memory, this run): `LIMIT -5` returned all 5 rows; `LIMIT 2.5` and `LIMIT NaN` raised `datatype mismatch`. Same semantics as the bun:sqlite probe behind #948 (Messaging limits).
- Contrast / fix pattern already in-tree: PR #946 added `branchListLimit` for plugin `vcs.branch.list` (`packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/branch-list.ts`) — missing or non-finite → default 50, otherwise `Math.min(Math.max(Math.trunc(limit), 1), 100)`.
- HTTP contrast: `packages/protocol/src/groups/session.ts:61` restricts `limit` to `PositiveInt`; `packages/server/src/handlers/session.ts:72` applies `ctx.query.limit ?? DefaultSessionsLimit`.

Dedup: `gh issue list --search "session.list limit"` and `--search "session list negative fractional"` (open + closed) return only #935 (missing-limit default; explicit limits explicitly out of scope) and #945/#948 (vcs.branch.list and Messaging surfaces — different code paths). No open or closed issue covers non-positive / fractional / non-finite limits on plugin `session.list`.

## Why it matters

- A plugin computing its page size (e.g. a remaining-count subtraction that goes negative, or a fractional share of a budget) either silently gets the whole session table — the exact unbounded read #935 was filed over, reached by a different value — or crashes its own list call with an opaque store defect instead of a clean validation result.
- The two surfaces of the same endpoint disagree: HTTP rejects these values at the schema; the plugin surface honours or defects on them.
- Plugins are JavaScript at runtime; the TypeScript `number` type on the plugin API is not a runtime guard.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plugin `session.list` normalises `limit` before it reaches the store, mirroring `branchListLimit` (PR #946): missing or non-finite → the default page size (50, as in PR #940); fractional → floored/truncated; zero or negative → a positive minimum (or a clean, documented rejection) — never an unbounded read and never a store defect.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test/plugin/session-list.test.ts` pin: `limit: -5` does not return every session, `limit: 2.5` does not defect and returns a floored page, `limit: NaN` falls back to the default page.
- [ ] Positive integer limits (including values above the default) behave exactly as today; HTTP `session.list` behaviour unchanged.
- [ ] Lands cleanly with or after PR #940 (which supplies the `?? DefaultSessionsLimit` half) — the normalisation should subsume that default, not conflict with it.

title: fix(core): Messaging limits are clamped only from above — a negative limit returns every row, a fractional one defects the read

labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The Messaging service clamps every caller-supplied `limit` only from above (`Math.min(limit, MAX_LIMIT)`) and never floors it. The contract schemas promise `PositiveInt` (schema/messaging.ts), and the HTTP/RPC layer and the built-in messaging tool do enforce that — but the service itself, which the plugin host calls directly (`messaging.query(input ?? {})`, `topics`, `sessions`, `log` in `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts`), applies no floor, so a limit that reaches the service unvalidated inverts or breaks the query:

| `limit` reaching the service | Result |
|---|---|
| negative (e.g. `-5`) | SQL `LIMIT -4`/`LIMIT -5` — SQLite treats a negative LIMIT as **no limit**: `query` returns every matching message, `topics`/`sessions` return every row (verified with bun:sqlite on the laptop) |
| `0` | `query` returns an empty page with `more: true` — a caller paging on `more` loops forever |
| fractional (e.g. `2.5`) or `NaN` | the SQLite bind fails with `datatype mismatch` (verified on the laptop); the read's `.pipe(Effect.orDie)` turns it into a defect that kills the caller's step |

Verified on main `f6a1b4c2ee` (code) plus a laptop bun:sqlite probe of the exact LIMIT semantics (probe-2026-10-29-creator-msg).

## Evidence (file:line, main f6a1b4c2ee)

- `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:693` — `read()`: `const limit = Math.min(input.limit ?? DEFAULT_LIMIT, MAX_LIMIT)` (20/500), no floor; `chronological()` at `:862` runs `.limit(limit + 1)` and pages with `rows.slice(0, limit)`, `more: rows.length > limit`.
- `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:1563,1572` — `topics()`: same `Math.min` only, then `.limit(limit)` with `.offset(input.offset ?? 0)` at `:1573`.
- `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:1764-1765` — `sessions()`: same pattern.
- `packages/core/src/messaging.ts:1833-1834` — `log()`: same ceiling-only clamp, then JS slice paging (`all.slice(offset, offset + limit)`) whose `more` arithmetic assumes a positive limit.
- `packages/schema/src/messaging.ts:184,266,362,390` — the contract the service fails to defend: `limit: PositiveInt` on Query, TopicsInput, SessionsInput, LogInput.
- Contrast: `packages/core/src/kv.ts:61` shows the house pattern for a service-level limit — `Math.min(Math.max(Math.floor(options.limit ?? 100), 1), 1000)` plus an explicit NaN case.

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "messaging limit", "messaging query limit negative" — no hits. #935/#945 cover the same no-floor class on `session.list`/`vcs.branch.list`; this is the messaging surface, a different service and code path.

## Why it matters

- The smallest request producing the largest response is the worst failure shape for a paging parameter: a negative limit silently disables paging on the service other agents use to read each other's messages, materialising whole topics instead of a page.
- A fractional limit — easy for a caller computing a page size from a ratio — doesn't degrade; it defects the read via `orDie`.
- Every other surface validates (schema, tool `Count`), so the gap only shows for direct service callers such as the plugin host: exactly the callers with no schema decode in front of them on the effect-plugin path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All four Messaging reads (`query`, `topics`, `sessions`, `log`) normalise `limit` to a positive integer (floor + clamp to `[1, MAX_LIMIT]`, NaN treated as absent/default) at the service boundary, the way `KV.scan` already does.
- [ ] A negative limit returns the default-sized page rather than every row; `limit: 0` no longer yields an empty page with `more: true`; a fractional or NaN limit no longer defects the read.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test` (messaging tests) pin the negative / zero / fractional / NaN limit behaviour for at least `query` and one of `topics`/`sessions`.
- [ ] Valid limits (including values above `MAX_LIMIT`) behave exactly as today.

body:
## Problem

The plugin host's `vcs.diff` passes a plugin-supplied `context` (diff context lines) through to the git adapter's `--unified=` argument untouched — no integer validation, no floor. The HTTP endpoint it mirrors restricts the same parameter to a non-negative integer. A negative, fractional, or NaN context does not degrade to a default; it fails the whole diff with a git usage error surfaced to the plugin. This is the same plugin/HTTP divergence class as #945 (`vcs.branch.list` limit), on the diff surface.

Verified on main `f6a1b4c2ee`, with the git failure modes reproduced on the laptop against a scratch repo:

| Plugin `context` | Plugin host result | HTTP `vcs.diff` result |
|---|---|---|
| `-1` | `--unified=-1` → `error: --unified expects a non-negative integer`, diff fails | rejected: query schema requires a non-negative integer |
| `1.5` | `--unified=1.5` → `error: --unified expects a numerical value`, diff fails | rejected |
| `NaN` | `--unified=NaN` → same git error | rejected (not a number string) |
| `0` | `--unified=0`, works | works |
| omitted | service default (full-file context) | service default |

## Evidence (file:line, main f6a1b4c2ee)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:551` — `diff: (input) => response(vcs.diff(input.mode, { context: input.context, base: input.base }))`: the caller's context passes through untouched.
- `packages/client/src/promise/generated/types.ts:9159` — the plugin-facing `VcsDiffInput.context` is a bare optional `number`; nothing in the plugin API surface restricts it to an integer (the effect-side definition input, `packages/plugin/src/effect/vcs.ts:22`, is likewise a bare `number`).
- `packages/protocol/src/groups/vcs.ts:27-32` — the HTTP `DiffQuery` restricts `context` to `Schema.NumberFromString.pipe(Schema.decodeTo(NonNegativeInt))`.
- `packages/core/src/vcs.ts:239` — the Vcs service forwards `context: options?.context ?? PATCH_CONTEXT_LINES` to the provider with no validation.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/git.ts:408,426,449,503` — every patch path interpolates `` `--unified=${options?.context ?? 3}` `` verbatim.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/hg.ts:208` — the hg adapter passes `String(options.context)` as `--unified` the same way (hg itself was not available on the verification laptop, so the hg failure mode is inferred from the identical construction, not reproduced).
- Laptop verification (scratch git repo): `git diff --unified=-1` → `error: --unified expects a non-negative integer`; `git diff --unified=1.5` → `error: --unified expects a numerical value`; `--unified=0` and `--unified=100000000` are accepted.

Dedup: searched open and closed issues for "vcs diff context", "unified", "diff context plugin", "context fractional" — no hits covering this; #945 covers `vcs.branch.list` only, a different parameter and code path.

## Why it matters

- A plugin computing its context dynamically (half a hunk, a ratio of file length) can easily produce a fractional or negative value; instead of a diff it gets a raw git usage error, and the failure looks like a repository problem rather than an input problem.
- The two surfaces of the same endpoint disagree silently: HTTP callers are protected by the schema, plugin callers — the audience least able to see the adapter's command line — are not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A negative, fractional, or NaN `context` no longer reaches `git diff --unified=` / `hg diff --unified`: it is rejected with a clear input error, or normalised (floored and clamped at 0) before the adapter builds the command — the chosen behaviour is the same for the git and hg adapters.
- [ ] Valid contexts behave exactly as today: `0` yields a zero-context diff, positive integers pass through, and an omitted context keeps the current service default.
- [ ] Tests pin the bad inputs (e.g. in `packages/core/test/vcs.test.ts` or the plugin host tests): `context: -1`, `context: 1.5`, and `context: NaN` do not surface a git/hg usage error.
- [ ] HTTP `vcs.diff` behaviour is unchanged.

body:
## Problem

The plugin host's `vcs.branch.list` passes a plugin-supplied `limit` through to `git for-each-ref --count=` untouched — no default, no cap, and no integer validation. The HTTP endpoint it mirrors applies all three. The sibling divergence for `session.list` was filed as #935; this is the same class on the VCS surface, with an extra failure mode: non-integer limits make the git call itself fail.

Verified on main `3a1c3a0c78`:

| Plugin `limit` | Plugin host result | HTTP `vcs.branch.list` result |
|---|---|---|
| omitted | **every** local + remote branch (no `--count` argument at all) | newest 50 |
| `10000` | `--count=10000` honoured verbatim | capped at 100 |
| `0` | falsy in the adapter, so `--count` is omitted → **every branch** (asking for none returns all) | rejected: query schema requires a positive integer |
| `-5` | `--count=-5` → `git for-each-ref` usage error, exit 129 (verified on laptop) | rejected: positive integer only |
| `1.5` | `--count=1.5` → `error: option 'count' expects an integer value` (verified on laptop) | rejected: positive integer only |

## Evidence (file:line, main 3a1c3a0c78)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/host.ts:547-549` — `branch.list: (input) => response(vcs.branches({ search: input?.search, limit: input?.limit }))`: the caller's limit passes through untouched.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/vcs/git.ts:261-276` — `branches()` builds `--count=${options.limit}` whenever `options?.limit` is truthy (line 270); an undefined or `0` limit omits `--count` entirely, so `for-each-ref` returns every ref.
- `packages/server/src/handlers/vcs.ts:87` — the HTTP handler the plugin surface mirrors applies `Math.min(ctx.query.limit ?? 50, 100)`: default 50, ceiling 100.
- `packages/protocol/src/groups/vcs.ts:21-25` — the HTTP query schema restricts `limit` to `PositiveInt`; the plugin input (`packages/plugin/src/effect/vcs.ts:14-17`, `packages/plugin/src/promise/vcs.ts:13`) is a bare optional `number` with no such restriction.
- Laptop verification of the git failure modes: `git for-each-ref --count=-5` → usage error, exit 129; `--count=1.5` → `error: option 'count' expects an integer value with an optional k/m/g suffix`; `--count=0` → all refs (0 means no limit to git, matching the adapter's falsy-omission behaviour).

Dedup: `gh issue list --search "vcs branch limit plugin"` and `--search "branch.list"` return nothing covering this; #935 covers `session.list` only, a different surface and code path.

## Why it matters

- The two surfaces of the same endpoint disagree silently: a plugin paging branches with the documented HTTP behaviour in mind gets the whole ref set on page one, and on a long-lived repo with thousands of remote branches that is an unbounded list materialised through the plugin host.
- `limit: 0` inverting to "return everything" is the worst case of the divergence — the smallest request produces the largest response.
- A fractional or negative limit (easy for a plugin computing a page size dynamically) doesn't degrade to a default; it fails the whole `for-each-ref` call with a git usage error surfaced to the plugin.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Plugin `vcs.branch.list` with no `limit` returns at most the HTTP default (50), and an explicit limit is capped at the HTTP ceiling (100) — or the divergence is explicitly documented in the plugin API docs with the unbounded behaviour called out.
- [ ] A limit of `0`, a negative number, or a non-integer no longer reaches `git for-each-ref --count=`: it is rejected, defaulted, or normalised to a positive integer before the adapter builds the command.
- [ ] Tests (e.g. in `packages/core/test/vcs.test.ts` or the plugin host tests) pin: no-limit returns the default page on a repo with more branches than the default, `limit: 0` does not return every branch, and a fractional limit does not surface a git usage error.
- [ ] HTTP `vcs.branch.list` behaviour is unchanged.

body:
# fix(core): OpenAI, OpenCode and xAI device poll intervals have no ceiling — a large server interval makes login expire before the next poll (the #915 class, in the three sibling flows #915 did not cover)

## Evidence (verified on main `3a1c3a0c78`, 2026-10-29, by line-level reading of each helper and its poll loop, plus the sibling tests)

#915 fixed this exact shape for GitHub Copilot only: its `deviceIntervalMs` is now clamped to **[1s, 60s]**, with the rationale recorded at `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/github-copilot.ts:21-33` — a large or unit-confused server `interval` "made the first sleep outlast the integration layer's 10-minute attempt lifetime, silently guaranteeing a login timeout" — and pinned at `packages/core/test/plugin/provider-github-copilot.test.ts:746-747` (`deviceIntervalMs(600)` → `60_000`, `deviceIntervalMs(999_999)` → `60_000`). The three sibling device flows kept the floor but never got the ceiling:

1. **OpenAI headless (ChatGPT device) flow — worst case: no ceiling and no deadline anywhere.**
   - `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/openai.ts:187-191`: `deviceIntervalMs` returns `Math.max(parsed || 5, 1) * 1000` — floored at 1s, unbounded above. `deviceIntervalMs("3600")` is a 1-hour sleep by direct evaluation of the expression; `"86400"` is a day.
   - The poll loop at `openai.ts:215-248` is `while (true)` sleeping `interval + pollingSafetyMargin`, and the authorize result (`openai.ts:210-214`) carries **no `expiresAt`** — unlike the OpenCode and xAI flows, nothing in or around this loop bounds the total attempt, so an oversized interval is an effectively hung login until something external cancels it.
   - Its tests pin only spelling/floor behaviour (`packages/core/test/plugin/provider-openai.test.ts:69-75`); no ceiling case exists.

2. **OpenCode Console flow — no ceiling; the poll loop itself is deadline-free.**
   - `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:34-37`: `deviceIntervalMs` returns `Math.max(seconds, 1) * 1000` — floored, unbounded above (`deviceIntervalMs(3600)` = 3,600,000 ms).
   - The authorize path does hand the integration layer an `expiresAt` (`opencode.ts:158-167`), but the comment there states the poll loop is "deadline-free", and `poll()` (`opencode.ts:672-694`) sleeps `wait + pollingSafetyMargin` **before** its first token request — so an interval past the attempt lifetime means the first poll fires only after the attempt is already dead. Repeated `slow_down` responses grow the wait by +5s from that unbounded base (`opencode.ts:688-690`).
   - Its tests pin only floor/fallback behaviour (`packages/core/test/plugin/provider-opencode.test.ts:136-145`); no ceiling case exists.

3. **xAI flow — no ceiling on the initial interval; the internal deadline is only checked between sleeps.**
   - `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/xai.ts:174`: the loop starts at `Math.max(positiveSeconds(device.interval, 5) * 1000, 1000)`; `positiveSeconds` (`xai.ts:241-244`) validates positivity/finiteness only — no upper bound.
   - `poll()` (`xai.ts:137-174`) checks its deadline (`deviceDeadline`, clamped to the 10-minute `MAX_DEVICE_LIFETIME_SECONDS`) at the top of an iteration, then sleeps the full `interval + pollingSafetyMargin` on `authorization_pending` — so one oversized interval overshoots the deadline by up to the whole interval before the timeout can fire. `slow_down` likewise grows the wait +5s per response from the unbounded base (`xai.ts:160-162`). When the device response carries no usable `expires_in`, the authorize result also carries no `expiresAt` (`xai.ts:61-67`), leaving this loop's own check as the only bound.

## Why it matters

The interval is **server-supplied** in all three flows (device-code responses from ChatGPT/OpenAI, the OpenCode Console, and xAI). The failure mode is silent and user-facing: login shows a code, the user approves it, and the CLI never polls again in time — it reads as "login is broken/hangs", the same symptom family as #431/#857, with no error to report. #915 already established the house position that this is a bug worth a ceiling plus regression pins; the sibling flows were simply not in its scope. A unit-confused server (interval in milliseconds: `600` meaning 600 ms… or a plain `3600`) triggers it without any attacker.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each of the three flows clamps its device poll interval to a stated ceiling (the Copilot 60s bound, or a per-flow bound with a comment justifying any difference), keeping the existing floor, fallback, and spelling rules byte-for-byte for in-range values.
- [ ] xAI's and OpenCode's `slow_down` growth starts from the clamped interval (it composes from the same helper), so repeated `slow_down` responses cannot rebuild an unbounded wait from an oversized server interval.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the ceiling in each flow's existing test file, mirroring the Copilot pins: e.g. OpenAI `deviceIntervalMs("600")` and `deviceIntervalMs("999999")`, OpenCode `deviceIntervalMs(600)` / `(999_999)`, xAI's initial-interval computation — all returning the ceiling, with the existing floor/fallback cases unchanged.
- [ ] Out of scope: the Copilot flow (fixed in #915), `expires_in` lifetimes (bounded by #879/#892/#899/#900), and the integration layer's attempt lifetime itself.

Filed by new-issue-creator-opencode, 2026-10-29 run. Cross-reference: #915 (closed, Copilot instance of this class), #880 (OpenCode floor), #771 (OpenAI spelling grammar).

body:
# fix(latex): parser command tables read through the prototype chain — `\constructor{x}` becomes an accent node holding the Object function

## Summary

The LaTeX parser (`packages/latex`) dispatches on command names taken verbatim from the document being rendered, using `in` checks and bare bracket reads on plain-object tables. Every `Object.prototype` member name is alphabetic, so it passes the command lexer and "matches" every table: `\constructor{x}` parses as an **accent** node whose `accent` field is the `Object` constructor function instead of falling through to the unknown-command path, and macro expansion **throws** for the same input whenever any unrelated macro is configured.

This is the #833 prototype-chain class in a package the core-only regression gate (#865/#912) does not scan: `packages/latex` has no own-property guard anywhere in its dispatch.

## Evidence (main `3a1c3a0c78`)

Unguarded sites in `packages/latex/src/parser.ts` (tables are plain object literals in `parser.ts:34` `accents`, `parser.ts:47` `variants`, and `packages/latex/src/symbols.ts:209` `symbolTable`, `:219` `largeOperators`, `:272` `delimiterTable`, `:300` `spacingCommands`):

- `parser.ts:242` `if (command in accents)` and `:245` `if (command in variants)` — `in` tests the prototype chain, so `constructor`/`toString`/`hasOwnProperty`/`valueOf` all "match", and the node fields receive the inherited functions.
- `parser.ts:314` spacingCommands, `:315` symbolTable, `:319` largeOperators — same `in` shape (shadowed today by the accents branch for alphabetic prototype names, but independently wrong).
- `parser.ts:330` and `:450` `delimiterTable[\\${command}] ?? delimiterTable[command]` — the `??` fallback never fires for `constructor`, so a function is returned where a delimiter string is required; `:456` `delimiterTable[token] ?? token` same shape.
- `parser.ts:517` text-group spacing lookup — same `in` read.
- `parser.ts:101` macro expansion: `macros[command] ?? macros[command.slice(1)]` — for `\constructor`, the second read returns the inherited `Object` function, which is not `undefined`, so expansion throws `TypeError: Macro \constructor must expand to a string` even though no such macro was defined.

Verified this run on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-latex-proto/`, `bun probe.ts` / `probe2.ts` importing the real `packages/latex/src/parser.ts` at `3a1c3a0c78`):

- Control `\hat{x}` → `{type:"accent", accent:"hat", ...}`; control `\nosuchcmd{x}` → unknown-command text fallback.
- `\constructor{x}` → `{type:"accent", accent:<<function Object>>, ...}`; `\toString{x}`, `\hasOwnProperty{x}`, `\valueOf{x}` → accent nodes holding the respective inherited functions.
- `\left\constructor x \right)` → `{type:"delimited", left:<<function Object>>, ...}` (control `\left(` gives `left:"("`).
- `expandLatexMacros("\constructor", { macros: { "\\R": "x" } })` → throws `TypeError: Macro \constructor must expand to a string`; `\nosuch` with the same macros passes through unchanged, and `\R` expands correctly.

## Why it matters

LaTeX input is document content — model output, notes, and shared documents rendered in the TUI/app surfaces that consume `@opencode/latex`. A single `\constructor` in a formula silently corrupts the render tree with a function where the types promise `AccentKind`/`string` (downstream layout/render code receives a value outside its contract), and with macros configured it is a hard `TypeError` that kills rendering of the whole document. The names are ordinary English words a document can plausibly contain (`\toString` in a CS text, `\valueOf` in a programming book).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `\constructor{x}`, `\toString{x}`, `\hasOwnProperty{x}`, `\valueOf{x}` (and the other alphabetic `Object.prototype` names) take the same path as any unknown command (non-strict text fallback / strict-mode `Unsupported command` error) — no node field ever holds an inherited function.
- [ ] `\left\constructor … \right)` no longer yields a function delimiter.
- [ ] `expandLatexMacros` with unrelated macros configured passes `\constructor` through unchanged instead of throwing; a macro actually defined under a prototype-colliding key in the caller's own object still works if it is an own property.
- [ ] All dispatch reads in `parser.ts` (accents, variants, spacingCommands, symbolTable, largeOperators, delimiterTable, macros, text-group spacing) use own-property semantics (`Object.hasOwn` or the shared guard pattern from #865).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/latex` cover the prototype-named commands for the parse, delimiter, and macro paths, plus controls (`\hat`, `\alpha`, a defined macro) still passing.

body:
## Problem

`ModelRouteTuning.predict()` turns a provider's quota-error text into a `skip` adjustment with **no upper bound on `until`** — and for a large enough relative reset it **throws**, taking the whole tuning review down with it.

Verified on main `c523a00fe7` with the real module (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-tuning-until`, since moved into `packages/core` for the run and removed after):

| Provider error text | Result |
|---|---|
| `quota exceeded; reset at 9999-01-01T00:00:00Z` | prediction `until=253370764800000` — a skip **2,912,077 days (~7,978 years)** out |
| `quota exceeded; try again in 100000 days` | prediction `until` 100,000 days out (~274 years) |
| `quota exceeded; try again in 999999999 days` | **`predict()` throws `RangeError: Invalid Date`** |
| `quota exceeded; try again in 3 hours` (control) | `until = now + 3h`, as expected |

## Evidence (file:line, main c523a00fe7)

- `packages/core/src/model-route-tuning.ts:132-149` — `predict()` calls `ModelRouteLimits.resetAtFromMessage(error.lastMessage, now)` and pushes `{ state: "quota-reset", until: reset }` with no clamp; the `detail` string is built with `new Date(reset).toISOString()` at line 146, which throws `RangeError` when `reset` exceeds the Date range (~8.64e15 ms).
- `packages/core/src/model-route-tuning.ts:176-190` — `parseQuotaReset()` has the same unbounded relative grammar: `back in 999999999 days` returns `86401767189600000`, beyond the maximum representable Date.
- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:124-145` — `resetAtFromMessage` / `relativeMs` sum `\d+(\.\d+)?` amounts × unit with no ceiling, and `parseAbsoluteTime` accepts year 9999.
- `packages/core/src/model-route-tuning.ts:261-285` (`review()`) — a `quota-reset` prediction becomes a `skip` adjustment with `until: prediction.until` verbatim; `ModelRoute.addAdjustment` (`packages/core/src/model-route.ts:901-913`) applies no cap either, and records the adjustment in the route log so it **survives a restart** (`onRestore`, model-route.ts:944-953).
- Contrast, same file: `noteAdjustments` (`model-route-tuning.ts:217-232`) caps a **user-written** note's reset at `now + 30 days` with the comment "A user-stated reset can be days out; only a runaway value is bounded." Provider error text — untrusted input — gets no such bound.
- Blast radius of the throw: `schedule()` wraps `review()` in `Effect.catchCause(() => Effect.succeed([]))` (`model-route-tuning.ts:311`), so one poisoned error message silently discards **every** adjustment from that review cycle, every cycle, while the poisoned error stays in the window.

Related, already-fixed analogues (different code paths, not duplicates): #913 (WebSearch `Retry-After` cooldown unbounded), #879/#892/#899/#900 (OAuth `expires_in` unbounded). Dedup: `gh issue list --search "parseQuotaReset" / "resetAtFromMessage" / "quota-reset predict"` returns only the closed grammar/calendar fixes #523/#526/#532/#533/#609/#666/#798 — none covers a bound or the throw.

## Why it matters

A single malformed or hostile provider 429 message can (a) bench a target effectively forever — the skip persists across restarts via the route log — or (b) crash `predict()` and silently disable the entire tuning review (all weight/skip suggestions) for as long as that error remains in the breakdown window. Both outcomes are the opposite of what the tuner is for, and (b) is invisible: the `catchCause` swallows it to an empty result.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A quota-reset prediction's `until` is bounded by the same ceiling the file already applies to user notes (30 days from `now`), or another single named constant with a comment explaining the choice — applied so both the absolute (year-9999) and relative (100000 days) forms are capped.
- [ ] `predict()` (and `parseQuotaReset` / `resetAtFromMessage` if the bound is placed there) never throws for any provider text: an out-of-Date-range reset is capped or treated as no reset, never a `RangeError`.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/model-route-tuning.test.ts` (and `model-route-limits.test.ts` if the parser changes): year-9999 absolute, `in 100000 days`, and `in 999999999 days` cases, plus the existing 3-hour control still passing.

body:
# fix(core): MessagingEmbedding.download has no in-flight size bound — an oversized or endless body fills the disk before the size/sha checks in finish() ever run

## Evidence (verified on main `c9edb37fda`, 2026-10-29, laptop probe driving the real module)

`MessagingEmbedding.download` (`packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts:297`) streams a remote body into `<dest>.part`, but nothing bounds how much it writes while streaming:

- The chunk loop (`embedding.ts:335-347`) only does `progress.received += chunk.byteLength` (`:341`) and reports progress — it never compares `received` against `input.size` or any cap.
- The declared length is computed into `total` (`:328-330`, from `content-range`/`content-length`) and used **only** for progress display — a `content-length` far above the known size does not fail the download before the body is read.
- All verification lives in `finish()` (`:351-357`), which runs only **after** the stream completes: the sha256 comparison, and the size check — which does not even run when a digest is present (`digest === undefined && input.size !== undefined`).

Both call shapes are affected:

- **Model files** — `ensureModel` (`:596-609`) passes the catalog's exact `size` (tiers at `:52-94` run 25,008,064 to 15,141,156,384 bytes) plus `sha256`; the known size is available at the call site and inside `download`, just never enforced in flight.
- **llama.cpp server archive** — `installServer` (`:550-558`) passes **only** `sha256` (`LLAMA_ASSETS`, `:104`, carries no size), so this path has no bound of any kind, at any point, until the digest check at the very end.

### Probe (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-embedding-download`, real `MessagingEmbedding.download` via the repo's own test harness, local HTTP fixture)

- Control: 100,000-byte body with matching sha256 + size → succeeds.
- Declared `size: 100_000`, server serves 5,000,000 bytes → download consumed/wrote **all 5,000,000 bytes** (`onProgress` max received = 5000000) before failing in `finish()` with `size mismatch … expected 100000 bytes, got 5000000`.
- Sha-only call (the `installServer` shape), server serves 5,000,000 bytes → again consumed **all 5,000,000 bytes** before failing with `sha256 mismatch`.

A body that never ends (or a redirect/compromised mirror serving far more than the real file) therefore writes to the user's disk until the disk fills or the body ends; the integrity checks only fire afterwards. Retries compound it: a digest mismatch deletes the part and the next attempt re-downloads from zero.

## Why it matters

This is the disk-side sibling of #923 (four paths that buffer whole bodies into memory with no cap). This path streams, so memory is safe — but it is the one downloader in the system whose expected size is *known exactly in advance* for models, and it still cannot stop early. The embedding pipeline autostarts in the background, so the download is not something the user is watching; a bad Hugging Face / GitHub mirror response turns into a filled disk and a wedged pipeline instead of a prompt, clear error. The house pattern already exists: `collectBoundedResponseBody` (`packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts`) does a declared-size pre-check plus a per-chunk cap for webfetch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When `input.size` is known, `download` aborts as soon as the received bytes exceed it (and fails fast, before reading the body, when a declared `content-length` / `content-range` total exceeds it), with a clear "larger than expected" error; the oversized part does not survive as a resumable `.part`.
- [ ] The sha-only llama.cpp asset path gains a bound too (e.g. record the asset sizes in `LLAMA_ASSETS` alongside the digests, or a named, justified cap constant well above the real archive sizes).
- [ ] Chunked / undeclared-length bodies are bounded by the same in-flight check, not just the header pre-check.
- [ ] Normal downloads behave exactly as today: resume via Range, 416-as-complete, digest-mismatch deletion and restart (existing tests in `packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts` keep passing).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts` pin the early-abort behaviour for both call shapes (declared size exceeded; sha-only over cap), asserting the download stops before the whole oversized body is consumed.

Cross-link: #923 (memory-side download caps — different paths, different failure mode; this path was not in its scope or out-of-scope list).

title: fix(ai): ResponsesHostedTools.isItem reads through the prototype chain — an output item typed "constructor" kills the Responses stream with a TypeError defect
