body:
## Problem

`ResponsesHostedTools.isItem` tests membership with the `in` operator, which reads through the prototype chain — so a provider-supplied output item whose `type` is a prototype member name is classified as a hosted-tool item, and `onDone` then dies with an untyped `TypeError` defect instead of falling through to the baseline Responses step.

- `packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/responses-hosted-tools.ts:29-30` — `export const isItem = ... => item.type in tools`
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/responses-hosted-tools.ts:38` — `const tool = tools[item.type]`, then `tool.name` / `tool.input(item)` at `:46-47` — for a prototype name, `tool` is an inherited `Object` member (e.g. the `Object` constructor for `"constructor"`, `Object.prototype` for `"__proto__"`), which is truthy, has no `input` function, and kills the step.

This is the same prototype-chain class as the Anthropic server-tool gate fixed in #856, where the comment at `anthropic-messages.ts:1198-1201` already explains exactly this failure shape ("a streamed block typed `constructor` … would pass this gate and kill the stream") and guards with `Object.hasOwn`. The hosted-tools gate missed that treatment.

## Reachability

`isItem` gates the `response.output_item.done` branch in four Responses protocols, all fed by provider-controlled stream items:

- `packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-responses.ts:286-287`
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/meta-responses.ts:145-146`
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/xai-responses.ts:71-72`
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/alibaba-responses.ts:88-89`

Providers ship new hosted-tool item types constantly (this package's own AGENTS.md forward-compatibility principle), and a hostile or buggy compatible endpoint can send any `type` string — including a future type that happens to collide, or an outright `"constructor"`.

## Evidence (verified on main `7696be82a4`, this run)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-hosted-tools-proto/probe.ts`, run with bun from `packages/ai` on the laptop) importing the real `ResponsesHostedTools` module — the file is md5-identical (`a1bc4be8a0d0924d4478039cc6c9df91`) in the sandbox clone at `7696be82a4` and the laptop clone — with a one-entry definitions table mirroring the OpenAI one (`web_search_call`):

| item `type` | `isItem(...)` | `onDone(...)` |
|---|---|---|
| `web_search_call` | `true` | OK — 3 events, tool named `web_search` (control ✓) |
| `future_hosted_call` (unknown) | `false` | — falls through to baseline step ✓ |
| `constructor` | **`true`** | **Failure: `Die(TypeError: tool.input is not a function … tool.input is undefined)`** |
| `toString` | **`true`** | **same TypeError defect** |
| `__proto__` | **`true`** | **same TypeError defect** |
| `hasOwnProperty` | **`true`** | **same TypeError defect** |
| `valueOf` | **`true`** | **same TypeError defect** |

The failure is a `Die` (defect), not a typed `AIError` — so it is not a provider-output error the caller can classify or recover from; it kills the stream step.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "hosted tools prototype", "ResponsesHostedTools", "isItem", and "output_item.done constructor" — no hits. #856 covers the Anthropic-messages gate only; #912 tracks extending the `check:proto-reads` CI gate to `packages/ai` (this site is an `in`-operator read, which that gate's P-A/P-C bracket patterns would not catch anyway).

## Why it matters

One malformed or adversarial `response.output_item.done` item from any OpenAI-/Meta-/xAI-/Alibaba-Responses provider (including OpenAI-compatible endpoints, which this fork routes to broadly) crashes the whole generation with an untyped defect, instead of the item being ignored / handled by the baseline step like every other unknown item type. The fix is the established house pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `isItem` (and the `tools[item.type]` read in `onDone`) use own-property membership (`Object.hasOwn`), so only keys actually present in the protocol's definitions table classify as hosted-tool items.
- [ ] An output item typed `constructor`, `toString`, `__proto__`, `hasOwnProperty`, or `valueOf` falls through to the baseline `OpenResponses.step` in all four caller protocols — no defect, no fabricated tool call.
- [ ] Known hosted-tool items (`web_search_call`, `code_interpreter_call`, `image_generation_call`, `mcp_call`, …) still produce their provider-executed tool-call + tool-result events unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the prototype-named types against at least one caller's definitions table (or the shared helper directly), plus a known-type control.

body:
# fix(core): route-overrides.json is written in place, not atomically — a crash or concurrent read mid-write silently drops every route override

## Evidence (verified on main `61b359a25b`, 2026-10-29)

`ModelRouteOverrides.save` writes the store **directly over the live file**:

- `packages/core/src/model-route-overrides.ts:189-195` — `fs.writeFileSync(file, JSON.stringify({ version: 1, overrides: live }, null, 2))`. `writeFileSync` truncates the destination first, so for the whole write window the file on disk is empty or partial JSON. There is no temporary file, no rename, no retry.

The reader treats a partial file as "no overrides, no error":

- `packages/core/src/model-route-overrides.ts:171-186` — `current()` documents itself: "A missing or unreadable file is no overrides, never an error". `JSON.parse` of a truncated body throws, the `catch` sets `list = []`, and the empty result is **cached** against the file's mtime, so routing proceeds with every override silently gone until the file changes again.

### Laptop probe (real module, this run)

Probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-overrides/probe.ts`, run with bun against the laptop checkout at the same main `61b359a25b`, importing the real `model-route-overrides.ts`:

```
after save, current(): [ "ov1" ]
after truncated write, current(): []
file still on disk (bytes): 163 of 327
```

i.e. simulating exactly the on-disk state a crash/kill mid-`save` (or a reader racing the write) leaves behind: the saved `avoid` override vanishes from `current()` with no log, no error, and no recovery — the next `save` from any caller starts from `current()` (`add`/`remove`, :197-207) and permanently overwrites the file from the empty base, so the loss is not even self-healing.

## Why it matters

- These overrides are user routing instructions (`avoid` / `prefer` / `allow-over-budget`, some time-boxed). Losing them silently changes which providers/models serve sessions — the opposite of what the override was created to prevent — and nothing surfaces that it happened.
- The file is explicitly shared: the header at `model-route-overrides.ts:157-159` says it lives in the data directory "so OpenChamber can read the same file". A second process reading during the write window sees the same truncated JSON.
- The sibling store solved exactly this: `ModelPlan.writeStore` (`packages/core/src/model-plan.ts:151-167`) writes a temp file in the same directory and renames it over the destination, with a retry loop for transient Windows rename errors (`EPERM`/`EACCES`/`EBUSY`, :124-149, "the update would be lost" — kept in sync with the desktop `atomic-write.ts`). The overrides store, added on the same routing surface, did not get the same treatment.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `save` writes `route-overrides.json` atomically: temp file in the same directory + rename over the destination (reuse or mirror `ModelPlan.writeStore`'s pattern, including the Windows rename retry), and cleans up the temp file on failure.
- [ ] A reader can never observe a partially written store: a file left truncated by an old-version crash is still tolerated as today (no throw from `current()`), but new writes never produce that state.
- [ ] Regression tests in the overrides test suite: `save` leaves no temp files behind, the file content round-trips through `current()`, and the write path is the atomic one (e.g. the destination is never opened for direct writing).
- [ ] Behaviour otherwise unchanged: expired overrides are still dropped on save, the `{ version: 1, overrides }` shape is unchanged, and OpenChamber's read of the same file keeps working.

title: fix(ai): speech finish-path tables read through the prototype chain — PCM_CODECS, HEADERLESS_ENCODINGS and SpeechStream media types

body:
## Problem

Three speech table reads in `packages/ai` are still bare prototype-chain reads (#833 class), on caller-supplied format/encoding strings:

- `packages/ai/src/protocols/elevenlabs-speech.ts:176` — `const encoding = PCM_CODECS[codec]`, where `codec` is the first segment of the caller-supplied output format (`providerOptions.outputFormat`, e.g. `"pcm_44100"`). A format of `"constructor_44100"` makes `encoding` the Object function (not `undefined`), so the container fallback is skipped and `SpeechStream.pcm` is called with a function as the encoding.
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/deepgram-speech.ts:106` — `const headerless = HEADERLESS_ENCODINGS[format.encoding ?? ""]`, where `format.encoding` can come verbatim from `providerOptions.encoding`. An encoding of `"constructor"` makes `headerless` the Object function (not `undefined`), so a WAV container and a bogus PCM encoding/sample-rate path are taken for an unknown encoding.
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/utils/speech-stream.ts:57,71` — `CONTAINER_MEDIA_TYPES[format]` in `SpeechStream.container()` and `PCM_MEDIA_TYPES[encoding]` in `SpeechStream.pcm()`. `container()` is called with caller-derived format strings (e.g. OpenAI speech `finish` passes the sent body's `response_format` verbatim; ElevenLabs passes the split codec above), so a format of `"constructor"` yields the Object function as the reported `mediaType`.

#907 guarded the Deepgram/Cartesia/ElevenLabs *format rejection* tables; these are the remaining finish-path tables, found while dispositioning the `packages/ai` hits for #912. Filed separately per #912's acceptance criteria rather than allowlisted silently.

## Evidence (main `61b359a25b`)

- None of the three sites has an `Object.hasOwn` / `ownValue` guard.
- JS-semantics probe on the laptop (table literals copied verbatim): for `PCM_CODECS`, `CONTAINER_MEDIA_TYPES`, and `HEADERLESS_ENCODINGS`, keys `"constructor"`/`"toString"` → function and `"__proto__"` → object; control keys resolve to their real entries.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each read is own-key guarded at the site, or guarded centrally in `SpeechStream.container`/`pcm` for the shared tables, so prototype-named formats/encodings take the existing unknown-format paths (container with `undefined` media type / unsupported error as appropriate at each caller).
- [ ] A test or probe shows a `"constructor"` format/encoding no longer yields a function as encoding or media type, and known formats (`pcm`, `mp3`, `linear16`) still resolve.
- [ ] `bun run check:proto-reads` still passes (guarded lines keep their allowlist disposition, updated to "guarded at the site").

title: fix(core): Copilot device poll interval has no ceiling and slow_down can speed polling up — a large interval makes login expire before the first poll

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

body:
## Problem

The GitHub Copilot device-code flow trusts the server-supplied poll `interval` with a floor but no ceiling — and its `slow_down` handling can make polling *faster*. Two defects in `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/github-copilot.ts`:

1. **Initial interval unbounded** (`:87`): `const interval = Math.max(device.interval, 1) * 1000`. Any large value becomes the first poll wait verbatim. The Copilot `authorize` returns no `expiresAt`, so the integration attempt expires after the default 10 minutes (`packages/core/src/integration.ts:266` `attemptLifetime`, `:621` `authorization.expiresAt ?? created + attemptLifetime`; the scrub at `:552-570` closes the attempt scope on expiry). An `interval` of 600 already makes the first sleep 603s (interval + the 3s `pollingSafetyMargin`) — the attempt expires before the first token poll, so the login can *never* succeed, and larger values (3600, 86400) fail the same way with no diagnostic naming the interval.
2. **`slow_down` can speed polling up** (`:142-145`): `const next = token.interval && token.interval > 0 ? token.interval * 1000 : wait + 5000`. When the token response carries a positive `interval` smaller than the current wait, the wait *shrinks* — the exact opposite of RFC 8628 §3.5 `slow_down` semantics. Both sibling device flows treat `slow_down` as a monotonic increase: opencode `poll` does `loop(wait + 5000)` (`opencode.ts:689-691`) and xAI does `interval + 5000` (`xai.ts:159-161`). Copilot is the only flow that replaces the wait with a raw server value.

A non-finite initial interval also slips through: `Math.max(NaN, 1)` is `NaN`, so the first `Effect.sleep(wait + pollingSafetyMargin)` receives `NaN`. The sibling guards reject non-finite values (opencode `deviceIntervalMs`, `opencode.ts:34-37`; xAI `positiveSeconds`, `xai.ts:241-244`).

## Evidence (verified on main `72290b030a`, this run)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-copilot-interval/probe.mjs`, node) evaluating the verbatim expressions spliced from `github-copilot.ts` — the file is md5-identical (`6dc68e205196720397c45329c7b45e8b`) in the sandbox clone at `72290b030a` and the laptop clone:

Initial interval → first wait / first sleep (wait + 3000ms margin):

| `device.interval` | first wait | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| `5` | 5,000 ms | control ✓ |
| `0` / `-5` | 1,000 ms | floor ✓ |
| `60` | 60,000 ms | slow but workable |
| `600` | 600,000 ms | sleep 603,000 ms > 600,000 ms attempt lifetime — first poll never happens before expiry |
| `3600` | 3,600,000 ms | login can never complete |
| `86400` | 86,400,000 ms | login can never complete |
| `NaN` | `NaN` | non-finite wait |

`slow_down` with current wait 5,000 ms:

| `token.interval` | next wait | verdict |
|---|---|---|
| absent / `0` | 10,000 ms | `wait + 5000` fallback ✓ (matches siblings) |
| `1` | 1,000 ms | **speeds up after being told to slow down** (sleep drops 8,000 → 4,000 ms) |
| `2` | 2,000 ms | speeds up |
| `5` | 5,000 ms | unchanged |
| `3600` | 3,600,000 ms | unbounded, same expiry failure as above |

Repeated `slow_down` with `interval: 1` drives the wait sequence 5000 → 1000 → 1000 → …

There is no test covering the Copilot device poll: `packages/core/test/github-copilot/` contains only message-conversion tests.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for "copilot interval", "copilot device", "slow_down" — no issue covers this flow's interval handling. #880 floored the *opencode* provider's interval; #900 bounded device-code *lifetimes* in opencode + xAI. Copilot's device flow was not part of either, and neither defect (no ceiling; non-monotonic `slow_down`) is tracked.

## Why it matters

Device login is a user-waiting flow against endpoints this code does not control — including GitHub Enterprise / data-residency domains, which this same function explicitly supports (`enterpriseUrl`). A unit-confused or simply generous `interval` from such an endpoint silently turns a login into a guaranteed 10-minute timeout with no error pointing at the cause, and a `slow_down` response that carries a small `interval` makes the client poll *faster* against an endpoint that just asked it to back off — the response shape RFC 8628 designed `slow_down` to prevent.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The initial poll interval is validated like its siblings: non-finite / non-positive values take a sane fallback, and the result is bounded above by a stated ceiling low enough that at least one poll happens well within the 10-minute attempt lifetime.
- [ ] `slow_down` never reduces the wait: the next wait is at least the current wait plus the established 5s increase (a larger server-supplied interval may be honoured only when it exceeds that, and still subject to the ceiling).
- [ ] Ordinary behaviour is unchanged: `interval: 5` polls every ~8s (5s + margin); `slow_down` with no usable interval still adds 5s.
- [ ] Regression tests pin: an oversized initial interval, a non-finite initial interval, and a `slow_down` carrying a smaller positive interval.

body:
## Problem

`WebSearch.cooldownMillis` (`packages/core/src/websearch.ts:221`) validates the *spelling* of a provider's `Retry-After` header but never bounds its *magnitude*. A 429 response carrying a huge `Retry-After` sidelines that websearch provider for the rest of the process lifetime.

## Evidence (verified on main `427f20399e`, this run)

Code (`packages/core/src/websearch.ts:221-238`):

- Delay-seconds branch: `/^\d+$/` + `Number.isFinite(seconds)` → returns `seconds * 1000`, no upper bound.
- HTTP-date branch: returns `Math.max(0, date - now)`, no upper bound.

Laptop probe importing the **real** `cooldownMillis` from the laptop clone at the same HEAD (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-websearch-cooldown/probe.ts`, `now = 1_800_000_000_000`):

| input | result |
|---|---|
| `undefined` / `""` | 60_000 (fallback ✓) |
| `"60"` / `"120"` | 60_000 / 120_000 ✓ |
| `"0x10"` / `"1e3"` | 60_000 (grammar guard from #686 ✓) |
| `"31536000"` (1 year in seconds) | 31_536_000_000 ms |
| `"999999999"` | 999_999_999_000 ms ≈ **31.7 years** |
| `"999999999999999999999"` | 1e24 ms (passes the finite check) |
| `"Fri, 01 Jan 9999 00:00:00 GMT"` | 251_570_764_800_000 ms ≈ **7,973 years** |

Impact path: the cooldown map is process-lifetime state (`websearch.ts:92`, pruned only when `cooldown.until <= now` at `:136-137`), and providers in cooldown are excluded from random selection (`:140-142`). One malformed or hostile 429 (unit-confused servers sending milliseconds-as-seconds is the classic case — `7200000` already buys ~83 days) silently removes Exa/Parallel from rotation until restart, with no log line naming the duration.

Sibling surfaces are bounded, which is the house pattern this one missed:

- Session retry caps a provider-stated retry-after at 15 minutes: `packages/core/src/session/runner/retry.ts:31-38` (`RETRY_AFTER_MAX`, "so a hostile or buggy retry-after cannot stall a session for hours").
- OAuth `expires_in` takes the fallback past 30 days: `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/expires.ts` (#879/#892/#899 family).

Dedup: #686 covered the spelling grammar of this same function and #713 its calendar-rollover date branch; neither bounds magnitude. No open or closed issue covers an upper bound here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `cooldownMillis` never returns a cooldown longer than a stated bound (clamp to the bound, or take the 60s fallback past it — either is acceptable if named in a comment; the session-retry 15-minute cap and the 60s fallback are the local precedents to weigh).
- [ ] The bound applies to **both** branches: delay-seconds and HTTP-date.
- [ ] Ordinary values are unchanged: `60`/`120` behave as today; blank/hex/exponent spellings still take the 60s fallback (#686); calendar-invalid dates still fall back (#713).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/websearch.test.ts` pin an oversized delay-seconds value and a far-future HTTP-date.

title: fix(ai): open-responses item-ID prefix reads through the prototype chain — an item typed "constructor" mints an ID containing the Object function source

body:
## Bug

`packages/ai/src/protocols/open-responses.ts:954` mints a fallback output-item ID from a plain-object table read through the prototype chain:

```ts
`${ITEM_ID_PREFIX[item.type] ?? "item"}_${crypto.randomUUID().replaceAll("-", "")}`
```

`item.type` comes from the provider's streamed item payload. The `?? "item"` fallback never fires for `Object.prototype` member names, because the inherited member is not nullish:

- `item.type === "constructor"` → the prefix is the `Object` function, so the minted ID is `function Object() { [native code] }_<uuid>` — spaces, braces and parentheses included.
- `item.type === "__proto__"` → the prefix is `Object.prototype`, so the ID is `[object Object]_<uuid>`.
- `item.type === "toString"` → the ID embeds the `toString` function source.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `80225ac023`)

- Site: `ITEM_ID_PREFIX` table at `packages/ai/src/protocols/open-responses.ts:934-939`, read at `:954` inside `resolveItem`, which normalizes every streamed item that lacks an ID (`normalize`, `:958-962`).
- Laptop probe of the exact expression: `ITEM_ID_PREFIX["__proto__"] ?? "item"` yields the prototype object (`[object Object]_uuid` after interpolation); `ITEM_ID_PREFIX["constructor"] ?? "item"` yields the `Object` function.
- Item IDs in this parser are not cosmetic: they key `state.outputItems` routing for `item_id` on later events and are carried on the normalized items downstream, so a garbage ID with whitespace/function source can break ID matching and any provider round-trip that echoes the ID.
- The `check:proto-reads` gate (`script/check-proto-reads.ts`) scans only `packages/core/src`; the #833/#865 prototype-chain sweep never covered `packages/ai`. The Anthropic sibling of this shape was filed and fixed as #856.

## Why it matters

A gateway or provider that emits an unusual item type (the parser already defends against gateway quirks — see the `namespace` null comment at `:949`) can poison every ID minted for that item. Real types (`message`, `reasoning`, `function_call`, `compaction`) and genuinely unknown types (which correctly fall back to `"item"`) are unaffected — only prototype names break, which is exactly the signature of the #833 class.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An item with `type` `"constructor"`, `"__proto__"`, or `"toString"` and no `id` gets a minted ID with the `"item"` fallback prefix (matching unknown types).
- [ ] Known types keep their prefixes (`msg`, `rs`, `fc`, `cmp`); items that carry their own `id`, or adopt one from `state.outputItems`, are unchanged.
- [ ] Regression tests in the `packages/ai` open-responses parser tests pin the three prototype names.
- [ ] Fix uses an own-property guard (the `ownValue`/`ownOr` pattern from #865, or `Object.hasOwn`) — not a blocklist of names.

body:
## Bug

Three speech protocols validate a caller-supplied `request.format` against a plain-object table and treat "lookup result is not `undefined`" as "format is supported". The lookups read through the prototype chain, so a format named after an `Object.prototype` member — `"constructor"`, `"__proto__"`, `"toString"` — passes validation with an inherited function/object as its format descriptor:

- **Deepgram** — `packages/ai/src/protocols/deepgram-speech.ts:75`: the rejection fires only when `FORMATS[request.format] === undefined`. For `"constructor"` the lookup returns the `Object` function, so no rejection; `audioFormat` (`:50`) then reads `.encoding`/`.container` off the function (both `undefined`) and the request goes out with the bogus format silently dropped instead of the designed `route.unsupported("media.format", …)` error.
- **Cartesia** — `packages/ai/src/protocols/cartesia-speech.ts:81-82`: `CONTAINERS[format] === undefined` is the only rejection. For `"constructor"` the "container" is the `Object` function; it is returned as `container` in the request body object (`:95-96`), where JSON serialization silently drops a function value — the request goes out with no container instead of the "supports the pcm, wav, and mp3 formats" error.
- **ElevenLabs speech** — `packages/ai/src/protocols/elevenlabs-speech.ts:99-100`: `OUTPUT_FORMATS[request.format ?? "mp3"] === undefined` is the only rejection. For `"constructor"` the "format" is the `Object` function: in stream mode `format.startsWith("wav_")` (`:105`) throws a `TypeError` (functions have no `startsWith`), and in generate mode the function flows into `describeOutput`, which calls `format.split("_")` (`:166`) — same crash, at response-finish time.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `80225ac023`)

- Laptop probe of the exact tables: for `constructor` / `__proto__` / `toString`, `FORMATS[k] === undefined` is `false` with `FORMATS[k].encoding === undefined`; `CONTAINERS[k] === undefined` is `false`; `OUTPUT_FORMATS[k] === undefined` is `false` and `typeof OUTPUT_FORMATS[k].startsWith === "undefined"`.
- `request.format` is a caller-supplied string on the media request (not a schema enum at these sites — the `=== undefined` checks exist precisely because arbitrary strings arrive here).
- The `check:proto-reads` gate (`script/check-proto-reads.ts`) scans only `packages/core/src`, so this class was never swept in `packages/ai` (the #833/#865 audit was core-scoped). Sibling speech parsing has been hardened repeatedly (#687, #690, #697) — these three validation sites were missed.

## Why it matters

An unsupported format is supposed to fail fast, locally, with a message naming the supported formats. Instead, a prototype-named format either silently sends a malformed request to the provider (Deepgram, Cartesia — confusing provider-side errors, possibly a differently-shaped audio response) or crashes with a bare `TypeError` (ElevenLabs). The same guard-the-table fix pattern as #865 applies.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `request.format` of `"constructor"`, `"__proto__"`, or `"toString"` is rejected with each protocol's existing `media.format` unsupported error in Deepgram, Cartesia, and ElevenLabs speech — no request is sent, no `TypeError`.
- [ ] All real formats (`mp3`, `wav`, `pcm`, `opus`, `flac`, `aac` as applicable per protocol) behave exactly as before, including Deepgram's `providerOptions.encoding` escape hatch.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the three prototype names for at least the validation path of each of the three protocols.
- [ ] Fix uses own-property guards (the `ownValue`/`ownOr` pattern from #865, or `Object.hasOwn`) at the lookup/validation sites — not a blocklist of names.

body:
## Bug

`mediaTypeExtension` and the file-extension lookup in `packages/ai/src/utils/media-type.ts` read plain-object tables through the prototype chain, so an `Object.prototype` member name is returned where a media type / extension string is expected:

- `packages/ai/src/utils/media-type.ts:52` — `extensionMediaType`: `EXTENSIONS[path.slice(path.lastIndexOf(".") + 1).toLowerCase()]`. The extension is lower-cased, so the lower-case prototype names hit exactly: a file named `notes.constructor` or `notes.__proto__` whose bytes match no magic-byte sniffer gets `EXTENSIONS["constructor"]` (the `Object` function) or `EXTENSIONS["__proto__"]` (`Object.prototype`) as its "media type".
- `packages/ai/src/utils/media-type.ts:69` — `mediaTypeExtension`: `EXTENSION_ALIASES[type] ?? …`. The `??` fallback never fires for prototype names because the inherited member is not nullish: `mediaTypeExtension("constructor")` returns the `Object` function, `mediaTypeExtension("__proto__")` returns `Object.prototype`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `80225ac023`)

- Laptop probe of the exact tables/lookups: `EXTENSIONS["constructor"]` → `function`, `EXTENSIONS["__proto__"]` → `object`, `EXTENSION_ALIASES["constructor"]` → `function`; a template-built filename becomes `audio.function Object() { [native code] }`.
- Callers that trust the result:
  - `packages/ai/src/media.ts:313` / `packages/ai/src/promise.ts:116` — `Media.file` / file reads pass `fileMediaType(data, path)` into `Media.bytes`, whose `mediaType` is typed `string` (`packages/ai/src/media.ts:274`); a function/object is stored as the asset's media type and propagates to providers.
  - `packages/ai/src/protocols/openai-transcription.ts:167-175` — `mediaTypeExtension(...) === undefined` is the designed rejection ("cannot name a … upload"); for `"constructor"`/`"__proto__"` the check is bypassed and the upload filename becomes `audio.function Object() { [native code] }` instead of the clear local error.
  - `packages/ai/src/protocols/elevenlabs-transcription.ts:111-117` — same filename construction, same garbage name.
- The `check:proto-reads` gate (`script/check-proto-reads.ts`) only scans `packages/core/src`, which is why this class survived in `packages/ai` after the #833/#865 sweep.

## Why it matters

Both inputs are external: file paths/extensions come from user files, and audio media types come from callers/providers. A mistyped or hostile value produces a function/object where every consumer assumes a string — bypassing a designed validation error in OpenAI transcription and corrupting asset metadata elsewhere — instead of the intended `undefined` fallback.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `mediaTypeExtension("constructor")`, `mediaTypeExtension("__proto__")` and `mediaTypeExtension("toString")` return `undefined`; real aliases (e.g. `audio/mp3` → `mp3`) unchanged.
- [ ] `fileMediaType(bytes, "x.constructor")` and `fileMediaType(bytes, "x.__proto__")` return `undefined` for unsniffable bytes; known extensions unchanged.
- [ ] OpenAI transcription again rejects an unnameable media type with its existing `invalidRequest` message for these names.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/ai` test suite next to the existing media-type tests pin all three names for both functions.
- [ ] Fix uses an own-property guard (the `ownValue`/`ownOr` pattern from #865, or `Object.hasOwn`) — not a blocklist of names.

title: fix(core): ModelPlan.readNotes fractional limit in (0,1) returns every note — slice(-0.5) is slice(0), the #542 break between the guarded cases (PR #741)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

body:
## Summary

PR #741 (for #733) extended `ModelPlan.readNotes`' limit guard so a non-finite limit keeps no notes, closing the `slice(-Infinity)` / `slice(-NaN)` hole left by #542. One numeric class still slips past the same guard: a **fractional limit in (0, 1)**.

`readNotes({ limit: 0.5 })` returns **every** matching note — more than `limit: 1` returns (one), and the opposite of `limit: 0` (none). The newest-N contract breaks in the unbounded direction for exactly the input range between the two guarded cases.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main `5c8375cd3b0`)

Source PR in this review batch: PR #741 (merge `d4a020cdcd71`, closes #733) changed the guard in `packages/core/src/model-plan.ts`:

- `:352-356` on current main — `filter.limit === undefined ? matching : !Number.isFinite(filter.limit) || filter.limit <= 0 ? [] : matching.slice(-filter.limit)`. A limit of `0.5` is finite and `> 0`, so it reaches `matching.slice(-0.5)`.
- `Array.prototype.slice` converts `-0.5` via ToIntegerOrInfinity to `-0`, and `slice(-0)` is `slice(0)` — the whole array. This is the same `slice(0)` trap the #542 comment at `:352` names; it re-enters through truncation instead of through `0`/`NaN`/`Infinity` themselves.
- `NoteFilter.limit` (`model-plan.ts`, the interface above `readNotes`) is a plain `number` with no integer constraint, and `readNotes` is exported — any direct caller can pass a fractional limit. (The plan-info tool at `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/plan-info.ts:49` validates its own input to `1..500`, but that schema still admits fractional values ≥ 1, and the exported function's contract is what #542/#733 were filed against.)

Logic probe (plain `node -e` evaluating the exact guard + slice expression from main, no repo build):

```text
limit 0   -> []
limit 0.5 -> [1,2,3,4,5]   (every matching note)
limit 0.9 -> [1,2,3,4,5]   (every matching note)
limit 1   -> [5]
limit 1.5 -> [5]           (floors by truncation)
limit 2.5 -> [4,5]         (floors by truncation)
```

Dedup: searched open + closed issues for `readNotes` and for fractional/non-integer limit — #542 (limit 0), #557 (unparseable `since`), #621 (sort order), #717 (calendar rollover), #733 (NaN/non-finite) are the sibling filings; none covers a fractional limit in (0, 1).

## Why it matters

The guard's whole purpose, per its own comments (#542, #733), is that a limit which cannot mean "keep the newest N" must keep **no** notes rather than silently keep **all** of them — an unbounded return is the failure mode, because callers use `limit` to bound what they render/store. A fractional sub-1 limit is the one remaining input that produces the unbounded return while sitting between two inputs (`0` and `1`) that behave sanely.

## Acceptance criteria

- `readNotes` with a fractional limit in (0, 1) no longer returns every matching note: the effective limit is a non-negative integer (e.g. floored, so `0.5` keeps none — consistent with `limit: 0` keeping none), or such limits are otherwise treated as keeping no notes.
- Integer and positive fractional ≥ 1 behaviour stays sane and bounded: `limit: 1` keeps the newest 1, `limit: 2.5` keeps at most 2 (floored, as today), `limit: 0` / negative / `NaN` / `Infinity` keep none (the #641/#733 behaviour is unchanged).
- Tests beside the existing limit cases in `packages/core/test/model-plan.test.ts` pin `limit: 0.5` (and a `2.5` control) alongside the existing `0` / `-1` / `NaN` / `Infinity` assertions.

title: fix(core): device-code expires_in has no upper bound — a millisecond-scale value polls the token endpoint for days (opencode + xAI)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

body:
## Problem

The device-code flows bound the poll *interval* (#880 floored it) but never bound the device code's *lifetime*: both providers take the server-supplied `expires_in` verbatim as the poll deadline / attempt expiry. A millisecond-confused or hostile value (e.g. `600000`, intended as 10 minutes in ms) stretches a login attempt from minutes to days of periodic token-endpoint polling, and the attempt never times out on any human timescale.

## Evidence (main `e030d19257`, read-verified this run; behaviour is deterministic from the quoted paths)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:158` — `const lifetime = Number.isFinite(device.expires_in) && device.expires_in > 0 ? device.expires_in : 0` — positivity only, no upper bound; `:163` turns it into `expiresAt: Date.now() + lifetime * 1000`.
- `packages/core/src/integration.ts:621` — the attempt's expiry is `authorization.expiresAt ?? created + attemptLifetime`, where the default `attemptLifetime` is 10 minutes (`integration.ts:266`). A supplied `expiresAt` replaces that bound entirely.
- `packages/core/src/integration.ts:556` (scrub) — a pending attempt is expired and its scope closed only when `attempt.time.expires <= now`, so the far-future `expiresAt` is the only thing standing between the poll and indefinite running — and it has been pushed out by the unvalidated value.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:669-691` — the poll loop itself has no deadline: it recurses on `authorization_pending` (sleeping `interval + pollingSafetyMargin` each round) until the attempt scope is closed, so it polls for the full fabricated lifetime.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/xai.ts:128` — same shape in xAI's device flow: `const expires = started + positiveSeconds(device.expires_in, 300) * 1000` is the loop's only deadline (`xai.ts:131-133`), and `positiveSeconds` (`xai.ts:233-236`) checks only finite-and-positive. A ms-scale `expires_in` of `600000` makes the xAI poll run ~6.9 days instead of ~10 minutes.

## Why it is not already tracked

#880 (closed) floored the poll *interval* for the opencode provider only (and xAI's interval is floored at `xai.ts:166`); neither it nor any other issue bounds the lifetime. #892 (open) covers xAI/Poe *credential* `expires_in` in `tokenExpiration` and explicitly excludes device-code handling. Search (open + closed) for "device-code lifetime" / "device expires_in poll deadline" / "authorization_pending" returns only #880.

## Why it matters

A device login is a user-waiting flow: the attempt sits pending in the UI and the client keeps hitting the token endpoint. A unit-confused response from either server — the same classic ms-vs-seconds bug this repo has now fixed in five-plus credential paths (#879, #885, #892) — turns a 10-minute login window into days of polling and an attempt that never visibly expires, with no user action able to distinguish it from a slow login.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both device flows clamp the server-supplied lifetime to a documented sane maximum (the integration default attempt lifetime of 10 minutes, or a stated bound of the same order) — an oversized `expires_in` behaves as that maximum, not as days.
- [ ] Valid lifetimes behave exactly as today: opencode `expires_in: 60` still bounds the attempt at 60s (#880 behaviour preserved), xAI's 300s default still applies when `expires_in` is absent/non-positive.
- [ ] Regression tests cover a ms-scale device `expires_in` (e.g. `600000`) for both providers' poll/attempt bounds; CI green.

body:
## Problem

Third companion to #879 (five providers, fixed via the shared `expires.ts` helper) and #892 (xAI + Poe, open): DigitalOcean is the remaining OAuth provider whose `expires_in` guard has no upper bound. #771 fixed its *spelling* grammar (bare `parseInt` reinterpreting `"1e3"`), but any plain unsigned decimal — however large — is still stored verbatim as the credential lifetime. The classic server bug of returning the lifetime in milliseconds (`7200000` for a 2-hour token) therefore stores an ~83-day expiry, and a larger value stores years.

## Evidence (main `e030d19257`, read-verified this run; behaviour is deterministic from the quoted paths)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/digitalocean.ts:44-47` — `expiresInSeconds` returns `Number.parseInt(text, 10)` for any `/^\d+$/` spelling, with no upper bound (contrast the shared helper at `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/expires.ts:26-29`, which caps at `MAX_EXPIRES_IN_SECONDS` = 30 days and falls back).
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/digitalocean.ts:83-88` — the callback accepts any finite positive result verbatim: `expiresIn: Number.isFinite(expires) && expires > 0 ? expires : 60 * 60 * 24 * 30`. A ms-scale `7200000` passes; so does `315360000` (10 years in seconds).
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/digitalocean.ts:116` — the stored credential is `expires: now + payload.expiresIn * 1000`, unbounded.
- Consumer: `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/digitalocean.ts:145` — `load()` skips the credential only when `credential.expires <= now`. With a fabricated far-future expiry, the plugin keeps presenting the credential as live after the real token dies: router discovery keeps failing with the dead token, the last inventory is retained, and nothing prompts a re-login until the fabricated expiry passes.
- Existing test coverage confirms the gap: `packages/core/test/plugin/provider-digitalocean.test.ts:209-217` tests `expiresInSeconds` for spelling only (`"3600"`, `"0"`, malformed spellings → NaN); no oversized-value case exists.

## Why it is not already tracked

#771 (closed) covered only the spelling direction for this provider. #879's fix scope was its five named providers via the shared helper — DigitalOcean does not import that helper (it has its own string-typed variant because its implicit-flow callback delivers `expires_in` as a string). #892 scopes xAI and Poe only. Search (open + closed) for "DigitalOcean expires" returns only #771, #879, #885, #880 — none bounds this provider's lifetime.

## Why it matters

DigitalOcean credentials are long-lived stored OAuth credentials, and the expiry timestamp is the only local signal that the token is dead. One ms-confused token response silently wedges the provider: models keep being advertised from the retained inventory while every call fails, with no re-login prompt, for weeks to years.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An implausibly large `expires_in` in the DigitalOcean callback is clamped to a documented sane bound or falls back to the existing 30-day default, consistent with the shared bound in `expires.ts` (`MAX_EXPIRES_IN_SECONDS`) — reusing that bound is preferred over a third spelling.
- [ ] Valid positive `expires_in` values (e.g. `"3600"`) behave exactly as today, and the #771 spelling behaviour is unchanged (malformed spellings still yield NaN → fallback).
- [ ] Regression tests cover a ms-scale `expires_in` (e.g. `"7200000"`) for DigitalOcean's credential construction / `expiresInSeconds` path; CI green.

`bun run check:proto-reads` (the #865 prototype-chain regression gate, run in CI on Linux in `.github/workflows/test.yml`, "Check prototype-chain reads are dispositioned") fails on current main `580c277358`. The gate's allowlist was written against the pre-#878 shape of `variant.ts`; PR #878 then changed that read to a multiline `Object.hasOwn` guard, and PR #883 (the #865 gate itself) merged afterwards carrying the now-stale entry. The guarded read is correct — the gate's bookkeeping is what is broken — so every CI run of the `test` workflow on main fails this step until the allowlist is updated.

## Evidence (main `580c277358`, verified this run)

- `packages/core/src/variant.ts:30-37` — the current read is multiline:
  ```ts
  const protocol =
    model.package === undefined
      ? undefined
      : Object.hasOwn(PROTOCOLS, model.package)
        ? PROTOCOLS[model.package]
        : undefined
  ```
  The trimmed hit line `? PROTOCOLS[model.package]` (variant.ts:36) matches the gate's P-A pattern (`script/check-proto-reads.ts`, `PATTERNS`) and is NOT in the allowlist.
- `script/check-proto-reads.allowlist.txt:50` — the only variant.ts entry is the old single-line form:
  `packages/core/src/variant.ts :: const protocol = model.package === undefined ? undefined : PROTOCOLS[model.package] :: tracked: #862, fix in flight on PR #878; migrate to ownValue when it lands …`
  That exact line no longer exists in the source, so the entry is stale, and its disposition ("fix in flight on PR #878") is also out of date: #878 has merged and the read is now guarded at the site.
- Replicated the gate's exact scan/parse/stale/unlisted logic (`scanSource`, `parseAllowlist`, `unlistedHits`, `staleEntries` from `script/check-proto-reads.ts`) over `packages/core/src` at `580c277358`: 45 hits, 44 allowlist entries, exactly **1 unlisted hit** (variant.ts:36 above) and exactly **1 stale entry** (the allowlist line above). No other file is affected.
- Merge order confirms the cause: `d0dd344d84` (Variant own-property guard, PR #878) landed before `a5c18ea45e` / merge `580c277358` (PR #883, the #865 gate), whose allowlist still carried the pre-guard line.

## Why it matters

A regression gate that is red on main trains everyone to ignore it — the exact failure mode #865/#833 built it to prevent — and it fails the Linux `test` workflow step for unrelated PRs until fixed. The fix is bookkeeping only; the underlying prototype-chain read is already correctly guarded.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `script/check-proto-reads.allowlist.txt`: replace the stale variant.ts entry with the current trimmed hit line from `packages/core/src/variant.ts:36`, with disposition "guarded: Object.hasOwn ternary at the same site (#862)".

- [ ] No source change to `variant.ts` (its `Object.hasOwn` guard is correct as-is), and no other allowlist entries added, removed, or reworded.
- [ ] CI `test` workflow's "Check prototype-chain reads are dispositioned" step is green.

title: fix(core): xAI and Poe expires_in guards have no upper bound — a millisecond-scale value disables refresh for weeks (companion to #879)

body:
## Problem

Companion to #879 (five providers) and #885 (MCP path, fixed): the two providers #879 cites as the *precedents* guard only the non-positive direction of `expires_in`. The oversized direction — the classic server bug of returning the lifetime in milliseconds (`7200000` for a 2-hour token) — passes both guards verbatim and disables credential refresh for weeks, the exact harm #879's acceptance criteria clamp for the five providers it touches.

## Evidence (main `159df45744`, read-verified this run; behaviour is deterministic from the quoted paths)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/xai.ts:233-236` — `positiveSeconds`: `Number.isFinite(seconds) && seconds > 0 ? seconds : fallback` — no upper bound.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/xai.ts:215` — `tokenExpiration`: `Date.now() + positiveSeconds(tokens.expires_in, 3600) * 1000`. A ms-scale `expires_in` of `7200000` stores an expiry ~83 days out; a year-scale value stores ~a year.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/poe.ts:16` — schema allows any non-negative int; `:157-160` — `expires = now + token.api_key_expires_in * 1000`, rejected only when the resulting *timestamp* is not a safe integer or exceeds `maxExpiry = 8_640_000_000_000_000` — the JavaScript Date maximum, not a lifetime bound. A ms-scale `7200000` (83 days) or a 10-year value passes.
- Consumer (same gate as #879): `packages/core/src/integration.ts:751` — a credential whose `expires` is more than 5 minutes out is returned as valid and never refreshed, so once the real token dies every API call fails 401 with no recovery until the fabricated expiry passes.

## Why it is not already tracked

#879's evidence and acceptance criteria name exactly five providers (GitLab, Snowflake Cortex, ChatGPT, OpenAI, opencode) and cite xAI's `positiveSeconds` and Poe's schema as the in-repo precedents — neither provider is in its fix scope, and both precedents predate the oversized-direction requirement. Search (open + closed) for "xai expires_in oversized" / "poe expiry" returns only #879 and the closed #885.

## Why it matters

xAI and Poe credentials are stored through the same integration refresh gate as the #879 five. One ms-confused token response from either endpoint silently wedges the credential into permanent 401s with refresh disabled — the stored credential looks well-formed, so nothing surfaces the cause.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An implausibly large `expires_in` in xAI's `tokenExpiration` path is clamped to a documented sane bound (or falls back to the 3600s default), consistent with whatever bound #879 adopts for its five providers — one shared bound/helper is preferred over a third spelling.
- [ ] Poe's `api_key_expires_in` gets the same lifetime sanity bound (its existing safe-integer/Date-maximum check stays as the overflow guard).
- [ ] Valid positive `expires_in` values behave exactly as today in both providers, including xAI's JWT-`exp` fallback when `expires_in` is absent.
- [ ] Regression tests cover a ms-scale `expires_in` (e.g. `7200000`) for both providers' credential construction; CI green.

body:
## Problem

Per-target context limits shipped in #710 / PR #811 (merged 2026-10-29, main `159df45744`) are inert in live sessions: the eligibility mechanism exists, but no production caller ever supplies the request size it filters on.

- `packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts:164-170` — `ModelResolver.resolveModel(model, variant, sessionID, requestTokens?)`: "`requestTokens` is the request's context size in tokens, when known: a route target whose ceiling the request does not fit is skipped like any other ineligible target."
- `packages/core/src/model-route.ts:614-618` — `ModelRoute.overLimit(definition, index, requestTokens)`: `if (requestTokens === undefined) return false` — an unknown size never filters.
- `packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts:120` — the only production caller: `resolver.resolveModel(selected, target.variant, session.id)` — three arguments, no `requestTokens`. A repo-wide search shows every other `resolveModel` call site is a different service (`session/context.ts`) or a test.

PR #811's own body named this as follow-up work ("Threading live session prompt sizes through the runner is follow-up work; the eligibility mechanism is complete and covered by tests"), but no issue was filed for it — #710 is closed and a search for `requestTokens` across open and closed issues returns only #710.

## What works today, and what does not

The *presented* limit does compose (route presents `min(route cap, leaf ceilings)`, so compaction respects the smallest ceiling). What never happens live is *selection*: a session whose prompt has grown past a small leaf's per-target ceiling is still routed to that leaf instead of skipping it with the `over-limit` reason the resolver, review dump, and `route_stats` already implement and test. The feature's stated purpose — "selection skips over-limit targets" — only fires in unit tests that pass `requestTokens` by hand.

## Why it matters

A user who configures `limit: { context }` per target (the flat motivating case in #710: one `small` route with 100k/100k/200k leaves) gets compaction behaviour but not routing behaviour: oversized requests land on leaves that cannot serve them well instead of the leaf sized for them, and `route_stats` will never show an `over-limit` skip in production, making the configured ceilings look decorative.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The session runner (or the session-context layer that calls it) supplies a real request/context token size to `ModelResolver.resolveModel` for live turns, sourced from the same accounting compaction uses for the presented limit.
- [ ] With per-target ceilings configured, a request larger than a leaf's ceiling skips that leaf in a live session and the skip is attributed `over-limit` in the resolver dump / `route_stats`.
- [ ] Unknown size keeps today's behaviour exactly (never filters), and sessions without per-target limits are unaffected.
- [ ] Tests cover the runner-level threading (not only resolver-level `requestTokens` passing); CI green.

## Evidence

Read-verified on main `159df45744` this run: `model-resolver.ts:164-175` (interface + doc), `model-route.ts:614-618` (`overLimit` undefined-guard), `session/runner/model.ts:120` (sole production caller, 3 args), plus a repo-wide `resolveModel` call-site search. Dedup: `gh issue list --search requestTokens` (all states) returns only #710 (closed by #811).

title: fix(core): governance pruning of requested-variant leaves can bypass subagent exclusions for retarget-added leaves (Codex P1 on #871)

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.description: Not yet triaged; needs a first look

labels.name: effort/m

body:
## Problem

Found by Codex review on PR #871 (head 07e72e8d48, P1, `packages/core/src/session/model-governance.ts`): governance (`routeTargets`/`leaf()`) prunes a leaf that cannot produce the pinned/route-requested variant, mirroring plugin expansion (#869). But in the retarget path, a model transform can add a leaf without the requested variant while the route still advertises that variant; `ModelResolver.resolveSelected()` then accepts the variant and `model-resolver.ts` loads that deployment with an undefined variant — it runs bare on failover. Because governance omitted the deployment entirely, a subagent exclusion naming that deployment no longer blocks it.

## Why this is not a one-line fix

PR #871 deliberately implements — and tests — the opposite semantics for the catalog path (`model-governance.test.ts`: "a leaf that cannot produce the requested variant is pruned from governance, as in expansion (#869)"), where expansion really does drop the leaf and it never runs. The bypass needs the retarget/resolver path, where the leaf survives and runs bare. Reconciling the two needs a design call: either governance keeps a bare ref for leaves the resolver can run bare (and the #869 pruning test is re-scoped to the pure-expansion case), or runtime resolution guarantees such leaves cannot execute (resolver-side), or governance judges the retargeted definitions rather than the catalog.

## Acceptance

- A retarget-added leaf that the resolver can run bare under a route-requested variant is judged by governance (an exclusion naming it denies), or the resolver demonstrably cannot run it bare, with a regression test for the transform + retarget + exclusion scenario from the Codex thread on PR #871.
- The existing #869 governance semantics for the pure catalog/expansion path stay intact or are explicitly re-decided in the PR.
- CI green.

Refs: PR #871, issue #869, task 3411. Filed by repo-queue-worker Lane A, 2026-10-29.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A retarget-added leaf that the resolver can run bare under a route-requested variant is judged by governance (an exclusion naming it denies), OR the resolver demonstrably cannot run it bare — with a regression test for the transform + retarget + exclusion scenario from the Codex thread on PR #871
- [ ] The existing #869 governance semantics for the pure catalog/expansion path stay intact (the pruning test re-scoped, not deleted, if semantics change)
- [ ] The chosen reconciliation (governance keeps a bare ref / resolver-side guarantee / governance judges retargeted definitions) is recorded on this issue with its rationale

title: fix(core): Copilot model release dates roll calendar-invalid versions over — "2026-02-30" becomes a March 2 release and outranks newer models

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The GitHub Copilot model builder derives `Model.Info.time.released` from the catalog version string with bare `Date.parse`, guarded only by `Number.isFinite`:

```ts
const version = remote.version.startsWith(`${remote.id}-`) ? remote.version.slice(remote.id.length + 1) : remote.version
const released = previous?.time.released || Date.parse(version)
...
time: { released: Number.isFinite(released) ? released : 0 },
```

The finite guard stops NaN, but not calendar rollover: V8 rolls overflow days into the next month instead of returning NaN, so a catalog version ending in a calendar-invalid date fabricates a release instant that was never real. `released` feeds the released-descending model sort (`packages/core/src/model.ts:229`, `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/opencode.ts:249`), so a fabricated March date for a "February 30" model outranks genuinely newer models.

## Evidence (main cbe84e94ee, verified this run)

- `packages/core/src/github-copilot/models.ts:150-153` and `:176` — the code above.
- Laptop probe (verbatim lines 150-153 + the finite guard, node): `gpt-5-2026-06-01 → 2026-06-01` (correct); `gpt-5-2026-02-30 → 1772409600000 = 2026-03-02` (fabricated); `gpt-5-2026-02-29 → 2026-03-01` (2026 is not a leap year — fabricated); non-date suffixes (`preview`) → NaN → 0 (correctly unknown).
- The in-repo rollover-safe helper already exists: `Model.parseReleaseDate` (`packages/core/src/model.ts:326-340`) round-trips components through a real calendar date and returns `undefined` for invalid ones. It is used for config and models.dev release dates but not here.
- Existing tests (`packages/core/test/github-copilot/models.test.ts:16,43,55,74,128`) only use valid date suffixes.

Not a duplicate of closed #502: that issue fixed the models.dev consumer, and its sweep explicitly cleared this Copilot site as "the `Number.isFinite`-guarded copilot version parse" — that clearing was incomplete, because the finite guard does not stop the rollover case that #471/#502 were about. This site remains on current main.

## Why it matters

The Copilot catalog is fetched live from GitHub's API, not bundled, so OpenCode does not control the version strings it parses. One calendar-invalid version silently invents a release date, skewing model recency ordering for every Copilot user — the same flaw class the repo has already fixed twice elsewhere (#471, #502), in the one consumer those fixes missed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A calendar-invalid version suffix (e.g. `2026-02-30`, `2026-02-29`, `2026-13-01`) yields `released: 0` (the existing unknown sentinel), e.g. by routing the parse through `Model.parseReleaseDate(...) ?? 0` or an equivalent round-trip check.
- [ ] Valid date suffixes, including real leap days, produce exactly the same instants as today.
- [ ] Non-date version strings keep today's behavior (0 when unparseable).
- [ ] A unit test in `packages/core/test/github-copilot/models.test.ts` covers the rollover case alongside a valid case; CI green.

title: fix(core): MCP OAuth toCredential trusts expires_in — a negative value stores a born-expired credential, a millisecond-scale value disables refresh for weeks

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

`MCPOAuth.toCredential` computes the stored MCP credential expiry straight from the remote MCP server's token response with only a truthiness check:

```ts
expires: input.tokens.expires_in ? Date.now() + input.tokens.expires_in * 1000 : 0,
```

`expires_in` is an arbitrary number from an arbitrary, user-configured remote MCP server's token endpoint (the SDK's `StoredOAuthTokens` type places no positivity or bound on it). Two failure directions:

- **Negative `expires_in`** (truthy, so the guard passes) → the credential is born expired: `expires` is in the past.
- **Oversized `expires_in`** — the classic server bug of returning the lifetime in milliseconds (e.g. `7200000` for a 2-hour token) → expiry ~83 days out. `toTokens` then round-trips that fabricated lifetime back to the MCP SDK (`expires_in: Math.max(0, Math.floor((credential.expires - Date.now()) / 1000))`), so the SDK sees a fresh token for weeks and never refreshes; once the real token dies, every call to that MCP server fails auth with no recovery until the fabricated expiry passes.

## Evidence (main cbe84e94ee, verified this run)

- `packages/core/src/mcp/oauth.ts:250` — the line above; `:260-266` — `toTokens` round-trip that feeds the fabricated expiry back to the SDK.
- Both entry points funnel through it: `authorize`'s finalize (`oauth.ts:466`) and the SDK store's `saveTokens` (`oauth.ts:302-313`), which runs on every token response including refreshes — so a single bad response poisons the stored credential persistently.
- Laptop probe (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-mcp-oauth-expires, verbatim line-250 expression, node): `3600 → +3600s` (correct), `-3600 → -3600s` (born expired), `7200000 → +7200000s ≈ 83 days`, and the round-trip hands `7200000` back to the SDK as `expires_in`; `0`/`undefined` → `0` (non-expiring, intended per the comment at :249).
- Existing test coverage (`packages/core/test/mcp-oauth.test.ts:132`) only exercises `expires_in: 3600`.
- In-repo precedents: `xai.ts:233-236` `positiveSeconds` (finite + > 0 or fallback) and DigitalOcean's guarded `Number.isFinite(expires) && expires > 0 ? expires : <default>` before its `* 1000` at `digitalocean.ts:88`.

Distinct from #879 (open), which covers the five integration providers' credential construction and explicitly left this MCP site out of scope (noted as a same-class site on PR #884). This is a different code path (MCP SDK token store), different consumer (the SDK's refresh decision), and a less-trusted input source (any remote MCP server, not a named provider).

## Why it matters

MCP servers are third-party endpoints the user points OpenCode at. One malformed or ms-confused token response either wedges that server's credential into permanent auth failures with refresh disabled for weeks, or stores a born-expired credential. Both fail silently: the stored credential looks well-formed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-positive or non-finite `expires_in` in `toCredential` does not produce a past or fabricated expiry (fall back to the existing non-expiring `0` semantics or another documented sane default — pick one and say why).
- [ ] An implausibly large `expires_in` is clamped to a documented sane bound (or treated like the invalid case), so a milliseconds-confused response cannot disable refresh for weeks.
- [ ] A valid positive `expires_in` behaves exactly as today; absent/`0` keeps the non-expiring semantics.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/mcp-oauth.test.ts` cover negative and oversized `expires_in` for `toCredential`/`toTokens`; CI green.

title: fix(core): opencode device-code poll trusts the server interval with no floor — interval 0 or negative busy-polls the token endpoint for the full 10-minute attempt window

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Problem

The opencode provider's own device-code flow polls with the server-supplied interval verbatim:

```ts
// packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:146
callback: poll(http, server, device.device_code, Duration.seconds(device.interval)),
```

`Device.interval` is an unbounded `Schema.Number` (`opencode.ts:66`). Inside `poll()` (`opencode.ts:651-673`) each iteration is `Effect.sleep(wait)` followed by a POST to `${server}/auth/device/token`, recursing on `authorization_pending`. There is **no floor and no safety margin**:

- `interval: 0` or negative → `Effect.sleep` returns immediately; the loop polls as fast as HTTP round-trips allow.
- `interval: 0.1` → 10 requests/second for the whole authorization wait.

The only bound is the integration layer's generic 10-minute attempt lifetime (`packages/core/src/integration.ts:266`), so a malformed or hostile server response buys up to ~10 minutes of maximum-rate POSTs against the token endpoint — precisely the behavior RFC 8628 §3.5 polling discipline and provider rate limits punish; the likely real-world outcome is the client getting throttled so the legitimate login then fails with `slow_down`/429s.

Secondary: `authorize` never passes the device code's own `expires_in` as the authorization `expiresAt` (the integration layer supports it — `integration.ts:621`, `authorization.expiresAt ?? created + attemptLifetime`), and `poll()` never reads `device.expires_in` — the decoded field is unused, so a short-lived device code is polled for the full generic 10 minutes instead of its own lifetime.

## The in-repo precedent

The OpenAI device flow got exactly this hardening in #771 — `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/openai.ts:179-188`:

```ts
export const deviceIntervalMs = (raw: string): number => {
  const text = raw.trim()
  const parsed = /^\d+$/.test(text) ? Number.parseInt(text, 10) : Number.NaN
  return Math.max(parsed || 5, 1) * 1000
}
```

(clamped to at least 1 second, 5-second fallback), and its poll loop sleeps `interval + pollingSafetyMargin` (`openai.ts:243`). The opencode provider's own flow — the one for this fork's own Console server — never got the same treatment. #771 covered DigitalOcean and OpenAI only; dedup search for the opencode device flow found no open or closed issue.

## Evidence (main 5664199a79, read-verified this run)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:62-67` — `Device` schema: `expires_in: Schema.Number`, `interval: Schema.Number`, both unbounded.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:146` — `Duration.seconds(device.interval)` passed raw into `poll`.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:651-673` — `poll`/`loop`: `Effect.sleep(wait)` → POST → recurse on `authorization_pending` with the same `wait`; `slow_down` adds 5s, but nothing ever raises a too-small initial `wait`.
- `packages/core/src/integration.ts:266` — `attemptLifetime = Duration.minutes(10)` is the only outer bound; `:621` shows `expiresAt` is supported but unset by this provider.

## Why it matters

This is the sign-in path for the fork's own provider. A Console server bug (or any endpoint that answers the device request with a bad interval) turns every login attempt into a request flood against that same server, degrading it for everyone and likely getting the user throttled out of the login they were trying to complete.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The poll interval is floored (≥1s, mirroring `deviceIntervalMs`) with a sane fallback for non-positive/non-finite values, and a small safety margin is added like the OpenAI flow, or an explicit reason is recorded for differing.
- [ ] `authorize` passes the device code's `expires_in` as the authorization `expiresAt` (when positive), so polling stops at the code's own lifetime instead of the generic 10 minutes.
- [ ] A normal server interval (e.g. 5s) behaves exactly as today; `slow_down` backoff still applies on top.
- [ ] Regression tests cover interval 0, negative, and sub-second values for the poll setup; CI green.

title: fix(core): OAuth expires_in stored unvalidated in five providers — negative makes a born-expired credential, an oversized value disables refresh for weeks

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Five OAuth providers compute the stored credential expiry straight from the token response's `expires_in` with no positivity or sanity check:

```ts
expires: now + (tokens.expires_in ?? <default>) * 1000
```

The `??` default only covers an *absent* value. A present-but-wrong value flows through verbatim:

- **Negative or zero** → the credential is born expired. The consumer (`packages/core/src/integration.ts:751`) refreshes whenever `expires <= now + 5 minutes`, so every request triggers a token refresh — a refresh storm against the provider, and with rotating refresh tokens (GitLab) constant rotation churn.
- **Oversized** — the classic server bug is returning the lifetime in milliseconds (e.g. `7200000` for a 2-hour token). That stores an expiry ~83 days out; `integration.ts:751` then treats the credential as valid and *never refreshes*, so once the real token dies every API call fails 401 with no recovery until the fabricated expiry passes.

## Evidence (main 5664199a79, read-verified this run)

- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/gitlab.ts:38` — `expires_in: Schema.optional(Schema.Number)`; `:432` — `expires: now + (tokens.expires_in ?? 7200) * 1000`. GitLab is self-hostable (`instanceUrl` metadata), so the token endpoint is not necessarily gitlab.com's well-behaved one.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/snowflake-cortex.ts:29` — same optional `Schema.Number`; `:75` — `expires: (yield* Clock.currentTimeMillis) + (tokens.expires_in ?? 600) * 1000`.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/chatgpt.ts:521` — `expires: Date.now() + (tokens.expires_in ?? 3600) * 1000`; the response type (`:60-67`) is a plain TS type, so nothing validates the value at runtime at all.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/openai.ts:424` — same `?? 3600` shape in `credential()`.
- `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/opencode.ts:65-71` — `Token`/`Device` schemas declare `expires_in: Schema.Number` (required, unbounded); `:168` and `:697` — `expires: Date.now() + token.expires_in * 1000`.
- Consumer: `packages/core/src/integration.ts:751` — `if (credential.value.expires > now + Duration.toMillis(Duration.minutes(5))) return credential.value` (no refresh); otherwise the credential is refreshed on use. Both failure directions above follow directly from this comparison.

## The in-repo precedent

`packages/core/src/plugin/provider/xai.ts:233-236` already solves exactly this:

```ts
function positiveSeconds(value: unknown, fallback: number) {
  const seconds = Number(value)
  return Number.isFinite(seconds) && seconds > 0 ? seconds : fallback
}
```

used at xai.ts:61, :128 and :215 for every `expires_in` it consumes. `poe.ts:16` likewise constrains its expiry at the schema (`Schema.Int.check(Schema.isGreaterThanOrEqualTo(0))`). The five providers above are the ones that never got the guard.

Distinct from closed #771, which covered *string-spelling* parsing (`parseInt("1e3")`) of duration fields in the DigitalOcean/OpenAI device flows; this is the numeric JSON `expires_in` on the authorization-code/token paths of five other providers.

## Why it matters

Credential expiry is the fork's auth backbone for routed providers. A single malformed or ms-confused token response — most plausible from a self-hosted GitLab instance or a custom Snowflake account endpoint — either wedges the credential into permanent 401s with refresh disabled, or turns every request into a refresh call. Both fail silently: the stored credential looks well-formed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-positive or non-finite `expires_in` falls back to each provider's existing default lifetime (7200 GitLab, 600 Snowflake, 3600 ChatGPT/OpenAI) instead of producing a past expiry; the opencode provider's schemas reject or replace non-positive values.
- [ ] An implausibly large `expires_in` is clamped to a documented sane bound (or rejected to the default), so a milliseconds-confused response cannot disable refresh for weeks.
- [ ] A valid positive `expires_in` behaves exactly as today.
- [ ] Regression tests cover negative, zero, and oversized `expires_in` for each touched provider's credential construction; CI green.

body:
# fix(cli): `service set port` parses with bare Number() — "0x10" stores port 16, "1e3" stores 1000, "8080.0" stores 8080

## Evidence (verified this run, main 4080825c68)

`packages/cli/src/services/service-config.ts:272-276` (the `port` case of `ServiceConfig.set`, reached by `opencode service set port <value>`):

```ts
const port = Number(value)
if (!Number.isInteger(port) || port < 1 || port > 65_535) throw new Error("Port must be between 1 and 65535")
yield* Service.stop(yield* options())
yield* write({ ...(yield* read()), port })
```

The range/integer check rejects NaN, fractions, and out-of-range values, but bare `Number()` still reinterprets non-decimal spellings before the check runs. Laptop probe (~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-29-creator-grace-port/probe.ts, verbatim validation lines; service-config.ts md5-identical between the sandbox checkout at 4080825c68 and the laptop checkout):

```
port "8080"   -> 8080    (control)
port "0x10"   -> 16      FAIL: hex spelling silently becomes a different port
port "1e3"    -> 1000    FAIL: exponent spelling
port "8080.0" -> 8080    FAIL: decimal-point spelling passes the integer check
port "+8080"  -> 8080    sign spelling accepted
port " 8080 " -> 8080    surrounding whitespace accepted
port "0"      -> REJECT  (control)
port "65536"  -> REJECT  (control)
port "abc"    -> REJECT  (control)
port "80junk" -> REJECT  (control)
port ""       -> REJECT  (control)
```

## Why it matters

The stored port is what the managed service binds and what clients connect to. A user (or a script generating the value) who passes `0x10`, `1e3`, or `8080.0` gets no error — the service restarts on a port nobody asked for by that name (16 instead of a literal reading), and the mismatch surfaces later as a connection failure against the port the user believes is configured. This is the same bare-`Number()` grammar family the repo has been closing surface by surface — interactive form numbers (#844), rate-limit counts (#711), OAuth durations (#771) — where the accepted grammar is a plain decimal integer and every other spelling is rejected rather than reinterpreted. A port is the canonical plain-decimal-integer value; there is no caller for whom hex/exponent/decimal-point spellings are intentional.

Note the neighbouring fixed parsers for contrast: the systemd `LISTEN_FDS` reader (`packages/cli/src/systemd.ts:11`) uses `Number.parseInt(…, 10)`, and the managed-port derivation (`service-config.ts:58`) is computed, not parsed.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `service set port` accepts only plain decimal integer spellings in 1–65535 (leading/trailing whitespace handling decided and pinned by test).
- [ ] `"0x10"`, `"1e3"`, `"8080.0"`, and `"+8080"` are rejected with the existing "Port must be between 1 and 65535" error (or a grammar-specific message), and nothing is written and the service is not stopped.
- [ ] `"8080"`, `"1"`, and `"65535"` keep working; `"0"`, `"65536"`, `"abc"`, `"80junk"`, and `""` stay rejected.
- [ ] Tests in the cli package cover the accepted and rejected spellings above for `ServiceConfig.set` port handling.
