title: fix(core,ai,tui,cli): calendar checks skip non-ISO date strings — 'Feb 30 2026' rolls to Mar 2 in all six date parsers

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai
labels.description: Package: ai (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Summary

The calendar checks added for #656/#609/#666 (PRs #658, #667, and the copies made for #713/#727/#780) only round-trip a date part that matches the ISO prefix `/^(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})/`. Every copy then explicitly returns the bare `Date.parse` result for any other shape (`if (!iso) return date` / `return true`). V8's non-ISO parsing rolls overflow days over the same way the ISO path did: `new Date("Feb 30 2026")` is Mar 2 2026, not Invalid. So a calendar-invalid date written in a non-ISO form still passes every one of these validators/parsers and is silently read as a different, real date:

- `"Feb 30 2026"`, `"Feb 30, 2026"`, `"30 Feb 2026"`, `"2026/02/30"` → 2026-03-02 (node probe, below)

Valid non-ISO forms (e.g. `"Jan 5 2026"`) keeping their lenient behaviour is documented intent (PR #658 body; `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts` comment on the `parseAbsoluteTime` path) — this issue is only about non-ISO forms whose day/month components overflow the calendar, which no decision has ever accepted.

## Evidence (verified this run on current main `43cef26f6cef`)

Source PR in this review batch: PR #658 (merge `205db4ec1069`, for #656) added the round-trip to `Form.isDateTime` with the `if (!iso) return true` escape; PR #657 (merge `c1479327be0f`, for #655) routed `QuotaSnapshot` explicit `resetAt` through the same-shaped `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime`. All six current copies share the escape, at these lines on current main:

- `packages/core/src/form.ts:474` — `isDateTime` (function at :466): `if (!iso) return true`. A `date-time` form answer of `"Feb 30 2026"` passes `Form.validateAnswer`.
- `packages/core/src/model-route-limits.ts:57` — `parseAbsoluteTime` (export at :53): `if (!iso) return date`. Shared by `resetMs`/`resetAtFromMessage`, `ModelRouteTuning.parseQuotaReset`, `QuotaSnapshot` resetAt, `MessagingTemplate.parseTime`, Exa/Parallel published dates — a quota message saying a reset happens "Feb 30 2026" yields a Mar 2 reset instant.
- `packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:41` — `parseHttpDate`: `if (!iso) return date` (retry-after HTTP-date branch).
- `packages/ai/src/protocols/replicate-images.ts:134` — its `parseHttpDate` copy: `if (!iso) return date` (Replicate `completed_at` expiry).
- `packages/tui/src/util/form.ts:149` — `validDateTime` (function at :142): `if (!iso) return true`.
- `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/form.ts:205` — `validDateTime` (function at :198): `if (!iso) return true`.

Probe (plain `node -e`, no repo build): `new Date("Feb 30 2026")` → `2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z`; same rollover for `"2026/02/30"`, `"30 Feb 2026"`, `"Feb 30, 2026"`. Each function above returns that rolled instant / `true` because none of the strings match the ISO prefix.

Dedup: searched open + closed issues 2026-10-28 for the non-ISO/lenient angle — #656, #666, #609, #647, #655, #713, #717, #727, #780, #785 all cover ISO-prefixed forms (or bare `Date.parse` sites that have since been routed through these checked parsers); none covers a calendar-invalid **non-ISO** string passing the checked parsers themselves. Note the `!iso` return also short-circuits the hour-24 check in these functions (the `/[T ](\d{2}):\d{2}/` test sits after it), so `"Feb 30 2026 24:00"` passes the form validators on both counts.

## Why it matters

These parsers are the fleet's designated fix for the Feb-30 rollover class: newer code is deliberately routed through them (#785, #779, #717 fixes all delegate here). A hole in the shared parser therefore re-opens the class for every consumer at once — a form respondent can submit a nonexistent date that validates, and a provider quota message can fabricate a reset two days late — while the code comments claim the rollover is checked.

## Acceptance criteria

- For each of the six sites above, a non-ISO date string whose calendar components overflow (e.g. `"Feb 30 2026"`, `"2026/02/30"`, `"30 Feb 2026"`, `"Feb 30, 2026"`) is rejected / returns `undefined`, while valid non-ISO forms (`"Jan 5 2026"`, RFC 9110 HTTP-dates such as `"Wed, 21 Oct 2015 07:28:00 GMT"` for the retry-after sites) keep parsing exactly as today.
- The fix does not regress the ISO checks (#656/#666 cases) or the hour-24 check, and triage decides whether the hour-24 check should also apply to non-ISO forms that reach it (currently the `!iso` return short-circuits before it in the form validators).
- Tests pin the non-ISO overflow rejections and the valid-non-ISO controls beside the existing calendar tests in each affected package (core form + model-route-limits at minimum; ai executor + replicate-images; tui + cli form validators).
- If triage decides some site's non-ISO input space cannot actually contain a month-name/slash date (e.g. a wire format that only ever carries ISO or IMF-fixdate), that site may be left unchanged — but the reasoning is recorded on this issue, not silently skipped.

body:
## Problem

On very large trees the whole-directory watcher silently never starts — the user gets no watching and no user-visible signal, only a server log line.

Two measured walls, both hit before any watch exists (benchmark harness and data: see the results comment on #195, task 2640, laptop `amd`, 2026-10-28):

1. **Production subscribe timeout (10s):** `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts` sets `SUBSCRIBE_TIMEOUT_MS = 10_000` around the @parcel/watcher subscribe. Measured subscribe time grows linearly with tree size: ~0.18s at 1k files, ~0.7s at 50k, **4.0–8.2s at ~510k files** — already within striking distance of the timeout. Trees around ~1M files will exceed it; on timeout/interruption `subscribeDirectory` abandons the subscription and the directory watch simply does not exist.
2. **inotify watch limit:** with 560,000 directories against `fs.inotify.max_user_watches = 524288`, the parcel subscribe ran 20.3s and then failed outright: `inotify_add_watch on '.../d414011' failed: No space left on device`. The failure is all-or-nothing (no partial watching, so no per-subtree staleness), but in production the cause is caught, logged as "failed to subscribe", and converted to `undefined` — the stream ends and nothing surfaces to the user.

## Evidence

- `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts`: `SUBSCRIBE_TIMEOUT_MS`, `subscribeDirectory` catch → log + `undefined`; `nativeLayer` shutdown of the pubsub on missing subscription.
- Benchmark: `~/git/fleet/watcher-bench-195/` on the laptop (harness mirrors the production subscribe call: `createWrapper` + glibc binding, inotify backend, ignore list from `packages/core/src/config/watch.ts`); full table on #195.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When a directory subscribe times out or fails (incl. ENOSPC at the inotify limit), the failure is surfaced somewhere a user or support can see it (e.g. a session/notice-level warning naming the directory and the cause class), not only a server log line.
- [ ] Subscribe timeout scales with tree size, is configurable, or the subscribe is chunked/resumed so that a >1M-file tree still ends up watched (or explicitly reports itself unwatched).
- [ ] A test or benchmark note pins the behavior at the inotify limit: subscribe failure is reported, not silently converted to an empty stream.

title: fix(core): MessagingTemplate.constant reads config vars through the prototype chain — "{constructor}" resolves to a function and crashes rendering when any messaging.vars are configured

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/low

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Summary

`MessagingTemplate.constant()` resolves a variable name through the prototype chain whenever the config carries **any** `messaging.vars` object — even an empty one. `constant("constructor", config)` returns the `Object` constructor function and `constant("__proto__", config)` returns `Object.prototype`, where a string-or-`undefined` is contractually expected. Callers then treat that non-string as a resolved template value and crash on string operations (`.includes` / `.split`), instead of leaving the unknown `{constructor}` placeholder untouched.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fd36da324a`)

- `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts:373-375` — `return config?.vars?.[name] ?? constants[name]?.value`. `config.vars` is a plain config object: for any name not its own property, `config.vars[name]` reads `Object.prototype` members. `constructor` and `__proto__` are not nullish, so `??` never falls through to the built-in `constants` table. (Without a config, `constants[name]?.value` happens to mask the same lookup on the second table — a function's `.value` is `undefined`.)
- Callers trust the result as a string:
  - `packages/core/src/messaging/vars.ts:286-288` — `const configured = MessagingTemplate.constant(name, input.config); if (configured !== undefined) return { value: configured, template: true }`, and `render()` (`template.ts:307-317`) calls `resolved.value.includes("{")` — a function has no `.includes`, so rendering a template containing `{constructor}` throws a `TypeError` defect.
  - `packages/core/src/messaging/template.ts:415-445` — `compile()` (topic classification) calls `expand(value, …)` on the same result; `expand` calls `text.split(TOKEN)` — same crash for a classified template containing `{constructor}`.
- The sibling guards in the same subsystem already use own-property checks — `vars.ts:203,211` (`Object.hasOwn(sessionFields/timeVars)`) and the membership tests fixed under #747 (`vars.ts:419-427`, `Object.hasOwn(constants, …)`) — `constant()` is the lookup those fixes missed.

Laptop probe importing the real module (file md5 `e13568b5e6…`, byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator3/probe-constant.ts`), run from `packages/core`:

- `constant("constructor")` (no config) → `undefined`; with `config = { vars: {} }` → **function** (`typeof` = `function`, `.split` undefined); with `{ vars: { myvar: "hello" } }` → function
- `constant("__proto__", { vars: {} })` → **object** (`Object.prototype`)
- Controls: `constant("separator", …)` → `"/"` in all configs; `constant("myvar", {vars:{myvar:"hello"}})` → `"hello"`; `constant("nosuchvar", {vars:{…}})` → `undefined`

## Why it matters

Messaging templates and topic presets are user/config-authored text; a `{constructor}` or `{__proto__}` token is exactly the kind of placeholder that should be reported as an unknown variable or left untouched in lenient rendering. Instead, the moment a user configures any messaging var at all, those tokens resolve to prototype objects and take down template rendering / topic classification with a raw `TypeError`, far from the actual cause. It also means `constant()` can hand a non-string "value" to anything else that consumes it as topic-name material.

## Acceptance criteria

- `constant("constructor", config)` and `constant("__proto__", config)` return `undefined` for every config shape (no config, empty `vars`, populated `vars`); built-in constants and configured vars still resolve exactly as today.
- Rendering a template containing `{constructor}` with `messaging.vars` configured leaves the placeholder untouched (lenient) or raises the standard unknown-variable `TemplateError` (strict) — never a `TypeError`.
- Both lookups in `constant()` (config vars and the built-in table) are own-property only.
- Tests pin the prototype names for `constant()` and for one downstream render/compile path.

title: fix(core): ShellParse ARITY table reads through the prototype chain — a "constructor" command head yields an empty permission prefix and a " *" saved pattern

body:
## Summary

`ShellParse.prefix()` looks the command head up in the `ARITY` table with a plain index, so a shell command whose head is an `Object.prototype` member name — `constructor`, `__proto__` — is treated as a known multi-word command and produces an **empty** permission prefix. The saved "always allow" pattern for that command becomes `" *"` instead of `"<command> *"`: the grant the user approves can never match a future command, and the permission prompt's saved pattern is meaningless.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fd36da324a`)

- `packages/core/src/shell/parse.ts:23-161` — `ARITY: Record<string, number>` is a plain object literal.
- `packages/core/src/shell/parse.ts:375-382` — `prefix()`: `const arity = ARITY[tokens.slice(0, length).join(" ")]`; `if (arity !== undefined) return tokens.slice(0, arity)`. For `constructor`, `ARITY["constructor"]` is the inherited `Object` function (not `undefined`), and `tokens.slice(0, <function>)` coerces the function to `NaN`, i.e. `slice(0, 0)` → `[]`. For `__proto__` the inherited value is `Object.prototype`, same result.
- Both scan paths consume it identically: legacy `parse.ts:198` (`save: `${prefix(tokens).join(" ")} *``) and portable `parse.ts:267-271` (`selected = prefix(...)`, `conventional = `${selected.join(" ")} *``, and `wordEnds[selected.length - 1]` is `wordEnds[-1]`).
- `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/shell.ts:150-166` — the scan's `save` patterns go into `permission.assert({ save })`; on an "always" reply `packages/core/src/permission.ts:299-306` persists them as saved allow rules, later matched with `Wildcard.match` (`packages/core/src/util/wildcard.ts`) — the pattern `" *"` compiles to `^( .*)?$`, which no real command resource (no leading space) can match.

Laptop probe (verbatim `ARITY` table, lines 23-161, plus `prefix()` spliced unchanged from `shell/parse.ts`, md5 `9c8057aa2…` byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator3/arity-table.ts`):

- `["constructor","foo.txt"]` → prefix `[]`, save `" *"`
- `["__proto__","x"]` → prefix `[]`, save `" *"`
- Controls: `["git","status"]` → `"git status *"`; `["ls","-la"]` → `"ls *"`; `["cargo","run","--release"]` → `"cargo run --release *"`; unknown head `["unknowncmd","arg"]` → `"unknowncmd *"` (the correct fall-through the prototype names bypass)

## Why it matters

This is the permission-analysis surface: the `save` pattern is what the user sees and approves as the persistent grant for a shell tool call. A command head colliding with a prototype name silently degrades that grant to a pattern that matches nothing, so "always" approvals for such a command never take effect (the user is re-prompted forever) — and the corrupted empty prefix also feeds the portable path's `wordEnds[-1]` boundary logic. Same prototype-chain class as #747/#774/#791, in a table none of those covered. Any executable, script, or package binary named `constructor` (e.g. invoked via a project-local bin) hits it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `prefix(["constructor", …])` and `prefix(["__proto__", …])` fall through to the unknown-head behaviour: `[firstToken]`, save `"<head> *"`.
- Known commands keep their exact arities (`git status`, `cargo run`, single-word heads, multi-word keys like `"bun run"`).
- The `ARITY` lookup is own-property only (`Object.hasOwn`, `Map`, or null-prototype table); no other change to scan output for ordinary commands.
- Tests pin prototype-named heads in the shell parse/scan tests, for the saved pattern in at least one scan path.

body:
## Summary

`ModelRouteSchedule.parse` reads day-of-week names through the prototype chain: `daysOfWeek: ["constructor"]` (or `["__proto__"]`, in any letter case) is accepted as a valid day instead of rejecting the window. The stored `daysOfWeek` then contains a function / `Object.prototype` where a number belongs, the window can never be active, and `describe()` renders an empty day list.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `fd36da324a`)

- `packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts:60-66` — `dayOfWeek()` lowercases the input and returns `DAY_NAMES[text]` with a plain index into a normal object literal (lines 34-51). Inherited members resolve: lowercasing makes `constructor` and `__proto__` the reachable prototype names.
- `packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts:207-219` — `parse()` only rejects an entry when the mapped value is `=== undefined`, so the inherited non-number passes, is cast `as number[]`, deduplicated and sorted with a numeric comparator (`NaN` comparisons).
- `packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts:277,318-319` — `dayMatches` uses `daysOfWeek.includes(parts.dayOfWeek)` (never true for the bogus entry) and `describe()` maps through `DAY_LABELS[day]` (undefined).

Laptop probe importing the real module (file md5 `90ef612d…`, byte-identical on both checkouts; probe at laptop `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator3/probe-schedule.ts`):

- `isDayOfWeek("constructor")` → `true`; `isDayOfWeek("__proto__")` → `true` (controls `"tostring"`/`"valueof"` correctly return false only because lowercasing renames them)
- `parse({daysOfWeek:["constructor"]})` → `{daysOfWeek:[<function>]}` (JSON `[null]`), **not** `undefined`
- `parse({daysOfWeek:["__proto__"]})` → `{daysOfWeek:[<Object.prototype>]}` (JSON `[{}]`)
- `parse({daysOfWeek:["mon","constructor"]})` → `{daysOfWeek:[1, <function>]}`
- `describe(that window)` → `" all day"` (empty day list); `active(window, a Monday noon UTC)` → `false`
- Controls: `parse({daysOfWeek:["mon"]})` → `{daysOfWeek:[1]}`; `parse({daysOfWeek:["frieday"]})` → `undefined`

## Why it matters

The module header (lines 15-17) and the pinned tests (`packages/core/test/model-route-schedule.test.ts:38-39`: `["mon","frieday"]` → `undefined`) state the contract: any unreadable day entry rejects the whole window, so a typo makes a rule disappear instead of applying at the wrong time. Prototype names break that contract in the worst direction — the window is *kept*, is silently never active, describes itself with an empty day list, and carries a non-number in a `number[]` that downstream consumers (`ModelRouteSchedule.active` via model-route.ts gates/overrides, route-adjust describe) trust. This is the same prototype-chain class as #747 and #774, in a table those fixes did not cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- `parse({daysOfWeek:["constructor"]})`, `["__proto__"]`, and mixed forms such as `["mon","constructor"]` return `undefined`; `isDayOfWeek` returns `false` for them (any letter case).
- Valid names, numeric strings, and numbers parse exactly as today (`"mon"` → 1, `"06"` → 6, dedup/sort unchanged).
- Lookup is own-property only (e.g. `Object.hasOwn`, a `Map`, or a null-prototype table) — no other behaviour change in `parse`/`active`/`describe`.
- Tests pin the prototype names alongside the existing unreadable-entry cases in `model-route-schedule.test.ts`.

title: fix(core): websearch result dates roll calendar-invalid dates over — Exa and Parallel published dates pass the isFinite guard as fabricated instants

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
## Finding

Both web-search providers that report a publication date parse it with a bare `Date.parse` guarded only by `Number.isFinite`:

- Exa — `packages/core/src/plugin/websearch/exa.ts:71-77`:
  ```ts
  const published = publishedText && publishedText !== "N/A" ? Date.parse(publishedText) : undefined
  …
  time: { ...(published !== undefined && Number.isFinite(published) ? { published } : {}) },
  ```
- Parallel — `packages/core/src/plugin/websearch/parallel.ts:90-95`: the same shape over `item.publish_date`.

`Date.parse` does not return NaN for calendar-invalid dates — it rolls them into the next month/day. The `isFinite` guard (correctly) drops unparseable strings, but a rolled date is finite, so it passes the guard and the `Schema.Finite` on the result field (`packages/schema/src/websearch.ts:29`) alike. The fabricated instant is then presented to the model as fact: `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/websearch.ts:157-160` renders `Published: ${new Date(result.time.published).toISOString()}` in the websearch tool output.

This is the one `Date.parse` surface #780 named as "guarded" — the guard covers NaN only, not the calendar-rollover class removed elsewhere with a round-trip check (#609 `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime`, #713, #717, #779, #780).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `76b8cafb6f`)

Line-level reading of exa.ts:71-77, parallel.ts:90-95, schema/websearch.ts:29 and websearch.ts:157-160, plus a laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator2/probe.mjs`, Node) evaluating the exact expression:

| provider date input | stored `published` | intended |
|---|---|---|
| `"2026-02-30T10:00:00Z"` | **2026-03-02T10:00:00Z** | omitted (unknown date) |
| `"2026-04-31"` | **2026-05-01** | omitted |
| `"2026-01-01T24:00:00Z"` | **2026-01-02** | omitted |
| `"2026-10-28T10:00:00Z"` (control) | 2026-10-28T10:00:00Z | ✓ |
| `"garbage"` (control) | NaN → omitted | ✓ (existing guard) |

No test pins either provider's published-date parsing: there is no exa/parallel websearch test covering a calendar-invalid `Published:` / `publish_date` value.

## Why it matters

- The `Published:` line is how the model (and the user reading the transcript) judges a result's freshness. A source dated Feb 30 presented as Mar 2 — or an Apr 31 item as May 1 — is a silently fabricated publication date, off by days, on an external-API surface whose spellings opencode does not control.
- Both providers share the hole, so the fix belongs in one shared shape (a calendar-checked parse both call, or the same round-trip guard applied at both sites), not two divergent patches.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A calendar-invalid provider date (Feb 30, Apr 31, hour 24) yields **no** `time.published` from either the Exa or the Parallel provider — never a rolled-over instant.
- [ ] Valid provider dates parse to exactly the same instants as today, and unparseable / `"N/A"` / absent values stay omitted.
- [ ] Tests pin both providers: calendar-invalid → omitted; valid → correct instant.
- [ ] No change to result ordering, content extraction, or the `Published:` rendering once a valid date exists.

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "exa published Date.parse", "parallel publish_date", "websearch published rollover" — no hits. #780 (Replicate) names these sites only as isFinite-guarded siblings; #713 covers WebSearch.cooldownMillis retry-after, not result dates.

title: fix(client,app): client-side session root walks ignore the fork link — a fork splits its family, cost and titlebar root from the source tree

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/app

labels.description: Package: client (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

Core defines a session tree's root by following **parent and fork links**: `SessionAffinity.resolveRoot` (`packages/core/src/session/affinity.ts:24-58`) walks `current.parentID ?? current.fork?.sessionID`, with the doc comment "The top-level Session ID grouping a Session tree's model requests: follows parent and fork links … until a Session with neither." A fork is projected top-level (`parent_id` null, `fork_session_id` set — `packages/core/src/session/projector.ts:160-161`), and #505 / PR #775 just extended the same fork-as-child rule to governance and subagent depth.

The two client-side root walks were missed — both follow `parentID` only:

1. `packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:626-641` — `resolveRoot()` walks `store.session.info[…]?.parentID` upward. It keys the **family index** (`registerSession`, :646-672), backs `data.session.root()` (:1493-1495) and `family()` (:1496-1498), and gates `cost()` (:1506-1513): a session with no `parentID` aggregates only its own family's costs.
2. `packages/app/src/shell/routes/session.ts:19-29` — `rootSession()` walks `current.parentID` only; its `SessionParent` type (`:17`) doesn't even include `fork`, although the API's session info carries it (`packages/schema/src/session.ts:41-44`; generated client type at `packages/client/src/promise/generated/types.ts:2791` — `fork?: { sessionID; boundary }`).

So for any chain that crosses a fork, both walks stop at the fork and report the fork as the root, while core reports the true root above the fork's source.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `76b8cafb6f`)

Line-level reading of the three walks above, plus a laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator2/probe.mjs`, Node) running the verbatim walk logic over the fixture `root → child (parentID=root) → fork (no parentID, fork.sessionID=child) → grand (parentID=fork)`:

| session | app `rootSession` | client `resolveRoot` | core `SessionAffinity` |
|---|---|---|---|
| fork | **fork** | **fork** | root |
| grand (child of fork) | **fork** | **fork** | root |
| child (control) | root | root | root |

Existing tests pin only parent chains: `packages/app/src/shell/routes/session.test.ts` (root resolution + cycle) and `packages/client/test/solid-data.test.ts:151` (`root("ses_a1x") === "ses_root"`) — no fork case in either.

## Why it matters

- **Family grouping and cost are split at every fork.** A forked session starts a new client "family": `data.session.family(root)` omits the fork subtree, and `cost(root)` never includes what the fork and its children spend — the session header / family cost views under-report exactly for forked work, which is the common power-user flow.
- **The titlebar resolves the wrong root.** `rootSession`'s result is used as the tab/root identity in `packages/app/src/shell/titlebar/titlebar.tsx:214-226,265,313`; for a child of a fork (or a fork of a child) the tab matching anchors at the fork instead of the tree root its siblings use.
- The divergence is silent and structural: core (affinity, governance #505, depth) treats the fork as part of the source's tree; the client treats it as a brand-new tree.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both client-side root walks follow the fork link when there is no parent link (`parentID ?? fork.sessionID`), matching core `SessionAffinity` semantics — including the differing missing/cycle behaviours each walk already documents (client `resolveRoot`: furthest-known ancestor + seen-set stop; app `rootSession`: cycle throws `Session parent cycle`).
- [ ] Fixture chain root → child → fork → grandchild-of-fork resolves to `root` in both walks; plain parent chains and cycles behave exactly as today.
- [ ] Tests: a fork case in `packages/app/src/shell/routes/session.test.ts` and in `packages/client/test/solid-data.test.ts` (root + family registration across a fork; root cost includes the fork subtree).
- [ ] No change to core affinity/governance, the session schema, or which sessions list as top-level in the UI (a fork still lists top-level; only root/family resolution changes).

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "rootSession fork", "resolveRoot fork client", "family root fork session" — no hits. #505 covers core governance/depth only; its fix (PR #775) does not touch `packages/client` or `packages/app`.

title: fix(ai): Replicate image expiry is NaN or rolled over for a malformed completed_at — bare Date.parse with no validity guard in replicate-images

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

body:
## Finding

`packages/ai/src/protocols/replicate-images.ts:143-145` derives the generated images' expiry from the prediction's `completed_at` with a bare `Date.parse` and **no validity guard at all**:

```ts
const completedAt = prediction.completed_at ?? undefined   // Schema.String, replicate-images.ts:38
const expiresAt =
  completedAt === undefined ? undefined : Date.parse(completedAt) + Duration.toMillis(OUTPUT_RETENTION)  // 1 hour
// → images: urls.map((url) => Media.url(url, { expiresAt }))
```

Two failure modes, both silent:

1. **Unparseable `completed_at` → `expiresAt` is NaN.** Unlike its sibling `Date.parse` sites in this repo — Exa (`plugin/websearch/exa.ts:71-77`), Parallel (`plugin/websearch/parallel.ts:90-95`), and GitHub Copilot models (`github-copilot/models.ts:153,175`) all check `Number.isFinite` before using the value — this site passes NaN straight into `Media.url`. A NaN expiry never compares as expired (`NaN < now` is false for every `now`), so the asset carries a poisoned expiry instead of "unknown expiry" (`undefined`).
2. **Calendar-invalid `completed_at` rolls over.** `Date.parse` turns `2026-02-30` into Mar 2 and `2026-04-31` into May 1, so `expiresAt` lands days after the real completion + 1-hour retention — the images are treated as live long after Replicate's output retention has actually lapsed. This is the rollover class removed elsewhere with a calendar round-trip check (#609/#647/#713; the ai package keeps its own equivalent in `route/executor.ts:31-52`).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5e77693704`)

Line-level reading of replicate-images.ts:38,143-147 and the sibling guards above, plus a laptop runtime probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-creator-20261028-1735/probe-replicate-expires.js`, Node 24) evaluating the exact expression with `OUTPUT_RETENTION = 3_600_000`:

| `completed_at` | `expiresAt` | Intended |
|---|---|---|
| `"2026-10-28T18:00:00Z"` | 2026-10-28T19:00:00Z | ✓ |
| `"2026-02-30T10:00:00Z"` | **2026-03-02T11:00:00Z** | undefined (unknown expiry) |
| `"2026-04-31T10:00:00Z"` | **2026-05-01T11:00:00Z** | undefined |
| `"garbage"` / `""` | **NaN** (`NaN < now` is false — never expires) | undefined |
| absent | undefined | ✓ |

There is also no test file for this protocol in `packages/ai/test/` pinning `completed_at` handling at all.

## Why it matters

`expiresAt` is the contract consumers use to decide whether a generated image URL is still fetchable ("Epoch milliseconds after which a url source stops resolving", media.ts:116). A NaN or rolled expiry silently defeats that: expired Replicate outputs are presented as live (broken images / failed downloads downstream with no explanation), and the NaN case can never expire by comparison. `completed_at` is server-supplied — exactly the untrusted-spelling surface the sibling guards were added for.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An unparseable or calendar-invalid `completed_at` yields `expiresAt: undefined` (unknown expiry), never NaN and never a rolled-over instant — calendar check equivalent to the ai executor's local `parseAbsoluteTime` (route/executor.ts:31-52) or a stated equivalent.
- [ ] A valid `completed_at` still yields exactly `completed + 1 hour`, and an absent `completed_at` still yields `undefined`.
- [ ] New tests for the replicate-images result path pin: valid, calendar-invalid (Feb 30 / Apr 31), and garbage `completed_at` values.

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "replicate completed_at expiresAt", "replicate-images Date.parse", and "replicate" — no replicate-images issue exists (list hits were unrelated issues mentioning the word in passing). The calendar-rollover issues (#609/#647/#713/#717) cover other files only.

title: fix(core): Azure CLI token expiry rolls calendar-invalid dates over — bare Date.parse on expiresOn fabricates a cache lifetime instead of the invalid-expiration error

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

The Azure CLI token path in `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/azure.ts:98` parses the CLI's string expiry with a bare `Date.parse`:

```ts
const expires = result.expires_on !== undefined ? result.expires_on * 1000 : Date.parse(result.expiresOn ?? "")
if (!Number.isFinite(expires))
  return yield* Effect.fail(new Error("Azure CLI returned an invalid token expiration"))
```

`expiresOn` is `Schema.optional(Schema.NonEmptyString)` (azure.ts:31) — the only guard is the `isFinite` check. But `Date.parse` does not return NaN for calendar-invalid dates: it silently rolls them into the next month/day. A malformed `expiresOn` therefore never reaches the existing "invalid token expiration" error — instead the token is cached (`tokens.set(scope, …)`, azure.ts:102) with a fabricated expiry, and the cache check `cached.expires - now > 5 * 60_000` (azure.ts:93) treats the token as fresh until that fabricated instant.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `5e77693704`)

Line-level reading of azure.ts:88-104 (above), plus a laptop runtime probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-creator-20261028-1735/probe-azure-expires.js`, run under both Node 24 and Bun 1.4.2 with identical results) evaluating the exact expression:

| `expiresOn` input | Result | Intended |
|---|---|---|
| `"2026-10-28T18:00:00Z"` | 2026-10-28T18:00:00Z | ✓ |
| `"2026-10-28 18:00:00.000000"` (az CLI shape) | parses | ✓ |
| `"2026-02-30T10:00:00Z"` | **2026-03-02T10:00:00Z** | invalid-expiration error |
| `"2026-02-30 10:00:00.000000"` (az shape) | **2026-03-02** | invalid-expiration error |
| `"2026-04-31T10:00:00Z"` | **2026-05-01T10:00:00Z** | invalid-expiration error |
| `"2026-01-01T24:00:00Z"` | **2026-01-02T00:00:00Z** | invalid-expiration error |
| `"not-a-date"` / `""` | NaN → error | ✓ (only these reach the error) |

This is the same defect class removed elsewhere with a calendar round-trip check: quota-reset parsers (#609, `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime`, model-route-limits.ts:54-71 — which already handles both the `T` and space separators and the hour-24 case), ModelPlan dates (#717), retry-after dates (#713). The Azure token parser is in the same package (`packages/core`) and was missed. Test gap: `packages/core/test/plugin/provider-azure.test.ts` exercises only the numeric `expires_on` form (its `cliToken` fixture, ~line 112); the `expiresOn` string path has no test at all.

## Why it matters

- The cached expiry decides when opencode re-runs `az account get-access-token`. A rolled expiry (up to ~2 days late for Feb 30, a day for hour 24) means an actually-expired Azure token is presented as fresh — management/deployment requests fail with auth errors while the client believes the credential is valid, instead of the clean refresh / invalid-expiration error the code intends.
- The value comes from an external process's JSON output — exactly the untrusted-spelling surface the calendar-check fixes were for.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A calendar-invalid `expiresOn` (Feb 30, Apr 31, hour 24, in both ISO and the space-separated az CLI shape) takes the existing `Azure CLI returned an invalid token expiration` error path — no fabricated cache expiry. Reusing `ModelRouteLimits.parseAbsoluteTime` is the natural shape; a stated equivalent calendar check is fine.
- [ ] Valid `expiresOn` values (ISO with zone, and the space-separated `YYYY-MM-DD HH:mm:ss.ffffff` az shape) parse to the same instants as today.
- [ ] The numeric `expires_on` path is unchanged.
- [ ] Tests in `provider-azure.test.ts` pin the string path: calendar-invalid → error; valid az-shape string → correct expiry (the existing fake-CLI fixture can return `expiresOn` instead of `expires_on`).

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "azure expires", "expiresOn", "azure expiresOn Date.parse", "Date.parse rolls" — hits were #609/#647/#713 only (quota, messaging-template, retry-after surfaces); no Azure token issue exists.

title: fix(core): AISDKNative package tables read through the prototype chain — a package named "constructor" resolves to a function, not a package string

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: status/in-progress
labels.description: Actively being worked

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: queue/claimed
labels.description: A queue worker has claimed the task for this item

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

`packages/core/src/aisdk-native.ts` looks up package and provider names in plain object literals through the prototype chain, so a package/provider named like an `Object.prototype` member is treated as a known entry and resolves to a **function or object instead of a package string**:

- `aisdk-native.ts:142` — `resolve()` gates on `npm in PACKAGES || npm in (HOSTS[context.providerID] ?? {})`. `in` walks the prototype chain: `"constructor" in PACKAGES === true` even though `PACKAGES` (lines 66–87) has no such key.
- `aisdk-native.ts:127` — `native()` returns `PACKAGES[npm]` directly; for `npm = "constructor"` / `"toString"` / `"hasOwnProperty"` that is an inherited **function**, and for `"__proto__"` the prototype object — despite the declared return type `string | undefined`.
- `aisdk-native.ts:123` — `native()` first reads `HOSTS[context.providerID]?.[npm]`; `HOSTS["constructor"]` and `HOSTS["toString"]` are likewise inherited functions, not host tables.

Callers trust the result as a string:

- `packages/core/src/models-dev.ts:88` — `nativePackage()` does `AISDKNative.native(npm, …) ?? Provider.aisdk(npm)`; a function is not nullish, so the function itself becomes the provider's package name for a models.dev / config entry whose `npm` is a prototype name.
- `packages/core/src/provider.ts:393,421` and `packages/core/src/model.ts:142` — `rewrite()` assigns the resolved value to `target.package` when it differs from the specifier, so `target.package` can be set to a function, corrupting the provider/model record that later loading, serialization and equality checks consume.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `0b51b19b33`)

Laptop probe (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-28-creator/probe.js`, Node) replicating the shipped tables' shape and the exact `in` / index expressions:

```
PACKAGES["@ai-sdk/openai"]  in=true  value=string "@opencode/ai/providers/openai"
PACKAGES["constructor"]     in=true  value=function (function!)
PACKAGES["toString"]        in=true  value=function (function!)
PACKAGES["__proto__"]       in=true  value=object {}
PACKAGES["hasOwnProperty"]  in=true  value=function (function!)
HOSTS["constructor"] -> function; HOSTS["toString"] -> function
```

The `npm` / provider names reaching these tables come from models.dev data and user provider config (`package` / `npm` fields) — authored strings, not a closed enum. This is the same prototype-membership defect class fixed for MessagingVars in #747 (`in` → own-property checks, PR #755), one subsystem over; `aisdk-native.ts` was not part of that fix.

## Why it matters

A provider or package literally named `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty` or `__proto__` — in a user config, a plugin-supplied catalog, or future models.dev data — is silently treated as a built-in AI SDK package and rewritten to a non-string value. The failure then surfaces far away (package loading / record serialization) with no pointer back to the name collision, instead of the name simply being treated as an unknown (non-native) package, which is the correct outcome: `resolve()` should return `undefined` and `nativePackage()` should fall back to `Provider.aisdk(npm)`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `resolve()` / `native()` use own-property lookups for `PACKAGES` and `HOSTS` (both the outer provider table and the inner per-host table); prototype names (`constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, `__proto__`, `valueOf`) are treated as unknown packages.
- [ ] `AISDKNative.native("constructor", …)` returns `undefined` (so callers fall back to `Provider.aisdk(npm)`), and `rewrite()` never assigns a non-string to `target.package`.
- [ ] Tests in `packages/core/test/aisdk-native.test.ts` pin the prototype names as unknown, alongside the existing known-package cases.
- [ ] No behaviour change for any real key of `PACKAGES` / `HOSTS`.

Dedup: searched open+closed issues 2026-10-28 for "aisdk-native prototype", "aisdk PACKAGES constructor", "native package prototype", "in PACKAGES" — no filing covers these tables; #747 covers `messaging.ts` variable tables only, #538 config alias `__proto__`.

title: fix(core): a config file in a .opencode directory created after startup is loaded once but never watched — later edits are ignored

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/sweep
labels.description: Filed or worked by an issue-sweep job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/m

body:
## Problem

In `packages/core/test/config/reload.test.ts`, the variants `loads references when .opencode/opencode.json is first created and keeps watching it` and `loads references when ../.opencode/opencode.jsonc is first created and keeps watching it` fail deterministically on the laptop (Linux) at current main `0b51b19b33`: 2 of 13 tests in the file fail, 3 of 3 runs, while the other 11 pass.

The first load works; the file is then never watched. Instrumented run (single variant, poll budget temporarily raised to 2000 attempts / ~20s, test timeout 60s):

- Poll 1 (create `.opencode/opencode.json` with `references: { docs: "./docs" }` after startup; wait for the `docs` reference) succeeds after 12 attempts (~120ms).
- Poll 2 (rewrite the same file with `references: { next: "./next" }`; wait for the list to become `next`) never completes — the full 2000-attempt budget expires with the reference list unchanged.

So a config file inside a `.opencode` directory that is itself created after startup is picked up once (presumably by the rescan that follows the directory-create event), but no live watch is established on it: later edits are silently ignored until something else triggers a rescan. The root-file variants (`opencode.json`, `../opencode.jsonc`) pass, so the gap is specific to the first-created `.opencode` directory path.

## Likely mechanism

Watch acquisition for the newly created `.opencode` directory (or for the config file inside it) either never happens or happens without a follow-up rescan, so an edit that lands before/around acquisition is the only one ever seen and subsequent edits have no watcher. Compare the skill plugin's ordering note in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/skill.ts` ("Subscribe before debouncing so no update slips through") and the mocked-watcher test in the same file, `loads the first config written while a new directory watch is starting`, which covers exactly this race for a mocked watcher — the native watcher path appears to have the same shape of gap for `.opencode` directories. Relevant code: `packages/core/src/config/watch.ts`, `packages/core/src/filesystem/location-watcher.ts`, `packages/core/src/filesystem/watcher.ts`, `packages/core/src/config/plugin/reference.ts`.

Note: these tests pass in CI as far as current evidence shows (they are not among the known CI failures), so the race may be timing- or environment-sensitive; on the laptop it is deterministic (3/3 runs, plus the instrumented run).

## Evidence

- Laptop, clean main `0b51b19b33`, worktree from the laptop primary: `bun test test/config/reload.test.ts` (from `packages/core`) = 11 pass / 2 fail, both failures the `.opencode` variants above, at ~1.5-1.7s with the stock 100-attempt poll budget.
- Same result with a 300-attempt budget (failures at ~3.9-4.4s) and with a 2000-attempt budget under a 60s test timeout (single variant, 26.6s, still failing) — this is not a polling-budget problem; the update never arrives.
- Instrumented `waitUntil`: poll 1 ok after 12 attempts; poll 2 dies. The failing step is therefore "keeps watching it", not first creation.
- Found while fixing #551 (the skills-variant poll-budget flake in the same file; PR #772). This issue is the references/watch half that #551's budget change does not and cannot fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Root cause identified in the watcher/config-watch path: why no live watch (or no post-acquisition rescan) covers a config file in a `.opencode` directory created after startup.
- [ ] Both `.opencode` variants of `loads references when ... is first created and keeps watching it` pass repeatedly on the laptop (e.g. 5 consecutive full-file runs) and in CI.
- [ ] The fix does not weaken the tests: all six poll steps (create, edit, delete, recreate, edit) still assert the reference list contents.
- [ ] No regression in the other `reload.test.ts` variants or the mocked-watcher "new directory watch is starting" test.

title: fix(core): McpxDiagnose.attemptParameterRepair still reinterprets non-decimal number spellings — "0x10" coerces to 16 while ToolInputRepair leaves it unrepaired

body:
## Finding

`McpxDiagnose.attemptParameterRepair` (packages/core/src/tool/plugin/mcpx-diagnose.ts) still coerces numeric strings with bare `Number()` grammar, so non-decimal spellings are silently reinterpreted in the repaired parameters it produces for MCP tool calls: `"0x10"` → 16, `"0b101"` → 5, `"0o17"` → 15, `"1e3"` → 1000, `"+42"` → 42. The sibling repair path in the same repo, `ToolInputRepair` (packages/core/src/plugin/tool-input-repair.ts), was deliberately restricted to a plain-decimal grammar for exactly this defect class in #715 / PR #719 ("Number() alone is too wide — it reinterprets hex/binary/octal/exponent spellings … the model never wrote as decimals, so those are left unrepaired"). The two parameter-repair paths now disagree: the same malformed tool input is left for schema validation by one path and silently rewritten to a different number by the other.

## Evidence

- PR #644 (commit 9b0371c9d8, fixing #595) hardened this coercion against flooring and non-finite values but explicitly pinned Number()'s grammar as accepted: the comment at mcpx-diagnose.ts:280-284 (current main 0b51b19b33) reads "The accepted grammar is Number()'s, so hex ("0x10") and exponent ("1e3") forms coerce when they satisfy those checks", and its tests pin `"0x10"` → 16 and `"1e3"` → 1000.
- Current main, mcpx-diagnose.ts:286-291: `const num = Number(trimmed)` with only finiteness / integer checks — no grammar restriction. Verified 2026-10-28 via `git show origin/main:`.
- Contrast on current main: tool-input-repair.ts (as changed by PR #719) tests the string against `/^-?\d+$/` (integer) or `/^-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?$/` (number) before parsing and leaves every other spelling unrepaired. The same plain-decimal stance was adopted for rate-limit counts (#711), retry-after (#682/#686), Modal pricing (#724) and file-URL line ranges (#728).
- One deliberate divergence to decide in triage: mcpx coerces integer `"3.0"` → 3; ToolInputRepair's integer grammar leaves `"3.0"` unrepaired. The triage should state which behaviour the mcpx path keeps, rather than leaving the two paths incidentally different.

## Why it matters

attemptParameterRepair's output is the repaired parameter set proposed/applied for an MCP tool call. Reinterpreting a radix or exponent spelling changes the number the tool actually receives from what was written — the exact failure #715 removed from the other repair path. Consistency also matters for diagnosis: the same input currently produces "repaired to 16" from the mcpx diagnose path and "unrepaired, schema error" from the input-repair path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] attemptParameterRepair coerces only plain-decimal spellings (the ToolInputRepair grammar, or a stated equivalent), for both `number` and `integer` parameters; `"0x10"`, `"0b101"`, `"0o17"`, `"1e3"`, `"+42"`, `"5."` are left unrepaired.
- [ ] The integer `"3.0"` divergence from ToolInputRepair is decided explicitly and pinned by a test either way.
- [ ] The pinning tests added by PR #644 in packages/core/test/tool-mcpx-features.test.ts are updated to the new grammar (finite/integral checks from #595 stay pinned).
- [ ] The in-code comment no longer states Number()'s grammar is the accepted grammar.

Found by the pr-diff-review job reviewing PR #644 against current main; dedupe: searches over open+closed issues for "mcpx repair hex", "attemptParameterRepair", "parameter repair", "decimal grammar mcpx" returned only #595 (the flooring bug #644 fixed) — no filing covers the grammar.

body:
## Support per-element (per-target) context limits in model routes

Today `limit: { context }` exists only at the route level (landed with the route context-limit feature). A pool whose members need *different* context ceilings must be expressed by nesting whole routes.

### Motivating case (live config, 2026-10-27 redesign)

The `small` pool needs three elements with two different ceilings:

- `haiku-plan#high` at ≤100k
- `luna-plan#xhigh` at ≤100k
- `haiku-plan#high` at ≤200k

Because per-target limits don't exist, this ships as a nested `small-100k` sub-route (100k cap) inside `small` (200k cap) — an extra route id, and the intent ("these elements, these ceilings") is split across two definitions.

### Request

Allow `limit` on individual route targets, composing with the route-level limit:

```jsonc
{ "model": "opencode-route/haiku-plan#high", "limit": { "context": 100000 } }
```

Semantics to define:

1. A target is eligible only when the request context fits BOTH the route limit (if any) and the target limit (if any).
2. Over-limit targets are skipped like other ineligible targets (quota-demoted, disabled, window-closed), with the exclusion visible in the resolved-route dump with its reason.
3. Nested-route references carrying their own limits keep working unchanged.

### Done when

`small` can be written as one flat route with per-element limits, the dump shows per-element ceilings and skip reasons, and tests cover mixed-ceiling pools.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `small` can be written as one flat route with per-element `limit: { context }` on individual targets — no nested `small-100k` sub-route needed (the body's "Done when", restated here as the criteria section).
- [ ] A target is eligible only when the request context fits BOTH the route-level limit (if any) and the target limit (if any); over-limit targets are skipped like other ineligible targets.
- [ ] The resolved-route dump shows per-element ceilings and the skip reason for each over-limit target.
- [ ] Nested-route references carrying their own limits keep working unchanged, and tests cover mixed-ceiling pools.

title: fix(server): PR #596 provider.get embeds models from the unfiltered state record while provider.list embeds only snapshot.available — disabled/stale-connection providers leak their catalog through get

body:
# Finding (pr-diff-review lane B, PR #596) — triage: confirm intended semantics

PR #596 (OPEN, head `4c0f8c5a`, for #560) embeds models into both provider endpoints, but the two endpoints now draw from **different provider sets**:

- **List** (`packages/server/src/handlers/provider.ts`, PR head): `providers.snapshot()` → `snapshot.available.map(withModels)` — only providers that pass the snapshot availability filter.
- **Get** (same file, PR head): the new nonblocking `Provider.definition()` (`packages/core/src/provider.ts`, PR head) returns `state.get().get(id)` — **any recorded definition**, with no availability check — and `withModels` embeds that record's full model map.

## Evidence

- The snapshot filter the get path bypasses (current main `41c8a35f`, `packages/core/src/provider.ts`, `Provider.snapshot`): a record is available only if its activation is not `disabled`, and — when it carries a `sourceConnection` — only if that connection still matches the current integration connection ("Never combine the previous account's discovered endpoints/models with a new connection"). Disabled and stale-connection records are excluded from `available`.
- Before this PR, `provider.get` returned only `Provider.Info` metadata through the equally unfiltered `Provider.get`, so the unfiltered read exposed little. The PR makes the unfiltered read the one that serves the provider's **model inventory** — models of a disabled provider, or of a provider whose recorded models belong to a previous account's connection, are now served by `GET /api/provider/:id` while `GET /api/provider` correctly omits that provider entirely.
- The PR's own new test (`packages/server/test/provider.test.ts`) covers only an enabled, available custom provider; no test pins the get/list relationship for a disabled or connection-stale provider.
- The core interface still documents the boundary the PR crosses (`packages/core/src/provider.ts:319` on main): "Internal definition/access snapshot; raw model inventories never cross the HTTP API."

## Why it matters

List/get disagreement is exactly the class of inconsistency #560's consumers (T3 Code's provider health check) trip over: a provider can be absent from discovery yet return a full model catalog when queried directly, including catalog data the snapshot layer deliberately withholds after a credential/account switch.

## Acceptance criteria

- Triage decides and records the intended contract: either `provider.get` serves only providers that would appear in `provider.list` (available set), or the unfiltered get is deliberate and documented in the handler/protocol description.
- If aligned to the available set: a disabled (or source-connection-stale) provider returns `ProviderNotFoundError` from get, with a server test pinning it; the nonblocking contract (no waiting on integration discovery) is preserved or the change in blocking behaviour is explicitly justified.
- If the unfiltered get is kept deliberately: the protocol endpoint description says so, and a test pins that get returns models for a provider absent from list.

Source PR: https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/596 · Parent issue: #560

## Problem

#240 established the mechanism in `packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts`: a field description annotated **outside** the package `optional` helper (`.pipe(optional).annotate({ description })`) lands only on the decoded side, so the encoded JSON schema — what the OpenAPI document and editors are generated from — shows nothing for the field. #240 fixed the pool/model-route schemas (completed by PR #597 and the #645 remainder), but the same ordering pattern exists in other schema files and has never been audited:

Preliminary grep evidence on main 3466af1d26 (`.pipe(optional)` followed by `.annotate`, per file):

- `packages/schema/src/messaging.ts` — the largest cluster
- `packages/schema/src/config.ts`

- `packages/schema/src/config/experimental.ts` (e.g. lines 10–37: aliases, portable_shell_scanner, subagent_depth, shell_timeout, model_routes, model_route_schedules, model_route_tuning, model_route_log)

labels.name: meta/enriched

body:
## Request: exclusion expressions for model route / plan pool definitions

Today a plan pool (e.g. `deepseek-flash-plan`) enumerates every leaf target explicitly. As the pool set grows (per-model pools × many doors × three OpenCode Go workspaces), enumeration is error-prone and hides intent: several pools we want are most naturally expressed as a model on a door set **minus** exclusions.

### Motivating examples (from the 2026-10-27 pool review)

- `deepseek-flash` on **all doors except ClinePass** — ClinePass's flat meter is more valuable reserved for MiMo; Flash burns better on Go (promo rate) and OpenDesign.
- `mimo-flash` **on ClinePass** (plus Go/OpenDesign) — the inverse reservation.
- The standing rule "any pool containing one OpenCode Go workspace contains all three (personal, lab, base)" is currently maintained by hand-enumerating three near-identical leaves per pool.

### Proposed shape

Allow a target/pool definition to express a model over a door set with exclusions, composing with the existing controls (selection mode, weights, per-target variant pins/remaps, context limits, and `disabled_providers` skipping):

```jsonc
{ "model": "deepseek-v4.1-flash", "doors": "all", "exclude": ["cline-pass"] }
```

or equivalently negative targets in the existing list form:

```jsonc
"targets": [
  { "model": "*deepseek-v4.1-flash" },        // all doors serving this model
  { "model": "-cline-pass/deepseek-v4.1-flash" }
]
```

Exact syntax is open; requirements are:

1. Expansion happens against the live provider catalog (a door is included iff it lists the model and is not disabled).
2. Exclusions win over inclusions, always.
3. Expansion is visible/verifiable — a way to dump the resolved leaf list per route so config reviews can check what a pool actually contains.
4. Existing fully-enumerated pools keep working unchanged.

### Why

Pool definitions become statements of intent ("Flash everywhere except the meter reserved for MiMo") instead of leaf inventories that silently drift when a door adds or drops a model.

## Acceptance criteria

- A pool/target definition can express a model over a door set with exclusions (e.g. deepseek-flash on all doors except ClinePass), composing with selection mode, weights, per-target variant pins/remaps, context limits, and `disabled_providers` skipping.
- Expansion resolves against the live provider catalog: a door is included only if it lists the model and is not disabled, and exclusions always win over inclusions.
- The resolved leaf list per route can be dumped/verified, so a config review can check what a pool actually contains (including the all-three-OpenCode-Go-workspaces rule).
- Existing fully-enumerated pools keep working and resolve unchanged.

title: Native quota intelligence: burn-rate estimation and dynamic reprioritization to consume quota before reset

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: New feature or capability request

labels.name: status/in-progress
labels.description: Actively being worked

labels.name: priority/high
labels.description: Important and time-sensitive

labels.name: effort/l
labels.description: Large: multi-day or open-ended; expect staged check-ins

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

Plan quotas that reset with unused headroom are wasted money; quotas blown early strand work. Today OpenCode's relationship to quotas is essentially binary — a model is available until it isn't. We want OpenCode to treat quotas as a **managed resource with a deadline**:

- Know each pool's current % used, its reset time, and its usage history.
- Know, empirically, **how much of a window a typical session costs** — e.g. a medium session on model X burns ~N% of the weekly window, a high/xhigh session ~M%.
- Then **reprioritize across the board at a calculated rate**: if projected usage won't consume a pool before reset, spend the surplus on quality — upgrade models and efforts. If it will overshoot, downgrade early instead of hitting the wall mid-session.

Examples of the intended upgrades when a pool is under-projected to be consumed:

- Sonnet medium → Sonnet xhigh, Opus medium, or Opus high (same provider, richer effort/model)
- DeepSeek → Muse Wonder (cross-provider substitution toward a pool with surplus)
- A small/fast model (e.g. Luna-class) → Sonnet or Flash High

…and the mirror-image downgrades when a pool is projected to exhaust early.

## Desired behavior

1. **Routine quota telemetry**: poll/refresh each pool's % used and next reset on a configurable interval; keep a history so rates are computed from data, not guesses. Stale data is marked stale and never treated as headroom.
2. **Per-session burn-rate model**: from history, estimate the typical % of window consumed per session, bucketed by provider/model/effort (low/medium/high/xhigh). Cold start uses configured priors.
3. **Projection + controller loop**: project end-of-window usage from remaining time, reset schedule, and recent burn rate. When the projection under-consumes by more than a configurable margin, raise effective weights/effort floors along a configured **upgrade ladder** (within a provider first, then across providers). When it over-consumes, step down the ladder. The goal: land near 100% at reset — **never into PAYG**.
4. **Safety bounds**: upgrades never exceed configured per-pool ceilings; the final-reserve pool (OpenAI/Codex in our fleet) is excluded from burn-up behavior unless explicitly opted in; every controller action is logged with its inputs (projection, margin, ladder step) so a human can audit *why* a model was upgraded.
5. **Safe default bets**: ship with a small set of conservative defaults (telemetry on, controller in observe/advise mode first, upgrades opt-in per pool) so this can land incrementally: measure → advise → act.

## Non-goals / boundaries

- No PAYG spend, ever, as a result of this controller.
- No silent behavior: reprioritization must be visible in status/logs.
- This issue owns the *intelligence*; the placement gates (quota % × session type, #566) and time-based weighting are separate companion issues, and this controller should adjust the same weight model they use rather than inventing a parallel one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Quota % + reset time are refreshed on an interval and persisted with history for every configured pool.
- [ ] Burn-rate estimates per model/effort bucket are computed from history and exposed for inspection.
- [ ] Given a scripted quota history and clock, the controller's projection and ladder decisions are deterministic and unit-tested (under-consume → upgrade; over-consume → downgrade; at-target → no change).
- [ ] Observe mode logs the action it *would* take without applying it; act mode applies it through the shared weight model.
- [ ] Controller never selects a PAYG route and never burns the configured final-reserve pool without explicit opt-in — covered by tests.
- [ ] All thresholds (poll interval, under/over margins, ladder steps, ceilings) are configuration.

## Context

Fleet rule (Drew, 2026-10-27): use plan quotas all the way to 100%, then stop until reset (or until a fresh read shows an early reset). Companion issues: #566 (quota-% × session-type placement filtering) and #567 (time-of-day weighting with temporary priority windows).

`/api/provider` should include each provider's resolved models (the same catalog `/api/config` already assembles), so model discovery works for API consumers without them having to parse the full config document.

1. Find where the `/api/provider` response is assembled; merge the resolved per-provider model lists (post config-load, post sync-models edits) into the provider resources it returns.

body:
## Problem

The `config plugin reloads` test `loads skills when <root> appears after startup` (`packages/core/test/config/reload.test.ts:57`, `it.live`, parameterized over `.agents`, `../.claude`, `home/.agents`, `home/.claude`) intermittently fails on Linux CI in PR runs whose diffs do not touch the config/plugin/skill/watcher subsystems.

Sightings:

1. PR #539 CI (linux unit) — `home/.claude` variant; recorded in the sweep backlog 2026-10-26 as a first sighting under WATCH (the PR diff touched only `model-route-overrides.ts` + its test).
2. PR #544 CI, run 40406527619 (linux unit) — `../.claude` variant, failed after 1360.79ms; log-verified 2026-10-26 by issue-sweep-rotating. That PR's diff touches only config alias normalization. The same run's other failures were the 2 known tui permission-focus flakes per OS (plus a first-sighting windows Git-objects 60s timeout, tracked separately as WATCH in the backlog).

Counter-evidence: the main push run for the #539 merge commit (5c72116653, test run 40404404133) failed ONLY the 2 known tui permission-focus flakes per OS — this test passed there. So it is intermittent, not a deterministic regression.

## Likely mechanism

The test polls with `waitUntil` (`reload.test.ts:394-400`): 100 attempts × `Effect.sleep("10 millis")` ≈ a ~1s budget for a filesystem-watcher event to propagate and the skill list to refresh. The 1360ms failure duration is consistent with that budget expiring under CI load. Either the polling budget is too tight for loaded runners, or watcher delivery latency has a long tail worth fixing in the watcher/skill refresh path itself — the fix should determine which, not just raise the timeout blindly.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Determine whether the failure is test-budget tightness or real watcher/refresh latency (e.g. instrument or reproduce under load).
- [ ] Fix so the test is reliable on loaded Linux CI: a justified polling/timeout change in the test, or a latency fix in the watcher/skill path if the latency is real product behavior.
- [ ] No blanket retry/flaky annotation without the root-cause note above recorded on this issue.

## Finding

The core unit test `fails over when a routed provider misses the first-output deadline` (`packages/core/test/session-step.test.ts`) is timing-flaky on CI: the failover itself succeeds, but the final assertion on the recorded LLM requests races and reads an empty list.

Failing assertion (both sightings):

```
expect(yield* llm.requests()).toHaveLength(1)
Expected length: 1
Received length: 0
at packages/core/test/session-step.test.ts:998
```

The assertions immediately before it pass — the step result is a success with tag `Failover` and `ModelRoute.coolingDown(primary.ref)` is true — so the routed failover happened; only the request recording is observed too early (or is lost) under CI load.

## Evidence

- Sighting 1 — 2026-10-20, PR #186 CI, unit (linux): sole failure in the job, ~31ms, untouched area; a rerun of the failed job passed. Recorded as a first sighting in the sweep backlog with a watch note ("file if it recurs").
- Sighting 2 — 2026-10-26, PR #486 CI, unit (windows), job 121400083369: same test, same assertion, 23.95ms; the PR's diff (session governance) does not touch the runner, model routes, or LLM request recording. Log-verified as the only non-tui failure in that job (the other two were the known tui permission-focus flakes).

This is the recurrence the watch note asked to be filed on.

## Acceptance criteria

- Determine why `llm.requests()` can read 0 after a completed failover: test-side race (the recording lands asynchronously after the step resolves) or a real product race in request recording under a first-output deadline.
- Make the test deterministic per the repo's unit-tests skill: control or await the actual condition (e.g. poll for the recorded request with a generous deadline, or await the recording at its source) — no larger timeouts, sleeps, or retries as the fix.
- If the race is in product code, fix it there and keep this test as the regression cover.
- The test passes repeatedly under load on both OS legs (or the fix demonstrably removes the race by construction).

## Notes

- Unrelated to PR #486's change; that PR merged on the strength of this being a previously documented flake plus its own green typecheck/build and locally passing governance suites.

title: fix(core): bare-alias variant is preserved by the session runner (PR #390) but dropped by ModelResolver (PR #382)

body:
## Finding

PR #390 and PR #382 implement the same empty-id bare-alias ref-string construction in two places — and they diverge on the variant.

- PR #390 (`packages/core/src/session/runner/model.ts`, head `bd51c78ce774`): for an empty-id target it builds `` `${providerID}#${variant}` `` when a variant is present, preserving the user's variant.
- PR #382 (`packages/core/src/model-resolver.ts`, head from its diff): for an empty-id target it builds only `String(target.providerID)`, dropping `target.variant` entirely.

Issue #385's acceptance criteria explicitly asked for the two paths to *share* the empty-id construction "instead of duplicating a divergent one". PR #390's body itself notes the variant point: "preserving the variant, which a provider-only string would drop" — that drop still happens in `ModelResolver.resolve`.

## Evidence

- `ModelAlias.resolveRef` (`packages/schema/src/model-alias.ts` on current main): the first `#variant` in the input becomes `explicitVariant` and wins over the alias target's variant (`initialVariant = explicitVariant ?? settledVariant`). So `flash#low` with `flash -> deepseek/deepseek-chat#high` resolves to variant `low`, while plain `flash` resolves to `high`.
- Therefore a bare-alias target `{ providerID: "flash", id: "", variant: "low" }`:
  - through `SessionRunnerModel.resolve` after PR #390: variant `low` (user's choice preserved);
  - through `ModelResolver.resolve` after PR #382: variant `high` (user's `low` silently replaced by the alias target's variant).
- `ModelResolver.resolve(requested)` is reachable with such a target: `Generate.text` (`packages/core/src/generate.ts:41`) passes `input.model: Model.Ref` straight to it. That is a programmatic path, not the main CLI session path, so impact is narrower than #385 — but the silent divergence is exactly what #385 set out to prevent.
- PR #390's own variant test does not catch the divergence: `packages/core/test/session-runner-model.test.ts` uses variant `high`, which is also the configured alias target's variant (`flash -> deepseek/deepseek-chat#high`), and asserts only `providerID`/`id`, not the resolved variant. A test with a variant *different* from the alias target's would distinguish preservation from replacement.

## Why it matters

Two resolvers expanding the same user input to different variants is a silent correctness bug: the same `-m flash#low`-style selection would run at different effort depending on which service resolves it, with no error. It also leaves #385's shared-construction acceptance unmet even after both PRs merge.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The empty-id ref-string construction is shared between `ModelResolver.resolve` and `SessionRunnerModel.resolve` (one helper), or `ModelResolver.resolve`'s branch is updated to preserve the variant exactly as PR #390's does.
- [ ] A test resolves a bare-alias target whose variant differs from the alias target's variant through *both* resolvers and asserts the user's variant wins in both.
- [ ] Existing model-resolver / session-runner-model / aliases tests still pass.

Found by pr-diff-review reviewing PR #390 (open, fixes #385) in developing-today/opencode; cross-checked PR #382's diff and `model-alias.ts` on current main.

title: Model pools cannot reach models that a model transform creates, such as Azure deployments

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: source/human
labels.description: Filed directly by a human

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: effort/m
labels.description: Medium: expected under 1 day of work

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Problem

A model pool can only reach models that exist in the provider definitions. A model that a model transform creates is invisible to it. Azure deployment discovery is the case that matters: `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/azure.ts` (around lines 397-407) removes the catalog models that are not deployed and adds each deployment under its deployment name, in a model transform.

- An explicit target such as `azure/prod-mini` is looked up in the provider definitions (`matchingModels(ref.id, definitions.get(ref.providerID))` in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`), so it is never placed. This is the behaviour on main today.
- The matching keys from #233 (`include`, `contains`, `match`) enumerate the same definitions and look each one up with `editor.get`, so `include: ["azure/*"]` never sees a deployment name, and the catalog templates it does see were removed. The pool can end up empty.

Raised in review of #233 by Codex and Copilot.

## Why it is not a one-line fix

The model editor has no way to list the current model ids without copying them. `editor.list()` drafts (structuredClone) every model it returns (`packages/core/src/model.ts`, `list` and `draft`). Calling it from the routes transform would copy every model of every connected provider on each rebuild, and an edited model loses the shared definition object that `Model.read` reuses across rebuilds.

Options:

1. Add a read-only way to list the current model ids per provider to `Model.Editor`, and enumerate that for matching keys and glob targets.
2. Accept the copy cost and call `editor.list()` only when a pool uses matching keys.
3. Have provider plugins that create models in a model transform also declare them at the provider stage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An explicit pool target naming a transform-created model (e.g. an Azure deployment name) is placed by the pool instead of being looked up only in provider definitions.
- [ ] Matching keys (`include`/`contains`/`match`, e.g. `azure/*`) enumerate transform-created model ids as well as definition ids.
- [ ] No per-rebuild full-catalog copy regression: the enumeration path does not `structuredClone` every model on each routes rebuild (or the cost is measured and recorded on this issue).
- [ ] Regression tests cover a transform-created model reached via both an explicit target and a glob.

body:
## Finding

Interrupting a session stops its foreground subagents, but not the ones it started in the background.

- **Foreground:** the `subagent` tool call waits on the child's job. If the call is interrupted, its handler interrupts the child and cancels its job, and the same handler in the child's own `subagent` calls carries the interrupt down the chain.
- **Background:** the tool call registers the job and returns at once. Nothing ties the child to the parent after that, so interrupting the parent leaves the child running, along with everything it launches.

Since PR #39, only a top-level session can start a background subagent; nested launches always run in the foreground. A background subagent therefore runs until it finishes or someone stops it directly, for example from the app's running menu. This was noticed while PR #39 was written, and nobody decided it or filed it.

## Evidence (main 5214f4d8ae)

- `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts:220-222`: `background` is honored only at depth 0.
- `subagent.ts:251-253`: the background path registers the job and returns.
- `subagent.ts:256-262`: the foreground path's interrupt handler interrupts the child, cancels its job and releases its mcpx session.
- `packages/core/src/session/session.ts:321-324`: `Session.interrupt` interrupts only that session's own execution.
- `packages/app/src/session/header/session-running-menu.tsx:165-169`: the app's running menu can stop a running subagent on its own.
- `services/www/src/docs/content/agents.mdx:116` and `:131-133` describe background child sessions and nesting, but not what stopping the parent does to them.

## Options

1. **Keep it.** Background work is independent by design. Document that stopping a session leaves its background subagents running, and how to stop them.
2. **Stop them too.** Interrupting a session also interrupts the background subagents it started, and so everything below them. The job's recovery record already names the parent (`parentSessionID`, `subagent.ts:242-248`).

## Acceptance criteria

- A decision recorded here or in the PR that closes this issue.
- With option 1: `agents.mdx` says what stopping a session does to its background subagents.
- With option 2: a test where interrupting a top-level session stops a background child and that child's own foreground subagent.
