## Direction (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Restructure the routing config surface from the flat `experimental.model_route_*` key family into a single nested schema:

    "experimental": {
      "routes": {
        "models":    today's experimental.model_routes,
        "providers": experimental.provider_routes (PR #1134),
        "windows":   today's experimental.model_route_windows,
        "schedules": today's experimental.model_route_schedules,
        "tuning":    today's experimental.model_route_tuning,
        "log":       today's experimental.model_route_log,
        "settings":  the routing-constants block (bench / demotion / quota-gate / escalation), when it lands
      }
    }

## Staging decision (Drew, 2026-10-31 22:11 CDT)

STAGED, not big-bang. The flat rename (synthetic_providers -> provider_routes) lands first on PR #1134. This conversion happens after BOTH provider_routes (#1134) and the constants/settings block have landed, so exactly one migration moves a settled surface.

## Why a compat shim is required

The fork's config loader is not the only reader of these keys:

- `bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs` (developing-today/code) parses the raw JSONC and resolves `model_routes` itself — no shared code with the fork.
- OpenChamber's `validateModelRoutes` reads the same flat keys.

A hard rename breaks both silently (proxy finds no routes; validator validates nothing). The fork's normalize layer already translates legacy keys (`disabled_providers` -> `policies`, `experimental.policies` -> `policies`, `experimental.mcp_timeout` -> `mcp`) — this conversion follows that exact pattern.

## Acceptance

1. Nested keys are the canonical schema; the routing plugins read the nested shape after normalization.
2. Every flat key (`model_routes`, `model_route_windows`, `model_route_schedules`, `model_route_tuning`, `model_route_log`, `provider_routes`) normalizes into the nested shape with a deprecation diagnostic; resolved config is identical either way (tests both directions, including a config that mixes flat and nested — nested wins, conflict is diagnosed).
3. Follow-on reader updates are filed and linked from here when this lands: the route proxy (developing-today/code) and OpenChamber's validator learn the nested shape; the flat shim is removed only after both stop needing it.
4. The live fleet config migrates in the same pass as the deploy of this change (config + readers move together); until then the shim carries it.


## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Routing config is readable in the nested `experimental.routes` shape (models/providers/windows/schedules/tuning/log/settings) after both prerequisite pieces land (PR #1134 provider_routes; the #1141 settings block).
- [ ] Flat `experimental.model_route_*` keys keep working through the normalize compat shim, including external readers named in the body.
- [ ] Config tests cover nested, flat, and mixed inputs.

title: fix(core): ripgrep archive download has no integrity check — a version-pinned executable is extracted and run with no sha256 pin, unlike the embedding downloads

labels.name: kind/security

labels.name: task/triage
labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/core
labels.description: Package: core (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Improvement

The ripgrep fallback download in `packages/core` fetches a version-pinned release archive, extracts it, marks the binary executable and runs it as the search tool — with **no integrity verification at all**. A size cap is the only check on the bytes. Every other pinned-artifact download in the same package (messaging embedding models) pins a sha256 per artifact and verifies the digest before accepting the download; the ripgrep path is the outlier.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-31 on main `fdd26aa63c`)

`packages/core/src/ripgrep/binary.ts` (whole file read, 142 lines; `grep` for `sha256|checksum|createHash` over the file returns nothing):

- `:15` — `VERSION = "15.1.0"` is pinned, and `:21-29` the `PLATFORM` table pins each platform's target triple and archive extension — but carries **no digest field**.
- `:105-106` — the archive filename and URL are built purely from version + platform: `https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases/download/${VERSION}/${filename}`.
- `:109-128` — the response is collected through `collectBoundedResponseBody` (the 32 MiB cap from #923), written with `fs.writeWithDirs`, then `extract(archive, config, target)` unpacks it with the system tar; `:88-89` copies the extracted binary to the global bin dir and `chmod 0o755`. The resulting path is returned as the `rg` executable the search tooling spawns.
- Nothing between the network and execution ever hashes the bytes: a wrong, corrupted, or substituted archive of plausible size is extracted and run as-is (extraction only fails if the bytes are not a readable archive at all, and the "did not contain executable" check at `:86` only checks a filename exists).

Contrast — the house standard in the same package, `packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts`:

- `:33` and the tier tables (`:54-137`) pin `sha256` (and `size`) for every built-in artifact; `finish()` computes the digest of the downloaded bytes and rejects on mismatch before the file is accepted. The unpinned custom-URL shape there was itself treated as a defect (#929/#1071).

Dedup: `gh issue list --state all --search "checksum OR sha256 OR ripgrep OR integrity"` — #923 (closed) added the size caps to this path and #72 (closed) covered test-harness binary resolution; no open or closed issue covers integrity verification of the ripgrep download.

## Why it matters

`rg` is spawned constantly by the search/grep tooling, and the downloaded copy lands in the user's global bin directory, where it also shadows future lookups. Today only TLS and a 32 MiB cap stand between the network and code execution: a compromised release asset, a bad mirror/proxy substitution, or a future upstream asset mix-up would install an arbitrary binary silently. Pinning the digests is cheap because the version and platform set are already pinned constants — the `PLATFORM` table is exactly where the digests belong, mirroring the embedding tier tables.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Each `PLATFORM` entry in `packages/core/src/ripgrep/binary.ts` carries the pinned sha256 of the ripgrep 15.1.0 archive for that platform (digests taken from the upstream 15.1.0 release), with a comment that a `VERSION` bump must update the digests in the same change.
- [ ] The download path hashes the collected bytes and fails closed on a digest mismatch **before** the archive is written or extracted: no archive left behind, no binary installed at the target path.
- [ ] Regression tests: a body whose digest does not match the pin is rejected (and installs nothing); the digest-verification seam is covered without a network download (the existing `packages/core/test/ripgrep.test.ts` skips without an ambient `rg`, so the new coverage must not depend on one).
- [ ] Behaviour is unchanged when a system `rg` or an already-installed binary is found (no download, no hashing on those paths).

labels.description: New feature or request

body:
## Drew's directive (2026-10-31)

> make synthetic providers a concept which allow ordered round-robin weighted same as models except provider level

## The concept

Model routes compose **models**: a pool (e.g. `terra-plan`) holds `provider/model` leaves and applies a selection mode (`ordered` / `round-robin` / `weighted`). Route expansion passes no model context into a nested route, so **provider-level** composition is impossible today. Tonight proved it: the GPT account pair had to be instantiated as three separate pools — `openai-plan-terra`, `openai-plan-sol`, `openai-plan-luna` in the laptop config — each an ordered `[openai.alternate/<model>, openai/<model>]` pair, because the account order is a property of the *providers*, not of any one model.

A **synthetic provider** is a virtual provider defined by a selection over concrete providers, with the same selection modes as model routes — `ordered`, `round-robin` (including the tiered weights semantics of #1122), and `weighted`. A model route then uses `<synthetic-provider>/<model>` as a leaf, and resolution picks the member provider per the synthetic provider's selection, yielding a concrete `provider/model` call.

Canonical first instance: synthetic provider `openai-plan` = ordered `[openai.alternate, openai]` — one definition serving every GPT model.

## Design answers

Settled from the codebase's actual grammar (`packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts`, `packages/core/src/model-route.ts`); the implementation follows these.

**1. Config grammar.** Declared in a new top-level block `experimental.synthetic_providers`, a record keyed by synthetic provider id (same id pattern as route ids). Each entry: `providers` (the member provider ids, in configured order), `selection` (`ordered` default, `round-robin`, `weighted`), and `weights` (keyed by member provider id; unset weighs 1). A route references a synthetic provider exactly like a concrete one — `openai-plan/gpt-6.1-terra`, string or object target form, `#variant` included — because the reference site is what makes the concept useful. That means synthetic ids share the provider-id namespace at reference sites, so collisions are **rejected at config load**: an id that names a concrete provider in the catalog, the routes provider (`opencode-route`), or a configured route id is dropped, loudly (a warning naming the id and the reason — never silently, cf. #734). Concrete providers always win a reference.

**2. Member eligibility per dispatch.** Mirrors the leaf rule exactly. A member contributes a leaf for a requested model only when its catalog lists the model (glob patterns match per member) and it can produce the requested variant — natively, through the target's remap table, or as a suffixed catalog id (#985). Otherwise the member is skipped for that dispatch; it is never an error. A synthetic target whose members contribute no leaf for the model attaches nothing, like a glob that matches nothing.

**3. Health interaction.** Resolution produces concrete `provider/model` leaves, and every health mechanism is keyed on concrete targets — per-target and per-credential cooldowns and the bench ladder, quota demotion, quota gates, rate-limit holds, budgets. A benched or walled member leaf is simply absent from the walk's ready set, and selection falls through per the synthetic group's own mode — including #1122's tier rule inside a round-robin synthetic (a demoted member sorts below the live tiers there). No synthetic-level health state exists; member readiness is judged by the same walk that judges nested route groups.

**4. Nesting.** No in v1. Members must be concrete provider ids; a member naming another synthetic provider (or the routes provider) is dropped at load with a warning. Expansion stays one level deep, like the door-set target (#637). Revisit only when a real composition need appears.

**5. Decision records.** Expansion gives the synthetic group its own node, marked with the synthetic id. The walk records a decision for that node — `route_id` is the synthetic id, candidates are the concrete member leaves, `chosen` is the member that served — and the parent decision names the group by its synthetic reference (`openai-plan/gpt-6.1-terra`). A walk stays explainable end to end, the way #1122's `tiers` detail made tiered choices explainable.

**6. The route proxy door.** The proxy in developing-today/code (`bin/opencode-route-proxy.mjs`, OpenClaw's door) resolves routes **itself** from the same config file — its own expand/rotate/weightedOrder, its own `providerBaseURL` and credential-store reads. It does not share the fork's expansion or selection code. Synthetic providers are therefore **v1 server-side only**: a route using a synthetic leaf will not resolve through the proxy until the proxy learns the concept. That follow-up belongs to the code repo and is **not** part of this work.

## Implementation shape

- Schema: a `SyntheticProvider` class and a `SyntheticProviders` record in `packages/schema/src/config/model-routes.ts`; `experimental.synthetic_providers` in `packages/schema/src/config/experimental.ts`.
- Runtime: `ModelRoute.SyntheticProvider` (the validated form); the node tree gains an optional synthetic marker so decisions can name the group (answer 5).
- Plugin: a `configuredSynthetics` reader (validation + loud drops, exported like `configuredWindows`) threaded through `expand()` and `retargetDefinition()` as an optional parameter, like windows. Expansion treats a synthetic target as a per-model group node — one group per matched model id, so a glob model pattern fans out per model and a group never mixes models — reusing the existing leaf machinery (variant producibility, dedup, ceilings, budgets, cache formats) verbatim. The group's selection and weights are honored when the referencing route uses rules, mirroring how the referencing route's own selection is gated by its autonomy; a `fixed` route sees the group as ordered with unit weights.

## Acceptance criteria

- A config declaring `openai-plan` once can serve `openai-plan/<model>` leaves in any number of routes, for every model both members offer.
- All three selection modes behave per their model-route semantics at provider level, including tiered round-robin after #1122.
- A member that does not offer the model or the variant is skipped for that dispatch; a benched or demoted member falls through (last-resort rules unchanged).
- A synthetic id colliding with a concrete provider, the routes provider, or a route id is rejected at load with a warning; the concrete provider keeps the reference.
- Decision records show the synthetic resolution (`openai-plan` → the member that served).
- Tests cover: ordered synthetic (first ready member; fall-through on failure/bench), round-robin synthetic (even rotation; tiered weights), weighted synthetic, member skipped for a missing model/variant, benched member excluded with fall-through, a synthetic leaf inside a model route resolved end to end, collision rejection, and the decision record.

Design: #1127 (bounded by default — one deadline-and-cap contract for every outbound HTTP call). Design doc: `files/designs/opencode-bounded-outbound-http.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

### Scope

Add `script/check-bounded-http.ts` + `script/check-bounded-http.allowlist.txt` + its test, modelled directly on the proven `script/check-proto-reads.ts` shape (#865: sweep patterns + allowlist dispositions + stale-entry failure), and wire it as `check:bounded-http` in the root `package.json` alongside `check:proto-reads`.

Sweep, over the `packages/*/src` trees (roots listed in the script, extensible like `SCAN_ROOT`):

- **P-A:** a `fetch(` call whose options carry no `signal` (and which is not composed through the bounded-call helpers of design #1127 phase 1 / core's `tool/http-body.ts`).
- **P-B:** a response body read through `.text()`, `.json()`, or `.arrayBuffer()` on a fetch/HttpClient response that does not pass through a bounded or excerpt reader.

Every hit must appear in the allowlist with a disposition — bounded at the site (name the helper), local/test/generated read (say why it is not an outbound response), or tracked by an issue (name it). An unlisted hit fails the gate; an allowlist entry whose line no longer exists is stale and also fails. The initial allowlist is the inventory this gate produces on current main — writing it **is** the remaining-surfaces inventory for the contract.

The console/renderer instances of the contract are this phase's named work items, linked as sub-issues of design #1127 and expected to close or be allowlist-dispositioned as this net lands: #1110 (console proxy routes, no deadline), #1098 (console openapi.json route), #1097 (console Salesforce fetches), #1081 (renderer theme/whats-new fetches, no deadline).

### Out of scope

- Migrating the adopted issues' code itself — they keep their own issues and queue lifecycle; this issue is the net + inventory + wiring.
- Effect HttpClient call sites in core (covered by core's canonical pair; disposition them in the allowlist as bounded-at-site where they use it).
- Any new cap or deadline value.

### Acceptance

- `bun run check:bounded-http` runs in CI and fails on an unlisted hit and on a stale allowlist entry (both pinned by the script's test, as in `check-proto-reads.test.ts`).
- Every hit on current main is allowlisted with a disposition; the four adopted issues (#1110/#1098/#1097/#1081) are either closed or named as the tracking issue on their hits.

## Phase 1 of design #1127 — the shared bounded-call pair in `@opencode/util`

Design: #1127 (bounded by default — one deadline-and-cap contract for every outbound HTTP call). Design doc: `files/designs/opencode-bounded-outbound-http.md` in the keep-the-four-repos-healthy goal workspace.

### Scope

Add a dependency-free native-fetch bounded-call module to `packages/util/src/` (util currently has no http module — verified on main `1fd02338f6`):

- `readBoundedResponseText(response, maximumBytes, tooLarge)` — refuse semantics: declared `content-length` over cap fails before reading; chunked body bounded in flight, read cancelled at the cap. Behaviour-identical to core's existing native reader in `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts`.
- `readExcerptResponseText(response, maximumBytes, signal?)` — excerpt semantics (diagnostics-only): returns the prefix read up to the cap, tied to the signal so a deadline cancels the read — generalising the shape `packages/function/src/discord.ts` hand-rolled in #1114 (`readErrorBodyExcerpt`).
- A deadline-composition helper: given a caller `AbortSignal | undefined` and a timeout in ms, return the composed signal (`AbortSignal.any([caller, AbortSignal.timeout(ms)])` where available). It introduces **no** default timeout value; call sites pass their own, under #992's `timeoutMs` ceiling.

One table-driven conformance suite in `packages/util` over the shared edge table: declared length over cap refuses before any read; chunked drip over cap refuses at the cap; deadline firing mid-body aborts the read; caller signal aborting first wins; excerpt cut at cap returns exactly the prefix; empty body returns empty; no-stream body fallback still enforces the cap.

Then: core's native `readBoundedResponseText` in `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts` delegates to the util implementation (core depends on `@opencode/util` already). Core's Effect `collectBoundedResponseBody` stays in core. Existing core tests (`packages/core/test/http-body.test.ts`) pass unchanged.

### Out of scope

- No call-site migrations (phase 2 adopts #1029/#1049/#1078 in core; phase 3 covers console/renderer + the net).
- No new caps, deadlines, or default values anywhere; no behaviour change at any existing call site.
- `packages/function` / `packages/ui` copies are untouched (phase 3 / open question on the design issue).

### Acceptance

- Util module + conformance suite land; every edge-table row above is a test.
- Core's native reader is a delegation, not a copy; `packages/core/test/http-body.test.ts` passes unedited.
- `bun run check` from repo root passes, or pre-existing base-branch failures are named in the closing note; tests run from package directories, never repo root (per repo convention; verification via CI).

body:
## Bug

The console Honeycomb webhook route forwards alerts to Discord with a `fetch` that has no timeout. If the Discord webhook endpoint accepts the connection but never responds (or stalls before headers), the webhook handler hangs forever.

## Evidence (verified 2026-10-31 on main `eae7941be1`)

`packages/console/app/src/routes/honeycomb/webhook.ts`:

- `:66-73` — `postDiscordMessage()` calls `fetch(Resource.DISCORD_INCIDENT_WEBHOOK_URL.value, { method: "POST", headers, body })` with **no `signal`**.
- `:102` — the `POST` handler does `const response = await postDiscordMessage(parsed.data)` and only then checks `response.ok` — so a never-arriving response means the handler never returns, holding the request/worker open indefinitely and leaving Honeycomb without a delivery verdict (retries can then duplicate the alert once the endpoint recovers).

The neighbouring Discord relay in `packages/function` had exactly this defect and was fixed after #1114 (extracted `packages/function/src/discord.ts` carries a timeout); this console route is a separate call site that was not covered.

### Probe (laptop, `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-honeycomb-webhook/probe.mjs`)

Replicates the exact call shape (POST + JSON body, no signal) against a local server that accepts and never responds:

- current pattern (no signal): **STILL-PENDING >5s**
- control with `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)`: **REJECTED TimeoutError ~3002ms**

## Why it matters

This route is the incident-alert path (Honeycomb → Discord role ping). A stalled Discord endpoint silently wedges alert delivery instead of failing fast with the route's existing `502 discord webhook failed` response, and the wedged handler can accumulate on every new alert.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The Discord POST in `postDiscordMessage` carries a named timeout (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, in line with the timeouts used elsewhere in console/function).
- [ ] A stalled Discord endpoint makes `POST` return the existing `502` response within the timeout instead of hanging.
- [ ] Regression test: a never-responding (or slow) webhook endpoint yields a 502 in bounded time; a fast 2xx endpoint still returns `200 { message: "sent" }`.

body:
## Finding

PR #926 (open, head `70cf2bf8349816876849dbd70f5a236f19861abb`, for #923) adds a 5 MiB cap to skill-file downloads: an over-cap file now makes `SkillDiscovery.download` return `false`. But the unversioned / same-version branch of `pull` discards every download result, so a skill whose `SKILL.md` downloaded while a reference file failed — over-cap under #926, or any download error today — is still returned as a successfully pulled skill directory with that file silently missing.

CodeRabbit raised exactly this on PR #926 (review 5705464133, outside-diff comment on `discovery.ts:169`): "Do not publish a skill after a file exceeds the limit… Check all download results before returning the directory, as the versioned refresh branch does." It received no reply and was never filed.

## Evidence (verified on current main `7e12117b4d22b441c57edf8d235216e39a888933`)

- `packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts:78-89` — `download` returns `true` on success and `false` on any caught error (`Effect.as(false)` after logging).
- `packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts:153-156` — the `version === undefined || current === version` branch runs `Effect.forEach(files, (file) => download(...), { concurrency: fileConcurrency, discard: true })`: the Boolean results are thrown away.
- `packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts:193-196` — afterwards `pull` returns `[root]` whenever `SKILL.md` (or `<name>.md`) exists, regardless of whether the skill's other files downloaded.
- Contrast `packages/core/src/skill/discovery.ts:162-167` — the versioned refresh branch collects the results and refuses to publish when `!downloaded.every(Boolean)`.
- On PR #926's head the same discarding branch is unchanged, and its new `MAX_SKILL_FILE_BYTES` rejection is a new, routine way for a reference file to return `false` (a >5 MiB reference file in an unversioned skill).

## Why it matters

A pulled skill is presented to the model/user as complete. A silently missing reference file degrades the skill in a way nothing surfaces — no error, no marker — and under #926's cap this becomes the expected outcome for any unversioned skill carrying one large reference file, instead of the clear "do not publish" behaviour the versioned branch already implements.

## Acceptance criteria

- In the unversioned / same-version branch of `SkillDiscovery.pull`, if any file's `download` returns `false`, the skill directory is not returned as pulled (matching the versioned branch's `downloaded.every(Boolean)` gate), or the failure is otherwise surfaced to the caller instead of being discarded.
- A regression test pins: `SKILL.md` succeeds, a second listed file fails (e.g. over the #926 cap or a fetch error), and `pull` does not return the directory.
- The versioned refresh branch's behaviour is unchanged.

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PR #926 against current main; dedupe: searched open+closed issues for skill discovery / incomplete download / SkillDiscovery pull on 2026-10-31 — #923 covers the missing size caps only, no issue covers the discarded download results.

body:
## Problem

A quota bench planted during a provider's short quota window escalates on the generic failure ladder (quota base 15m, doubling per consecutive failure, capped at 24h) and is decoupled from the provider's actual window reset. While benched, the leaf is excluded from candidacy at selection time, so it can never earn the success that resets the ladder (`bench()` in `packages/core/src/model-route.ts`: "The count survives recover() and resets only on a success"). The bench therefore outlives the real quota wall by many hours, silently demoting a healthy account for up to a day.

## Evidence (laptop fleet server, 2026-10-31, all times UTC)

- Provider `openai.alternate` (ChatGPT account B) hit its genuine 5-hour usage wall in the afternoon; attempts failed `QuotaExceeded` 429 ("The usage limit has been reached").
- `route_health` for `openai.alternate/gpt-6.1-terra` credential `cred_17514e929001...` shows the ladder planting `cooldown-start` rows with until-now deltas of 15m, 30m, 1h, 2h, 4h, 8h, 16h, then capped 24h: the last start (id 1723, 21:02 UTC) set `until` = 2026-11-01 21:02 UTC.
- The account's 5-hour window reset at 00:00 UTC (19:00 CDT). After that, the SERVER made zero attempts on the account (the only later `route_attempt` rows are the route proxy's `UnknownProvider` rows from code#3256, a different process).
- `route_decision` for terra-plan after 00:00 UTC repeatedly shows: `excluded: [{"candidate":"openai.alternate/gpt-6.1-terra","reason":"credential-cooldown-until:1793566934902"}]` — candidacy exclusion, exactly as designed, with no probe ever offered.
- Net effect: a ~5h wall produced a ~24h bench, ~21h of it after the account was actually usable again. The fleet burned the other ChatGPT account (the reserve) all evening with no signal anywhere except the decision-detail exclusion string.

## Why this is not #1116 / #996

- #1116 is restart-restore of attempt quota snapshots ignoring `credential_id`. This bench was planted and held by the LIVE process; no restart was involved.
- #996 is quota-reset relative parsers disagreeing on compact units. Adjacent: if the router can parse/know a window's reset, the bench should use it — but the defect here exists even when the reset time is known to the quota machinery, because the bench ladder never consults it.

## Ask

Any of these shapes fixes the incident class; the first is the smallest:

1. **Cap a quota bench at the credential's known window reset.** When a quota snapshot/window for the target+credential has a `reset` in the future, `cooldownUntil = min(ladder, reset)` — a stated retry-after is already believed as-is; a known window reset deserves the same trust.
2. **Half-open probe at window reset.** When a benched credential's underlying quota window rolls over during the bench, admit one probe attempt; success clears the ladder, failure re-benches.
3. **Surface the bench.** The exclusion already names `credential-cooldown-until:<ts>` in decision detail; route stats/diagnostics should also expose active benches with until + reason so a day-long demotion is visible without reading decision JSON.

## Workaround used in the incident

Appended a `cooldown-end` row for the key to `route_health` (reason `manual-clear credential:<id>`, so restart restore replays start-then-end and restores nothing) and restarted the server — there is no live admin path to clear a credential bench. An operator-facing clear (CLI or API) would make shape 1/2 above less urgent but is not a substitute for the bench respecting the window.



## Acceptance criteria

- A quota bench for a credential whose quota window has a known future `reset` does not extend past that reset (`cooldownUntil = min(ladder, reset)`), or an equivalent half-open probe is admitted at the reset.
- After the window resets, the previously benched credential returns to candidacy with no operator intervention and no server restart; a successful probe/attempt clears the failure ladder.
- Regression tests cover: a bench planted inside a short quota window does not outlive the window reset, and the first post-reset success resets the ladder.
- The 2026-10-31 incident shape is reproducible in test: 5h wall, escalating ladder, window resets mid-bench, credential becomes eligible again at reset.

title: feat(routes): round-robin weights as priority tiers — rotate within a tier, fall through when it is exhausted
body:
## Ruling

Drew (2026-10-31 ~20:19 CDT), on route pool selection:

> allow round robin to accept weight but instead of all of them even or all of them by weight, evenly go through each priority so lowest weight even until all fail then second lowest evenly and so on

## Semantics to implement

In a `round-robin` pool, `weights` stop being proportional shares and become **priority tiers**:

- Targets with equal effective weight form one tier. Within the active tier, selection rotates evenly across dispatches (the existing per-session draw + stickiness, restricted to the tier).
- Selection falls through to the next tier only when **every** member of the current tier has failed or is unavailable for that dispatch's candidate walk (not ready, already tried, gate-closed, cooling, quota-gated — the existing eligibility rules decide membership as today).
- All-equal weights (or no weights; unset weight still defaults to 1) collapse to a single tier, which is exactly today's plain even round-robin. Unweighted pools do not change behavior.
- `ordered` mode is untouched.

## Tier order: higher weight = earlier tier (interpretation, flagged)

Drew's wording says "lowest weight" first, but the fleet's pools already use weight as preference, larger = preferred:

- the GPT pools put alternate at weight 2 over main at 1 precisely so alternate burns first;
- luna-plan puts the Go leaves at 3/2 above the rest;
- the DeepSeek plan pool uses a weight-100 guard to keep plan doors ahead of PAYG.

A literal lowest-first reading would invert every one of those pools. This issue therefore implements **descending** order (highest weight is the first tier). If Drew reverses the call, the change is the tier sort comparator and nothing else.

The tier key is the target's effective **pre-demotion** weight: configured pool weight after scheduled rules, user preferences, and learned adjustments — the same layers `tracedWeightOf` already computes, stopping before the demotion layer.

## Interaction with quota demotion

Demotion today scales the effective weight by 0.01, which under tiering would smear a demoted heavyweight into the middle tiers (100 x 0.01 = 1 ties it with nominal 1s). Rule instead:

- While demoted (>= `quota.demoteAfter` quota errors inside `quota.windowMs`, per target or per serving credential as today), a leaf sits in a **demoted tier below every non-demoted tier**, whatever its configured weight. Demoted leaves still order among themselves by weight, and they still serve as last resort when nothing else is left.
- A nested group counts as demoted only when **every** currently eligible leaf under it is demoted; a mixed group stays in its nominal tier and its own walk applies the same rule one level down.
- The 0.01 factor itself is unchanged for `ordered` and `weighted` modes, whose ranking keeps using the final effective weight exactly as today.

## `weighted` mode: left as-is

`weighted` remains the proportional mode (random draw by ratio) for pools that genuinely want shares. The ruling redefines round-robin only; removing the only proportional mode is not part of it.

## Acceptance criteria

Tests in the model-route suite cover at least:

1. Single-tier pools rotate evenly, as today.
2. Two-tier strict fall-through: the second tier is never drawn while any first-tier member is ready; it engages once every first-tier member has failed / left the candidate set, within a single dispatch walk and across dispatches.
3. Within-tier rotation persists across dispatches (successive sessions cycle through the tier, not the pool).
4. An unset weight lands in the same tier as weight 1.
5. A quota-demoted leaf sorts below all non-demoted tiers regardless of nominal weight, and serves again as last resort.
6. A nested route reference participates as a tier member with its group weight.

No config changes; selection logic and its tests only.

body:
## Problem

OpenCode stores multiple credentials per provider, and different sign-in methods wire the SAME provider to DIFFERENT backends with different token requirements:

- `chatgpt-browser` / `chatgpt-headless` (openai plugin) -> Codex backend (`chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex`), accepts Codex-flow OAuth tokens
- `chatgpt-token-sharing` (chatgpt plugin) -> platform API (`api.openai.com/v1`), requires a token minted for a registered agent client carrying `resource.invoke` + `chatgpt.tokens.use.direct` scopes

Nothing validates that the ACTIVE credential method matches a backend its token can actually serve. Activating a token-sharing credential whose stored token was minted by the Codex flow makes every call to that provider fail with 401 `Missing scopes: api.responses.write`, and the failure presents as an opaque provider auth error rather than a credential misconfiguration.

## What happened (2026-10-31, developing-today/code#3216, fixed + closed)

On the fleet laptop, provider `openai` (main ChatGPT Pro account) had both credential types stored; a credential-row update flipped the active one to the token-sharing row at 15:40 CDT. Its token was byte-identical to the live Muse token (Codex client `app_EMoamEEZ73f0CkXaXp7hrann`; scp `openid, profile, email, offline_access, api.connectors.read, api.connectors.invoke`) — valid for the Codex backend, unusable at the platform API. Every fleet session whose route reached the GPT leg failed at its first model call for ~4 hours; quota walls coexisting at the time masked the cause. Fix was `opencode auth switch` back to the browser credential; verification was 9 consecutive successes in the route ledger from the same sessions that had been failing.

## Ask

Guard the activation boundary so a credential cannot silently become active for a wiring its token cannot serve. Any of these shapes satisfies the issue, in increasing strength:

1. **At activation/switch time:** warn or refuse when the credential method implies a different backend than the provider other active-path configuration expects, and surface the method + backend in `opencode auth list` output.
2. **At call time:** when the platform API returns a scopes 401 for a token-sharing credential, classify the error as a credential-method mismatch (not a generic provider auth failure) and name the active credential method in the error surfaced to routes/sessions.
3. **At storage time:** refuse to store/activate a token whose decoded client_id/scopes cannot satisfy the method it is being stored under.

Acceptance: a reproduction (two stored credentials, mismatched one activated) produces an explicit mismatch signal at one of the three boundaries instead of a generic 401 at first model call; the #3216 scenario is the test case.



## Acceptance criteria

- A reproduction — two stored credentials for one provider, the token-sharing credential holding a Codex-flow token activated — produces an explicit credential-method mismatch signal at the activation, call, or storage boundary, instead of a generic 401 at the first model call.
- The signal names the active credential method and the backend its token cannot serve.
- Correctly matched credentials activate and call with no new warnings or refusals.
- The developing-today/code#3216 scenario is covered as a test case.

# fix(core): restart restore of stored attempt quota snapshots ignores credential_id — one credential's snapshot is restored target-wide (#1113 residual)

## Evidence (verified on main `6f68462488`, 2026-10-31, by line-level reading)

Since PR #1113 (for #1106), every `route_attempt` row stores the serving credential and its quota snapshot side by side: `credential_id` (`packages/core/src/model-route-log/sql.ts:44-47`) and `quota` are written on the same row (`packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts:129,133` — `credential_id: request.credentialID`, `quota: fields.quota ?? (seen.snapshot && { ...seen.snapshot })`).

The restart restore in `restoreCooldownsFrom` (`packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts`) treats the two stored histories inconsistently:

- The **health-row branch is credential-aware** (`:370-381`): it reads `row.credential_id` (falling back to a `credential:<id>` reason suffix), keys windows as `provider/model#credential`, and passes `credentialID` through — the #870/#1055 behavior, with tests (`packages/core/test/model-route-log.test.ts:774-900`).
- The **attempt-snapshot branch is not** (`:388-421`, "Cold targets get the provider's last word back too"): its select pulls only `provider_id, model_id, quota, time_ended` — never `credential_id` — and keys every snapshot as `` `${providerID}/${modelID}` `` (`:405`), merging into or creating a **target-wide** window entry with no credential.

Downstream, `seedLimits` (`packages/core/src/model-route.ts:992-1008`) already supports credential scoping (`row.credentialID ? credentialKey(...) : key(...)`) — the snapshot rows simply never supply one, so each restored snapshot is planted under the target-wide `limits` key.

## Consequences

1. **Misattribution after restart.** A quota snapshot observed on credential A's attempt (e.g. A nearly spent: remaining 2 of 60) is restored as the *target's* last word. Credential-less reads — `ModelRoute.rateLimitOf(target)` (`model-route.ts:963-964`) and the per-target diagnostics `rateLimitOfAny` / route_stats (`model-route.ts:976-990`) — present A's window as the whole target's, the same misattribution class #1113 fixed for live derivation and #870 fixed for cooldowns/limits, surviving in the restore path PR #1113 did not touch.
2. **The credential's own snapshot is lost.** Health-row windows restore under `target#credential`, snapshot windows under `target` — different keys, so the merge at `:419` never lands the snapshot on the credential's own entry: after a restart `rateLimitOf(target, credA)` misses the snapshot the live path held for credA.
3. **Last-attempt-wins across credentials.** Rows are applied in ascending `time_ended` order into a single target slot, so when credentials A and B alternate, whichever attempted last owns the target-wide snapshot regardless of which credential it describes.

## Test gap

The only cold-target snapshot restore test (`model-route-log.test.ts:1013-1045`, "brings back the provider's last word, not just the hold") records an attempt with **no** `credential_id` and asserts the target-wide restore — correct for uncredentialed attempts, but no test records a credentialed attempt and checks where its snapshot lands.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The snapshot branch of `restoreCooldownsFrom` selects `credential_id` and keys/merges snapshot windows with the same credential scoping as the health-row branch (column first, consistent with #1055); attempts with a null `credential_id` keep today's target-wide restore exactly (env-served / pre-column rows must never be assigned to a credential, per the sql.ts:44-47 contract).
- [ ] After restart, `rateLimitOf(target, credA)` returns credA's restored snapshot, and `rateLimitOf(target)` / `rateLimitOfAny` no longer present a credentialed attempt's snapshot as the target's own (or the diagnostics' attribution is explicitly documented as any-credential).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/model-route-log.test.ts`, mirroring the #870/#1055 restore describes: (a) two credentials with different snapshots restore onto their own keys, target-wide slot untouched; (b) an uncredentialed attempt still restores target-wide (existing test keeps passing); (c) a credentialed attempt's snapshot merges onto that credential's restored health-row window rather than creating a parallel target entry.

## Dedup

#1106/PR #1113 scoped live quota *derivation* (`QuotaSnapshot.deriveAll`, `targetUsage`) and added the column; its diff did not touch this restore branch. #870/#1055 credential-scoped cooldown and rate-limit-window restore from the *health* table. No open or closed issue covers the attempt-snapshot restore branch.

body:
# fix(cli): session import remote fetch has no timeout — a stalled or slow-dripping source hangs the import forever (#942 residual)

## Evidence (verified on main `6f68462488`, 2026-10-31, by line-level reading + laptop probe)

`packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/session/import.ts:27-30`: when the import source starts with `http://`/`https://`, the handler does

```ts
fetch(input.file).then((response) => {
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Failed to fetch session data: ${response.statusText}`)
  return readBoundedResponseBody(response, MAX_SESSION_TRANSFER_BYTES)
})
```

PR #944 (fixing #942) bounded the body **size** at 256 MiB via `readBoundedResponseBody` (`packages/cli/src/util/io.ts`), but neither the `fetch` nor the bounded reader carries any **time** bound: the fetch passes no `signal`, and the reader's pump (`io.ts`) only cuts when the running byte total passes the cap. Two hang shapes result:

- A server that accepts the connection and never sends response headers: `fetch` itself never settles.
- A server that sends headers and then drips body bytes slowly (or stalls mid-body) while staying under 256 MiB: the reader waits forever — the cap is a size bound, not a deadline.

`fetch` follows redirects, so the effective host is not necessarily the host in the pasted URL. The URL is arbitrary user input (a shared session link), so a dead, hostile, or merely slow host wedges the CLI command with no error and no way out but killing the process.

The CLI's own convention is a named `AbortSignal.timeout`: `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/login.ts:190,248` (5s), `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/stats.ts:74` (30s), `packages/cli/src/services/updater.ts:335` (10s). This fetch is the outlier. Same residual class as #1091 (desktop extension download: size-capped pump, no timeout), in a different package and call site.

Secondary, same handler: the import POST to the resolved server (`import.ts:51-58`) also passes no signal, and its response is read with an unbounded `response.text()` (`import.ts:66`). The target is the user's own server rather than an arbitrary URL, so this is lower severity, but `--server` can name a remote host (cf. #987 for `opencode api`).

## Probe (laptop, this run)

`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-import-timeout/probe.mjs` — the handler's exact call shape (bare `fetch`, then a verbatim copy of `readBoundedResponseBody` with the 256 MiB cap) against a local HTTP server:

- stall-headers (server accepts, never responds), handler pattern: **STILL-PENDING after 5006ms**
- drip 1 byte/sec under the cap, handler pattern: **STILL-PENDING after 5001ms**
- stall-headers with `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)` control: **REJECTED TimeoutError after 3001ms**

## Why it matters

`opencode session import <url>` is the documented way to pull a shared session. A single stalled connection hangs the command indefinitely with no diagnostic; in scripts/CI it burns until an outer timeout kills it, indistinguishable from a slow legitimate download of a large session (p90 exports are 7.55 MiB per #942's triage, so a generous timeout costs nothing).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The remote-source fetch in `import.ts` carries a named timeout (house precedent: `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, sized generously for a 256 MiB legitimate transfer — e.g. an overall deadline well above the stats command's 30s, or a stall/inactivity deadline; the choice and rationale recorded on this issue).
- [ ] The timeout also bounds the body-read phase (a signal on `fetch` covers the reader in Bun/Node fetch implementations — verify, don't assume).
- [ ] A stalled-headers server and a slow-drip server both fail the import with a clear timeout error instead of hanging.
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/cli/test/import-export.test.ts` (or the established cli test home) cover: stalled source rejects with the timeout error; normal remote import still succeeds.
- [ ] Secondary (same PR or a scoped follow-up note): the import POST at `import.ts:51` gets a timeout and its response read at `:66` is bounded, or an explicit note explains why the own-server path is exempt.

## Dedup

#942 covered size only (its body lists "no size cap, no content-length pre-check, and no streaming bound"; PR #944 added exactly those). #987 is `opencode api`'s response buffering, a different handler. #1091 is the desktop extension download. No open or closed issue covers a timeout for the session-import fetch.

## Problem

The support-relay handler in `packages/function/src/api.ts` (Mattermost → Discord) calls Discord with no deadline and reads its error body unbounded:

- `packages/function/src/api.ts:238` — `const response = await fetch(https://discord.com/api/v10/channels/${...}/messages, { method: "POST", headers, body })`: no `signal`, so a stalled Discord API holds the function invocation open until the platform kills it, and the incoming support message is neither relayed nor answered.
- `packages/function/src/api.ts:253` — on a non-OK response the handler does `console.error(await response.text())` with no byte cap, buffering the whole error body into memory just to log it.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 05b37bd71f)

- Code read: `api.ts:238-255` — the fetch passes only `method`/`headers`/`body`; the error path awaits `response.text()` whole.
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-jwks-per-request/discord.mjs` (replicates the exact call shapes against a local server):
  - Hanging upstream: the no-signal POST is `STILL-PENDING after 5000ms`.
  - Endless 500 error body: `response.text()` is `STILL-PENDING after 5000ms`, RSS +528 MiB in the completed probe run (a second run measured +524 MiB) and climbing.
  - Control with the house-precedent bound: the same POST with `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)` rejects `TimeoutError` at ~3003 ms.
- Dedup: `gh` search (open + closed) for `discord` in this repo returns workflow/deploy items only (#179, #118); no filing covers this relay handler. The console/stats unbounded-fetch filings (#1097/#1098/#1104/#1110/#1111) are different packages and call sites.

## Why it matters

This is a public support ingress: every relayed support message goes through this fetch. One stalled Discord response pins the invocation (and the sender's request) indefinitely, and a misbehaving error body grows function memory without limit on the log path — the same failure shape the recent console/stats bounds work closed on those surfaces, still open here in `packages/function`.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Discord POST carries a timeout (house precedent: `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, 3–10 s) via a named constant; on timeout the handler returns its existing 502 error response instead of hanging.
- The error path reads the response body through a bounded reader with a named byte cap (the log line only needs a short excerpt), never `response.text()` whole.
- Success behavior unchanged: a 2xx Discord response still returns `{ ok: true }`, and the non-OK path still returns 502 with the same error body shape.
- Regression coverage for: stalled upstream (times out, 502), oversized/endless error body (bounded, 502), normal relay (unchanged).

## Problem

Four console proxy routes fetch their upstream with no deadline. Each handler forwards the request and returns the upstream response, but none passes a `signal`, so a stalled or slow-dripping upstream holds the console request open indefinitely:

- `packages/console/app/src/routes/docs/index.ts:15` — `fetch(targetUrl, { method, headers, body: req.body })`, no `signal` (proxies to docs.opencode.ai / docs.dev.opencode.ai)
- `packages/console/app/src/routes/docs/[...path].ts:20` — identical handler, no `signal`
- `packages/console/app/src/routes/s/[id].ts:15` — identical handler, no `signal`
- `packages/console/app/src/routes/t/[...path].tsx:13` — `fetch(targetUrl, { method, headers, body: req.body })`, no `signal` (proxies to enterprise.opencode.ai)

The bodies are streamed (`new Response(response.body, response)`), so this is not a memory/cap problem like #1104 — it is purely a time bound: the fetch never settles when the upstream never sends headers, and the proxied body stream never ends when the upstream drips forever.

Every other console upstream fetch this fleet has audited is now time-bounded (#1097 Salesforce, #1098 openapi.json route, #1104 stats proxy, console-account.ts's 3 s timeout). These four proxy routes are the remaining unbounded ones in `packages/console/app/src/routes`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main 05b37bd71f)

- Code read: all four handlers above construct the fetch with exactly `{ method, headers, body }` — no `signal` anywhere in any of the four files (grep-verified this run).
- Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-console-proxies` (replicates the exact call shape against a local server):
  - Hanging upstream (never sends headers): `STILL-PENDING after 5000ms` — the fetch never settles.
  - Slow-drip body through the proxy wrap (`new Response(response.body, response)`): body read `STILL-PENDING after 5000ms`, bytes arriving but the stream never completes.
  - Control with the house-precedent bound: the same fetch with `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)` rejects `TimeoutError` at 3001 ms.
- Dedup: `gh` search (open + closed) for `proxy` / `docs proxy` / `enterprise proxy` returns #1104 (the separate `/data/*` stats proxy in `lib/stats-proxy.ts`, which additionally buffers HTML) and #1098 (the openapi.json route) — no filing covers these four routes.

## Why it matters

These are public console routes (`/docs/*`, `/s/*`, `/t/*`). One stalled upstream response pins a console worker request forever per hit, and a slow-dripping upstream holds the connection and worker slot indefinitely — the same hang shape #1097/#1098/#1104 were filed to close, on the proxy routes they didn't cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- All four proxy fetches carry a timeout (house precedent: `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`; a named constant per route file or a shared proxy helper) so a stalled upstream fails the request instead of hanging it. The timeout must also cover the streamed body (an abort after headers must terminate a dripping body read), not just time-to-first-byte.
- Streaming behavior is otherwise unchanged: method/headers/body forwarding, the locale `set-cookie` append on the docs/share routes, and in-bounds responses pass through untouched.
- Regression coverage for: stalled upstream (request fails at the timeout), slow-drip body (stream terminates at the timeout), normal upstream response (proxied unchanged).

const rows = yield* ModelRouteLog.targetUsage(db, since)

Rows are filtered by provider only — no credential dimension — and the provider-wide totals feed `QuotaSnapshot.deriveAll` per plan. ## Why it matters

This is a public console route (`/data/*`). One stalled upstream response pins a console worker request forever, and one misbehaving/oversized HTML response can OOM the worker — the same failure shape the console bounds in #1089/#1096/#1097/#1098 were filed to close, on the one proxy they didn't cover.

## Acceptance criteria

- The upstream fetch carries a timeout (house precedent: `AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, 3–10 s as in console-account.ts / salesforce.ts) so a stalled upstream fails the proxy request instead of hanging it.
- The HTML rewrite path reads the body through a bounded reader with a named byte cap (house precedent: 1 MiB, cf. download route #1089); an over-cap body fails or is passed through unrewritten, never buffered whole.
- Non-HTML responses keep streaming through untouched, and the cache-put / locale-rewrite behavior is unchanged for in-bounds responses.
- Regression coverage for: stalled upstream (times out), oversized HTML body (bounded), normal HTML body (rewrite + cache behavior unchanged).

title: feat(core): config changes should auto-apply to a running server — no reload, no restart
body:
## Ask (Drew, 2026-10-31)

Config-file changes should apply AUTOMATICALLY and COMPLETELY to a running OpenCode server — no manual reload step, no restart, no polling. Drew: "If there are other properties that we can just make the whole thing update automatically, I would even prefer that. I know there's a reload, but do we even need a reload?"

## Current state (evidence, to be re-verified in the audit)

- Route/agent config edits DO take effect for new sessions on a long-running server with no restart (observed live 2026-10-31: routes change synced to the laptop primary, new sessions used the new routes, server pid unchanged).
- 2026-10-24 operational notes: `opencode reload` did NOT reliably apply `disabled_providers` (post-reload /api/provider still showed disabled providers as available), and plugin-registered models stayed loaded until a full restart.
- Related watcher history in this repo: #773 (config file created after startup never watched — fixed), #797 (directory watcher silent failure on large trees), #968, #195 (watcher benchmarking). The pieces exist; the coverage is uneven.

## Scope

1. AUDIT: per-config-property table — for each property (routes, agents/prompts, providers/models incl. plugin-registered, disabled_providers, permissions, MCP servers, other opencode.jsonc sections): how does a running server pick up a file change today? (fresh-per-session / reload-only / restart-only / reload-broken), with file:line evidence.
2. DESIGN: event-driven watching (fs.watch) on the loaded config files/dirs → debounced invalidation → re-derive everything safely re-derivable, live for new work with zero reload calls and zero constant re-reading. Properties that genuinely cannot hot-apply get named with the technical reason and the least-bad fallback — nothing silently requires a restart.
3. IMPLEMENTATION slices: (a) watch-driven application for routes/agents + the properties already read fresh per session; (b) providers/disabled_providers if the audit shows it is safe; (c) tests: edit file → new session sees it with no reload call; no change → no re-reads; the disabled_providers case covered explicitly.

## Acceptance

- Editing opencode.jsonc on a running server changes behavior for new sessions without any reload/restart, for every property the audit marks hot-appliable.
- The audit table is checked in (docs or issue comment) and every restart-only property carries its reason.
- No polling loops introduced; watching is event-driven with debounce.

Filed by Muse at Drew's request; implementation in flight 2026-10-31.

title: fix(ai): native-route executor reads provider error bodies unbounded — response.text in statusError buffers the whole body and stores it whole on the error, though the message uses only 2,000 chars

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai
labels.description: Package: ai (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

Every provider request made through the native AI route passes through the shared executor's error path, and that path reads the **whole error body into memory and keeps it whole on the resulting error**:

```ts
// packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts:169-179 (main f6987d3324)
const statusError = (response: HttpClientResponse.HttpClientResponse) =>
  Effect.gen(function* () {
    if (response.status < 400) return response
    const result = yield* response.text.pipe(Effect.result)   // :172 — unbounded
    return yield* httpFailure({
      message: providerMessage(response.status, result._tag === "Success" ? result.success : undefined),
      ...
      responseBody: result._tag === "Success" ? result.success : undefined,  // :178 — retained whole
    })
  })
```

`statusError` is applied to **every** executed request (`executor.ts:315` and `:323`, both the plain and middleware paths), so this is the single choke point for all native-route provider errors.

The body is then passed as `rawBody` into failure classification (`executor.ts:201` → `classifyProviderFailure`, `packages/ai/src/provider-error.ts:236-237`), where it is stored on the error reason as `details.body`. Only the human-readable message is truncated — `providerMessage` caps it at `MAX_BODY_CHARS = 2000` (`executor.ts:156,166`) — while the retained body has no cap at all.

## Verified this run (laptop probe, real module)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-ai-executor-error-body/probe.test.ts` on the laptop — drives the real `RequestExecutor` (`fetchLayer`) from `packages/ai/src/route/executor.ts` against a local `Bun.serve` upstream:

- **Huge error body:** upstream returns HTTP 500 with a 32 MiB chunked plain-text body. The executor consumed all **33,554,432 bytes**, process RSS grew by **~133 MB**, and the resulting `AI.Error` (reason `ProviderInternal`) retained a body of exactly **33,554,432 chars** while its message was only 2,040 chars — proof the message path is capped and the retained body is not.
- **Endless error body:** upstream returns HTTP 500 and a body stream that never delivers and never closes. The execute call was **still pending after 5 s** (`STILL-PENDING`) — there is no read deadline at this layer, so a stalled error body hangs the request (and the session step waiting on it) indefinitely instead of surfacing the HTTP 500.

## Why it matters

- The body size is provider/gateway-controlled: any misbehaving or hostile endpoint (custom provider base URLs are user-configured) can answer an error with a multi-GB or never-ending body. One such response OOMs or wedges the whole opencode process, not just the failing request.
- The retained copy outlives the request: the whole body sits on the error reason (`details.body`), which is what gets logged, shown, and carried into retry/classification logic — memory and log volume scale with the largest error body a provider chooses to send.
- This is the same unbounded-error-body class already fixed/filed for sibling surfaces — #1049 (core MCP OAuth + Snowflake error reads), #1079 (MessagingEmbedding error text read whole to use 500 chars, fixed with a 64 KiB cap), #1029 (provider OAuth error responses in gitlab/poe/snowflake). The native-route executor is the uncovered central case: it is not an auth helper or a single provider, it is every native provider request.

## Suggested bound

Read the error body through a bounded reader (declared-length pre-check plus a streaming cap) with a named cap in the spirit of the house precedents (64 KiB error-body cap as in #1079's fix), and truncate the retained `rawBody` to the same bound. Classification scans the raw body for codes/phrases (`provider-error.ts`), and those signals live in ordinary small JSON error documents, so a generous-but-finite cap preserves classification for real providers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `statusError` no longer reads an error body unbounded: a declared `content-length` above the cap fails/ truncates before the body is read, and a streamed/chunked body is cut off at the cap while reading.
- [ ] The body retained on the error (`rawBody` / `details.body`) is at most the stated cap; the existing message behaviour (status line + body excerpt capped at `MAX_BODY_CHARS`) is unchanged for normal-sized error bodies.
- [ ] Failure classification (quota / auth / rate-limit / context-overflow / content-policy signals in `classifyProviderFailure`) still works for error bodies under the cap, including bodies whose signal JSON is close to the cap.
- [ ] A stalled/endless error body no longer leaves the execute call pending forever at this layer: it settles as the HTTP error within a bounded read (cap-triggered truncation is acceptable).
- [ ] Regression coverage in `packages/ai` (following its existing test conventions, e.g. the fake-HTTP test helpers) pins: oversized declared length, oversized streamed body, and normal error body classification.

title: fix(console,stats): GitHub metadata queries have no timeout and no body cap — console lib/github.ts and stats getGitHubStars hang past their own fallbacks when GitHub stalls

body:
## Problem

Two server-side GitHub API metadata queries — one in the console app, one in the stats app — fetch with **no timeout and no body cap**:

- `packages/console/app/src/lib/github.ts:12-16` — the `github` server query fires three fetches in `Promise.all` (`api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode`, `.../releases`, `.../contributors?per_page=1`) with headers only and **no `signal`**; two of the three bodies are read with `.then((res) => res.json())`, buffering whole bodies. The `catch` at `:25-27` only handles rejections — a stalled GitHub response never rejects, so the query never settles and the fallback (`return undefined`) never fires. Consumers: the console footer and pages (`component/footer.tsx:17`, `routes/black.tsx:16`, `routes/black/workspace.tsx:16`, `routes/index.tsx:32`, all via `createAsync(() => github())`).
- `packages/stats/app/src/routes/stats-shell.tsx:27-33` — `getGitHubStars` fetches `https://api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode` with headers only, **no `signal`**, and reads the body with `response.json()` unbounded. Its `.catch(() => githubLink.fallbackStars)` at `:40` likewise never fires on a hang, so the header star count's fallback is unreachable exactly when it is needed. Consumers: the stats shell header on the index, lab/model, compare, and model-compare pages (e.g. `routes/index.tsx:85`, `component/model-compare-detail.tsx:161`).

## Verification (this run)

Line-level verification on main `42869cd3f7` (the #942 precedent): neither call site passes a `signal`, and neither bounds the body read; both wrap the fetch in a rejection-only `catch` whose fallback a hang defeats by construction. The identical bare-fetch shape was probe-verified this same run against the real console download-route handler (sibling surface, #1089): a never-delivering body left the handler STILL-PENDING after 5 s and a paced endless body handed 60,555,264 bytes to the buffering `.json()` read in 5 s (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-github-meta/`). Both functions here are SolidJS `query()` server functions and cannot be invoked outside a request context (the probe's direct call fails with Solid's client-only-API error), so no real-function probe is claimed for these two.

Dedup: #1082 explicitly listed the stats-shell GitHub-stars fetch as **out of scope** ("Out of scope: `packages/stats/app/src/routes/stats-shell.tsx` GitHub-stars fetch…"), and #1083 covers only the console changelog loader (`lib/changelog.ts`), a different function and endpoint set. Neither issue covers `lib/github.ts` or `getGitHubStars`.

## Why it matters

These are per-render server queries on two public sites, backed by a third-party API. A stalled GitHub API response stalls the console footer/pages query and the stats header indefinitely — the coded fallbacks (`undefined`, `fallbackStars` "208K") exist precisely for GitHub being unavailable, but a hang is the one failure mode that bypasses them. An oversized or endless body buffers without limit in the server process. Sibling fetches in the same apps already bound their time: console `console-account.ts:17` uses `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)`, `salesforce.ts`'s helper uses `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)`, and stats-core `catalog-identity.ts:14` uses `AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)` (its missing cap is #1082's scope).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both queries carry a named timeout (house precedent range 3–10 s) so a stalled GitHub response settles into the existing fallbacks: `github` returns `undefined`, `getGitHubStars` returns `fallbackStars`.
- [ ] Both JSON body reads are bounded by a named cap sized for repo-metadata / release-list payloads (declared `content-length` over the cap fails fast where available; a streamed body is cut off at the cap), settling into the same fallbacks rather than buffering without limit. The console `releases` read (full release records) gets a cap sized with that payload in mind, stated in a comment.
- [ ] Happy paths unchanged: star counts, latest-release name/url/tag, and contributor count render exactly as today when GitHub responds normally.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the never-resolving and over-cap behaviours for both queries (settling into their fallbacks), following each app's existing test conventions; if a query's server-function wrapper resists direct testing, the bounded fetch/read is factored into a testable helper and the test pins the helper.
- [ ] Out of scope: the console changelog loader (#1083), the stats catalog fetchers (#1082), the console download route (#1089), and the third console `github.ts` fetch (contributors — only its headers are read; bounding its body read is not required, but its time bound comes free with the shared timeout).

Filed by new-issue-creator-opencode, 2026-10-31 run. Cross-references: #1082 (stats-shell explicitly out of scope there), #1083 (console changelog, same class, different surface), #1089 (console download route, same class, probe-verified this run).

body:
## Problem

The console site's desktop-download redirect route fetches its release-metadata body with **no timeout and no size cap**:

- `packages/console/app/src/routes/download/[channel]/[platform].ts:28-30` — `GET` awaits `fetch("https://opencode.ai/update/api/<channel>/desktop/opencode")` with **no `signal`** — a stalled update API leaves the route handler pending indefinitely; there is no fallback to fire (the handler's only error paths are the non-OK status passthrough at `:31` and the 502 at `:33`, neither of which a hang ever reaches).
- `packages/console/app/src/routes/download/[channel]/[platform].ts:32` — the body is read with `await release.json()`, which buffers the whole response before parsing. The handler only needs `metadata.files[<asset>].url` out of the document; nothing bounds what a compromised or misbehaving update endpoint can make the console server buffer per request.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe with the real handler)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-github-meta/` (laptop), importing the real `GET` handler from `packages/console/app/src/routes/download/[channel]/[platform].ts` (main `42869cd3f7`) with `globalThis.fetch` stubbed:

- **Hang:** fetch returns 200 with a body stream that never delivers and never closes. Result: `PROBE download-GET mode=hang outcome: STILL-PENDING` — `GET` still pending after 5 s, with no deadline at which it would settle.
- **Unbounded:** fetch returns 200 with a paced endless body (256 KiB every 20 ms). Result: `PROBE download-GET mode=endless outcome: STILL-PENDING bytesEnqueued=60555264` — over 60 MB handed to the buffering `response.json()` read in 5 s, still pending, never rejected.

## Why it matters

`/download/<channel>/<platform>` is a public console route — the link users hit to get the desktop app. Today a stalled update API stalls every download request with it (no timeout, no error), and an oversized response buffers without limit in the console server process, once per request. Sibling console fetches already bound their time (`packages/console/app/src/lib/console-account.ts:17` uses `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)`, `salesforce.ts`'s request helper uses `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)`) — this route is an outlier with neither a time nor a size bound. It is a different surface from the console changelog loader (#1083, `lib/changelog.ts`): that is the releases feed for the changelog page; this is the update-API fetch behind the download redirect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The update-API fetch in `GET` carries a named timeout constant (console precedent range 3–8 s), so a stalled response settles the handler — with a 502-style error response — instead of hanging the route.
- [ ] The release-metadata body is read through a bounded read with a named cap constant sized for a metadata document (declared `content-length` over the cap fails fast where available; a streamed body is cut off at the cap), failing as a 502 rather than buffering without limit.
- [ ] Happy path unchanged: a normal metadata document still resolves the asset URL and returns the same 302 redirect; unknown platform still 404s before any fetch; a non-OK upstream status still passes through as today.
- [ ] A regression test pins the over-cap and never-resolving behaviours for `GET` (the handler is a plain exported function, directly callable with a stubbed `globalThis.fetch`), following the console app's existing test conventions.
- [ ] Out of scope: the changelog loader (#1083), the console GitHub-metadata fetches and the stats GitHub-stars fetch (filed separately), and the redirect target itself (the asset URL is only read out of the metadata, never fetched by this route).

Filed by new-issue-creator-opencode, 2026-10-31 run. Cross-reference: #1083 (console changelog loader, same no-timeout/no-cap class, different surface).

title: fix(ci): check:proto-reads gate misses computed-key reads and lets one allowlist entry cover duplicate lines

labels.name: kind/ci
labels.description: CI/CD pipelines, workflows, and build automation

labels.description: Queue packet kind: verify, reproduce, and route this item

labels.name: source/pr-diff-review
labels.description: Filed by the pr-diff-review job

labels.name: priority/low
labels.description: Nice to have; do when convenient

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Finding

PR #883 (merged, merge commit 580c277358e409905a620d65ec13c3cdc7ef1cc0) introduced `script/check-proto-reads.ts`, the CI regression net that is supposed to stop the prototype-chain dictionary-read class regrowing "one bare read at a time" (#865). CodeRabbit raised two soundness gaps in the gate itself on PR #883 (comments 4413402382 and 4413402399); neither was replied to or filed, and both are still present on current main 42869cd3f76c0bd935303d94cdacb2d1e8ada19a.

## Evidence

1. **Computed keys evade both sweep patterns.** `script/check-proto-reads.ts:30`:
   `PATTERNS = [/\b[A-Z][A-Z_0-9]{2,}\[[a-zA-Z_]/, /\[[a-zA-Z_.]+\] \?\?/]`
   Probe against these exact regexes: `const a = TABLE[key] ?? 1` matches (true), but `const b = values[key.trim()] ?? 1` matches neither pattern (false) — the parenthesised computed key breaks the P-C bracket shape, and a lowercase receiver defeats P-A. `values[key.trim()]` with `key === "constructor"` still reads an inherited value, yet the line passes the gate with no disposition.
2. **One allowlist entry silently covers duplicate lines.** `hitKey` (:38) is `file :: exact trimmed line` with no occurrence identity. `unlistedHits` (:63-64) filters by key presence and `staleEntries` (:66-68) compares key sets, so adding a second identical matched line in the same file is covered by the first line's existing allowlist entry — the new site never gets its own disposition review. `script/check-proto-reads.test.ts` pins only single-occurrence accounting.

## Why it matters

The gate's value is that every hit gets a human disposition. Both gaps let a new prototype-chain read land in `packages/core/src` with no disposition and a green CI check — the exact silent regrowth the gate exists to prevent, in the two shapes a hurried edit is most likely to take (a normalising computed key, a copy-pasted line).

## Acceptance criteria

- `scanSource` flags a bracket read with a computed key (e.g. `values[key.trim()] ?? fallback` and the uppercase-table equivalent), with tests pinning the new shapes and no regressions on the existing test cases.
- Allowlist accounting is occurrence-aware: a second identical matched line in a file is reported as unlisted (or stale accounting fails) until it has its own disposition; tests pin the duplicate-line case.
- `bun run check:proto-reads` still passes on the current tree (any newly flagged existing lines are guarded with `ownValue`/`ownOr` or dispositioned).

Found by pr-diff-review lane B reviewing PR #883 against current main; dedupe: searched open+closed issues for check-proto-reads computed/occurrence/duplicate on 2026-10-31 — #912 (scan root covers only core) and closed #896 (stale variant.ts entry) are different gaps; no existing issue covers these two.

body:
## Finding

PR #883 (merged, merge commit 580c277358e409905a620d65ec13c3cdc7ef1cc0) added the prototype-chain regression net and dispositioned the two `state.toolNames[...]` reads in `packages/core/src/aisdk.ts` in `script/check-proto-reads.allowlist.txt:9-10` as:

> internal: state map keyed by provider event ids and written by own code before any read; ids are provider-assigned, not user text

That disposition is wrong for prototype-named ids, and CodeRabbit raised exactly this on PR #883 (comment 4413402360); it was never replied to or filed. Provider event ids are provider-supplied input — the same trust class this audit treats as untrusted everywhere else (e.g. PR #910's provider-supplied `item.type`).

## Evidence (verified on current main 42869cd3f76c0bd935303d94cdacb2d1e8ada19a)

- `packages/core/src/aisdk.ts:747` — `toolNames` is a plain object: `const state: StreamState = { step: 0, toolNames: {}, open: {} }` (type at :777).
- Writes at :820 (`tool-input-start`) and :842 (`tool-call`) use bare assignment `state.toolNames[event.id] = event.toolName`.
- Reads at :831 (`tool-input-delta`) and :837 (`tool-input-end`) use `state.toolNames[event.id] ?? "unknown"`.
- Node probe of the exact shapes:
  - An unrecorded id of `"constructor"` or `"toString"` (a `tool-input-delta`/`tool-input-end` whose start event never arrived, or used a different id) reads through the prototype chain: `toolNames["constructor"] ?? "unknown"` evaluates to the Object function, not `"unknown"` — inherited members are not nullish, so the fallback never fires. The resulting `LLMEvent.toolInputDelta`/`toolInputEnd` carries a function/object as its `name` instead of a string.
  - Writing `toolNames["__proto__"] = "name"` does not create an own property (the `__proto__` setter ignores a string value), so a tool legitimately started under the id `__proto__` is never recorded, and later reads return `Object.prototype` instead of the tool name.

## Why it matters

A provider (or a compromised/misbehaving provider endpoint) that emits tool events with prototype-named ids — or a delta/end for an unstarted id — puts a non-string `name` into LLM events that downstream session/runner code treats as a string, instead of the intended `"unknown"` fallback. This is precisely the defect class #833/#865 set out to eliminate; the allowlist disposition currently blesses the two remaining sites.

## Acceptance criteria

- `tool-input-delta` and `tool-input-end` for an unrecorded id of `constructor`, `toString`, `hasOwnProperty`, or `__proto__` produce `name: "unknown"`.
- A tool started under the id `__proto__` is recorded and its later delta/end events carry its real tool name.
- The reads/writes go through an own-property guard (e.g. `ownValue` from `packages/core/src/util/record.ts`) or the state map gets a null prototype; the two allowlist entries in `script/check-proto-reads.allowlist.txt` are updated/removed accordingly.
