body:
## Problem

The console site's changelog loader fetches a remote JSON body with **no timeout and no size cap**:

- `packages/console/app/src/lib/changelog.ts:42-52` — `loadChangelog()` calls `fetch("https://api.github.com/repos/anomalyco/opencode/releases?per_page=20", { headers, cf: {...} })` with **no `signal`** — a GitHub API response that stalls or slow-drips leaves the promise pending indefinitely; the `.catch(() => undefined)` only handles rejections, and a hang never rejects.
- `packages/console/app/src/lib/changelog.ts:56` — the body is then read with `await response.json()`, which buffers the whole response before parsing. Twenty release records with full markdown bodies are not small, and nothing bounds what a compromised or misbehaving endpoint (or a future `per_page` bump) can make the server buffer.

Consumers (main `42869cd3f7`):

- The SolidJS server query `changelog` (`changelog.ts:74-79`, `"use server"`) backing the console `/changelog` page.
- `packages/console/app/src/routes/changelog.json.ts:13` — the `/changelog.json` route awaits `loadChangelog()`; its `.catch(() => ({ ok: false, releases: [] }))` fallback likewise never fires on a hang, so the route hangs instead of serving the empty fallback.

This is a different surface from the gui-extensions whats-new changelog (#1061, size cap landed; #1081, renderer timeout): that is renderer code fetching a highlights JSON; this is the console web app's server-side GitHub-releases fetch, which has neither bound.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe with the real function)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-console-changelog/` (laptop), importing the real `loadChangelog` from `packages/console/app/src/lib/changelog.ts` with `globalThis.fetch` stubbed:

- **Hang:** fetch returns 200 with a body stream that never delivers and never closes. Result: `PROBE-CHANGELOG-HANG outcome: STILL-PENDING` — `loadChangelog()` still pending after 5 s, with no deadline at which it would settle.
- **Unbounded:** fetch returns 200 with a paced endless body (256 KiB every 20 ms). Result: `PROBE-CHANGELOG-UNBOUNDED outcome: STILL-PENDING bytesEnqueued: 63700992` — over 63 MB handed to the buffering `response.json()` read in 5 s, still pending, never rejected.

## Why it matters

The changelog page and `/changelog.json` are public console surfaces backed by a third-party API call made per server render. Today a stalled GitHub response stalls the request with no fallback, and an oversized one buffers without limit in the console server process. Sibling console fetches already bound their time (e.g. `packages/console/app/src/lib/console-account.ts` uses `AbortSignal.timeout(3000)`, `salesforce.ts`'s request helper uses `AbortSignal.timeout(8000)`) — this loader is the outlier with neither a time nor a size bound.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `loadChangelog()`'s fetch carries a named timeout (`AbortSignal.timeout(...)`, consistent with the 3-8 s console precedents or justified otherwise) so a stalled response settles into the existing `{ ok: false, releases: [] }` fallback.
- [ ] The releases body is read through a bounded reader (streaming cap, named constant sized generously above 20 releases' real payload) instead of an unbounded `response.json()`; an over-cap body lands in the same empty fallback.
- [ ] Regression tests cover a never-resolving body (settles via timeout fallback) and an over-cap body (empty fallback, not fully buffered), in the console app's existing test setup (e.g. alongside `packages/console/app/src/lib/console-signup.test.ts` / `salesforce.test.ts`).
- [ ] No behavior change for a healthy GitHub response under the cap.

## Dedup / scope notes

- Searched open + closed issues for `loadChangelog`, console changelog, and changelog fetch: the only hit is #1061 (gui-extensions whats-new + ui theme loader, renderer surfaces) — this console server-side loader is not covered by #1061 or by #1081 (renderer timeout residual of #1061).
- Out of scope: the Salesforce token fetch in the same package and the stats catalog fetchers (filed separately as #1082).

## Problem

The stats site's model-catalog fetches are unbounded in **time** and **size**:

1. `packages/stats/app/src/routes/model-catalog.ts:351-355` — `fetchCatalogPayload(url)` is a bare `fetch(url)` (no `signal`, no timeout) followed by `response.json()`, which buffers the whole body before parsing.
2. `packages/stats/app/src/routes/model-catalog.ts:357-365` — `fetchLabCatalogPayload(url)` is the same shape: bare `fetch(url)`, then `response.text()` unbounded.
3. `packages/stats/core/src/domain/catalog-identity.ts:14-19` — `loadCatalogIdentity()` does bound time (`AbortSignal.timeout(10_000)`) but then reads `await response.json()` with no size cap.

Callers / blast radius (main `42869cd3f7`):

- `fetchModelCatalog()` (`model-catalog.ts:85-91`) runs all three app fetchers in `Promise.all` against `https://models.opencode.ai/catalog.json`, `https://models.opencode.ai/api.json`, and `https://models.opencode.ai/labs` (`model-catalog.ts:5-7`).
- `loadModelCatalog()` (`model-catalog.ts:69-84`) caches the in-flight promise, so one hanging upstream is shared by every concurrent caller; its settle-based eviction never fires while the fetch is pending.
- `loadModelCatalog()` is awaited in middleware (`packages/stats/app/src/middleware.ts:102,113`) and page data (`packages/stats/app/src/lib/page-data.ts:22,47,69,101`) — a hung catalog fetch hangs user-facing stats requests, not just a background refresh.
- The file itself notes the legitimate payload is large: "The catalog is about 11 MB of JSON to fetch and parse" (`model-catalog.ts:68`). Any cap must be sized with generous headroom over that, not copied from the small-body precedents.

## Verification (this run, laptop probe with the real function)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-stats-catalog/` (laptop), importing the real `loadModelCatalog` from `packages/stats/app/src/routes/model-catalog.ts` with `globalThis.fetch` stubbed per URL:

- **Hang:** `catalog.json` returns 200 with a body stream that never delivers and never closes (other two sources return small valid bodies). Result: `PROBE-HANG outcome: STILL-PENDING` — `loadModelCatalog()` still pending after 5,010 ms; there is no deadline at which it would ever settle.
- **Unbounded:** `catalog.json` returns 200 with a paced endless body (256 KiB every 20 ms). Result: `PROBE-UNBOUNDED2 outcome: STILL-PENDING bytesEnqueued: 63700992` — over 63 MB had been handed to the buffering `response.json()` read in 5 s, still pending, never rejected. (A first unpaced variant starved the event loop so hard the harness had to be killed at 60 s.)

## Why it matters

`models.opencode.ai` is a remote dependency of the stats site: a stalled, slow-drip, or oversized response currently translates directly into hung stats requests and unbounded memory in the stats server process. The sibling core catalog fetch was already treated as a bug for the size half of this pattern (#1078, configurable ModelsDev source, 10 s timeout but unbounded `res.text()`); the stats surfaces were never covered — the app fetchers lack even the timeout, and stats-core's identity fetch lacks the cap.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] All three fetch sites get a named timeout via `AbortSignal.timeout(...)` (app fetchers) and a named maximum body size enforced while streaming (not after a whole-body `json()`/`text()` read), with the cap(s) sized generously above the current ~11 MB catalog and documented in a comment next to the constant.
- [ ] On timeout or oversize, the fetchers fail soft exactly as they do today for network/HTTP errors: app fetchers resolve `undefined`/empty so `buildModelCatalog` proceeds with an empty catalog and the cache entry is evicted for retry; `loadCatalogIdentity` falls back to `{ catalog: cache.value, stale: true }`.
- [ ] Regression tests in the inventoried homes — `packages/stats/app/src/routes/model-catalog.test.ts` and `packages/stats/core/src/domain/catalog-identity.test.ts` — cover: a never-resolving body settles via the timeout path, and a body over the cap is rejected without being fully buffered.
- [ ] No behavior change for a healthy catalog response under the cap.

## Dedup / scope notes

- Searched open + closed issues for `stats catalog`, `model-catalog`, `catalog-identity`, `stats-core`: no existing issue covers these fetchers. #1078 is the separate core ModelsDev fetch (`packages/core/src/models-dev` / catalog) and stays separate; #143 (stats tests not run by CI) is unrelated.
- Out of scope: `packages/stats/app/src/routes/stats-shell.tsx` GitHub-stars fetch and the R2 SQL read in `packages/stats/core/src/r2-sql.ts` (the latter already has a timeout signal).

body:
## Problem

`MessagingEmbedding.request()` — the call that sends texts to an embeddings endpoint — reads **both** of its remote response bodies unbounded:

1. On a non-200 status it buffers the whole error body with `response.text`, then uses only the first 500 characters.
2. On success it decodes the whole body with `HttpClientResponse.schemaBodyJson(EmbeddingResponse)`, which buffers the stream without bounds.

The remote target is user-configured (`config.remote.url` / `key`, resolved at `embedding.ts:213-218` and built at `:549-558`), i.e. a third-party server; the same function also talks to the local llama server, whose responses are equally unchecked. The only bound is the 60-second request timeout (`:145,691-695`), which is not a size bound on a fast connection. This is the #1029 unbounded `response.text`/`schemaBodyJson` pattern on a surface #1029 does not list (its sites are gitlab/poe/snowflake OAuth), and distinct from the embedding **download** bounds in #929/#1071 (`download()` in this same file is carefully bounded — `request()` is not).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `8dab871ace`)

- `packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts:678-681` — error path: `const text = yield* response.text.pipe(Effect.orElseSucceed(() => ""))`, then `text.slice(0, 500)` is embedded in the error. The whole body is buffered to use 500 chars.
- `packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts:683` — success path: `HttpClientResponse.schemaBodyJson(EmbeddingResponse)(response)` buffers the whole JSON body before decode; no `collectBoundedResponseBody` (the house primitive in `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts:4`) or any cap.
- `packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts:537-558,671-676` — `target.url` comes from the configured remote endpoint (or the local server) and the request is `POST ${target.url}/embeddings` with the configured bearer key.
- Contrast in the same file: `download()` (`:351+`, fixed under #929/#1071) pre-checks declared length and bounds the stream in flight — `request()` has neither.
- Test check: `packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts` has a fake remote server (`:389-404` pins path/auth/batching for a 41-text embed) but no oversized error-body or success-body case.
- Laptop probe this run (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-unbounded-catalog-embedding/probe.mjs`, Node): a 32 MiB chunked body was buffered whole by the same `.text()` primitive in 477 ms — far inside the 60 s timeout — and only 500 bytes of it would have been used on the error path.

Dedup: `gh issue list --search` (all states) for embedding response/body bounds returns #929/#1071 (the `download()` path only) and #1029 (gitlab/poe/snowflake OAuth only) — neither covers `request()`.

## Why it matters

Embeddings run on the messaging/search path, automatically and repeatedly. A hostile or broken remote embedding endpoint (user pastes a provider URL + key) can return an endless or multi-GB error body — exactly on the failure path meant to degrade gracefully to text matching (see the timeout comment at `:690`) — and OOM the whole process instead of producing the small `HTTP <status>: <first 500 chars>` error the code intends.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The error path reads through a bounded path (`collectBoundedResponseBody` or equivalent) with a named, documented cap comfortably above the 500 chars actually used (e.g. the 64 KiB OAuth-error precedent); an over-cap error body degrades to the status-only/short error instead of buffering whole.
- [ ] The success path is bounded in flight with a named, documented cap sized for legitimate embedding responses (batch × dimensions floats — justify the value in a comment; the request batches inputs, cf. the 32/9 split pinned in the existing test), with a declared-length pre-check where the client exposes it.
- [ ] Normal behaviour is unchanged: small error bodies still surface their first 500 chars, and ordinary remote/local embedding responses still decode and return vectors in index order.
- [ ] Regression tests using the existing fake-server harness in `packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts`: oversized error body (declared and streamed) is rejected/degraded without buffering whole, and an oversized success body fails cleanly.

body:
# fix(cli): config migration writer renames over symlinks and always resets mode to 0600 — the one writer of cli.json that #1067/#1070 missed

## Summary

`packages/cli/src/config/config.ts`'s main writer for the global CLI config (`cli.json`) was hardened in #1067 / PR #1070: it resolves the destination through any symlink first (dotfiles setups), uses a unique temp name, and never widens an existing file's permissions (`existing & 0o600`). The **migration writer in the same directory, writing the same file**, has none of the symlink/mode hardening:

- `packages/cli/src/config/migrate.ts:23-35` — `persist()` does `fs.rename(temp, input.file)` directly on the unresolved path, and creates its temp with a fixed `{ mode: 0o600 }` (migrate.ts:27). There is no `realPath` and no `stat` anywhere in the file (grep-verified).
- `input.file` is exactly the file #1070 hardened: `packages/cli/src/config/config.ts:34` sets `file = path.join(global.config, "cli.json")` and config.ts:61 passes that same `file` to `ConfigMigration.run({ file, ... })`.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `bc2013f05e`)

`persist()` is reached on both migration paths:

1. Existing `cli.json` with legacy content — legacy keybind renames or `terminal.copy_on_select` (migrate.ts, `return yield* persist(updated, info)` at the end of the existing-file branch): a **symlinked** `cli.json` (the standard dotfiles setup #1067 was about) has its symlink **replaced by a regular file**; the real target in the dotfiles repo is never updated, and the next migration/update sees a different file than the user's version-controlled one.
2. Fresh migration from `tui.json`/`kv.json` (migrate.ts:107, `persist(JSON.stringify(migrated, null, 2) + "\n", migrated)`).

Mode defect, same class as #1067 item 3: because the temp is always created `0o600` and then renamed over the destination, an existing `cli.json` with mode `0400` (read-only, the exact case PR #1070's tests pin for the main writer) comes out of a migration as `0600` — permissions silently widened by a background migration the user did not invoke as a config edit.

What is NOT defective here: the temp name is already unique (`${input.file}.${process.pid}.${randomUUID()}.tmp`, migrate.ts:24), so there is no shared-`.tmp` collision, and the write is atomic (temp + rename with cleanup in `Effect.ensuring`). This is a two-of-three-guarantees residual, not a repeat of the whole #1067 shape.

Test gap: `packages/cli/test/config.test.ts` covers migration behaviour extensively (tui/kv migration, keybind renames, `copy_on_select`, persistence-failure fallback) but has no symlink or mode case (grep-verified: no `symlink`/`chmod` in that file). The sibling guarantees ARE pinned for the main writer in `packages/cli/test/cli-config-write.test.ts:45` ("preserves a symlinked cli config and updates its target") and cli-config-write.test.ts:75-89 (a `0400` config stays `0400`) — the migration path bypasses both pins because it is a different writer.

## Why it matters

Migration runs automatically at startup, before the first update (config.test.ts: "migrates before the first update and does not remigrate afterward"). A user who keeps `cli.json` in dotfiles and still has one legacy key — one legacy keybind name or `terminal.copy_on_select` — loses the symlink on a routine launch, silently forking their config: the dotfiles copy stops receiving every later update, with no error anywhere. And a deliberately read-only config silently becoming writable undermines the permission posture #1070 explicitly chose to preserve.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `ConfigMigration.persist` resolves the destination through any symlink first (e.g. `fs.realPath(file)` with fallback to the raw path, mirroring config.ts's `write()`), so the rename lands on the real file and the symlink at `cli.json` survives a migration.
- [ ] The migrated file's mode is `existing & 0o600` when the destination already exists (a `0400` file stays `0400`), and `0o600` for a genuinely new file — same rule as config.ts's `write()`.
- [ ] New tests in `packages/cli/test/config.test.ts` (or a sibling migration-write test file) mirroring cli-config-write.test.ts: migration of a symlinked `cli.json` with legacy content updates the target and leaves the symlink in place; migration of a `0400` `cli.json` leaves its mode at `0400` (POSIX-only assertions guarded like the sibling tests).
- [ ] Existing migration tests in config.test.ts still pass; no behaviour change when `cli.json` is a regular file with default permissions.

body:
# fix(core): custom embedding model downloads have no size bound at all — the custom-URL shape carries neither sha256 nor size, so `download()` streams unbounded to disk (#929 residual)

## Evidence (verified on main `9ba3fb98d2`, 2026-10-31, laptop probe driving the real module)

#929 bounded `MessagingEmbedding.download` (`packages/core/src/messaging/embedding.ts`) for the two call shapes it enumerated: tier models (exact `size` known) and the llama.cpp archive (sizes recorded in `LLAMA_ASSETS`). Every bound in `download` is keyed on `input.size`:

- Declared-length pre-check, `embedding.ts:351`: `if (input.size !== undefined && total !== undefined && total > input.size)` — skipped when size is undefined.
- In-flight per-chunk bound, `embedding.ts:369`: `if (input.size !== undefined && progress.received + chunk.byteLength > input.size)` — skipped when size is undefined.
- `finish()` verification, `embedding.ts:394-399`: the digest check needs `input.sha256`; the size check needs both `digest === undefined && input.size !== undefined` — with neither, **any** completed body is renamed from `<dest>.part` to `dest` and accepted.

The third call shape has neither value:

- `resolve()`'s custom branch (`embedding.ts:243-254`) builds the `Local` for a user-supplied URL (`config embedding.url`, schema `packages/schema/src/config/messaging.ts:23` — "GGUF download URL used instead of the tier's model" — or the `OPENCODE_EMBEDDING=https://…` override) with **no `sha256` and no `size`**, unlike the tier branch (`embedding.ts:273-274`, which sets both). The config schema offers no `sha256`/`size` fields for a custom URL at all, so a user cannot supply them either.
- `ensureModel` (`embedding.ts:650-655`) passes `sha256: local.sha256, size: local.size` straight through — both `undefined` for custom models. The existing resolve test even pins this (`packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts`, "derives pooling and query for custom models": `expect(qwen?.sha256).toBeUndefined()`), but no download test uses the custom call shape — all three #929 regression tests pass an explicit `size`.

### Probe (laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-embedding-custom`, real `MessagingEmbedding.download` via the repo's own test harness, local HTTP fixtures; 3/3 pass)

- `resolve({ url: "https://example.com/x/model.gguf" })` → local `{ tier: "custom", sha256: undefined, size: undefined }`.
- Custom call shape (`sha256: undefined, size: undefined`) against a chunked (no `content-length`) server serving 5,000,000 bytes → download **succeeded**, dest holds all 5,000,000 bytes; nothing rejected or truncated it.
- Custom call shape against an **endless** chunked server → the download never self-terminates; after an external 3-second timeout killed it, `<dest>.part` already held **244,022,673 bytes** (~233 MiB) and was still growing.

## Why it matters

This is exactly #929's failure mode — an oversized or endless body fills the user's disk before any check can run — surviving on the one download path #929's fix could not bound, because the bound is keyed on a value this path never has. The embedding pipeline autostarts in the background (`autostart` defaults to true), so the download is not something the user is watching: a compromised/misbehaving mirror, a redirect to a huge file, or a server that streams forever turns into a filled disk and a wedged pipeline instead of a prompt, clear error. Tier models run 25 MB–15 GB, so the fix cannot be a small generic cap: it needs a deliberate bound for the unknown-size shape (a named, justified maximum well above the largest legitimate GGUF, and/or optional `sha256`/`size` config fields for custom URLs that, when present, restore the exact #929 checks).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A custom-URL embedding download is bounded in flight even when neither sha256 nor size is known: it aborts with a clear "larger than expected"-style error once the body passes a named, justified cap constant (sized for the largest legitimate GGUF models), and the oversized `.part` does not survive as a resumable download.
- [ ] A declared `content-length` / `content-range` total above the cap fails before the body is read, mirroring the known-size pre-check at `embedding.ts:351`.
- [ ] Tier and llama.cpp downloads behave exactly as today (existing `MessagingEmbedding.download` tests keep passing, including resume/416/digest-mismatch behaviour).
- [ ] Regression tests in `packages/core/test/messaging-embedding.test.ts` pin the custom call shape (`sha256` and `size` both undefined): declared-oversized and chunked-oversized bodies abort early, asserting the download stops before the whole oversized body is consumed.
- [ ] Out of scope: changing tier/llama asset sizes or digests; the memory-side body caps (#923 family) — this path streams to disk.

Cross-link: #929 (closed — bounded the known-size shapes; this is its residual custom-URL shape).

## Evidence (verified this run, main `9989fd3dd5`)

`packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts` holds the canonical bounded response-body readers that the recent body-cap fixes (#1017, #1019, #1025, #1026, #1023) converged on:

- `collectBoundedResponseBody` (http-body.ts:4) — Effect `HttpClientResponse` variant, with hand-rolled buffer growth: initial `Buffer.allocUnsafe(min(max, declared || 64 KiB))`, doubling growth capped at `maximumBytes` (http-body.ts:17-25).
- `readBoundedResponseText` (http-body.ts:39) — native fetch `Response` variant, with declared-length pre-check, streamed in-flight bound, and a no-readable-stream fallback that byte-counts via `TextEncoder` (http-body.ts:56-62).

Call sites depending on these two functions (grep on main): `config/plugin/instruction.ts:159` (remote instructions read into model context, #1025), `github-copilot/models.ts:97`, `modal/models.ts:74` (#1017), `mcp/oauth.ts:141` (#1019), `plugin/provider/chatgpt.ts:520`, `plugin/provider/github-copilot.ts:474,498,565`, `plugin/provider/openai.ts:234,431`, `plugin/provider/xai.ts:30` (#1026 OAuth flows), `plugin/websearch/mcp.ts:56`, `plugin/websearch/tinyfish.ts:122`, `tool/plugin/webfetch.ts:78`, `tool/plugin/mcpx.ts:252,259` (#1023).

**No test file references either function.** Verified twice this run: `grep -rln "collectBoundedResponseBody|readBoundedResponseText" packages/core/test packages/cli/test packages/ui` returns nothing, and there is no `http-body` test under `packages/core/test/`. By contrast, each of the three layering copies written because the packages cannot import core's helper IS tested: cli `updater-install.test.ts:340,362` (declared + streamed cases for the #1031 copy), ui `theme/loader.test.ts` (3 cases for the #1061 copy), gui-extensions `updater/changelog.test.ts` (4 cases, incl. the no-readable-stream multibyte case, #1063/#1064). The original is the only untested copy — and it is the one with the most call sites and the trickiest code (the `collectBoundedResponseBody` growth arithmetic has no counterpart in the copies).

## Why it matters

These helpers are the single bound standing between a hostile or broken upstream and unbounded buffering in OAuth token flows, model-list loaders, MCP discovery, webfetch, and remote instruction loading. A regression in the growth arithmetic (e.g. an off-by-one that truncates a body at a chunk boundary, or a cap comparison flipped to `>=`/`>`) or in the no-stream fallback would either silently un-bound every one of those surfaces at once or break legitimate responses — and nothing in CI would catch it, because the copies' tests exercise different code.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] New test file for `packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts` (e.g. `packages/core/test/http-body.test.ts`) covering `readBoundedResponseText`: normal body, declared-oversized rejected before reading, streamed-oversized rejected in flight, exactly-at-cap body accepted, and the no-readable-stream oversized case with a multibyte body pinning the byte-count (not `text.length`) check — mirroring `changelog.test.ts`'s cases.
- [ ] Same file covers `collectBoundedResponseBody`: normal multi-chunk body that crosses the initial 64 KiB allocation (pinning the growth path), declared-oversized, streamed-oversized, zero-length chunks skipped, and exactly-at-cap accepted.
- [ ] Tests run under the existing core test suite (`bun test` in packages/core) with no network access.
- [ ] No production-code change is needed to make the helpers testable (both are already exported); if a case cannot be driven without one, note it on this issue instead of refactoring silently.

body:
## Summary

Two CLI config writers still persist through a **fixed-name temp file** (`<file> + ".tmp"`) followed by a bare `rename` onto the destination — the exact shape that #1056 / PR #1057 just hardened in the plugin writers and that `mcp add` (#977 / PR #978) was built to avoid. They break the same three guarantees:

1. **A symlinked config is destroyed.** The rename lands on the symlink path itself, so the symlink is replaced by a regular file and the real (dotfiles-managed) config is never updated.
2. **Concurrent writers collide** (service config only — see below). All invocations share the one `.tmp` name, so parallel writers consume each other's rename source and fail with `ENOENT`, or silently rename another writer's content.
3. **An existing file's permissions are not preserved.** The temp is always created `0o600`, so a read-only `0o400` config silently becomes `0o600` after a write.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `3d2f849e37`)

Code:

- `packages/cli/src/services/service-config.ts:169-175` — the private `write()` behind `ServiceConfig.set` / `unset` / `password` / `remote` / `acceptRemote` and the legacy-repair path in `read()`:
  `const temp = configFile + ".tmp"`, `writeFileString(temp, ..., { mode: 0o600 })`, `rename(temp, configFile)`. No `realpath`, no unique temp name, no mode preservation — and **no lock anywhere in the module** (contrast `cli/src/config/config.ts`, whose updates at least run under `Flock`). Callers are independent CLI processes (`opencode service set/unset`, `pair`, and server startup via `server-process.ts:158` calling `ServiceConfig.password()`), so concurrent invocations are realistic. This file holds the managed service's **password and the unguessable remote-access route** (`Info` schema, same file), so a lost/clobbered write has credential-grade consequences.
- `packages/cli/src/config/config.ts:42-47` — the `write()` behind CLI `Config.update` (`cli.json`): identical fixed-temp + bare-rename shape. Its callers are flock-serialised, so the concurrency defect is mitigated there, but the symlink destruction and mode reset are not — the flock does not resolve the destination.
- Contrast the hardened siblings: `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/mcp/add.ts:68-84` and (after #1057) `plugin/add.ts` / `plugin/remove.ts` do `realpath` first, preserve `existing.mode & 0o777`-style owner bits, and use `destination + ".tmp-" + process.pid + "-" + randomUUID()`; `packages/cli/src/config/migrate.ts:23-27` (`persist`) already uses a pid+UUID temp; `packages/cli/src/services/service-registration.ts:22` uses a per-service-id temp. These two writers are the remaining outliers.
- No test pins any of the three behaviours for either writer: `packages/cli/test/plugin-config-write.test.ts` covers the plugin writers and `mcp-add-write.test.ts` covers `mcp add`; grep finds no symlink/concurrent/mode test referencing `service-config` or the CLI config writer.

Reproduction (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-service-config-write/probe.ts`, bun, replicating the exact write sequence above — temp name, mode, rename — against temp dirs):

```
SYMLINK:    isSymlinkAfter=false targetHasNew=false linkTextHasNew=true
CONCURRENT: rejected=["ENOENT","ENOENT"] final={"writer":2}
READONLY:   modeAfter=600 (was 400)
```

So: after a write against a symlinked `service.json` the link is gone and the real config never gains the change; two of three concurrent writes fail with `ENOENT`; and a `0o400` config comes back `0o600`.

## Why it matters

Dotfiles-managed configs (config dir symlinked into `~/.config/opencode/`) are a common setup — `mcp add` and `plugin add` were both fixed for exactly this user. Today `opencode service set password …`, pairing/remote toggles, and CLI config updates silently detach those files from the dotfiles repo and write into a shadow regular file, so the change is invisible to (and later overwritten by) dotfiles sync. For `service.json` the stakes are higher: it stores the service password and remote route, and its writer is the only one of the set with no serialisation at all, so scripted or overlapping `service` commands can lose each other's updates or fail spuriously.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both writers resolve the destination through any symlink (`realpath`, falling back to the given path) so the rename lands on the real file and the symlink survives, matching `mcp add` / `plugin add`.
- [ ] Both writers use a per-invocation unique temp name (pid + random suffix, following `migrate.ts` / the plugin writers), so concurrent writers cannot consume each other's rename source; the service-config writer additionally must not lose a concurrent update silently (unique temp at minimum; flock or equivalent if the triage finds read-modify-write loss in scope).
- [ ] An existing file's permissions are preserved (never widened: a `0o400` file stays `0o400`); a fresh file is created `0o600`.
- [ ] Regression tests, following `packages/cli/test/plugin-config-write.test.ts` / `mcp-add-write.test.ts` conventions, pin for at least the service-config writer: symlink preserved + target updated, concurrent writes all succeed, read-only file stays read-only; the CLI `cli.json` writer gets at least the symlink and mode cases.
- [ ] Existing CLI config / service tests stay green (`bun run test` + typecheck in `packages/cli`, on laptop or CI).

Out of scope: core `Config.update` (#998, in-place writer of `opencode.jsonc`) and the already-hardened mcp/plugin/migrate/registration writers.

body:
## Finding

PR #846 made interactive form numeric answers parse with the strict plain-decimal grammar (`formNumberValue`, `/^-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?$/`), but the form clients still pre-fill a numeric field's default with `String(field.default)`. For any default whose `String()` form is exponent notation, confirming the pre-filled value unchanged is now rejected as "Expected a number" — the field's own valid default cannot be submitted.

JS renders numbers in exponent notation outside the plain-decimal range (verified with a node probe of the exact expressions):

- `String(1e-7)` → `"1e-7"` — fails the grammar
- `String(1e21)` → `"1e+21"` — fails the grammar
- `formNumberValue("1e-7")` → `NaN` → validators report "Expected a number"

## Evidence

- Source PR: #846 (merged, commits d451cfe0, 5c24c77e), which introduced `formNumberValue` for typed answers, closing #844.
- Review source: CodeRabbit Minor on PR #846 (packages/tui/src/util/form.ts:84) — raised on the PR, never dispositioned or filed.
- Still present on current main `3d2f849e3794c91a74e6ddf6b330de1a3f0c90c2`:
  - `packages/tui/src/util/form.ts:81-85` — `formNumberValue` accepts only plain-decimal spellings, everything else is `NaN`.
  - `packages/tui/src/component/dialog-integration.tsx:1104` — `initial = field.default === undefined ? undefined : String(field.default)`, and the confirm path at `:1115-1122` runs that text through `formNumberValue` + `formValidateValue`.
  - `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/auth/form.ts:143` — the CLI text prompt's `initialValue` is the same `String(field.default)`, validated by `validateText` (same grammar) and converted with `formNumberValue` at `:149`.
  - Related display path: `formDisplayValue` (`packages/tui/src/util/form.ts:127-133`) also renders a numeric answer via `String(item)`, so the session/mini forms can show the same exponent text for an existing answer.

## Why it matters

A form definition (e.g. an integration/auth form) that legitimately defaults a number field to a very small or very large value — a rate like `1e-7`, a cap like `1e21` — becomes unsubmittable in the TUI dialog and the CLI auth form: the user is told their untouched, server-supplied default is not a number, and must guess a plain-decimal rewrite of it. This is a regression introduced by the #844 strict-parsing fix: before it, bare `Number()` accepted the pre-filled text.

## Acceptance criteria

- A numeric/integer field whose default renders in exponent notation (test with `1e-7` and `1e21`) can be confirmed unchanged in the TUI integration dialog and in the CLI auth form, submitting the original numeric value.
- User-typed exponent spellings (`1e3`, `0x10`) are still rejected with "Expected a number" (the #844 behavior does not regress).
- Tests pin the pre-fill path for both clients (parser/render-level tests are acceptable where the dialog itself is not unit-tested).
- The fix renders or carries the default in a plain-decimal form (or bypasses text parsing for an untouched default) rather than loosening the typed-input grammar.

# test(gui-extensions): the whats-new changelog size cap (#1061) has no regression test — its bounded reader is private, unlike both tested siblings

## Evidence (verified on main `3d2f849e37`, 2026-10-31)

PR #1062 (fix for #1061, merged today) added three implementations of the same bounded-remote-JSON pattern. Two of them shipped with regression tests; the third shipped with none, and as written it cannot get one without a code change:

1. **CLI updater release check (#1031)** — bounded reader in `packages/cli/src/services/updater.ts`, tested in `packages/cli/test/updater-install.test.ts:340-388`: a declared `content-length` of `releaseMaxResponseBytes + 1` is rejected before the body is read (`bodyRead` stays false), and a streamed body of 8 × cap/2 chunks is rejected in flight (`pulled < totalChunks`).
2. **Theme loader (#1061)** — bounded reader in `packages/ui/src/theme/loader.ts`, tested in the new `packages/ui/src/theme/loader.test.ts` (added by PR #1062 itself): normal body loads, declared-oversize rejected before read, streamed-oversize rejected in flight.
3. **Whats-new changelog (#1061)** — bounded reader in `packages/gui-extensions/src/updater/whats-new.tsx:19-56`: `changelogMaxResponseBytes` is exported, but `readBoundedChangelogText` (lines 22-56) is a private `const`, and the only caller is `showWhatsNew` (line 113), which requires a full extension `SetupContext`. There is no test: `grep -rn changelogMaxResponseBytes packages/gui-extensions/src packages/ui/src` returns only the definition site itself, and no `*.test.*` file in `packages/gui-extensions` references `whats-new` (the package does colocate bun tests, e.g. `packages/gui-extensions/src/updater/machine.test.ts`, and its `package.json` test script is `bun test`).

So the cap that protects the desktop renderer's automatic startup fetch of `https://opencode.ai/changelog.json` is the only one of the three with nothing pinning its behaviour. A future refactor that drops the declared-length pre-check, the in-flight bound, or the no-body fallback check would pass every existing test in the repo.

## Why it matters

This exact class — an unbounded remote body buffering whole into memory — has bitten this repo repeatedly (#923, #1017, #1018, #1025, #1026, #1029, #1031, #1049, #1061), and the house defence is a named cap **plus** a regression test, as both siblings demonstrate. The untested copy is also the one in the renderer at startup, against a remote endpoint the user does not control. Per `packages/gui-extensions/AGENTS.md`, unit tests are for "pure logic that carries a contract: path and security checks, storage migration, protocol parsing, archive validation" — a response-size security bound is exactly that category, not UI behaviour duplicated from e2e.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The whats-new bounded read is reachable from a test (export `readBoundedChangelogText`, or extract it to a testable module — following the sibling pattern: `packages/ui` exports its reader's cap and tests `loadThemeFromUrl` directly; `packages/cli` tests through the public service).
- [ ] A colocated bun test (e.g. `packages/gui-extensions/src/updater/whats-new.test.ts(x)`, run by the package's existing `bun test`) pins at least: (a) a normal changelog-sized body returns its text; (b) a declared `content-length` above `changelogMaxResponseBytes` rejects before the body is read; (c) a streamed/chunked body above the cap rejects in flight without consuming the whole stream.
- [ ] No behaviour change to `showWhatsNew`: a failed/oversized fetch still leaves the version un-marked and is retried on the next start, exactly as today.
- [ ] `bun run test` and `bun run typecheck` pass in `packages/gui-extensions` (on laptop or CI, per repo rules — not from the repo root).

## Dedup

`gh issue list --state all --search whats-new` on 2026-10-31 returns only #1061 (closed, the fix itself). No open or closed issue covers test coverage for the whats-new cap; #1061's acceptance criteria required over-cap regression tests "for at least one path", and PR #1062 satisfied that with the theme loader only — this issue is the residual for the other path, not a duplicate.

body:
# fix(ui,gui-extensions): two renderer remote-JSON fetches buffer the whole body — whats-new changelog and theme loader read response.json() with no size cap

## Evidence (verified on main `9ffaaeb959`, 2026-10-31)

Two remote JSON reads in the desktop-facing UI layer buffer the entire response body into memory with no size cap, no `content-length` pre-check, and no streaming bound:

1. **What's-new changelog (runs at desktop startup)** — `packages/gui-extensions/src/updater/whats-new.tsx:8,64-65`: `fetch(CHANGELOG_URL /* https://opencode.ai/changelog.json */, { signal: ctx.signal }).then((response) => (response.ok ? response.json() : undefined))`. The only signal is the extension teardown signal — there is no timeout and no body bound. Caller: `packages/gui-extensions/src/updater/renderer.tsx:107-110` invokes `showWhatsNew` on every start where the version changed and release notes are enabled. The changelog is normally small, but the decode that follows (`decodeChangelog`) is explicitly lenient about malformed entries — the size of the body is the one input it does not defend against.
2. **Theme loader (public `@opencode/ui` API)** — `packages/ui/src/theme/loader.ts:82-90`: `loadThemeFromUrl(url)` does `fetch(url)` then `return response.json()`, for an arbitrary caller-supplied URL, with no timeout and no cap. It is exported from `packages/ui/src/theme/index.ts:38`.

### Laptop probe (real module, this run)

Probe on the laptop (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-ui-remote-json/probe.ts`, bun, laptop clone at main `9ffaaeb959`): imported the real `loadThemeFromUrl` from `packages/ui/src/theme/loader.ts` and pointed it at a local server streaming a ~50 MiB chunked JSON body (no `content-length`):

```json
{"ok":true,"padLength":52428800,"rssBefore":19066880,"rssAfter":131158016,"rssDeltaMiB":107}
```

The 50 MiB body was accepted and parsed whole; RSS grew by ~107 MiB. A larger or endless body grows the renderer until it dies — there is no point at which this code says no.

## Why it matters

The house pattern for untrusted remote bodies is a bounded read with a named cap: core's `readBoundedResponseText` / `collectBoundedResponseBody` (`packages/core/src/tool/http-body.ts`), the generated client's 16 MiB JSON bound, the service probe's cap (#1018), and the updater release check's 1 MiB cap (#1031) — the sibling updater code in this same feature area already does this. These two renderer paths are the remaining `response.json()` reads of remote bodies in `packages/ui` + `packages/gui-extensions` (grep-verified this run: the only other hits are a local canvas blob and IPC payloads). One oversized or hostile response — a compromised changelog endpoint, a bad theme URL, a MITM'd plain connection downstream — OOMs the desktop renderer instead of failing a decorative feature.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both paths enforce a stated per-path size cap (changelog and theme JSON are both small documents; a named constant with a comment justifying the size, in the spirit of the updater's `releaseMaxResponseBytes`), failing with a clear "response too large" style error instead of buffering past the cap; a declared `content-length` above the cap fails before the body is read.
- [ ] Streamed/chunked bodies without a declared length are bounded in flight, not buffered whole and checked afterwards.
- [ ] Normal behaviour is unchanged: a real changelog still drives the whats-new dialog (and a failed/oversized fetch still leaves the version un-marked for the next start, as today), and a normal theme JSON still loads via `loadThemeFromUrl`.
- [ ] Regression tests pin the over-cap behaviour for at least one of the two paths (oversized declared length and oversized streamed body), following the package's existing test conventions.
- [ ] Out of scope: the console/stats websites' server-side fetches, local blob/IPC `arrayBuffer()` reads, and the already-bounded core/cli/client paths.

## Dedup

`gh search issues` (all states) for "whats-new changelog", "theme loadThemeFromUrl", and "unbounded" on 2026-10-31: no issue covers either path. The bounded-body family (#923, #1017, #1018, #1025, #1026, #1029, #1031, #1049) covers core/cli/client paths only; the updater sibling fixed in #1031 is `packages/cli/src/services/updater.ts`, not this gui-extensions whats-new fetch.

body:
## Problem

The route-window documentation never mentions the date-aware fields that #821 added: `dates`, `excludeDates`, and `excludeWindows`. The feature merged (PR #1043, commit 8ca25e5eb0 `feat(routes): date-aware route windows — dates/excludeDates + excludeWindows holiday exclusion`), but an operator reading the docs cannot discover it — including for the docs' own motivating example.

## Evidence (verified this run on main 93e1084cc2)

- `packages/web/src/content/docs/config.mdx`, "Windows" section (~lines 697–722): the field list documents `daysOfWeek`, `daysOfMonth`, `start`/`end`, `timezone`, and `from`/`until` — and nothing else. A repo-wide grep of the docs tree finds zero mentions of `dates` (as a window field), `excludeDates`, or `excludeWindows`.
- The fields are live in code: `packages/core/src/model-route-schedule.ts:26-40` (the `Window` interface documents `dates`, `excludeDates`, `excludeWindows`), parse/validation at `model-route-schedule.ts:118-135,282-299`, exclusion resolution in `packages/core/src/config/plugin/model-routes.ts:266-294`, with tests in `packages/core/test/model-route-schedule.test.ts`.
- The docs example window is `deepseek-peak` — exactly the #821 use case (DeepSeek peak pricing suspends on Chinese public holidays) — yet the holiday-exclusion mechanism that use case needs is the part that is undocumented.
- History: #866 (closed) documented the `model_routes` family before #821 landed; #821 itself stays open only for a cross-repo config remainder, not for docs.

## Why it matters

Date windows and holiday exclusions are operator-facing config: their whole value is an operator writing them by hand in `opencode.json`. Undocumented, the feature is effectively invisible, and the semantics that matter (entries are read in the window's timezone, exclusions win over every other field, an unknown or cyclic `excludeWindows` name drops the window rather than applying it unexcluded) are exactly the ones an operator cannot guess safely.

## Acceptance criteria

- The Windows section of `packages/web/src/content/docs/config.mdx` documents:
  - `dates` — `"YYYY-MM-DD"` entries and inclusive `"YYYY-MM-DD/YYYY-MM-DD"` ranges, read in the window's timezone; an unreadable entry invalidates the window (same rule as the day lists).
  - `excludeDates` — same entry shape; exclusions win over every other field.
  - `excludeWindows` — names a window from `model_route_windows`; while any named window is active this window is not; an unknown or cyclic reference drops the window (with the same "check names carefully" warning style the section already uses for gate names).
- A worked example shows the holiday pattern end to end: a `cn-holidays`-style calendar window (dates only) referenced via `excludeWindows` from a peak window such as the existing `deepseek-peak` example.
- No code changes; docs build/lint for the web package passes if CI runs it.

Cross-links: #821 (feature), #866 (original family docs).

body:
## Summary

`opencode plugin add` / `opencode plugin remove` write the global config through a
fixed-name temp file (`configPath + ".tmp"`) followed by a bare `rename`, and in doing
so break three guarantees that the sibling `mcp add` writer (`writeMcpConfig`, fixed for
#977 in PR #978) was explicitly built — and test-pinned — to keep:

1. **A symlinked config is destroyed.** The rename lands on the symlink path itself, so
   the symlink is replaced by a regular file and the real (dotfiles) config is never
   updated. `mcp add` resolves `realpath` first so the rename lands on the target.
2. **Concurrent writers collide.** All invocations share the one `.tmp` name, so
   parallel `plugin add` runs consume each other's rename source and fail with
   `ENOENT`. `mcp add` uses a per-invocation unique temp name for exactly this reason
   (see the comment in `writeMcpConfig`).
3. **An existing config's permissions are not preserved.** The temp file is always
   created `0o600`, so a read-only `0o400` config silently becomes `0o600` after a
   plugin add. `mcp add` preserves the existing file's owner bits.

## Evidence (verified this run, main `c9d194341d`)

Code:

- `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/plugin/add.ts:70-72` — `writePluginConfig`:
  `const temporary = configPath + ".tmp"`, `writeFile(temporary, ..., { mode: 0o600 })`,
  `rename(temporary, configPath)`. No `realpath`, no unique temp name, no mode preservation.
- `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/plugin/remove.ts:61-63` — `removePluginConfig`:
  identical fixed-temp + bare-rename shape.
- Contrast `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/mcp/add.ts:68-84` — `writeMcpConfig`
  does `realpath`, preserves `existing.mode & 0o600`, and uses
  `destination + ".tmp-" + process.pid + "-" + randomUUID()`, with a comment naming the
  concurrent-writer hazard.
- `packages/cli/test/mcp-add-write.test.ts` pins all three behaviors for `mcp add`
  (fresh `0o600`, no widening, symlink preserved + target updated, concurrent writes,
  read-only stays read-only). There is no equivalent test file for the plugin writers.

Reproduction (laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-31-plugin-config-write/probe.ts`,
real exported `writePluginConfig` / `removePluginConfig` / `writeMcpConfig` from main
`c9d194341d`, bun):

```
PLUGIN symlink: isSymlinkAfter = false | targetHasPlugin = false | configTextHasPlugin = true
MCP    symlink: isSymlinkAfter = true  | targetHasServer = true
PLUGIN concurrent: rejected = ["ENOENT","ENOENT"] | finalPlugins = "{ \"plugins\": [ \"pkg-three\" ] }"
PLUGIN readonly: modeAfter = 600 (was 400)
MCP    readonly: modeAfter = 400 (was 400)
PLUGIN remove symlink: isSymlinkAfter = false | targetStillHasPlugin = true
```

So: after `plugin add` against a symlinked config the link is gone and the real config
never gains the plugin; after `plugin remove` the real config still lists the plugin
while the link is destroyed; two of three concurrent adds fail with `ENOENT`; and a
`0o400` config comes back `0o600`.

## Why it matters

Dotfiles-managed configs (config symlinked into `~/.config/opencode/`) are a common
setup — `mcp add` was fixed for exactly this user. Today `plugin add`/`remove` silently
detach the user's config from their dotfiles repo and write the change into a shadow
regular file, so the change is invisible to (and later overwritten by) their dotfiles
sync. The fixed temp name also makes scripted/parallel plugin installs flaky, and the
mode clobber silently widens a deliberately read-only config.

## Acceptance criteria

- `writePluginConfig` and `removePluginConfig` match `writeMcpConfig`'s write
  discipline: resolve the config through any symlink (`realpath`) before writing,
  use a unique per-invocation temp name in the destination directory, and preserve an
  existing config's owner permission bits (fresh config still created `0o600`).
- New tests mirroring `packages/cli/test/mcp-add-write.test.ts` for the plugin writers:
  symlinked config preserved with the target updated (add and remove), concurrent
  adds do not fail or consume each other's temp file, read-only config stays
  read-only, fresh config is `0o600` with no temp file left behind.
- Existing CLI tests still pass; `mcp add` behavior unchanged.

## Finding (from PR #854 review)

PR #854 (merged, head `c14559939`, closes #6) added per-credential routing health — benches, quota gates and demotion are all keyed by `(target, credentialID)` — but its body explicitly deferred the persistence half:

> `route_health` gains no credential column — that requires a DB migration/schema regen; the credential dimension is carried in the health-row reason (`credential:<id>`) and the gate state. Flagged rather than silently dropped.

No issue was ever filed for that flagged follow-up (searched `route_health`, `"credential column"` on 2026-10-31: only #6, #984, #1014, none tracking it). It is still live on current main `79ebc5bc066e`.

## Evidence (current main, verified 2026-10-31)

- `packages/core/src/model-route-log/sql.ts` — `RouteHealthTable` columns are `id, time, route_id, provider_id, model_id, kind, reason, until`: no `credential_id`.
- `packages/core/src/model-route.ts` — `logHealth()` writes the credential only inside the free-text `reason`: bench writes `"<class> credential:<id>"` (~L371), `recover()` writes `"expired credential:<id>"` (~L297), the quota gate writes `"credential:<id> quota-known-full"` (~L532).
- `packages/core/src/model-route-log.ts` — restart replay (`restoreCooldownsFrom`, ~L365) recovers the credential dimension by regex-parsing that free text: `/credential:(\S+)/.exec(row.reason ?? "")` (#870). Any future reason-wording change silently breaks per-credential cooldown restore (a credential bench would restore onto the whole target, or not at all), and per-credential health history cannot be queried/filtered by credential without `LIKE` scans over `reason`.

## Why it matters

The credential dimension is now load-bearing for routing correctness on restart (replay), yet it exists in the persisted record only as an undocumented string convention inside a human-readable field. A typed column makes replay robust and per-credential health (quota-gated / readmitted / benched) directly queryable for the routing diagnostics built on `route_health`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Migration + schema regen adding a nullable `credential_id` column to `route_health` (existing rows stay valid with NULL).
- [ ] `logHealth` / its callers in `model-route.ts` populate `credential_id` for credential-scoped rows (bench, recover, quota-gated/readmitted); target-scoped rows leave it NULL. The `reason` text may keep its current wording for human readers.
- [ ] `restoreCooldownsFrom` reads the credential from the column, falling back to the existing reason-regex only for pre-migration rows; a test pins that a credential-scoped cooldown-start row restores onto that credential only, from the column.
- [ ] A test/query demonstrates filtering `route_health` by `credential_id` without scanning `reason`.
- [ ] No behaviour change for target-scoped (credential-less) health rows.

body:
# fix(client): family sync drops its target snapshot when the covering plain sync fails — and the family key still completes, so the stale snapshot sticks (the #1051 residual)

## Problem

The #1051 fix (PR #1052) guards the family sync's target with `unread` at publish
time: if a plain sync of the same session is in flight (its read "covers" the
target), the family sync does not publish its own snapshot of the target. But
nobody owns the snapshot if that covering read then **fails**:

- the family sync drops its target snapshot (the newest one it holds),
- the covering plain sync rejects, so its snapshot never lands either,
- and the family sync still completes normally — `session.family:<id>` is marked
  complete — so no later family sync ever re-reads the target. The pre-walk
  snapshot in the store sticks until some unrelated invalidation or live event.

The truncated-walk path already handles its version of this: when the ancestor
walk or descendant listing is incomplete, the sync invalidates the family key
so the next sync retries. A target dropped solely because a covering read was
in flight gets no such retry.

## Evidence (main `79ebc5bc06`)

- `packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:601-603` — `unread(session)` is
  `!store.session.info[session.id] || !sync.current('session:' + session.id)`:
  a merely in-flight covering read (not a completed one) makes the target
  "read" and the family snapshot is filtered out.
- `packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:1804-1811` — the family publish is
  `[info].filter(unread)` for family syncs (#1051), `ancestors` fill-only,
  `children.filter(unread)`.
- `packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:1814-1816` — the family key is invalidated
  only for `!ancestorsComplete || !descendantsComplete`; a dropped target does
  not count as incomplete.
- `packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:182-200` — `createSync.start`: a load that
  resolves without invalidation marks its key complete (`state.set(key, true)`);
  a rejected load deletes its own key only. So the failed plain sync leaves
  `session:<id>` incomplete, but the completed `session.family:<id>` key makes
  later `session.sync(id, { children: true })` calls no-ops.
- Contrast: the ancestor filter is existence-only
  (`!store.session.info[ancestor.id]`), so an ancestor that is in the store was
  actually published by someone — nothing is lost there. The `unread` guard is
  the only publish filter that defers to a read that may never publish.

## Reproduction (verified this run, laptop probe)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-family-cover-fail/probe-family-cover-fail.test.ts`
(real `createData` + `OpenCode.make` with a scripted fetch, run with
`bun test` in `packages/client` on main `79ebc5bc06`):

1. Plain sync publishes the target at location `/old`; `session.invalidate(id)`.
2. Family sync re-reads the target at `/mid`; its ancestor read is held.
3. A concurrent plain sync starts (covering read in flight), held, then fails.
4. The family walk completes: at publish time `unread` filters the target out —
   store still `/old`.
5. The plain sync rejects — store still `/old`.
6. A second family sync performs **no new read** (child `session.get` count
   stays 3) and the store still shows `/old`, even though the family sync's own
   `/mid` read was the newest snapshot anyone successfully held.

Probe result: `PROBE final: /old childGets: 3 second family sync re-read: false`
— 0 pass / 1 fail against the expected `/mid`.

## Why it matters

Session views that open a family (children: true) can show stale target state —
location, title, model, status — indefinitely after a transient read failure
that coincides with the walk, with no retry until an unrelated event or
invalidation. It is the failure-side hole in the otherwise correct #1051 guard:
the guard trades "overwrite a newer snapshot" for "lose my snapshot if the
newer read never lands".

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] When a family sync drops its target solely because a covering read was
      in flight, and that covering read does not publish the target, the
      target is recovered: either the family snapshot is published once the
      covering read settles without publishing, or the family key is left
      incomplete (invalidated, like the truncated-walk path) so the next
      family sync re-reads the target.
- [ ] Regression test in `packages/client/test/solid-data.test.ts` mirroring
      the #1051 test, with the concurrent plain sync **failing** after the
      family publish: the target ends at the family sync's snapshot (or is
      re-read by a follow-up family sync), never stuck at the pre-walk one.
- [ ] The #1051 behavior is preserved: a covering read that **succeeds** with
      a newer snapshot still wins over the family sync's older snapshot.
- [ ] Audit the sibling `children.filter(unread)` publish paths
      (`data.ts:589` and the family publish) for the same dropped-on-cover-failure
      loss; either fix them the same way or state in the PR why children cannot
      lose their snapshot this way (e.g. the descendant walk re-syncs them).
- [ ] Existing client tests pass (`bun test test/solid-data.test.ts` from
      `packages/client`, on laptop or CI), including the #631/#1038/#1039/#1051
      family-sync tests.

Related: #1051 / PR #1052 (the guard this is the residual of), #1038, #1039.

# fix(client): family sync publishes its own target's snapshot unconditionally — a newer snapshot that arrived during the ancestor walk is overwritten (the #1038 residual)

## Evidence (verified this run, main 4eea01f4b4)

`packages/client/src/solid/data.ts`, `session.sync` (family path):

- Line 1756: a family sync runs under the key `session.family:<id>`, a plain sync under `session:<id>` — the two run **concurrently**, neither joins the other.
- Lines 1761–1764: the family sync reads its target (`api().session.get`) and its direct children first, then walks ancestors one sequential read at a time (lines 1770–1793). That walk is the window during which the target's snapshot ages.
- Lines 1798–1801 (the #1038 fix, PR #1047): ancestors are published fill-only — `ancestors.filter((ancestor) => !store.session.info[ancestor.id])` — and children go through the `unread` guard (line 601). **The target itself, `info`, is published unconditionally** as the first element of the same `publishSessions` call.
- `publishSessions` (lines 608–624) then writes `draft[session.id] = session` for it and calls `sync.complete("session:<id>")`, marking the reverted snapshot as the settled read — nothing re-reads the session until the next invalidation/event, so the regression sticks.

Reproduced on the laptop (probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-family-target`, copy of the #1038 test pattern in `packages/client/test/solid-data.test.ts`):

1. Family sync of `ses_child` starts; its first `session.get` returns location `/old`; the ancestor read of `ses_parent` is held open.
2. A concurrent plain `session.sync("ses_child")` re-reads the session (now location `/new`, e.g. after a `session.moved`) and publishes it — store shows `/new`.
3. The ancestor read is released; the family sync completes.
4. **Observed: the store's location for `ses_child` is `/old` again.** Expected: `/new`.

Probe result: `PROBE RESULT final directory: /old` — 0 pass / 1 fail on current main. This is exactly the failure #1038 fixed for ancestors ("a live event refresh … is newer than the snapshot the walk holds"), left open for the one session the walk is about.

Note the `session.renamed` handler (line 822) only re-applies the *title* after a racing sync, so a title change happens to be rescued; every other field a newer read carries (location/project after a move, permissions, parentID, time) is silently reverted.

## Why it matters

Opening a session's family view (deep link into a nested subagent, #631) races with the plain syncs the event handlers start constantly. When the target was moved/updated between the family sync's first read and its publish, the client shows — and treats as confirmed — the stale location/state, with no further read scheduled to correct it.

## Acceptance criteria

- A family sync no longer overwrites store state for its target that a completed newer read published after the family sync's own `session.get` (e.g. guard `info` the way children are guarded, or re-check freshness at publish time — implementer's choice, consistent with the `unread` / fill-only precedents in this function).
- Regression test in `packages/client/test/solid-data.test.ts` mirroring the #1038 ancestor test but for the target session: concurrent plain sync publishes a newer snapshot mid-walk; after the family sync completes, the newer snapshot survives.
- Existing family-sync tests (#631 ancestors, #1038, #1039 retry) still pass; no behavior change when no concurrent update lands during the walk (the family sync's own read still publishes and completes normally).

# test(tui): two direct-footer tests skipped since 2026-10-17 — one passes today, the other fails on the composer frame lookup; the stated OpenTUI crash does not reproduce

## Evidence (verified this run, main `77de2fcb69`)

`packages/tui/test/mini/footer.view.test.tsx` carries two permanent `test.skip`s, both introduced in commit `1fc489d878` (2026-10-17, "feat(core): add session messaging and searchable logs"):

- `:1605` — "direct footer recreates the frame across command panel transitions", under the comment at `:1603-1604`: "OpenTUI currently crashes Bun in the full `test/cli/run` directory run here. Re-enable after the upstream OpenTUI fix lands in this repo."
- `:1629` — "direct footer dispatches leader variant binding only when leader is registered", with no explanatory comment of its own.

The stated precondition has never been re-checked and nothing tracks it (no open or recently closed issue mentions these tests or re-enabling them). `@opentui/core` was already at 0.5.17 when the skips landed and is still pinned at 0.5.17 in the root catalog today; the 0.6 upgrade attempt and its revert both predate the skips (2026-10-13).

Verified on the laptop (probe worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-10-30-footer-skips`, main `77de2fcb69`, the two `test.skip`s removed there only; Bun 1.4.2, `packages/tui`):

- "dispatches leader variant binding only when leader is registered" **passes** standalone (1 pass, 2 expect() calls). The skip is simply stale — this coverage has been silently absent for ~2 weeks.
- "recreates the frame across command panel transitions" **fails**, standalone and in the full-file run, with no Bun crash anywhere: `TypeError: undefined is not an object (evaluating 'boxPath(root, "TextareaRenderable").at')` at `footerComposerFrame` (`footer.view.test.tsx:732`), called from the test at `:1777` in the probe numbering. The helper finds no `TextareaRenderable` in the rendered tree at that point.
- Full-file run with both tests unskipped: **78 pass / 1 fail** — the "crashes Bun" precondition does not reproduce for this file on current main.

## Why it matters

The footer is the always-visible composer surface of the TUI. These two tests pin exactly its fragile interactions: recreating the composer frame across command-panel open/close transitions, and leader-key gating of the variant-cycle binding. One has been dead weight hiding a real failure (either the frame no longer recreates / the composer renderable changed shape, or the test helper's tree lookup is brittle against the current render tree — both need diagnosis, not a skip), and the other is passing coverage the suite has not run since 2026-10-17. A skip whose precondition is never re-verified is indistinguishable from deleted coverage.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] "dispatches leader variant binding only when leader is registered" is unskipped and passes in CI (it passes on current main per the probe above).
- [ ] The frame-recreation failure is diagnosed: if `footerComposerFrame`'s `TextareaRenderable` lookup is brittle against the current render tree, fix the helper; if the composer frame genuinely no longer recreates across command-panel transitions, fix the product code. The test is then unskipped and passes in both single-file and full-directory runs.
- [ ] If a genuine OpenTUI/Bun crash still reproduces in some broader run configuration, capture the crash output and a minimal repro in a comment here (and file upstream if it is upstream's) instead of restoring a bare skip.
- [ ] No `test.skip` remains in `footer.view.test.tsx` without an adjacent comment naming a tracking issue.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

In PR #843's family sync (packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:1768-1790 on main), when an ancestor session.get fails (the .catch(() => undefined) at :1780-1782) the walk simply breaks and the sync completes 'successfully' with a truncated ancestor list. The only incompleteness invalidation is for the descendant walk (:1789-1790: syncDescendants returning false invalidates session.family:<id>); a truncated ANCESTOR walk triggers no invalidation, so createSync caches session.family:<id> as complete and later family syncs — including reopening the same session — never retry the missing ancestor until an unrelated invalidation (e.g. reconnect). resolveRoot then keeps grouping the family under the furthest-known ancestor, the #631 symptom. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR; the asymmetry is unchanged on current main.

- Source PR: #843 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/843 (merged, 71608cb8 (head 04834693))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

One transient GET failure during a deep-link open permanently (for the session's cache lifetime) reinstates the wrong-root grouping #631 fixed — with no error surfaced, so it reads as an intermittent app bug rather than a retryable fetch failure.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A family sync whose ancestor walk stopped early because a parent GET failed invalidates session.family:<id> (mirroring the descendant-walk rule at :1789), so the next sync retries the walk.
- [ ] A regression test: first family sync with a failing ancestor GET, second sync after the GET recovers, resolves the true root.
- [ ] A walk that ends because the chain genuinely terminates (no parentID / known ancestor) is still cached as complete — no invalidation loop.

## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #843's ancestor walk in session family sync (packages/client/src/solid/data.ts:1768-1787 on main) collects ancestor SessionInfo snapshots across awaited session.get calls, then publishSessions([info, ...ancestors, ...]) at :1787. publishSessions only guards staleness by sync generation: when the generation is still current it writes every published session over the store entry (draft[session.id] = session at :608-622). An ancestor that was updated while the walk awaited a later parent — e.g. a session.renamed event loading the parent with its new title — is overwritten by the walk's older snapshot, reverting the newer state. ## Why it matters

Renames/titles (and any other info updates) applied during a family sync silently revert — the exact class of stale-store bug #631's family work was meant to eliminate, now introduced on the ancestor path it added.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Publishing walked ancestors does not overwrite a store entry that is newer than the snapshot (e.g. skip ids whose info changed since the walk read them, or re-read/merge at publish time).

## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #828 deliberately gives main-broken.yml a per-run concurrency group (group includes the workflow_run id, .github/workflows/main-broken.yml:43 on main) so watcher runs never displace each other — but that also means two watchers for two near-simultaneous main failures of the same workflow run fully concurrently. The filing step does EXISTING=$(gh issue list --search $BID) at :112 and only later creates via the pm-dispatch step; two watchers with the same Breakage-ID can both observe no existing issue and both file, defeating the one-issue-per-Breakage-ID dedupe the workflow exists to guarantee. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR; the per-run group and the unguarded lookup-then-create are both unchanged on current main.

- Source PR: #828 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/828 (merged, 4abddad7 (head 0c0d51ef))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

Duplicate main-broken issues for one breakage split the fleet's response (two critical tasks, two holders) and break the Breakage-ID contract the remediation chain and the backlog rely on for dedupe.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Filing is serialized per Breakage-ID (or per workflow) — e.g. a second concurrency dimension/queue for the filing step, or a create-then-reconcile pass that closes a duplicate it created as a race loser with a pointer to the survivor.
- [ ] Two simultaneous same-Breakage-ID failures produce exactly one open main-broken issue and the second run's link appended to it.
- [ ] Watcher runs still never cancel each other (cancel-in-progress stays false).

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #828's main-broken.yml gates on workflow_run.head_branch == 'main' (job if at .github/workflows/main-broken.yml:57 on main) and re-checks only head_branch in the filing step (:94). The watched workflows (test, check) also run on pull_request; a run from a fork PR whose source branch is literally named 'main' has head_branch == 'main' while belonging to the fork's repository/sha, not this repo's main. Neither the job condition nor the shell check inspects workflow_run.head_repository / head_sha against this repo's main, and the dispatch fallback path likewise trusts branch name alone. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR; it was not addressed before merge and the checks are unchanged on current main.

- Source PR: #828 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/828 (merged, 4abddad7 (head 0c0d51ef))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

A failing fork PR can file a priority/critical main-broken issue (and enqueue a critical fleet task) for a main branch that is actually green — crying wolf at the highest priority the fleet has, and training responders to ignore real main-broken filings.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The watcher only files for runs of this repository's main: it verifies the run's head repository is this repo (and/or that the run event is a push to main), in both the job if and the shell re-check.
- [ ] A fork-PR-shaped workflow_run payload (head_branch main, head_repository a fork) is skipped with a clear log line; a genuine push-to-main failure still files.
- [ ] The dry-run dispatch path exercises the same guard.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #827 converted release-github-action.yml to the standard concurrency pattern: dispatches are keyed by github.run_id (unique group) with cancel-in-progress: true (.github/workflows/release-github-action.yml:32-40 on main). That is correct for push-to-main/tag runs, but this workflow ONLY runs on workflow_dispatch (its on: block has no push trigger), so the run_id keying removes the serialization the previous ref-keyed group provided: two dispatches on the same branch now run concurrently instead of queuing. The release step runs ./github/script/release after git fetch --tags; the script reads the latest github-v* tag and computes its successor, so overlapping runs can select the same next version and race to create the same tag/publish. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR; the merged workflow still keys dispatches by run_id on current main.

- Source PR: #827 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/827 (merged, 6d0090e9 (head c462ce17))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

A double dispatch (maintainer retry, two maintainers, a dispatch plus an accidental second click) can produce a failed or duplicated release — the exact mid-publish interference the workflow's own comment says must never happen ('Releases are never cancelled mid-publish').

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Manual dispatches of release-github-action serialize (e.g. a stable dispatch group keyed by workflow+ref with cancel-in-progress: false / queue), while distinct runs are never cancelled mid-publish.
- [ ] ci-policy.md / the workflow header comment accurately describe the dispatch grouping after the change.
- [ ] YAML validates and the concurrency expression is covered by the repo's workflow-shape checks if any exist for this file.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #826 made every non-retry-after bench double per consecutive failure (bench() increments state.consecutiveFailures, model-route.ts:347, bench = base x 2^(n-1) at :352). Its networkSuspect undo path (model-route.ts:381-393 on main) clears the earlier correlated targets' cooldowns (prior.cooldownUntil = 0 at :387, samples reset) but does NOT reset prior.consecutiveFailures. So after a local outage that tripped the correlation window, the first two benched targets keep their incremented counts; their next genuine failure — after the correlation window has expired — is benched at double length even though the outage failure was explicitly judged 'not this target's fault' and its cooldown was undone. Codex raised this as a P2 on the PR (model-route.ts:299 in the PR diff); it was not addressed before merge and the undo loop is unchanged on current main.

- Source PR: #826 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/826 (merged, e9c1c196 (head 83d9fd15))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

The networkSuspect mechanism exists so a local outage does not punish healthy providers; leaving the escalation counter incremented silently re-imposes half that punishment on the next unrelated failure, benching a healthy target for 2x the intended first-offence cooldown (up to the quota-length base for auth/quota classes).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The networkSuspect undo also resets consecutiveFailures for every health/credential entry whose cooldown it clears (or otherwise records that the undone failure does not count toward escalation).
- [ ] A regression test: two targets benched, a third network failure trips networkSuspect, then a later single failure on one target benches at the first-offence (1x) length.
- [ ] Existing model-route / session-step-failure tests still pass.

body:
## Finding (PR diff review, lane B)

PR #817's burn-sample construction in `route_usage` (packages/core/src/tool/plugin/route-usage.ts:153-164 on main) emits one sample per (session window share x session target on that provider) with the session's FULL window percent each time, and the sample carries no plan/window identity. Two consequences: (1) a session that used the same provider/model through multiple pools (session.targets preserves separate per-route rows) contributes its full window share once per target, so multi-pool sessions are over-weighted in the bucket mean; (2) shares from distinct quota windows of the same plan/provider (different limits/denominators, e.g. 10% of a 100-request window and 1% of a 1,000-request window) land in the same provider/model/effort bucket (QuotaBurnRate.buckets keys on provider/model/effort only, quota-burn-rate.ts:78-89), producing a mean that describes neither window. Codex raised both as P2s on the PR (comments at route-usage.ts:155 and :158); neither was addressed before merge and both shapes are still present verbatim on current main.

- Source PR: #817 https://github.com/developing-today/opencode/pull/817 (merged, e9b3851d (head edc135ab))
- Verified against current main `e0b7706e83e6f2163732b97182f25dff106c90fb` on 2026-10-30: the cited code is present and unchanged in effect.
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for this defect's terms on 2026-10-30 — no existing issue covers it. (Filed by pr-diff-review lane B; the primary lane's watermark is independent.)

## Why it matters

burnRates are the #568 observe-mode signal the quota/failover work reads; systematically skewed estimates (over-weighted multi-pool sessions, cross-window averaging) mislead exactly the capacity decisions this signal exists to inform, silently — the numbers look precise (rounded to 0.1) while describing no real window.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A session's window share is sampled at most once per (session, window, provider/model) — duplicate pool targets for the same model do not multiply the sample.
- [ ] Samples from distinct quota windows are not averaged together: either the sample/bucket key carries the plan+window identity, or sampling is restricted per window with the window named in the estimate.
- [ ] Regression tests in quota-burn-rate / route-usage tests pin both shapes (multi-pool same-model session; two windows of one provider with different limits).
- [ ] Existing quota-burn-rate and route-usage tests still pass.
