body:
## Problem

The shared quota window builder `toUsageWindow` (`packages/ai/src/quota/utils.ts:113-135`) derives `remainingPercent` from the published `usedPercent` at `utils.ts:125`:

```ts
remainingPercent: hasFiniteUsedPercent ? Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent) : null,
```

The derivation guards only one side. It floors the result at 0, so an over-100 `usedPercent` correctly derives 0% remaining — but it never caps at 100, so a negative `usedPercent` derives a `remainingPercent` **above 100%**, a percent that cannot exist. That violates the window contract in `packages/ai/src/quota/types.ts` (rule 5: "A window's fields agree — derived fields are computed from the published (post-disposition) values"): the one shared place every parser's derived field is computed can publish a derived field outside the percent range.

## Evidence (verified this run on main `2d11e0f649436d6c4d20a64ce13fd7e0501bdd96`)

Probe `probe-usage-window.ts`, run with `bun` in a laptop worktree of `origin/main` (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-creator-1935`), calling the real `toUsageWindow`:

```
usedPercent=-20 -> remainingPercent=120
usedPercent=-5  -> remainingPercent=105
usedPercent=0   -> remainingPercent=100
usedPercent=50  -> remainingPercent=50
usedPercent=100 -> remainingPercent=0
usedPercent=150 -> remainingPercent=0
```

Caller audit (same main): every current parser happens to clamp its own percent before calling `toUsageWindow` (antigravity, claude, cline-pass, codex, command-code, groq, meta, mistral, opencode-go, opendesign all clamp; openrouter caps above; turso filters negative ratios), so no live parser publishes this today. That is exactly how the sibling shared-converter defect shipped and was fixed in #1845 (`toTimestamp` published 1969/1970 resets until the guard moved into the shared converter): the per-parser clamping saga (#1785, #1821, #1879, #1897, #1882) shows parsers repeatedly arrive without a clamp, and a new parser that computes a raw percent from a remaining-above-limit payload — the groq/opendesign shape — would publish `remainingPercent: 120` straight to consumers of the quota shape (aggregator gatherer / dashboard, code#6125) with nothing downstream re-checking the range. `toUsageWindow` itself has no direct pin in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` today (grep: 0 references).

## What NOT to do

Do not clamp `usedPercent` itself in `toUsageWindow`. Turso deliberately publishes over-100 usage truthfully (code#6227, `turso.ts`: "Over-100 is a real state, not bad data"), and its `remainingPercent: 0` for those windows is correct. The defect is only in the *derived* field's missing upper cap.

## Fix shape

Cap the derived field on both sides, e.g. `Math.min(100, Math.max(0, 100 - usedPercent))`. This is a no-op for every conforming input (any `usedPercent >= 0` derives exactly what it derives today, including turso's over-100 → 0) and changes only the negative-input derivation (120 → 100).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `toUsageWindow({ usedPercent: -20 })` derives `remainingPercent: 100`, and `-5` derives `100`; `usedPercent` itself is published unchanged (provider disposition preserved, turso over-100 case included: `150` still derives `0`).
- [ ] New pins in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` for the out-of-range derivations (negative, zero, 100, over-100) — the shared builder's first direct pins.
- [ ] Existing quota suite passes unchanged for all in-range inputs; `packages/ai` typecheck clean.

body:
## Finding

`convertSchema` in `packages/ai/src/protocols/antigravity.ts` still forces `type: "OBJECT"` onto two self-describing root shapes that PR #1669 (fixing #1667) did not cover: **enum-only roots** and **items/prefixItems-only roots**. The root guard on current main (antigravity.ts:299-306) only exempts roots carrying `anyOf` / `oneOf` / `allOf` / `not`; every other typeless root gets `converted.type = "OBJECT"`.

- An enum-only root is unsatisfiable after conversion: `enum` is a value key (`SCHEMA_VALUE_KEYS`, antigravity.ts:127) copied verbatim by `convertSchemaNode`, with no type inference. A root `{ enum: ["a", "b"] }` — a legitimate string-enum parameter schema — becomes `{ enum: ["a", "b"], type: "OBJECT" }`: no JSON value is both an object and equal to `"a"` or `"b"`. This is exactly the defect class #1667 fixed for allOf roots ("a string branch plus a forced OBJECT is unsatisfiable"), one keyword over.
- An items/prefixItems-only root (an array parameter whose element schema is given without an explicit `type`) gets its array keywords stranded on an OBJECT root: `{ items: { type: "string" } }` becomes `{ items: { type: "STRING" }, type: "OBJECT" }`, and `{ prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }] }` becomes `{ items: {}, prefixItems: [{ type: "STRING" }], type: "OBJECT" }` (the prefixItems→items synthesis at antigravity.ts:193 runs, then the root default overrides the shape it describes). Under JSON Schema semantics `items`/`prefixItems` constrain arrays only, so on an OBJECT root the element constraint is unreachable — the same "narrowing" #1667's guard comment describes for `not`.

## Evidence

- Source PR: #1669 — "fix(ai): stop forcing OBJECT onto allOf/not-only roots in antigravity convertSchema (#1667)", merged, merge commit `141e69708bab64be578e5878379111a62bce98dc` (head `1b68e7a72a438542264cfec534ce0bd246b99a9c`). Its guard extends the exemption to `allOf`/`not` only; its new test covers allOf/not/plain roots, not enum or items-carrying roots.
- Current main `2d11e0f649436d6c4d20a64ce13fd7e0501bdd96` (verified twice via the commits API): guard at `packages/ai/src/protocols/antigravity.ts:299-306` checks only `type`/`anyOf`/`oneOf`/`allOf`/`not` before assigning `type: "OBJECT"`.
- Verbatim-extract probe (the `SCHEMA_FIELDS`/`resolveSchemaRefs`/`convertSchemaNode`/`convertSchema` code copied byte-for-byte from current main, run on the laptop under Node `--experimental-strip-types`):
  - `convertSchema({ enum: ["a", "b"] })` → `{"enum":["a","b"],"type":"OBJECT"}` (same with `anthropic=true`)
  - `convertSchema({ items: { type: "string" } })` → `{"items":{"type":"STRING"},"type":"OBJECT"}`
  - `convertSchema({ prefixItems: [{ type: "string" }] })` → `{"items":{},"prefixItems":[{"type":"STRING"}],"type":"OBJECT"}`
  - Controls: `convertSchema({})` → `{"type":"OBJECT"}` (intended default, must be preserved); `convertSchema({ allOf: [{ type: "string" }] })` → `{"allOf":[{"type":"STRING"}]}` (the #1667 fix working).
- Dedupe: searched open + closed issues for "convertSchema enum", "convertSchema root OBJECT", "antigravity root" (2026-11-06). Hits are #1667 (allOf/not only, CLOSED by the source PR), #1556 (multi-valued type unions, CLOSED), #1573 (boolean false, CLOSED), #1820 (union ARRAY branch prefixItems, CLOSED), and #1557 (OPEN, `const` dropping — a different keyword and failure: `const` is absent from `SCHEMA_FIELDS` entirely; its probe confirms nested typed `enum` passes through fine, which is exactly the context the root guard breaks). The OPEN design #1684 (one fidelity contract for tool-schema projections) is the umbrella this file's specific fixes hang off — #1667 was filed and fixed under the same pattern — but it does not disposition the root guard. Nothing covers enum-only or items/prefixItems-only roots.

## Why it matters

Tool input schemas reach `convertSchema` verbatim from MCP/custom tools (`convertSchema(tool.inputSchema ?? …)`, antigravity.ts:456). A tool whose top-level parameter is an enum or an array without an explicit `type` is sent to the Gemini/Anthropic doors with a root schema that either can never validate (enum) or silently drops its element constraint (items) — the same silent-corruption shape this file's #1548/#1550/#1556/#1573/#1667 series has been eliminating one keyword at a time.

## Acceptance criteria

- `convertSchema({ enum: [...] })` no longer gains `type: "OBJECT"` when the enum values are not objects (at minimum the homogeneous non-object case), for both Gemini and Anthropic targets; an enum of objects, if treated differently, is pinned by a test saying why.
- `convertSchema({ items: … })` and `convertSchema({ prefixItems: […] })` roots without an explicit type no longer gain `type: "OBJECT"` (they stay self-describing, like the #1667 roots), for both targets.
- Plain roots keep the OBJECT default byte-identically (`{}`, `{ properties }`, `{ description }` — the existing #1667 regression cases stay green).
- New tests in `packages/ai/test/provider/antigravity.test.ts` next to the #1667 root-composition test cover each shape above; the oracle is JSON Schema conjunction semantics, as in #1667.

body:
# fix(ai): vibe-auth caches its credential forever — invalidate() has no caller, no TTL, and no 401 recovery, so a rotated or revoked key 401s until the process restarts

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `2d11e0f649` (merge of PR #1896), with a runtime probe in a laptop worktree (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-vibe-cache`, kept). Gates this run: not re-run — the defect is in the auth bridge, not a gate surface; the identical gate state was verified by the two preceding creator runs today (workflows/doc-env GREEN; bounded-http 7 / numeric 3 / proto 4 = exactly #1724's set).

## The defect

`packages/ai/src/providers/vibe-auth.ts` resolves the Vibe credential once and caches it for the life of the process, with no recovery path:

- :222-238 — `cached` / `inflight` are process-global; `loadApiKey` (the no-sources path every real route uses) returns `cached` forever once set. There is no TTL and no expiry check.
- :226-229 — `invalidate()` exists and clears both, but **nothing calls it**: a repo-wide grep for `VibeAuth` outside `vibe-auth.ts` itself finds only the import and the `vibeAuth(...)` wiring in `packages/ai/src/providers/vibe.ts` (:29, :140). The function is dead code.
- `packages/ai/src/providers/vibe.ts` :94/:136 — the provider rides `MistralChat.route` unchanged, whose transport is the plain SSE transport (`packages/ai/src/protocols/mistral-chat.ts`: `httpTransport`, no auth-retry wrapper). So a 401 from Mistral is terminal for every request, forever: the stale key is re-sent on each one.

Both sibling direct providers built in the same pattern have a working recovery loop, and the other bridges avoid the trap entirely:

- muse-direct: minted key cached 10 min (`MINTED_KEY_TTL_MS`), and its transport invalidates + re-prepares + retries exactly once on a 401 (`packages/ai/src/protocols/muse-direct-responses.ts` :205-228, `MuseDirectAuth.invalidate()` at :228). Its api_key-only path is re-read per request.
- antigravity: token cached only until 60 s before its expiry, and its transport calls `AntigravityAuth.invalidate()` on a 401 and retries (`packages/ai/src/protocols/antigravity.ts` :895).
- commandcode-auth: no cache at all — the login file is re-read per request, so a re-login takes effect immediately.

vibe-auth is the only bridge whose credential can go stale with no way back short of restarting the host process.

## Runtime probe (laptop worktree, `probe-vibe-cache.ts`, kept in the worktree)

Drives the real `vibeAuth({})` through `auth.apply` (the test suite's own harness shape in `packages/ai/test/provider/vibe-auth.test.ts`), with `MISTRAL_API_KEY` as the winning tier:

- env = key-A → `authorization: <redacted> A`
- env rotated to key-B, no invalidate → `authorization: <redacted> A` (stale)
- env removed entirely, no invalidate → `authorization: <redacted> A` (even sign-out / key removal never takes effect)
- after a manual `invalidate()` → `authorization: <redacted> B` (the mechanism works; it is simply never invoked)

## Why it matters

The vibe route's billing follows the KEY (the provider's own header comment in `vibe.ts`: the keyring sign-in key bills the Vibe plan budget; any other key bills its own). A key rotation, a revoked key, a re-run of `vibe --setup`, or removing a shadowing env key — all plausible on a long-lived serve process — leave the route either spending the wrong account's budget or 401ing on every request until someone restarts the process, with no diagnostic pointing at the stale cache. #1717's doctrine says auth must auto-renew for the direct providers; this bridge cannot even re-read.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A vibe credential that stops working is recoverable without a process restart: on a 401, the cached credential is invalidated, re-resolved, and the request retried once — the muse-direct/antigravity transport shape — OR the cache gains a bounded lifetime / per-request re-read like the sibling bridges. The chosen shape is recorded in the fix.
- [ ] `VibeAuth.invalidate()` has at least one real caller (or is removed in favour of the chosen mechanism); no dead recovery code remains.
- [ ] Tests pin the recovery: a rotated source key takes effect after the trigger (401 or expiry), and the pre-rotation key is not sent again. The caching behaviour is covered in `packages/ai/test/provider/vibe-auth.test.ts`, which today never mentions the cache or `invalidate`.
- [ ] Explicit-source calls (tests, embedding hosts) keep bypassing the process cache, as they do today.

Related: #1899 (the muse-direct cache's distinct defect — it ignores the credential source), #1717 (direct-provider doctrine: auth must auto-renew), #1653 (the vibe provider), #1809 (vibe-auth tier-shadow diagnostic).

labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai
labels.description: Package: ai (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

body:
## Problem

`connectWs` in `packages/ai/src/quota/cdp.ts` can hang forever during connection establishment. #1846 (for #1803) bounded the *request* phase — a per-request timeout in `send()` plus close/error settlement of pending requests — but the connect phase settles only from `ws.onopen` / `ws.onerror` / `ws.onclose`. An endpoint that accepts the TCP connection but never completes the WebSocket handshake (a wedged DevTools endpoint, a port answered by something that is not a WS server) fires none of the three, so the promise returned by `connectWs` never settles — regardless of the `requestTimeoutMs` argument, which only bounds requests sent *after* open.

`cdpPageFetch` awaits `connectWs(...)` directly (cdp.ts, in the `try` whose `finally` closes the client and any page this call created), so one stalled handshake hangs the whole quota read forever and the cleanup in that `finally` never runs — the page created for the read is leaked as well. This is the #1803 hang class surviving in the one phase #1846 did not bound.

## Evidence (verified this run, on main f2a11425d3)

Source: `connectWs` (packages/ai/src/quota/cdp.ts:87 ff.) creates `new WebSocket(wsUrl)` and resolves in `ws.onopen`, rejects in `ws.onerror`/`ws.onclose` when `!opened`; there is no timer anywhere in the connect phase. `CDP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS` / `requestTimeoutMs` is used only inside `send()`.

Probe (laptop worktree `probe-2026-11-06-creator-1535`, `probe-cdp-connect.ts`): a `node:net` server that accepts the connection and never speaks; `connectWs(wsUrl, 150)` called against it:

```
after 3000ms (requestTimeoutMs=150): settled=PENDING
```

Control: the existing `packages/ai/test/cdp.test.ts` modes (silent / close-on-request / reply / wedge-after-location) all settle — they exercise only the post-open request phase; no fake stalls the handshake itself.

## Why it matters

The meta quota provider reads through CDP (`cdpPageFetch`'s consumer in `providers/meta.ts`); a wedged local browser endpoint turns a quota read into a permanent hang of the calling command/session instead of the `cdp-unavailable:` classification every other CDP failure mode now produces — and leaks the DevTools page the call created.

## Acceptance criteria

- `connectWs` rejects within a bounded time when the socket never opens (the existing request bound, or a dedicated connect bound in the same spirit as this file's other bounds: 10s HTTP, 20s page-wait, 5s close).
- On a connect timeout the underlying socket is closed/abandoned so no half-open WebSocket lingers, and a late `onopen` cannot resolve a promise already rejected for timeout.
- `cdpPageFetch` against a handshake-stalling endpoint surfaces `cdp-unavailable:` and runs its cleanup (created page is closed), mirroring the wedge-after-location test.
- A regression test stalls the handshake (e.g. a raw TCP accept-and-hold server) and pins the bound; the existing cdp tests still pass and the ai package typechecks.

title: fix(ai): muse-direct key exchange reads its response unbounded — response.text() with no byte cap (new bounded-http gate site, not in #1724)

labels.name: task/small-fix

labels.name: app/ai

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The muse-direct key exchange buffers its whole response body with no byte cap. It has a deadline (15s `AbortSignal.timeout`) but no size bound — the one half of the bounded-by-default contract (#1127) the sibling claude-code exchange got in the #1862 fix, this exchange never got.

Site, on current main `e0199c6429`:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/muse-direct-auth.ts:151` — in `exchangeMintedKey`:
  ```ts
  const text = await response.text()
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`Muse key exchange failed: HTTP ${response.status}: ${text.slice(0, 200)}`)
  ```
  The full body is buffered before the 200-char slice for the error message, and before the JSON parse on the success path. The module's own header says the endpoint "returns a small JSON struct" — nothing enforces that.

Landed in `d6f0dcd27f` ("muse-direct: native Meta wire provider (#1825)", merged via PR #1872) — after #1724's bounded-http inventory, so the site has no disposition.

## Evidence

Gate, run on main `e0199c6429`:

```
$ bun run script/check-bounded-http.ts   # exit 1, 8 unlisted sites
Unlisted bounded-http candidate at packages/ai/src/providers/muse-direct-auth.ts:151:
  const text = await response.text()
```
The other 7 sites are exactly #1724's known set (cdp.ts ×5, turso.ts:204, quota/utils.ts:176) — this is the only new one. (numeric-boundaries still 3, proto-reads still 4 — both exactly #1724's sets, no other new drift.)

Runtime probe (laptop worktree `probe-2026-11-06-creator-1435` of origin/main, `probe-muse-exchange.ts`, fake `fetchFn` injected via the module's own `CredentialSources`):

- Success body of **3,145,800 bytes** (valid JSON, `api_key` present, ~3 MiB pad): **ACCEPTED** — `exchangeMintedKey` returned the minted key. Compare the in-package caps this blows past: `readQuotaJson`'s 1 MiB and the claude-code OAuth exchange's `OAUTH_TOKEN_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1024 * 1024` (`claude-code-auth.ts:75`).
- Error body of **5,000,000 bytes** (HTTP 500): fully buffered, then the thrown message uses only its first 200 chars (`msgLen: 236` total).
- Control (small valid body): key returned as expected.

## Why it matters

This exchange runs on the plan-backed Meta route's auth path, in-process, on every minted-key refresh (10-minute cache). A compromised, misconfigured, or MITM'd endpoint (or a future server change) can make every session process buffer an arbitrarily large body in memory before any check fires — the exact failure the bounded-http gate and #1127's deadline-and-cap contract exist to prevent. The claude-code exchange in the same package was filed and fixed for the same shape (#1862); leaving the newer muse-direct exchange unbounded re-opens it.

## Acceptance criteria

- `exchangeMintedKey` reads the response through a byte cap (in-package precedent: 1 MiB, as in `claude-code-auth.ts` via `readBoundedResponseText` from `@opencode/util/http-body`); an over-cap body — success or error — fails with a named, token-free error instead of being buffered whole.
- `bun run script/check-bounded-http.ts` drops to exactly #1724's 7 sites (this site bounded at the site, not allowlist-only).
- Tests in `packages/ai/test/provider/muse-direct.test.ts` pin both over-cap cases (oversized success body, oversized error body); the existing muse-direct suite still passes and the ai package typechecks.

body:
## Finding (fork side)

Cross-session messaging **works** — DM + wake delivery, and a receiver blocked in unread-with-wait gets the reply inside its turn — but it is reachable only through mcpx code mode, and **nothing in the fork's prompt or tool surface points at it**. A session must already know (or luck into) `mcpx_discover` for the `comms` namespace.

## Workshop evidence

Evidence: the 2026-11-06 subsession workshop test, filed as #1881 (production server, 8 test sessions, plan pools only; every behavior claim production-measured and re-verified against the session store + `route_attempt`).

#1881 Q4 + Q7.4: the sender's first `mcpx_discover` call errored before the retry succeeded; the `msg`/`topics`/`sessions` tool descriptions in `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/messaging.ts` are thorough — but sessions reach messaging through code mode, where discoverability is the weak link.

(The fleet-side doc gap — developing-today/code's `.opencode/instructions/mcpx.md` omitting `comms` from its namespace table — is handled in the code repo separately; this issue is only about fork-side discoverability.)

## Desired

- The base-prompt delegation/messaging block (filed separately) names `comms` as the messaging path.
- Consider registering `msg` as a **plain tool** as well as a code-mode projection, so messaging does not depend on code-mode discovery succeeding.
- `mcpx_discover` failure modes for a valid namespace should not require a blind retry (error text should name valid namespaces or the discovery call should be reliable).

## Acceptance sketch

- A fresh session, from its prompt + tool list alone, can find and use cross-session messaging without prior knowledge of the `comms` namespace.

## Acceptance criteria

- A session with no prior knowledge can discover cross-session messaging (`comms`) from the fork's own prompt or tool surface (e.g. via `mcpx_discover` guidance or a prompt mention), without external documentation.
- The `msg`/`topics`/`sessions` entry points are named where a session naturally looks for them.
- No behavior change to messaging delivery itself.

title: feat: serving leaf is invisible to the session — expose the resolved provider/model per step

labels.name: kind/feature

body:
## Finding

A session's declared model **ref never drifts**, but the **serving leaf varies per step** — and the session cannot observe which leaf served it. Asked "which model are you on", a session can only answer from its route ref or guess.

## Workshop evidence

Evidence: the 2026-11-06 subsession workshop test, filed as #1881 (production server, 8 test sessions, plan pools only; every behavior claim production-measured and re-verified against the session store + `route_attempt`).

#1881 Q3, from `route_attempt`:

- The messaging pair's turns ran `openai.main/gpt-6-luna#xhigh` for the tool steps and `vibe-direct/mistral-small-latest#high` for the closing step — all under the single session ref `opencode-route/workhorse`.
- After an API model switch to the `speed` route, the first step hit `opencode-go.drewrypope/muse-spark-1.3-contributor#xhigh` → **429** (pool walled) and failed over to `vibe-direct/mistral-small-latest#high`, success — the failover was invisible from inside the session.

## Why it matters

- **Debugging:** leaf-level behavior differs (prompt policy differs by family — filed separately; tool-call quirks differ by provider). Without leaf identity, session behavior is not reproducible or explainable after the fact from inside the session.
- **Correctness of self-reports:** sessions asked about their own model currently confabulate or answer with the route ref.

## Desired

- Expose the resolved provider/model (leaf) for the current/last step somewhere a session can see: e.g. a field in its context/status surface, or in the `sessions`/self tool output — including failover events (attempted leaf → served leaf).
- Historical per-step leaf data already exists in `route_attempt`; this is about an in-session surface, not new telemetry.

## Acceptance sketch

- A session can state, from a sanctioned surface, which leaf served its last step and whether a failover occurred.
- No change to routing behavior itself.

## Acceptance criteria

- A session can observe, per step or on request, which provider/model leaf actually served it (e.g. via session info or a route_attempt-backed readout).
- The readout distinguishes the declared route ref from the serving leaf, including after an API model switch.
- No change to routing behavior itself.

body:
## Finding

The `subagent` tool description (`packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts`) is the best text in the system — nesting, background, stop policies, and continuation by sessionID are all there. The workshop found it omits four things a launching session needs:

1. **Inheritance:** children inherit the parent's directory, and (without a `model` argument) the parent's model/route. Observed in all 5 workshop children; stated nowhere in the result or description.
2. **Depth cap:** nesting is capped (`experimental.subagent_depth`, default 5) — the description alludes to a limit via governance wording but the launching session can't see the number or its remaining depth.
3. **Background completion semantics:** a `background=true` child's completion (or error) is delivered to the parent unprompted as a synthetic turn — the parent does not need to poll. (Errors work the same way: the child reports its error verbatim as its result.)
4. **Question-stall warning:** a child's `question` call blocks the foreground `subagent` call until an external actor answers — no warning exists (see the very-high-priority stall bug, filed alongside).

## Evidence

Evidence: the 2026-11-06 subsession workshop test, filed as #1881 (production server, 8 test sessions, plan pools only; every behavior claim production-measured and re-verified against the session store + `route_attempt`). — #1881 Q1–Q3, Q6.

## Desired / acceptance

- Description updated with all four points, in the same register as the existing text.
- The launch result (or description) states the effective directory + model/route the child actually got, so intent is confirmed back instead of assumed.

## Acceptance criteria

- The `subagent` tool description states: children inherit the parent's directory and (absent a `model` argument) its model/route; the nesting depth cap and the launching session's remaining depth; background completion/error delivery semantics (synthetic turn, no polling); and the detached-context `question` warning.
- All four points match workshop-observed behavior.
- Description-only change in `packages/core/src/tool/plugin/subagent.ts`.

title: fix(ai): codex quota spend_control label publishes used/limit raw — "150 / 100 used" at a clamped 100%, "-5 / 100 used", "5 / 0 used"

body:
## Defect

In `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/codex.ts` (spend-control block, lines 158–173 on main `e0199c6429`), the `credits` window's percent and its label are derived from different dispositions of the same figures:

- Line 164: `usedPercent = clampPercent(toNumber(spendLimit.used_percent))` — clamped into [0, 100].
- Lines 162–163: `valueLabel = \`${used.toFixed(0)} / ${limit.toFixed(0)} used\`` — `used` and `limit` published **raw**, with no range check on either.

So an out-of-range payload produces a window whose percent and label contradict each other — the exact failure the window-contract rule 5 disposition exists to prevent (#1821, command-code: percent and label must derive from one clamped figure; same defect class as #1879, opendesign remaining).

## Evidence — probe against the real provider

Laptop probe `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-codex-spend/probe.ts` drives the real `codex` provider's `fetchQuota` with a stubbed `fetchImpl` returning crafted `wham/usage` payloads (same harness shape as the #1762 tests in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts`), on main `e0199c6429`:

| payload `spend_control.individual_limit` | published `credits` window |
| --- | --- |
| `{used: 40, limit: 100, used_percent: 40}` (control) | `usedPercent: 40`, label `"40 / 100 used"` |
| `{used: 150, limit: 100, used_percent: 150}` | `usedPercent: 100` (clamped), label `"150 / 100 used"` |
| `{used: -5, limit: 100, used_percent: -5}` | `usedPercent: 0` (clamped), label `"-5 / 100 used"` |
| `{used: 5, limit: 0}` (no percent) | `usedPercent: null`, label `"5 / 0 used"` |
| `{used: 150, limit: 100}` (no percent) | `usedPercent: null`, label `"150 / 100 used"` |

The label-only cases matter most: when `used_percent` is absent, the raw label is the *only* figure the window publishes, so nothing downstream can detect the contradiction.

## Why it matters

The `opencode quota` surface renders `valueLabel` verbatim. Impossible figures ("150 / 100 used", "-5 / 100 used", "5 / 0 used") erode trust in the whole quota readout, and an over-limit spend state — real information, cf. the #1744 annotation precedent — is presented as nonsense instead of being named. Sibling parsers have been hardened against this exact shape one by one (#1821 command-code, #1879 opendesign); codex's spend-control block is the remaining instance of the pattern in the quota providers.

## Acceptance criteria

- Percent and `valueLabel` for the spend-control `credits` window derive from one consistent disposition of `used`/`limit` — they can never contradict (the #1821 rule-5 shape).
- A negative `used` never renders as a negative figure in the label.
- `limit <= 0` never renders as a denominator (`"5 / 0 used"`); the disposition (drop the label, drop the window, or annotate) is chosen in the fix and pinned by a test.
- Over-limit `used` follows an explicit disposition — the #1744 annotation shape or a clamped label — chosen in the fix and pinned by a test.
- Tests in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pin the negative, over-limit, zero-limit, and in-range control cases for the codex spend-control window; the existing quota suite still passes.

title: fix(ai): readQuotaJson's 1 MiB cap is measured in UTF-16 code units, not bytes — a 1.2 MB multi-byte payload passes the "bytes" cap

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai

labels.name: effort/xs
labels.description: Trivial: expected under 30 minutes of work

body:
# fix(ai): readQuotaJson's 1 MiB cap is measured in UTF-16 code units, not bytes — a 1.2 MB multi-byte payload passes the "bytes" cap

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `90453b467f` (merge of PR #1874), in a laptop worktree (`~/git/probe-2026-11-06-creator-1235`, kept). Gates this run: `check:workflows`, `check:gates`, `check:doc-env-vars` GREEN; `check:bounded-http` 7 / `check:numeric-boundaries` 3 / `check:proto-reads` 4 RED = exactly #1724's set — no new drift.

## The defect

`packages/ai/src/quota/utils.ts:173-178` — the shared bounded reader every quota provider uses:

```ts
export const QUOTA_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024

export const readQuotaJson = async (response: Response): Promise<JsonValue> => {
  const text = await response.text()
  if (text.length > QUOTA_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES) {
    throw new Error(`Quota response exceeded ${QUOTA_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES} bytes`)
  }
```

The constant, the doc comment above it ("The most a quota provider answer may weigh"), and the error message all denominate the cap in **bytes**. The check measures `text.length` — the number of **UTF-16 code units** in the decoded string. For ASCII the two coincide; for multi-byte UTF-8 content they diverge by up to ~3× (a BMP character like `€` or CJK is 1 code unit but 3 UTF-8 bytes; astral characters are 2 code units but 4 bytes). A hostile or misconfigured quota endpoint — exactly the actor the comment says the cap exists for — can return a body roughly 3× the stated cap and pass.

## Runtime probe (laptop worktree, `probe-quota-caps.ts`, kept in the worktree)

Against the real `readQuotaJson` imported from main:

- **Multi-byte:** a valid JSON string payload of 400,002 characters / **1,200,002 UTF-8 bytes** (`"€" × 400,000`) — over the 1,048,576-byte cap — was **ACCEPTED** and returned in full.
- **ASCII control:** a 1,100,002-character / 1,100,002-byte payload was **REJECTED** with `Quota response exceeded 1048576 bytes`.

So the cap fires or not depending on the payload's alphabet, not its size in bytes.

## Why it matters

`readQuotaJson` is the one bounded reader the quota subsystem (#1127's bounded-by-default contract) relies on — the same reader #1862 pointed the claude-code sign-in exchange at. Its cap is a stated invariant ("cannot grow memory inside the deadline"); an enforcement that under-counts by up to 3× for non-ASCII bodies makes the invariant false and the error message a lie. Quota payloads are small per-account JSON, so legitimate responses are nowhere near the cap in either unit — byte-accurate enforcement changes nothing for conforming endpoints.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The cap is enforced on the body's UTF-8 **byte** length (e.g. `TextEncoder`), so a >1 MiB body is rejected regardless of its characters, and the error message stays accurate.
- [ ] A test pins both directions: an ASCII body just over 1 MiB rejected (existing behavior), and a multi-byte body whose character count is under 1 MiB but whose byte count is over 1 MiB rejected.
- [ ] A multi-byte body under the cap in bytes still parses normally (no false rejections of legitimate non-ASCII payloads).
- [ ] The quota test suite (`packages/ai/test/quota*`) passes and `bun run check:bounded-http` still lists exactly #1724's 7 sites for `quota/utils.ts` (this fix changes the check inside the reader, not its disposition).

title: fix(ai): claude-code sign-in callback caches its first failure — one bad paste kills the whole sign-in attempt and a retry can never succeed

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Something isn't working (prefixed form of the classic bug label)

labels.name: task/small-fix
labels.description: Queue packet kind: bounded fix with reproduction and targeted tests

labels.name: source/creator
labels.description: Filed by the new-issue-creator job

labels.name: priority/normal
labels.description: Ordinary priority (the default)

labels.name: app/ai
labels.description: Package: ai (pkgs/ or apps/ in this repo)

labels.name: effort/s
labels.description: Small: expected under 2 hours of work

body:
## Problem

The claude-code in-provider sign-in (#1852) can never recover from a failed paste. `beginClaudeCodeSignIn`'s callback memoizes its first attempt forever:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/claude-code-auth.ts:347-351` — `callback: (pasted) => { inflight ??= exchangeAndPersist(pasted); return inflight }`. The memoized promise is never cleared, on success or on failure.

Every failure mode of `exchangeAndPersist` is therefore terminal for the whole sign-in attempt, and a retry call ignores its new argument entirely and returns the original rejection:

- a malformed/blank paste (`claude-code-auth.ts`, "Malformed sign-in code") — no token exchange has even happened, the authorization code is unconsumed;
- a state mismatch (user pasted the code from an earlier attempt);
- a failed token exchange (HTTP error, timeout, oversized/token-less body, credential-write failure).

To try again the user must abandon the attempt, begin a brand-new sign-in (new PKCE verifier + state), reopen the authorize URL, and re-approve in the browser — because the verifier/state pair that the pasted code was issued for belongs to the dead attempt.

## Evidence (verified this run on origin/main 42f00d1b96)

Probe `probe-signin-retry.ts` in laptop worktree `probe-2026-11-06-creator-1135` (real `beginClaudeCodeSignIn`, stubbed fetch/store):

- Case 1: `callback("   ")` rejects "Malformed sign-in code" with **0 fetch calls**; a following `callback("<valid code>#<correct state>")` rejects with the *same* malformed error, still **0 fetch calls**.
- Case 2: `callback("auth-code-1#wrong-state")` rejects "state mismatch" (0 fetches); retry with the correct state rejects with the same mismatch error, still 0 fetches.
- Case 3: first exchange returns HTTP 400; retry with a *new* code (fetch stub would now succeed) rejects with the cached HTTP 400 error; fetch count stays 1.
- Control: a fresh sign-in with a valid first paste succeeds (1 fetch).

The sibling auth bridges in the same directory use the opposite, retry-safe pattern — the inflight promise is shared only while it is running and cleared when it settles:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/antigravity-auth.ts` `loadToken()`: `finally { inflight = undefined }`.
- `packages/ai/src/providers/vibe-auth.ts` `loadApiKey()`: `finally { inflight = undefined }`.

The existing test suite works around the defect: in `packages/ai/test/provider/claude-code-auth.test.ts` ("a malformed paste and a state mismatch fail named, with no exchange"), the second failure case is exercised on a *second* `beginClaudeCodeSignIn(...)` object instead of retrying the first one. The concurrent-callback test ("concurrent callbacks run exactly one token exchange") pins the legitimate purpose of the memoization — deduplicating simultaneous calls — which a failure-clearing fix preserves.

## Why it matters

Sign-in is the recovery path for the claude-code provider (#1852, and the loud-expiry failure in #1818's world): the user is already in a broken state when they reach it, and the paste step is the most error-prone part (the hosted page's `code#state` value is long and easy to paste partially or from the wrong attempt). One typo currently converts a recoverable paste error into a full restart of the OAuth flow.

## Acceptance criteria

- After a callback rejects (malformed paste, state mismatch, exchange HTTP/network failure, token-less body, or credential-write failure), calling the same sign-in's callback again with a new paste runs a fresh exchange attempt and can succeed — same authorize URL / PKCE / state, no new `beginClaudeCodeSignIn` needed.
- Concurrent callbacks still share exactly one token exchange (existing test stays green).
- A successful callback does not re-exchange on a later call (the authorization code is single-use; the persisted credential is the result).
- New tests pin retry-after-failure for at least the no-exchange failures (malformed / state mismatch) and one exchange failure; the full `claude-code-auth.test.ts` suite passes and the `ai` package typecheck is clean.

## Finding

# fix(ai): claude-code sign-in token exchange is unbounded — no deadline on the fetch, `response.json()` with no byte cap (new bounded-http gate site, not in #1724)

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `b0b56786682daf584f5216e12df0baaef65348ca`, in a laptop worktree (`~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-creator-1035`, kept), gates run twice with identical results.

## The gate drift

`bun run check:bounded-http` now reports **8** unlisted candidates, not the 7 of #1724's set. The new site:

- `packages/ai/src/providers/claude-code-auth.ts:301` — `const data: unknown = await response.json().catch(() => undefined)`

The other 7 (cdp.ts ×5, turso.ts:204, quota/utils.ts:176) are exactly #1724's bounded-http set at shifted lines. `check:numeric-boundaries` (3) and `check:proto-reads` (4) are unchanged subsets of #1724's set; `check:workflows`, `check:gates`, and `check:doc-env-vars` are green.

The site landed in `32c52e7c67` — `feat(ai): in-provider OAuth sign-in initiation for claude-code (#1852)`, merged via PR #1861 — after #1724's inventory was taken, so it has no disposition anywhere. (Same landing pattern as #1790 and #1841: a feature lands, a gate gains a site, nobody dispositions it.)

## The site is substantively unbounded, not disposition-class

Unlike the #1790/#1841 sites (a local file read; a clamped numeric index), this one is a real remote call with neither bound the #1127 contract requires:

- **No deadline.** `exchangeAndPersist` (claude-code-auth.ts:283-297) calls `(sources.fetchFn ?? fetch)(OAUTH_TOKEN_URL, { method, headers, body })` with **no `signal` at all** — no `AbortSignal.timeout`, no caller signal. Every quota provider in the same package uses `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`; the antigravity token refresh got exactly this fix in #1469.
- **No byte cap.** The success body is read with unbounded `response.json()` at :301. The package's own bounded reader (`readQuotaJson`, quota/utils.ts:175) caps at 1 MiB (`QUOTA_RESPONSE_MAX_BYTES`).

### Runtime probe (laptop worktree, `probe-signin-unbounded.ts`, kept in the worktree)

Injected via the module's own `fetchFn` test seam:

- **PROBE1** — a token endpoint that never replies: the sign-in `callback(...)` promise was **still unsettled after 2,500 ms**, and the captured fetch init shows `signal: undefined`. By source inspection there is nothing that would ever settle it — a stalled `https://platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token` hangs the sign-in flow forever.
- **PROBE2** — a 3,145,763-byte token response (`access_token` + a 3 MiB pad field): the callback **succeeded** and returned the token — the body was read and parsed with no cap, 3× the package's own 1 MiB quota cap.

## Why it matters

This is the user-facing claude-code sign-in path (#1852): a user pastes their `code#state`, the UI waits on this exchange, and a slow/stalled token endpoint (or a hostile/MITM'd response body within the deadline-free window) hangs sign-in indefinitely with no error and no recovery short of killing the app. It also re-opens the gate-drift window #1724 describes: while `check:bounded-http` is red for an undispositioned site, the gate cannot cleanly catch the *next* new unbounded call.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The token-exchange fetch carries a deadline (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)`, matching the package's quota providers, or a justified value), and a fetch that never replies settles as a named `ClaudeCodeSignInError` instead of hanging.
- [ ] The success body is read through a bounded reader with an explicit byte cap (the package's `readQuotaJson` or an equivalent), and an over-cap body fails named rather than being parsed.
- [ ] Error behavior is preserved for the existing cases: non-OK status still fails named with the HTTP status and persists nothing; a non-JSON or token-less success body still fails with the "no access token" error (or an equally named one).
- [ ] `bun run check:bounded-http` on main no longer lists claude-code-auth.ts (back to #1724's 7 sites, or fewer if #1724 lands first) — no bare allowlist disposition for this site; it is bounded at the site.
- [ ] New tests pin both bounds via the `fetchFn` seam (never-replying endpoint settles with the deadline error; over-cap body rejected), and the existing `claude-code-auth.test.ts` sign-in suite still passes.

title: Plugin/provider ownership hardening: conflicting-package settings folding + unscoped model.request baseURL rewrites

labels.name: kind/security
labels.description: Security issue or security hardening

labels.name: meta/enriched
labels.description: Intake review done: acceptance criteria, links, and normalized labels added

body:
## Summary

A stale external plugin silently hijacked a config-seated provider and produced days of misleading `404 Not Found` failures against Anthropic. Two hardening gaps made it possible:

1. **Package-conflict settings folding.** The plugin `@openchamber/opencode-claude@1.3.8` declares provider settings for `claude-code` (including a `baseURL` pointing at its own loopback proxy). Those settings were folded into the config-seated native `claude-code` provider even though the plugin's declared `package` is not the package the config seats for that provider. A plugin whose declared `package` conflicts with the config-seated package for the same provider should not have its settings folded into that provider.
2. **Unscoped `model.request` hook ownership.** The same plugin registers a `session.model.request` hook that rewrites the `baseURL` of every claude-code request to its loopback proxy. Provider-scoped request hooks need an ownership rule: a hook may retarget a provider's requests only if it owns that provider (declared and seated as its package), or the rewrite must be surfaced (warned/logged) rather than silent.

## Root-cause evidence (2026-11-06, production laptop)

- Plugin: `@openchamber/opencode-claude@1.3.8`, present in the global config `plugins` array.
- Mechanism: its `session.model.request` hook rewrites every claude-code request baseURL to an ephemeral loopback proxy it starts; the native Anthropic provider then composes `POST http://127.0.0.1:<proxy-port>/v1/v1/messages`, and the proxy answers with its own plain-text `404 Not Found` (not Anthropic's JSON error shape — an early tell that the request never left the machine; route-attempt latency was ~2.7 ms loopback).
- Proven by recording-listener test: with a listener configured as the provider baseURL, the listener received nothing while sessions still 404'd in ~5 ms — the hook overrode the configured baseURL.
- Affected builds: fork `22c0a6d` (previous production) and fork main `5e9b135f` identically — the defect is external to the binary; the fork's provider composition is correct (bare origin + `/v1/messages`).
- Eliminated during diagnosis: credential/auth (CLI `claude -p` OK; credential subscriptionType "max", tokens healthy), config baseURL (no baseURL set in either config layer), the double-`/v1` endpoint bug (fixed earlier, `d66b463f`, predates both builds), server env overrides, stale process state.
- Fix: removal of the plugin entry from the global config. Production went GREEN immediately on the unmodified main build (both probe legs return PROBEOK; `route_attempt` outcome success; ~1.25 s real Anthropic round trips). Durable config fix: developing-today/code PR #6538 (merge `9c06d0c8a4e20629dbcd883f9f8338f54daed1d5`).

## Suggested acceptance

- A plugin whose declared `package` differs from the config-seated package for a provider it names: its provider settings are ignored (or refused with a loud startup warning), never folded in.
- A `model.request` hook that changes a provider's baseURL (or other routing fields) for a provider the plugin does not own is blocked or at minimum logged at warn level with plugin id + provider id.
- Regression test: conflicting-package plugin present in config; assert provider settings remain the config-seated ones and requests keep the provider's own baseURL.

Related: #1806 (session-cascade context where the 404s surfaced), #1825 (wire-only audit — this plugin is also how a binary-era proxy stayed load-bearing after decommission).

## Acceptance criteria
- Settings folding respects package ownership: a plugin whose declared package conflicts with the config-seated package for a provider does not have its settings folded into that provider (a regression test seats a native provider, loads a conflicting-package plugin declaring settings for it, and asserts the provider's effective settings are unchanged).
- Request-hook ownership is enforced or surfaced: a session.model.request hook from a plugin that does not own the targeted provider cannot silently retarget that provider's requests — the rewrite is refused, or at minimum warned/logged with the plugin and provider named.
- The diagnosed hijack shape is covered end-to-end in tests: with the conflicting plugin present, a claude-code request still goes to the configured/native baseURL (recording-listener style assertion, mirroring the root-cause probe).
- Legitimate plugins that DO own their provider keep working: a plugin seated as its provider's package can still fold settings and retarget its own provider's requests (no regression for the owned case).

title: fix(ai): claude quota credentialExpiresAt publishes 1969/1970 dates for non-positive expiresAt — normalizeTimestamp lacks toTimestamp's guard

body:
## Problem

The shared quota helper `normalizeTimestamp` (`packages/ai/src/quota/utils.ts:55-58`) has no non-positive guard — the exact defect #1845 fixed in its sibling `toTimestamp` (utils.ts:36-53: "A non-positive reset is null, never a 1969/1970 date"). `normalizeTimestamp` is used only for credential expiry, at both Claude credential sources:

- `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/claude.ts:80` — `expiresAt: normalizeTimestamp(oauth?.expiresAt)` (Claude Code credentials file / Keychain blob)
- `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/claude.ts:102` — `expiresAt: normalizeTimestamp(entry?.expires)` (OpenCode stored credential)

`claude.ts:118-123` (`withMetadata`) then publishes any non-null value as an ISO string: `credentialExpiresAt: new Date(credential.expiresAt).toISOString()`. So a non-positive `expiresAt` on either source is published as a real 1969/1970 credential expiry instead of being treated as absent:

- Numeric `0` returns `0` (not null) → `credentialExpiresAt: "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"`.
- A negative seconds spelling (`-5000`) returns `-5000000` → `"1969-12-31T22:36:40.000Z"`.
- A negative millisecond spelling is even scaled a second time (`-1893456000000` → `-1893456000000000`), since the `< 1e12` seconds test has no sign check.

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `a977b979cb`)

Probe: `probe-claude-expires.ts` in laptop worktree `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-creator-0935`, run with bun against the real modules:

- `normalizeTimestamp(-5000)` → `-5000000`; `normalizeTimestamp(0)` → `0`; `normalizeTimestamp(-1893456000000)` → `-1893456000000000`; controls `normalizeTimestamp(1893456000)` → `1893456000000` and `normalizeTimestamp(1893456000000)` → `1893456000000`.
- `findClaudeCredential` with fixture homes (`.claude/.credentials.json`): `expiresAt: 0` → expiresAt `0`, which `withMetadata` renders as `credentialExpiresAt "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"`; `expiresAt: -5000` → `-5000000` → `"1969-12-31T22:36:40.000Z"`; seconds and ms spellings of 2030-01-01 both render correctly.

No test pins this: `grep normalizeTimestamp|credentialExpiresAt` in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` returns nothing.

Dedup: #1845 covered `toTimestamp` (window `resetAt` fields) only; #1855 covered meta's raw `*1000` portal resets. Neither touches `normalizeTimestamp` or `credentialExpiresAt`.

## Why it matters

Per the module header (claude.ts:38-42, code#6125), the gatherer stamps quota entries from `credentialExpiresAt` instead of doing a side read. A published 1969/1970 expiry reads as a credential that expired over five decades ago — indistinguishable from a genuinely long-expired token — while the honest answer for a non-positive wire value is "expiry unknown" (field omitted, as `withMetadata` already does for null). This is the same payload-anomaly class #1821/#1845/#1855 keep out of published quota state; `normalizeTimestamp` is the remaining unguarded converter in the shared utils.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `normalizeTimestamp` returns `null` for non-positive inputs in both spellings (seconds and milliseconds, including numeric `0`); valid positive seconds/ms timestamps convert exactly as before.
- [ ] Neither Claude credential source can publish a 1969/1970 `credentialExpiresAt`; a non-positive `expiresAt` omits the field (the existing null path in `withMetadata`).
- [ ] Cases in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pin the non-positive shapes for `normalizeTimestamp` (or for `findClaudeCredential` with a fixture credentials file), including the epoch-zero spelling.
- [ ] Existing quota tests still pass and `packages/ai` typecheck is clean.

body:
# fix(ai): meta quota `parseSubscriptionQuota` publishes non-positive portal resets as 1969 dates — it bypasses the shared `toTimestamp` guard

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `5e9b135ffc` in a laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-06-creator-0835`), calling the exported pure parser `parseSubscriptionQuota` directly (probe `probe-meta-reset.ts`, kept in that worktree).

## Evidence

`packages/ai/src/quota/providers/meta.ts:99,104`:

```ts
resetAt: windowReset === null ? null : windowReset * 1000,
resetAt: weeklyReset === null ? null : weeklyReset * 1000,
```

The portal resets (`window_resets_at` / `weekly_resets_at`, read via `toNumber` at meta.ts:77-78) are multiplied raw, with no positivity check. This is the only reset construction in the quota providers that does not go through a guard: the shared converter `toTimestamp` (utils.ts) returns null for non-positive timestamps in both spellings (#1845, which fixed this exact 1969/1970 publication for every provider parsing resets *through* the converter — its call-site list covered meta.ts's other sites at the key endpoint, not this parser), command-code carries its own explicit `resetAt <= 0 ? null` guard (#1821), and groq's reset is a non-negative duration (#1793).

Probe results (control: window 50/100, weekly 25/100, duration 18000, resets 1893456000 / 1894060800):

- control → `5h.resetAt: 1893456000000`, `weekly.resetAt: 1894060800000` (correct)
- `window_resets_at: "-5000"` → `5h` publishes **`resetAt: -5000000`**, `resetAtFormatted: "Wed, Dec 31, 4:36 PM"` (1969-12-31), `resetAfterSeconds: 0` — a fabricated "resets now" on a 1969 date
- `window_resets_at: "0"` → `resetAt: 0`, formatted as the 1969/1970 epoch date
- `weekly_resets_at: "-86400"` → `weekly` publishes **`resetAt: -86400000`**, formatted "Tue, Dec 30, 6:00 PM" (1969-12-30)
- both resets absent → `resetAt: null` on both windows (correct — the parser's own comment at meta.ts:81-85 states the absent-reset-is-null disposition, and the shared probe matrix pins it)

The window contract in `packages/ai/src/quota/types.ts` rule 3: "Missing is null, and nulls the field... An absent reset is an honest null `resetAt` on the window" — and the types.ts inventory's shared-converter note states the #1845 disposition applies to "every provider parsing resets through the shared converter, so no consumer can publish a 1969/1970 resetAt". This parser is the remaining exception: a non-positive reset is not missing data, but it is equally not a real reset instant, and publishing it (plus the derived `resetAfterSeconds: 0`) is the same fabricated figure #1845/#1821 removed everywhere else.

Distinct from the open meta issues: #1849 covers this parser's zero/negative *limits* (whole-payload null gate, fabricated 0%); #1777 covers its rolling/weekly key collision. Neither touches the reset fields.

## Why it matters

The Meta pool is a sole-door pool for its models and the portal read is the system of record for its percentages; its quota row drives placement/rotation. A 1969 `resetAt` with `resetAfterSeconds: 0` tells consumers the window resets immediately, forever — the silent wrong-quota state the contract was written to stop, surviving in the one parser that bypasses the shared converter.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A zero or negative `window_resets_at` / `weekly_resets_at` publishes that window with `resetAt: null` (and null derived formatted/after fields), exactly like an absent reset; the window's figures still publish.
- [ ] Positive resets (seconds spelling) convert exactly as today; the unchanged control is pinned.
- [ ] `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pins: negative window reset, zero window reset, negative weekly reset, and the unchanged control.
- [ ] The fix routes through (or matches) the shared `toTimestamp` disposition, with the parser comment / types.ts inventory updated if the wording changes.

body:
## Gap: claude-code provider cannot initiate a sign-in — recovery still requires the `claude` binary

**Provider:** `packages/ai/src/providers/claude-code-auth.ts` (#6117 native wire emulation). Sibling of #1818 (renewal); the full-lifecycle design is recorded in a design comment on #1818 (2026-11-06).

### The gap
#1818's routed fix (queue task 10996) covers renewal of an existing login: refresh + mandatory atomic write-back. It does not cover **initiation**. Today, with no credential file — or after the stored refresh token is invalidated (`invalid_grant`) — the provider's only recovery path is a human running the real `claude` CLI interactively:

- `claude-code-auth.ts:50-52` — `NOT_SIGNED_IN_MESSAGE`: "Run `claude` once and complete the claude.ai sign-in."
- `claude-code-auth.ts:54-58` — `expiredMessage` gives the same instruction for renewal failures.
- `CredentialSources` (`:68-74`) has a `readFile` seam only — there is no write path, no authorize URL builder, no PKCE, no code exchange anywhere in `packages/ai` for this provider, and `packages/core/src/plugin/provider/` has no claude-code entry to host a login flow.

On 2026-11-06 this dependency turned a burned refresh token into a fleet outage: the laptop's login was destroyed by fleet action, and restoring it required driving the CLI binary's sign-in by hand. Drew's directive (2026-11-06): this must be the last time a binary command is run for a provider.

### The flow to implement (all constants verified — #1818 triage + public implementations of the same client)
- OAuth client (public id): `9d1c250a-e61b-44d9-88ed-5944d1962f5e`
- Authorize: `https://claude.ai/oauth/authorize` — `code=true`, `response_type=code`, PKCE S256, `state`, `redirect_uri=https://console.anthropic.com/oauth/code/callback` (Anthropic's **hosted** code page: the CLI's flow has no localhost listener; the page displays `code#state` for paste-back)
- Token endpoint: `POST https://platform.claude.com/v1/oauth/token`, form-encoded, snake_case response
- Persistence: the shared CLI file `~/.claude/.credentials.json` stays canonical — write the full `claudeAiOauth` blob atomically (temp + rename, 0600, unrelated fields preserved), sharing one atomic-write helper with task 10996

### Shape (mirrors the fork's existing authorize flows)
A claude-code sign-in surface in `packages/core` (plugin provider / Integration method, mirroring `plugin/provider/chatgpt.ts` `authorize()` → `{url, instructions, callback}`), with the paste-code variant as primary: it works when the browser is on any device, and no browser needs to stay open — sign-in is an on-demand action, as with chatgpt (loopback callback) and github-copilot (device code). Provider error messages are updated to name this in-product sign-in instead of the `claude` binary.

### Acceptance criteria
- With no credential file and the `claude` binary absent from PATH, the in-product sign-in completes end-to-end and the provider serves a request.
- Exchange-succeeds/write-fails: tokens discarded, named error, no file created/modified, no in-memory-only credential.
- Concurrent sign-in/refresh attempts produce exactly one token-endpoint exchange.
- Interop both directions: provider sign-in → real CLI reads signed-in from the file; CLI sign-in → provider serves (regression check).
- No provider message instructs running `claude`; tokens never logged; the `claude` quota provider still resolves the credential after a provider-managed sign-in.

body:
# fix(ai): meta quota `parseSubscriptionQuota` drops BOTH windows on a zero limit in either, and publishes a fabricated 0% window on a negative limit

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `67b276850c6c` in a laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-06-creator-0735`), calling the exported pure parser `parseSubscriptionQuota` directly (probe `probe1.ts`, kept in that worktree).

## Evidence

`packages/ai/src/quota/providers/meta.ts:84-90`:

```ts
if (
  windowUsed === null || windowLimit === null || weeklyUsed === null || weeklyLimit === null ||
  windowLimit === 0 || weeklyLimit === 0
) {
  return null
}
```

The zero-limit check is whole-payload, and negative limits are not checked at all. Probe results (control: window 50/100, weekly 25/100, duration 18000):

- control → `{5h: 50%, weekly: 25%}` (correct)
- `window_weighted_limit: "0"` (weekly still 25/100) → **`null`** — the valid weekly window is discarded
- `weekly_weighted_limit: "0"` (window still 50/100) → **`null`** — the valid 5h window is discarded
- `window_weighted_limit: "-100"` (used 50) → publishes `5h` at **`usedPercent: 0`, `remainingPercent: 100`** — a fabricated full-headroom window from a negative limit
- `weekly_weighted_limit: "-100"` (weekly used 50) → publishes `weekly` at **0% used / 100% remaining**, same fabrication

The window contract in `packages/ai/src/quota/types.ts` rule 4 is per-window: "an empty/all-null/**zero-limit** window-shaped object publishes **no window**" — it does not null the sibling window. The per-window precedents are #1799 (openrouter: zero/negative limit publishes no window, other data stands) and #1750 (opendesign: `limit <= 0` skips only that window). Rule 5 also bars the negative-limit outcome: a 0%-used window is a figure the payload never contained.

Caller impact: `meta.ts` fetch path treats a `null` parse as portal failure class `no-data` and falls through to the key-endpoint cross-check — so one zero limit on the portal (the system of record for percentages) silently demotes the whole read, and a negative limit poisons it with invented headroom instead.

## Why it matters

The Meta pool is a sole-door pool for its models; its quota row drives placement/rotation. Losing a valid window because its sibling hit a zero limit, or reporting 100% remaining on a negative limit, are exactly the silent wrong-quota states the window contract was written to stop.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A zero or negative limit drops only that window; the other window still publishes with its real figures. The parse returns `null` only when neither window survives.
- [ ] No window is ever published with a percent derived from a zero/negative limit (no clamped 0% fabrication).
- [ ] `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pins: window-zero/weekly-valid, weekly-zero/window-valid, a negative-limit case, both-zero → `null`, and the unchanged control.
- [ ] The disposition for each case is stated in the parser (comment) consistent with contract rule 4, and the types.ts inventory's meta row is updated if its known-lossy list changes.

# fix(ai): codex quota publishes non-positive `limit_window_seconds` as negative-duration windows (`-1h`, `-1d`, `windowSeconds: 0`)

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `67b276850c6c` in a laptop worktree (`probe-2026-11-06-creator-0735`), driving `provider.fetchQuota` for codex with a stubbed fetch (probe `probe1.ts`, kept in that worktree).

## Evidence

`packages/ai/src/quota/providers/codex.ts:122-129` is the only quota site that passes a raw upstream duration into both the window key and the published window with no positivity guard:

```ts
const windowSeconds = toNumber(window.limit_window_seconds)
return [{ role, label: resolveWindowLabel(windowSeconds),
  window: toUsageWindow({ usedPercent, windowSeconds, resetAt: toTimestamp(window.reset_at) }) }]
```

`packages/ai/src/quota/utils.ts:64-71` (`resolveWindowLabel`): `if (!windowSeconds) return "tokens"`, then `% 86400` / `% 3600` arithmetic — negative durations produce negative labels, and `0` is treated as missing for the label but still published as `windowSeconds: 0`.

Probe results (primary window, `used_percent` valid in every case):

- control `18000` → key `5h`, `windowSeconds: 18000` (correct)
- `-3600` → key **`-1h`**, `windowSeconds: -3600`
- `-86400` → key **`-1d`**, `windowSeconds: -86400`
- `0` → key `tokens` (the missing-duration label) but `windowSeconds: 0`, not `null` — the window's own fields disagree
- both windows `-3600` → keys `-1h-primary` / `-1h-secondary` (the #1762 collision qualifier faithfully propagates the fabricated label)

The in-package precedent is explicit: both meta call sites guard before labelling — `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/meta.ts:92` and `:218` use `duration > 0 ? duration : null`, so a non-positive duration is an unknown duration (honest `null` + the fallback label), never a negative one.

This violates the window contract in `packages/ai/src/quota/types.ts` (rule 3: missing/invalid is null, never a fabricated label; rule 5: a window's fields agree).

## Why it matters

Downstream consumers key and group by the window label and read `windowSeconds` as a real duration. A malformed or hostile upstream payload (or an upstream schema change) currently mints windows that sort/group as `-1h`/`-1d` and carry a negative duration into quota recording and pool-rotation logic, instead of the honest unknown-duration shape every sibling parser produces.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A codex primary/secondary window with `limit_window_seconds` ≤ 0 (or non-finite) publishes with `windowSeconds: null` and the same label the missing-duration case produces (`tokens`, with the #1762 `-primary`/`-secondary` qualifiers on collision); its `usedPercent`/`resetAt` still publish — the window does not vanish.
- [ ] Positive durations are byte-identical to today (18000 → `5h`, 604800 → `weekly`).
- [ ] `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pins the non-positive cases (negative, zero, collision) through `provider.fetchQuota` with a stubbed fetch, plus the positive control.
- [ ] The types.ts parser inventory's codex row is updated if the fix changes its conforming note.

body:
## Problem

The shared quota timestamp converter `toTimestamp` (`packages/ai/src/quota/utils.ts:38-49`) publishes non-positive resets as real 1969/1970 dates for every provider that uses it — nine of the thirteen quota providers. The window contract in `packages/ai/src/quota/types.ts` (design #1794) records the correct disposition — "a non-positive resetAt is null" — but only in the command-code inventory row, because #1821 fixed it parser-locally: command-code does its own conversion (`command-code.ts:97`: `resetAt === null || resetAt <= 0 ? null : …`) and its fix packet explicitly excluded "changing shared utils toNumber/toTimestamp semantics for other providers". The shared converter was never given the same guard:

- Numeric branch: `if (!value) return null` catches numeric `0` only; any finite negative returns `value < 1_000_000_000_000 ? value * 1000 : value` — e.g. `-5000` → `-5000000`.
- String branch: the `Date.parse` result is returned unchecked — `"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"` → `0`, published as a real epoch reset instead of null.

`toUsageWindow` then derives real fields from those values: `formatResetTime` renders a Dec 31, 1969 date and `calculateResetAfterSeconds` reports `0`, so the bogus reset looks like a reset that is due now.

Call sites (all reset / period fields): `codex.ts:130`, `opendesign.ts:103`, `meta.ts:149,222,230`, `claude.ts:176,200,207`, `opencode-go.ts:56,79`, `antigravity.ts:277,383`, `cline-pass.ts:93`, `mistral.ts:81`, `turso.ts:66-67` (period start AND end — two bogus bounds even fabricate a `windowSeconds` from their difference).

## Evidence (verified this run, laptop probe at origin/main `24a68f829b`)

Probe: `~/git/fleet/probe-2026-11-06-totimestamp/probe.ts` against the real modules in worktree `probe-2026-11-06-creator-0635`:

- `toTimestamp(-5000)` → `-5000000`; `toTimestamp(0)` → `null`; `toTimestamp("1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z")` → `0`; control `toTimestamp(1893456000)` → `1893456000000`.
- `parseOpenCodeGoUsage({ usage: { rolling: { percent: 50, resetsAt: -5000 } } })` → window with `resetAt: -5000000`, `resetAtFormatted: "Wed, Dec 31, 4:36 PM"` (1969), `resetAfterSeconds: 0`.
- `parseOpenCodeGoUsage` with `resetsAt: "1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"` → `resetAt: 0` with an epoch formatted date, not null.
- `tursoWindows` with `current_period_start: -10000, current_period_end: -5000` → window with `resetAt: -5000000` (1969 formatted) and a fabricated `windowSeconds: 5000` derived from the two bogus bounds.
- Control (valid positive reset) publishes correctly in both parsers.

The only non-positive-reset test in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` ("non-positive resetAt publishes resetAt null…", ~:343) pins command-code's private conversion; no case pins `toTimestamp` or any provider that uses it.

Note on scope interaction: opencode-go's parsers drop a window when `resetAt` is null — whether a bogus-reset window should drop or publish with a null reset is related to #1725's open rule-3 decision for that provider; the triage should state the interaction explicitly rather than silently changing it.

## Why it matters

Quota windows drive pool gating, the dashboard, and `opencode quota` rendering. A reset rendered as Dec 31, 1969 with `resetAfterSeconds: 0` reads as "reset due now" to consumers, and turso's fabricated `windowSeconds` invents a billing-period length from garbage. These are the same payload-anomaly shapes #1821 and #1793 exist to keep out of published quota state; the shared converter is the remaining unguarded path, and fixing it in one place covers nine providers instead of nine parser-local patches.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A non-positive timestamp (negative in seconds or ms spelling, numeric `0` handled as today, and a string parsing to `<= 0` ms) converts to `null` in `toTimestamp`; valid positive timestamps convert exactly as before.
- [ ] No provider publishing through `toTimestamp` can emit a window with a 1969/1970 `resetAt` or derived formatted/reset-after fields; turso cannot derive a `windowSeconds` from non-positive period bounds.
- [ ] Probe-matrix cases in `packages/ai/test/quota.test.ts` pin the non-positive shapes for `toTimestamp` and at least one exported parser that uses it (e.g. `parseOpenCodeGoUsage` or `tursoWindows`), including the epoch-string spelling.
- [ ] The types.ts inventory reflects the outcome, and the interaction with #1725 (opencode-go drop-on-null-reset) is stated in the fix or on that issue.
- [ ] Existing quota tests still pass, including #1821's command-code non-positive cases.

# fix(ci): check:proto-reads gained a 5th unlisted site — #1828's infra-hold ladder read in model-route.ts has no disposition

Verified 2026-11-06 on origin/main `cbfaa84514a2928cbc453f354e98628d9641805f`, in a laptop worktree of origin/main, gate run twice with identical results.

## Evidence

`bun script/check-proto-reads.ts` on current main reports **5** unlisted prototype-chain read candidates:

- `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/antigravity.ts:202` — in #1724's set
- `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/claude.ts:123` — in #1724's set
- `packages/ai/src/quota/providers/openrouter.ts:145` — in #1724's set
- `packages/cli/src/commands/handlers/quota.ts:266` — in #1724's set
- **`packages/core/src/model-route.ts:326` — NEW, not in #1724's set**

The new site landed with the provider-availability merge (commit `472d7b9a64`, feat(core): provider availability — one classification + stop/resume state machine (#1828), merged via PR #1832):

```ts
// packages/core/src/model-route.ts:311
const INFRA_LADDER_MS = [30_000, 60_000, 120_000, 240_000]
// packages/core/src/model-route.ts:326 (plantInfraHold)
const until = now + Math.min(INFRA_LADDER_MS[Math.min(failures - 1, INFRA_LADDER_MS.length - 1)]!, INFRA_CAP_MS)
```

The other two allowlist gates show no new drift on the same main: bounded-http 7 unlisted and numeric-boundaries 3 unlisted, both subsets of #1724's set; check:workflows and check:doc-env-vars are green.

## Assessment

The read itself is safe by construction — this is a disposition gap, not a prototype-chain vulnerability:

- `INFRA_LADDER_MS` is a module-local const array defined at model-route.ts:311 in the same change.
- The index is `Math.min(failures - 1, INFRA_LADDER_MS.length - 1)`, where `failures` is the in-module infra-hold counter computed at the same site as `(infraHolds.get(id)?.failures ?? 0) + 1` — always an integer ≥ 1, so the index is always an integer in `[0, length - 1]`.
- A numeric index cannot name a prototype member (`__proto__`, `constructor`, …); there is no externally supplied key at this site.

That is exactly the "safe: numeric index into an array" disposition class the allowlist already uses for the neighbouring model-route.ts weight reads and for `SHRINK_STEPS[rejections]` in session/compaction.ts. What is missing is the written disposition itself.

## Why it matters

This is the recurring pattern of #1540, #1600, #1655, #1688 and #1790: a feature lands, an allowlist gate gains an undispositioned site, and the gate stays red for an unrelated extra reason — during which window it cannot cleanly catch the *next* drift, and every later gate run has to be diffed against a growing remembered set (the last several creator runs all had to record "proto 4 RED = exactly #1724's set" by hand). #1724 tracks its own 4 proto sites; this 5th site arrived after its list was written, so it needs its own disposition, following the #1790 precedent for the bounded-http 8th site.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `bun script/check-proto-reads.ts` on main reports exactly the 4 sites tracked by #1724 — the model-route.ts:326 site is dispositioned.
- [ ] The disposition in `script/check-proto-reads.allowlist.txt` states why the read is safe (numeric clamped index into the module-local const ladder array; no externally supplied key) — not a bare allowlist line.
- [ ] `script/check-proto-reads.test.ts` still passes.
- [ ] No code behaviour changes: the infra-hold ladder values and capping are untouched.
